stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The article on p. 10 is your way in, and the class read it in the last lesson. Put the four photos up and ask who is who: who is waiting for a text, who is studying in New York, who uses Facebook for birthdays, who ends relationships by instant message. Two minutes – you want them remembering the people, not reading again.
stages.avoid: Do not set the article again. It was the whole of the previous lesson; your minutes belong to the grammar.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 3a on p. 11: four sentences, and they write present simple or present continuous on each line. Then send them back to the article on p. 10 for two more of each – I’m waiting for her text message, I’m studying in New York, I’m writing a blog, when I check my Facebook page, it tells me, I normally communicate. Board what they find in two columns without naming the columns yet.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning first, with ex 3b: pairs match the four sentences to the four uses – habits and routines, feelings and permanent situations, actions right now, temporary actions around now. Then check it with questions, not with the rule. Is Julie waiting now? Yes. Does she always wait for texts from Sara? We don’t know. Is Marc in New York for ever? No – so is his studying permanent or for now? Write questions like these for every sentence on your board before the lesson. Form is a review: be + -ing, and the -s on he, she, it, with Grammar Focus 1B on p. 142 as the reference. Point at the spelling box for writing, studying, putting. Then the tip box – like, prefer, hate, know, need are not normally continuous – which the article shows for you: I prefer writing a blog, never I’m preferring. Pronunciation last, the contractions: play 1.14 for them to repeat the table, then drill two sentences from the article at natural speed – I’m waiting for her text, she’s writing a blog – so the ’m and ’s can be heard.
stages.avoid: They are B1 and have met both tenses. Present the form from scratch and you will spend fourteen minutes on what they know and none on the choice between the two, which is what they get wrong.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Focus 1B on p. 143. Ex a first: four pairs of sentence beginnings, each matched to the ending that fits – I work in a bank… but I don’t enjoy it; I’m working in a café… but it’s only a summer job. It makes them choose by meaning. Then ex b, eight sentences with two choices each. They work alone, compare with a partner, and you go through only the items they disagreed on. Expect 5 and 8 to divide the room: friends who look at their phones every five minutes, and does your brother like.
stages.avoid: Ex c is a fourteen-gap conversation and will not fit. Leave it on the page.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 4 on p. 11: How often do you…? with the nine activities – send a message to say you are sick, share news on Facebook, read English websites, call friends on Skype. Pairs ask and answer, and every answer needs a reason. Put the book’s second speech bubble on the board – Not very often. But I’m planning a holiday in America… – because it shows the move you want: a habit, then something going on in their life now. Change partners halfway so everyone asks the questions twice. Write down sentences as you go round, right ones and wrong ones.
stages.avoid: The questions all start How often, so on their own they produce the present simple and nothing else. Without that second sentence about now, you will hear only half of what you taught.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: A quick survey: hands up for who does each activity most often and least often. Then a state verb you heard in the continuous – I’m knowing, she’s preferring – on the board next to a sentence someone got right. Pairs say which is which and fix the wrong one; you confirm.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have listened for gist and for specific detail to a conversation between two old friends who meet by chance in the street.
slots.sub: To introduce six phrases for greeting someone you know and someone you are meeting for the first time – Long time no see, How are you?, Great to see you, Where are you living these days?, by the way and Nice to meet you – and the usual replies to them.
slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 12 ex 1a–1d – audio track 1.15 (Part 1) / SB p. 12 ex 2a–2d – audio tracks 1.16, 1.17

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1a on p. 12: in your country, what do you say and do when you meet someone new, and when you meet someone you know well? Mime hug, kiss and shake hands as you set it, so the words are in the room. Pairs, then two or three answers to the class. In a mixed-nationality class the answers differ and this runs longer – let it, up to five minutes.

stages.name: Prediction
stages.todo: Ex 1b: the two photos. Do the people in each one know each other well, and how can you tell? Pairs, then board the class’s guesses. Do not say who is right.

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex 1c: play 1.15, Part 1 of the video or the audio if you have no screen, once. One question: were your guesses right? The two women are old friends; the man is meeting one of them for the first time. Pairs check, then ask what told them – the way they say each other’s names, or nice to meet you.

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex 1d, five true-or-false sentences: when Rachel and Annie last met, where Annie lives, when Rachel and Mark got married, whether Annie has a boyfriend, where the three of them go next. Give them a minute to read first, then play 1.15 again. They answer alone, compare, and correct the false ones – that half of the task is what makes them listen closely. Play it a third time with pauses if pairs still disagree. Answers: 1 true, 2 false (really close to the centre), 3 false, 4 true, 5 false (a café).
stages.avoid: Sentence 3 has a joke in it: Rachel says they married six months ago and Mark says eight. Neither is a year, so it is false either way – but expect the question.

stages.name: Language from the recording
stages.todo: Ex 2a: six phrases from the conversation, each with a piece missing. Pairs fill them from the box, then play 1.16 to check. Ex 2b sorts them – the first four for someone you know, by the way and nice to meet you for someone new. Then ex 2c: play 1.17 and they note the reply to each phrase. Collect one or two more replies to How are you? from the class – Fine, thanks, Not bad. Drill the six as phrase and reply, with the voice lifting on the pleased surprise: Long time no SEE! – Great to SEE you!
stages.avoid: Teach these as whole chunks. Long time no see has no grammar worth explaining, and trying to explain it costs you the speaking.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Each of them thinks of a friend they have not seen for a long time – who, where they used to meet, what they would ask now. Then groups of three, the same people as in the recording. Two meet in the street as old friends – greeting, how are you, where are you living these days – and the third, standing with one of them, introduces themselves as Mark does: my name’s…, by the way. Nice to meet you, and the conversation carries on with three. About ninety seconds a scene, then rotate so each person is the newcomer once. Books shut for the second round.
stages.avoid: With the page open they read the phrases; shut, they have to remember them, which is the point. Say so before they start.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One group shows its meeting to the room. Then two things from your notes: a phrase used well, and one used in the wrong place – nice to meet you said to an old friend is the likely one.

1B.context: Travel and tourism – saying yes to a holiday

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have read the first part of a holiday story for gist and for detail, and predicted what happens next.
slots.sub: To pre-teach the words that would block the story – travel agent, travel agent’s, receptionist and water skiing – so that students can follow Richard’s first two days.
slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 18 ex 1a–1d (article: ‘Yes Man changed my life’) / SB p. 19 (Day One and Day Two)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Books closed. Build a list of kinds of holiday on the board as they call them out – beach, city break, camping, cruise, safari, adventure – and take a quick vote on the one the class would choose. Then books open at p. 18, ex 1a, in small groups: where do you like to go, what new things do you try on holiday, what kind of holiday would you hate? Keep the third question until last. The story is about a man who ends up on exactly that holiday.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Four items: travel agent and travel agent’s, receptionist, water skiing. The pair is the useful part – which is a person and which is a shop? Where do you book a holiday? (In the shop, from the person.) Receptionist from a hotel desk you draw on the board; water skiing from the photo at the foot of p. 18. One concept question each, drill, and board them with the stress: TRAvel agent, reCEPtionist, WAter skiing.
stages.avoid: Leave accommodation, check in and unpack for later. They are in the story, but they are also in the vocabulary lesson at the end of this day, and the text makes them clear enough – a hotel? or a…? If anyone asks, a gesture will do.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 1b: they read only the introduction, the white text over the photo, and answer the two questions – what is Danny Wallace’s book about, and what did Richard do after he read it? Two minutes, alone, then pairs. Check: a man who said yes to every question for a year; Richard took a week off work and did the same. Then one question to the room before they read on: what could go wrong if you say yes to everything?

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 1c: Day One and Day Two on p. 19, four questions each. Set Day One, check it, then set Day Two – two short reads hold a class better than one long one. Alone, then pairs, with a finger on the line that gives the answer. Day One: he saw a poster in the travel agent’s window, he booked a beach holiday in Greece, no – he prefers cities, the flight was the next day. Day Two: the receptionist asked if he wanted to go, it was about 40°C, he bought two pairs of sunglasses, three hats, a watch and a necklace, and tomorrow is water skiing, which he dreads.
stages.avoid: Day One question 3 hides its answer in a list of things he hates. Weaker readers will say yes because he booked it. Ask them to find what he says about the beach.

stages.name: Response task
stages.todo: Ex 1d: would you like to try water skiing, and will Richard enjoy it? Two minutes in groups. Then take it one step further: each group writes Richard’s Day Three in four or five lines, in his voice – what happened on the water, how he felt by the evening. Groups read theirs out and the class votes on the most likely. End with one question to everybody: would you say yes to everything for a week?
stages.avoid: The Day Threes will be full of past simple slips. That is the next lesson’s target, not yours – note a few for your colleague if you like, but do not teach them here.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Content first: which Day Three won, and why. Ex 1e on p. 18 has the real Day Three as a recording, but it is not part of this lesson – tell them in one line that he ended up loving it, or leave them guessing. Then a sentence where a pre-taught word was used well, and two that went wrong, for pairs to fix.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have clarified and practised the positive form of the past simple, regular and irregular, including when the -ed ending adds a syllable, to tell the story of a day on holiday.
slots.sub: To give students practice in writing a short story in pairs, about a day on a holiday they invent.
slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 18 ex 2a–2c (the article from the previous lesson) / SB p. 19 ex 5a–5c – audio tracks 1.27, 1.28 / Grammar Focus 2A SB p. 144 / SB p. 145 ex a

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Books closed. Two sentences on the board with the verb gapped: Richard ___ to change his life. He ___ a Yes Man for a week. They call out what fits, and you board every possible answer. Books open to check against the introduction on p. 18 – wanted, became. Then ask: did this happen now, or before he wrote the article? That one question carries the meaning for the whole lesson.
stages.avoid: The class read this article in the last lesson. One line to remind them who Richard is, then straight on.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 2a: fifteen verbs in a box, and pairs underline the past form of each in the article. They appear in the same order, starting from the introduction, so make it a race. Then ex 2b: which end in -ed, and what happens to the others? Board the answers in two columns, regular and irregular, and leave them up.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning is quick – finished, in the past – and the lead-in has done most of it. Form takes the time. Regular verbs add -ed, and then the three spelling changes from the box on p. 144 that they will need for ever: live, lived; stop, stopped; study, studied. Elicit them from verbs on the board rather than reading the box. Irregular verbs have no rule, so say so: they are learnt, not worked out. Then pronunciation, with section 5 on p. 19. Ask where they stayed and what they visited on their last holiday, board stayed and visited, and ask which has an extra syllable. Play 1.27 for ex 5a and they tick the verbs that do – needed, decided, started, wanted. Ex 5b gives the rule: only after t and d. Ex 5c with 1.28: waited, included, shouted, ended. Then drill – as much on the verbs without the extra syllable as on the ones with it.
stages.avoid: The error you will hear all week is ask-ed and play-ed, said as two syllables. That is why asked, changed and played need drilling as much as wanted does.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 2c on p. 18: six sentences from Richard’s last day with the verb in brackets – worked, spent, stayed, won, took, went. Alone, then read to a partner aloud, so the endings are said and not only written. Then Grammar Focus 2A ex a on p. 145: fifteen verbs to put into the past, spelling included. Check on the board the three where the spelling rules bite: hurried, preferred, danced.
stages.avoid: Ex b and c on p. 145, and section 4 on p. 19, are negatives and questions. Not today – the positive form is the whole lesson.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Pairs invent a day of their own: a holiday nobody in the class would choose, and someone on it who says yes to everything. Six to eight sentences, every verb in the past. Give them a first line on the board so they start writing rather than discussing: At nine o’clock the hotel manager asked me… Pairs then swap stories and read another pair’s aloud, and the class votes for the worst day.
stages.avoid: Monitor the writing, not only the reading out. A slip in stopped or tried shows on paper and disappears in speech, which is why this stage is written.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two sentences from the stories on the board, one with a wrong past form or spelling. Pairs correct it.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have learnt and practised the travel phrases in Vocabulary Focus 2A – get a visa, exchange money, book accommodation, check into a hotel, unpack your luggage, do some sightseeing, buy souvenirs, stay in a hostel, stay on a campsite – to talk about their holidays.
slots.sub: To give students practice in speaking for fluency, telling a partner about a holiday they enjoyed and answering questions about it.
slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 19 ex 6a–6b, 7a–7b / Vocabulary Focus 2A SB p. 133 ex a, c – audio tracks 1.29, 1.30 / Workbook p. 10 ex 2a

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 6a on p. 19: which holiday items can they see in the pictures around the article – sunglasses, hats, suntan lotion, the beach chair – and what else do people take? Pairs, two minutes, then board their list. Then Vocabulary Focus 2A ex a on p. 133: eight items matched to the pictures, and play 1.29 for them to check and repeat. Passport, map and suitcase they know, so keep it moving; this is the way into the topic.
stages.avoid: Do not clarify the eight items. The pictures carry the meaning, and the minutes belong to ex c.

stages.name: Presentation
stages.todo: Ex c on p. 133: ten sentences about one holiday, from the visa to the last week by the beach, each with a noun missing. Pairs fill them from the box; holiday is done for them. Play 1.30 to check. Then send them back into the sentences with one question: which verb goes with each noun? They underline – get a visa, exchanged money, booked accommodation, checked into a hotel, unpacked luggage, did some sightseeing, bought souvenirs, stayed in a hostel, stayed on a campsite, had a great adventure.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: The phrases are the lesson, not the nouns, so clarify verb and noun together. Meaning, a question for each that needs one: a visa – from the embassy or the airport? A hostel – cheaper than a hotel, and do you share a room? Sightseeing – at home or on holiday? Then form, which is where they go wrong. The verbs: do sightseeing, not make it; stay in a hostel but on a campsite; check into, then check out of. Accommodation, luggage and sightseeing are uncountable – no -s, no a. And campsite, not camping: we stayed at a great camping is the classic mistake. Then stress, drilled inside the phrase: do some SIGHTseeing, book accommoDAtion, buy souveNIRS, have an adVENture. The page prints the phonemes, so point at them as you drill.
stages.avoid: Accommodation, sightseeing and souvenirs are hard to spell because they do not sound the way they look. Write them up slowly and leave them up.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 10 ex 2a: eight sentence halves to match – get a visa from the embassy, do some sightseeing this afternoon, book your accommodation before you go, check out of your hotel by eleven. Alone, then compare. In open class they say the whole sentence, not the letter, so the stress you drilled gets used. Answers: 1d 2e 3a 4f 5h 6b 7c 8g.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 7 on p. 19. First 7a: each of them chooses a holiday they enjoyed and reads the nine questions silently – when, where, how long, who with, what kind of accommodation, any sightseeing, any souvenirs. A minute to think. Then 7b: they tell a partner about it, and the partner asks the questions and some of their own. Swap. Then change partners once, so the phrases come out a second time with more confidence.
stages.avoid: Ex 7 is full of past simple questions. They are printed, so let students read them off the page; correcting did-questions here turns your vocabulary lesson into a grammar lesson.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One holiday from each pair to the room – whose was the biggest adventure? Then write up two phrases you heard – one right, one with the wrong verb or an extra -s – and let the class decide which needs fixing.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have learnt and practised nine verbs and phrases for describing a journey – travel around, set off, take off, land, hitchhike, give someone a lift, board a train, change trains, get to – and used them to retell a trip.
slots.sub: To give students practice in speaking for fluency, retelling a journey from a map and talking about how they like to travel.
slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 20 ex 1a / Vocabulary Focus 2B SB p. 134 ex a, b, f – audio track 1.31 / Workbook p. 11 ex 1a

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ask how they got here today and list the transport on the board as they answer. Then ex 1a on p. 20 – car, bus, train, plane, coach, on foot: which do they prefer, and why? Three prompts on the board give the pairs more to talk about: every day? on holiday? at the weekend?

stages.name: Setting the situation
stages.todo: Vocabulary Focus 2B on p. 134 with the nine sentences covered, so they see only the map. Play 1.31 once and they follow the journey with a finger: which cities, and how many kinds of transport? Pairs compare – a plane to Berlin, a car to Frankfurt, then trains to Paris with a change on the way.

stages.name: Presentation
stages.todo: Ex a: now uncover the sentences. Pairs match each phrase in bold – travelled around, set off, took off, landed, hitchhiked, gave us a lift, boarded a train, changed, got to – with a definition from a–i, using the map to help. Check in open class: 1h 2i 3d 4g 5e 6c 7a 8b 9f.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning goes fastest in pairs that contrast: set off and get to (start and end a journey), take off and land (only planes), hitchhike and give someone a lift (the same car seen from two sides – who is standing by the road?). Concept-check each pair against the map on the board. Then form. Set off and take off need no object; get to needs a place after it; give takes two – gave us a lift. Write up board a train with no on, because they will add one. The sentences are in the past and three of the verbs are irregular – set off, took off, gave – so point at them. Drill each phrase inside a short sentence: in set off and take off the stress falls on off, in get to it falls on the place – we got to PAris.
stages.avoid: Leave ex c, the travel problems, closed. It is a second set of ten words and will not fit in this lesson.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 11 ex 1a: four short travel stories with ten gaps, and the verbs in the box go into the past – hitchhiked, gave, set off, missed, took off, landed, boarded, changed, got to. Alone, a partner check, then the stories read aloud in open class. Then Vocabulary Focus ex b: sentences covered, and pairs retell the map journey from the pictures alone. Listen for the three irregular past forms.
stages.avoid: Miss is in the Workbook box and not among the nine. It is easy – give it in a line when it comes up.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Vocabulary Focus ex f, questions 2 to 5: a country you would like to travel around, the last time someone gave you a lift, how you feel when a plane takes off and lands, and whether hitchhiking is a good idea. New partners. Note what you hear.
stages.avoid: Question 1 is about the pictures in ex c, which you have not taught. Start at question 2.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One answer to the hitchhiking question that the room should hear, then two slips you caught while monitoring, for pairs to correct – a missing to after got, or boarded on a train.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have clarified and practised the past continuous with the past simple, to describe an action that was in progress when something else happened.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency, telling a partner about a problem they had while they were travelling.
slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 20 ex 2a–2b – audio track 1.33 / SB p. 21 ex 3a–3f, 3h–3i – audio tracks 1.34, 1.36 / Grammar Focus 2B SB p. 144 / SB p. 145 ex b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 2a on p. 20: the cartoon and the headline, Woman angry after flight in toilet. Pairs: what happened? Point at the flight attendant and say the word as you do – it is in the story and they need it. Take two guesses.

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex 2b: play 1.33 once, and they listen only to check their guess. Pairs, then thirty seconds in open class: why was she in the toilet? A flight attendant’s seat was broken, she was the last passenger to check in, so she lost hers.
stages.avoid: Play it once and stop. Ex 2c is a detail task and the story is not your lesson – the four sentences in ex 3a are. Everything before the grammar should be over inside ten minutes.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 3a on p. 21: four sentences from the story with the verb missing. Pairs try them from memory, then play 1.34 to check – was raining, were waiting, was reading, was sitting. Ex 3b: they underline the past simple verb in each – left, boarded, spoke, started. Board the four sentences with both verbs marked.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex 3c does the meaning, so put its questions to the room. Which action started first in every sentence? The past continuous one. Then the harder one: did the continuous action stop because of the past simple, or carry on after it? She was reading and the attendant spoke – she stopped. It was raining when she left – the rain went on. Draw the timeline from p. 144 under one sentence, a wavy line for the long action and a cross for the short one, and check two more: was she in the toilet before the turbulence started? Did it stop because of the turbulence? Form next: was or were with -ing, and when joins the two halves either way round. Then ex 3e–3f: play 1.36, and they notice that was and were are weak in the positive sentences and strong in wasn’t and weren’t. Drill the positives at speed: it was RAINing, I was READing my book when…
stages.avoid: Grammar Focus 2B puts positive, negative and question side by side. Teach the positive and let the other two stay on the page – one new structure is enough. Ex 3g is the negatives’ pronunciation and belongs with them.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 3h on p. 21: five sentences, each needing one verb in each tense – the train was leaving when I realised, someone stole my bag when I was standing in the queue. Alone, then a partner. Take the answers aloud so you hear the weak was. Then Grammar Focus 2B ex b on p. 145: seven sentences, choosing the right form for each verb. Check only the ones pairs disagreed on.
stages.avoid: Item 3 of ex 3h has three verbs: I was running for the bus when my bag opened and all my things fell out. Someone will put the third one in the continuous, and it is worth boarding when they do.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 3i: have they had an experience like the ones in ex 3h – a lost passport, the wrong train, a bag that opened? Tell a short one of your own first: I was getting off a bus when my phone fell out of my pocket. Then pairs, and the listener asks one question at the end, as in the book’s speech bubbles: What did you do? Swap, then change partners and tell it again.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One story to the room. Then two sentences from your notes on the board, one with the tenses the wrong way round, and pairs put it right.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have read a short news story about a difficult journey for gist and for detail, and told it to a partner who read a different one.
slots.sub: To give students practice in using the past simple and the past continuous to retell a news story.
slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 21 ex 4a–4d / Communication Plus 2B: Student A SB p. 127, Student B SB p. 128

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 4a on p. 21: the two headlines and pictures – Did you mean Capri? and Coach passengers asked to get out and push. Ask a student to find Capri and Carpi on the map and spell them both. Then pairs guess what happened in each story. Board one guess for each and leave them there.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Five items across the two texts, since half the class reads each: GPS, a spelling mistake, break down, push and pull. GPS and a spelling mistake come straight from the map – someone typed CARPI for CAPRI. Break down from a mime of a car that will not start; push and pull with a chair. Drill them, and board break down with its past, broke down.
stages.avoid: Five is enough. Coastline, grotto and tonnes can be guessed, and none of the questions turns on them.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Split the class into A and B. Students A turn to p. 127, Students B to p. 128. They read once, fast and alone, for one thing: was the guess on the board right? Then A pairs with A and B with B to compare.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: The five questions printed above both texts: where were they going, how were they travelling, what was the problem, who helped and how, what happened in the end. They read again, alone, and make notes – notes, not sentences copied out, because the next stage is telling. Then A with A and B with B check their answers together. Go round the pairs rather than checking in open class; the other half must not hear the answers.
stages.avoid: Question 4 in Text B has two answers – ten passengers pushed, and then a car pulled the coach with a rope. Make sure each B pair has both.

stages.name: Retelling
stages.todo: Ex 4c: now each A sits with a B. Books shut, notes open. Each tells their story using the five questions, and the listener asks at least two questions of their own. Board the book’s opening – Two Swedish tourists were on holiday in Italy. They… – and one sentence from the coach story: it broke down while it was turning a corner. Those are the shapes from the last lesson, and you want to hear more of them.
stages.avoid: If the notes turn into reading aloud, take the page away. A story told from memory with mistakes is the lesson; a story read out is not.

stages.name: Response task
stages.todo: Ex 4d in fours: which journey was worse for the travellers? Each group agrees on one answer and two reasons.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Each group’s verdict and one reason. Then two or three sentences from the retelling on the board, one of them a past continuous used well, and pairs correct the others.

2B.context: Travel and tourism – arriving somewhere new

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised six ways of asking for information in a public place – What time’s the next…?, How often do…?, Could you tell me where…?, How much is…?, Can I…?, Where can I…? – joining the words in them as fluent speakers do.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency in a role play between a tourist and a tourist officer.
slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 22 ex 1a–1c – audio track 1.38 (Part 1) / SB p. 22 ex 2a–2d, 3a – audio tracks 1.39, 1.40, 1.41, 1.42 / SB p. 23 ex 4c–4d / Workbook p. 12 ex 1a

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1a on p. 22: train stations, tourist offices, airports – two kinds of information people ask for in each. Pairs, then board a few: train times, platforms, ticket prices, places to visit.

stages.name: Listening for context
stages.todo: Ex 1b: the photo – where is Annie, and what is she asking about? Board their guesses. Then ex 1c: play 1.38, Part 1 of the video or the audio, and they check. She is at a station on her way to Birmingham, asking about the next train, how often they leave, the platform, the ticket office, the price and where to buy a magazine.
stages.avoid: Ex 1d is a second listening for detail. Skip it: this is a functional language lesson, and the recording has done its job once they know who she is and what she wants.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 2a: the six questions from Annie’s conversation, cut in half. Pairs try to remember the endings before they match, then match, then play 1.39 to check. Then ex 2b: play 1.40 for the assistant’s two questions – How can I help you? Is there anything else I can help you with? Board all eight.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning first, one question for the set: which opening asks about a time, a price, a place, how often, and which asks permission? Then form, where one question needs care. Could you tell me where the ticket office is – not where is the ticket office. After could you tell me the order goes back to a normal sentence; board the two side by side and ask which sounds more polite. Then the pronunciation, ex 3a: play 1.42 – Where can I buy a magazine? How much is a ticket? – and ask what happens between can and I, and between much and is. A consonant at the end of one word runs into the vowel at the start of the next, with no pause: ca-nI, mu-chis. Drill all six questions whole, slowly first, then at speed.
stages.avoid: Ex 3b–3d are different questions – Is anyone sitting here? – from a different situation. Leave them for another day.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 2c: a short dialogue at a tourist office with five gaps from the box. Alone, then play 1.41 to check, which is ex 2d. Pairs read it aloud in both roles; the joining you drilled should be audible. Then Workbook p. 12 ex 1a: eight questions with the words jumbled. Put any slip in item 2 on the board – Could you tell me where the information desk is?

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 4c on p. 23: A is a tourist officer, B a tourist in town. The flowchart gives them the frame, and two lines for coming back with more – Sorry, just one more thing and Actually, there is one more thing. Read those two aloud as you set it up; the task asks for two extra questions of their own. Then ex 4d: swap roles and do it again, books shut the second time.
stages.avoid: The officer has to invent answers. Give the As thirty seconds to decide where they are – which town, which bus station – or they will stall on every reply.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One pair performs its conversation for the room. Then one question from your notes that came out wrong – Could you tell me where is… is the likely one – for the class to fix.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have listened for gist and for detail to a phone conversation about arriving in a new country.
slots.sub: To pre-teach rainy season, storm, lightning, delay and turbulence, so that students can follow Karen’s memories of arriving in Jakarta.
slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 24 ex 1a–1c – audio track 1.46

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Say Jakarta and ask which country it is the capital of. Then ex 1a on p. 24, the five photos: what can they see, what do they know about Indonesia, would they like to go? Pairs, then open class – a traffic jam, a beach, a storm over a city, a temple, an orang-utan.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Five items: rainy season, storm, lightning, delay and turbulence. Photo c does the first three – what is happening in the sky? Is a rainy season one wet day or months of them? Delay from a departures board: the train was at ten, it left at eleven. Turbulence from a plane that shakes – mime it. One question each, drill, and board them with the stress: LIGHTning, deLAY, TURbulence.
stages.avoid: Do not pre-teach traffic jam. It is in photo a, and ex 1b asks them to find it.

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex 1b, three questions: why is Tim phoning, when did Karen go to Indonesia, and which photos does she describe? Play 1.46 once. Pairs, then check: for advice about arriving, about ten years ago, the traffic jam and the storm. Then ask why each of them went – Tim on holiday, Karen to work.

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex 1c, five questions. Let them read them and pencil in anything they remember. Play 1.46 again; they answer alone, then compare. Play a third time with pauses if pairs still disagree. Answers: by taxi; a long delay and turbulence; much noisier and longer than at home; she found them exciting; there was no internet connection in her flat.
stages.avoid: Question 1 is a trap. Karen suggests a bus to save money, but the question asks about Tim’s plan, and Tim says taxi.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: A phone call of their own. Pairs find a town that one of them knows and the other does not. The one who does not know it is going there next week and phones for advice: how to get from the airport or the station, what it is like when you arrive, what to watch out for. A minute to think, then the call – back to back so they cannot see each other, as on a real phone. Swap, with a different town.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Ask a few callers for the best advice they were given. Then three sentences you overheard during the calls, one with a pre-taught word used well; the class corrects the other two.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have written a short travel blog post about a holiday, a new place or a first day doing something new.
slots.sub: To practise using and, but, so, because and when to join short ideas into longer sentences.
slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 24 ex 1d, 2a (Tim’s blog, which runs on to p. 25) / SB p. 25 ex 3a–3c, 4a–4d

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: One line back to the last lesson: Tim has arrived in Jakarta, and Karen never wrote anything down. Then ex 1d on p. 24: do they keep a blog or a diary when they travel, and do they read other people’s? Pairs, two minutes.

stages.name: Model text
stages.todo: Ex 2a: Tim’s two posts, Tuesday on p. 24 and Wednesday on p. 25, and the one topic from the list he does not write about – animals. Three minutes, alone. Then a second pass with a different question: what is each part about? Arriving and the heat; the traffic and the taxi; the meal; the Old Town. Board it as four lines. That is the shape they will use.
stages.avoid: Ex 2b is five detail questions. This is a writing lesson; take two of them orally if you want them, and move on.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Ex 3a on p. 25: five sentences from the blog, a linking word in bold in each, and five uses – two things at the same time, a similar idea, a different idea, a reason, a result. Pairs, then check and board each word with its use. Then the pair they mix up: so gives the result, because gives the reason – I slept on the plane, so I’m not tired; I’m not tired because I slept. And the comma: a sentence that starts with When needs one after the first half. Ex 3b: they find more examples in the blog. Then ex 3c, eight sentences to complete with but, when, so or because. Alone, then check.

stages.name: Preparing to write
stages.todo: Ex 4a and 4b: they choose one of the three topics and make notes under the four headings – where you were, how you felt, what you saw and did, who you talked to. Notes, not sentences. Go round and help with words.

stages.name: Writing task
stages.todo: Ex 4c: they write the post, about 100 words, with a day and a place at the top as Tim has. Ask for at least four linking words, one of them When at the start of a sentence. Silence; answer questions quietly at the desk. Give a two-minute warning.
stages.avoid: Some will write a list of things they did. Point them back at Tim’s four lines: one day, a few parts, and a feeling in each.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Ex 4d: pairs swap posts. The reader looks for two things – which linking words did your partner use, and is the post like yours? – and writes a one-line comment at the bottom, as on a real blog. Finish with two sentences from the posts on the board, one that joins two ideas well and one that does not, and fix the second together.

slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 28 ex 1a–1e

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Books closed. Tell them three small kind things you did yesterday and let pairs guess the question you were answering. Then ex 1a on p. 28: what is happening in the photo, and how each of the two people might feel.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Three words block the way in: generous (and generosity — no u), hug and charity. Elicit each from a quick context or mime before you board it, and say generosity with them: five syllables, stress on the third.
stages.avoid: Leave the highlighted words in the forum alone. They are ex 1d, the text gives their meaning away, and that is the reason to read for them later.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 1b: the Generosity Day paragraph and a quick reaction in pairs — good idea or not? Then ex 1c, first question only: which of the five writers helped someone and which were helped. Three minutes for the forum, said out loud and kept.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 1c, second question: what kind of help each writer mentions. Then a task you write yourself — five true/false statements, one per post (Sally’s helper drove her home: false, it was the corner shop). Pairs check each answer against the line that proves it.
stages.avoid: ThatGeorgeKid is on both lists: his first line says strangers have helped him too. Expect pairs to file him under helping only.

stages.name: Vocabulary from the text
stages.todo: Ex 1d, the sub aim: the nine highlighted items worked out from context, then explained in their own words with an example of their own. Go past meaning into form — the verb each phrase takes (do volunteer work, give someone directions, make someone smile, no to), give away splitting round its object — and drill volunTEER and STRANGer.
stages.avoid: The posts are full of present perfect — I’ve given, has ever done. That is the next lesson’s target language; if it comes up, park it.

stages.name: Response task
stages.todo: Ex 1e in groups: which writer is the most generous, and why? Each group agrees one name and one reason, then the class votes.

stages.name: Feedback
stages.todo: One group’s reason the others disagree with, and two phrases from ex 1d that you heard used — one well, one not — for the class to judge.

slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 29 ex 2a–2f – audio track 1.48, ex 5a–5b / SB p. 146 Grammar Focus 3A – audio track 1.47 / SB p. 147 Grammar Focus 3A ex c

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The forum was read in the previous lesson, so do not set it again. Each pair retells one post with a single fact changed and the partner catches it — Sally didn’t fall off her bike, she was running.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 2a on p. 29: six forum sentences, gapped, filled from the box and checked against the posts. Then ex 2b: which are present perfect, which past simple. Take the answers and the saw/seen question; hold back the rule.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Start with two questions on the board — Did you help a stranger yesterday? and Have you ever helped a stranger? — and ask what time each is about. Then ex 2c: time expressions underlined, rules finished (ever, never, three times; a few weeks ago, on my fiftieth birthday). Grammar Focus 3A on p. 146 has the timeline and the table; drill it with track 1.47, for the contracted I’ve and the weak have in Have you ever. Draw your own timeline and write three concept questions beforehand.
stages.avoid: The Grammar Focus flags two traps: been, not gone, for a trip that is over, and no finished time with the present perfect. Expect I’ve given a big tip last week, and answer it with a concept question, not the rule again.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Focus 3A ex c on p. 147: seven sentences after the example, each with one wrong tense or form — I never saw that film, Have you ever gone to Canada?, I’ve worked in a hospital a long time ago. Alone, then pairs name the rule each one breaks; only the disputed ones go up.

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 2e on p. 29: three question pairs, a present perfect opener and a past simple follow-up (Have you ever done anything for a charity? What did you do?). They check with track 1.48 (ex 2f), then ask and answer in pairs.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 5a: find someone who has done each thing in the grid, and ask more. Make the grid into a slip they carry, with a second column for the detail from the follow-up question. Close with ex 5b — the most generous thing anyone heard — and two sentences you overheard for the class to repair.
stages.avoid: The follow-up is the lesson: a yes to Have you ever…? means the tense has to change. If they only collect names, the past simple never comes out.

slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 30 ex 1a–1c, 2a–2c / SB p. 135 Vocabulary Focus 3B ex a–b – audio track 1.50 / SB p. 130 (3B Results) / Workbook p. 17 ex 1b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The topic turns from giving to spending. Write 3 for 2 and BOGOF on the board and let them work out what the shop is offering. Then ex 1a on p. 30: is saving money easy, and why?

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 1b: three saving tips with four highlighted items. Then Vocabulary Focus 3B on p. 135, ex a: twelve sentences matched to the pictures to tell Carol’s story and Brian’s, checked with track 1.50. Take the order; the meanings are the next stage.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: The box lists fourteen items and they know several (cash, cost, spend, the sales). Teach seven or eight properly: lend and borrow, owe, get a loan, pay back, save up for, afford, discount. Lend and borrow need a picture and one question — who has the money at the start? Then the patterns: borrow from, lend to, spend on, save up for, can’t afford it, pay it back. The book prints the sounds of the hard ones; drill owe and loan (one vowel), afford, and acCOUNT against DIScount.
stages.avoid: Fourteen items is two lessons. Decide before class which ones you will only name, and do not let the known words eat the time lend and borrow need.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 17 ex 1b: saving for a car, eight gaps after the example, filled from the box. Alone, then compare, then only the gaps they argued over.

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
stages.todo: Vocabulary Focus ex b on p. 135: sentences covered, the pictures and the box words in view, one partner tells Carol’s story and the other Brian’s. Then they swap stories.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 2a–2c: the What kind of spender are you? quiz alone in three minutes, then compared in pairs with a reason for each choice, and the results on p. 130. Write a slip of four follow-up questions that need today’s words — What are you saving up for? Would you lend a friend £100? — so the talk goes past a, b or c.
stages.avoid: Keep the quiz reading short. It is a prompt for talk, not a second reading lesson, and this is the only stage where the words come out unprompted.

slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 31 ex 3a–3b – audio track 1.51, ex 4a–4e – audio tracks 1.52, 1.54, ex 4h / SB p. 146 Grammar Focus 3B – audio track 1.53 / SB p. 147 Grammar Focus 3B ex c / Teacher’s Book p. 209 (photocopiable)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 3a on p. 31: the three shoppers in the photos. Elicit what a big spender, a smart spender and a non spender are, then pairs decide who is who.

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Ex 3b with track 1.51: they check their guesses and note what each person bought. Three minutes of audio, one play, answers taken quickly.
stages.avoid: Ex 3c and 3d are not this lesson. The listening is the way into the grammar; ten minutes here and the clarification gets squeezed.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 4a: three sentences from the interviews with the past participle missing. They try from memory, then check with track 1.52 (ex 4b) and name the tense.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex 4c gives three rules: just for a short time ago, already for done (often sooner than expected), not … yet for not done but still expected. Check each on its sentence — do I have the food now? do you know when I spent it? — with questions you write beforehand. Grammar Focus 3B on p. 146 shows word order and questions; drill with track 1.53. Then ex 4e with track 1.54: the /dʒ/ in just against the /j/ in yet, which many learners merge, repeated and then said again inside the target sentences.
stages.avoid: Plan for three errors: just or already before have (I just have bought it), already in a negative, and a finished time on the end (I’ve already paid it yesterday).

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Focus 3B ex c on p. 147: Jeff’s to-do list, ticked and unticked, turned into already and not yet sentences. The tick decides the adverb and the adverb decides the position, so it tests meaning and form at once. Alone, then read aloud to a partner.

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
stages.todo: Teacher’s Book p. 209, adapted: cut it up and hand out only the bold prompts (Did you go to that new café? You’re late.). The partner answers with just, already or yet, then they compare with the printed reply that fits — that is the key, not the task.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 4h is the model: two speech bubbles, the second speaker capping the first. Each writes three true sentences about their own money this week — something just bought, something already spent, something not done yet — and they trade them in pairs the same way. Save the last minute for one sentence from your notes on the board.
stages.avoid: Monitor where the adverb lands, not whether the story is interesting.

slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 32 ex 1a–1g – audio tracks 1.56, 1.57, ex 2a–2b – audio track 1.58

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1a on p. 32: do they enjoy shopping, and for which of food, gifts, clothes and books? Then ex 1b: the photo of Mark and Rachel, and what they might be shopping for. Board two or three guesses.

stages.name: Setting the context
stages.todo: Ex 1c with track 1.56, Part 1, about forty seconds: they check their guesses — a birthday present for Leo. Then ex 1d in pairs: the four products, what each one is for, and who they would buy one for. This doubles as your pre-teaching: football in a tin, a weather station and a book money bank are the words Part 2 depends on.

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex 1e with track 1.57: one question only — which product do they buy? Pairs compare, then confirm.
stages.avoid: If your room can show the video, use it; the track is the same conversation. Know where Part 2 starts before the lesson.

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex 1f: four why-questions, one per product, on a second play of track 1.57. Write three or four true/false items of your own on what ex 1f leaves out — what else the weather station does, how the money bank opens, which of the two is sure Leo likes football — and give them out with the book’s questions. Pairs compare before you decide whether a third play is needed.

stages.name: Response task
stages.todo: Ex 1g: what they think of the present and whether Leo will like it — then which of the four they would have chosen, and why.

stages.name: Language focus
stages.todo: Ex 2a, which carries the sub aim: in threes they act the shop scene from memory first — assistant, Mark, Rachel — then fill the eight gapped phrases and check with track 1.58. Ex 2b sorts them by job — the assistant’s lines, asking to see something else, we’ll take it. Finish with the threes running the scene again with the phrases in front of them.
stages.avoid: This is a short focus on the phrases, not a second lesson. Meaning and who says what is the work here; leave sentence stress for another day.

slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 34 ex 1a–1b / SB p. 35 ex 2a–2b, 3a–3c, 4a–4d

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Books closed: R _ _ S _   M _ N _ Y   F _ R   CH _ R _ TY on the board, letters guessed until the phrase appears. Then ex 1a on p. 34, the three charities matched to what they do, and ex 1b, more ways to raise money. Leave their list on the board; it is material for their own email.
stages.avoid: Leave out ex 1c–1f. The lead-in collects ideas for the writing; it is not a second lesson.

stages.name: Model text
stages.todo: Ex 2a on p. 35: Anita’s email, and which of the six reasons she is writing for (four of them). Then ex 2b: how the team raised the money, how the National Trust will spend it, what else colleagues can do. Pairs compare.

stages.name: Paragraphing and useful language
stages.todo: Ex 3a–3b: the four paragraphs matched to their jobs, and what goes into the opening and closing ones. Then ex 3c, the Oxfam email in four jumbled paragraphs, put in order. Take the sub aim from the two emails: We’ve successfully raised £500 and many of you have bought tickets give news that counts now; we also sold our old books and others gave clothes in March tell what happened. Board two of each and ask why the tense changes.
stages.avoid: Raise and rise get confused in writing: raise money, never rise money. One example on the board saves a lot of correcting.

stages.name: Preparing to write
stages.todo: Ex 4a: they choose email 1 (a real experience) or email 2 (£1,000 raised at work or school). Ex 4b: a plan in four paragraphs. Make a one-page planning sheet with four boxes headed by the jobs from ex 3a and hand it out here.

stages.name: Writing task
stages.todo: Ex 4c: they write the email alone, from the plan, with the ex 1b list still up for ideas. When you spot a mistake, point at it and let them fix it — a finished time with the present perfect is the one to catch.

stages.name: Feedback
stages.todo: Ex 4d: emails swap — four paragraphs? the right thing in each? Then one opening paragraph read aloud because it does its job, and one tense slip from your monitoring for the room to repair.

slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 38 ex 2a–2d – audio track 1.65

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 2a on p. 38: the two photos at the bottom of the page — Marta at a Cambridge May Ball, Craig at his Indian wedding. Pairs say what each event is and what is going on in the picture. Most of them will not know ball in this sense: a big formal party with dancing. Take two or three ideas and leave the details open; the listening fills them in.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Three or four words stand between them and the listening: ceremony, rub (something on your skin), spice, and ball if the lead-in did not settle it. A picture or a mime for each, elicited before you board it. Bring the pictures yourself — a jar of turmeric does more than a definition.
stages.avoid: DJ, dress and breakfast they already know. Pre-teach only what blocks ex 2b and 2c, or the listening has nothing left to give them.

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex 2b: six sentences, and pairs guess who says each one, Marta or Craig, from what they now know about the two events. Then play track 1.65 once to check. Insist on an M or a C next to every line before you press play — the guess is what makes them listen.
stages.avoid: The six sentences are full of future forms — we’re going to stay, I’m meeting the others. They are the next lesson’s target language. Take the M and C answers and nothing else; if someone asks about the verbs, write the question on the side of the board and leave it there.

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex 2c: eight questions, the first four on Marta, the last four on Craig. Give them time to read before you play track 1.65 again, and pause between the two speakers so they can write. Pairs compare and say which answers they still need; play only those parts a third time. For fast finishers, make a small card of numbers from the recording — 8, 70, 9, 6 and the fourth day — and ask what each one refers to.
stages.avoid: Questions 6 and 8 have two parts (when the day starts and when it ends; who eats where). Accept the main point and move on — this is listening, not dictation.

stages.name: Response task
stages.todo: Ex 2d in groups of three or four: the biggest party and the best wedding they have ever been to. Ask each group to find one thing all their stories have in common. Once they are talking, stay out of the groups and note language for the close.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One story per group — the one the group chose — then four sentences you heard, two worth copying and two to fix. A question with ever will probably be among them; it is the present perfect from unit 3 and worth thirty seconds.

slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 38 ex 3a–3f – audio track 1.67 / SB p. 148 Grammar Focus 4A – audio track 1.66 / SB p. 149 Grammar Focus 4A ex d / Workbook p. 22 ex 2a

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Marta and Craig were heard and worked through in the previous lesson, so the text is done: two minutes on what they remember — what Marta has to do before the ball, what happens on Craig’s wedding day. Nothing goes on the board yet.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Books closed: the four sentences of ex 3a on the board with the verbs missing — My friends … early tomorrow, I’m … the house on Saturday, I’m … the whole night, A beautician … our make-up. Pairs rebuild them from memory; give the verbs (arrive, leave, stay, do) if they stall. Then books open, they check against ex 3a on p. 38 and answer the book’s question: present or future?

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex 3b splits the meaning: the present continuous for plans already arranged with other people (a beautician is doing our make-up — someone has booked her), going to for something decided but not arranged (I’m going to stay the whole night). Ask concept questions on the board sentences — has she already called the beautician? could Marta change her mind at three in the morning? Grammar Focus 4A on p. 148 adds that the present continuous usually comes with a time. Drill the going to table with track 1.66 — positive, negative, question. Then ex 3d with track 1.67: five speakers, which say /ˈgəʊɪŋtə/ and which say gonna. Make a visual of your own for the meaning — two diary pages, one with a booked time and a name, one with only an idea.
stages.avoid: In most situations both forms are correct, and the Grammar Focus says so. Do not teach a rule sharper than the language. And going to go usually becomes going (I’m going shopping on Saturday); if a student offers it, it is right.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Focus 4A ex d on p. 149: five pairs, each with two follow-up lines that make one form more natural — I’m having a party … it’s this Saturday, do you want to come? Alone, then in pairs with a reason for each choice. Then Workbook p. 22 ex 2a: five going to sentences and questions put in order after the example. That one is form only, so keep it brisk.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 3e–3f on p. 38: notes on their plans for each time expression in the box (true or invented), then they tell a partner, who asks a question every time — when are you going? who with? Model it on yourself first with one arrangement and one plan side by side, so they hear both forms before they need them.
stages.avoid: At this level will is the default for every future. Say before they start that you are listening for today’s two forms, and deal with any will at the close, not mid-flow.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two plans the room should hear, then three sentences from your notes: one where the form matched the plan, one with be missing (they going to visit), one will that should have been a booked present continuous.

slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 39 ex 4a–4d

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 4a on p. 39: do they celebrate their birthday and how, and are any ages special where they come from? The photos help — before anyone reads, pairs guess which country each one shows.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Fireworks, kimono and become an adult are the three that block the article. A picture does the first two in seconds; for the third, use the age it happens in their own country. Find or make the pictures yourself.
stages.avoid: Do not pre-teach apply, rent or borrow: ex 4c turns on them, and the reading should find them, not your board.

stages.name: Reading for specific information
stages.todo: Ex 4b: what do 1, 15, 20 and 100 refer to? A scan, not a read — three minutes, then pairs. Warn them that a number can have two answers; 100 is both the Queen’s card and the Vietnamese New Year greeting.
stages.avoid: The 1 is the hardest: it is not an age but the day the whole of Vietnam gets a year older together, at Tet. Let a pair that found it explain it to the room.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 4c: six things people do — wear clothes they can’t afford, ask for something, give and receive, party for days, wear special shoes, take a day off — matched to the four celebrations. Alone, then pairs, pointing at the line that decides each one. Write a second task yourself for the quick readers: three questions that need some thought, such as why twins get slightly different cards, or why so many families rent kimonos.
stages.avoid: Items 2 and 5 sit in a single sentence each — apply before the big day; her first pair of high heels. If a pair misses them, send them back to the paragraph rather than giving the answer.

stages.name: Response task
stages.todo: Ex 4d: which celebration they found most interesting, then the important celebrations where they live, from the book’s list — weddings, local festivals, religious festivals and new year. In a one-country class, ask each group to describe one celebration to a visitor who has never seen it. Give it the full time; this is where the topic becomes theirs.
stages.avoid: When the detail stage overruns, this is the stage that gets cut, and it should not be. Drop your second detail task instead.

stages.name: Feedback
stages.todo: The celebration from each group the others would most like to go to, then a few points of language from your notes. Today’s future forms may come out when they talk about next year’s festivals — praise them where you hear them.

4B.context: Social life – A day out and an invitation

slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 40 ex 1a–1b – audio track 1.68, ex 2a–2h – audio tracks 1.69, 1.72, 1.73 / SB p. 148 Grammar Focus 4B – audio tracks 1.70, 1.71 / SB p. 149 Grammar Focus 4B ex b–c / SB p. 131 Communication 4B Student A / SB p. 132 Communication 4B Student B
slots.tracks:
Track 1.68
Track 1.69
Track 1.70
Track 1.71
Track 1.72
Track 1.73

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1a on p. 40: what they know about Tokyo, and which of the five places in Tokyo Highlights (the photos run across the spread) they would choose for a day there.

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Ex 1b with track 1.68: Mike has one day in Tokyo and his friend Harry plans it. One play and two questions — which of the highlights they choose, and which three other places.
stages.avoid: Ex 1c is a second listening and belongs to no one today. One play, then on — the grammar is the lesson.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 2a with track 1.69: five lines from the conversation, gapped for ’ll, won’t and shall. Then ex 2b: are they talking about the present or the future, and what are the full forms of ’ll and won’t?

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex 2c matches the five lines to four jobs: will for promises and for decisions made while speaking, shall for offers and suggestions. Write a concept question for each — had Harry planned this before? is he offering or asking? Grammar Focus 4B on p. 148 gives the form; drill with tracks 1.70 and 1.71 and make the point that shall comes only in questions with I and we. Then ex 2e–2g: track 1.72 for the two vowels in want and won’t, and track 1.73 to hear the difference and repeat it.
stages.avoid: The Grammar Focus also gives will for requests. Leave it out — four uses is plenty for twelve minutes. And the answer to Shall I…? is Yes, please, never Yes, you shall.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Focus 4B ex b on p. 149: six short exchanges, will or shall chosen from the italics. Then ex c, the dinner conversation with ten gaps; let the slower pairs stop at five and check what they have.
stages.avoid: Item 6 of ex b (Will you cook dinner?) and gap 8 of ex c are requests — the use you left out. Say so when you check them; do not reopen it.

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 2h sends Student A to Communication 4B on p. 131 and Student B to p. 132: one reads a line (I don’t understand the menu), the other answers. Change the task slightly — the listener answers in their own words first, with I’ll or Shall I / Shall we, then looks at the printed replies to see which matches best.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Make role cards for a phone call the night before a visit. The visitor’s card lists three wishes and one worry (I land at 6 am; I hate crowds), the host’s lists four places in their own city. They plan the day with offers, promises and suggestions, then swap roles. A line per item is enough.
stages.avoid: Without a reason to offer or promise, they will narrate in going to. The worry on the visitor’s card is what draws out I’ll — make sure every card has one.

slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 41 ex 3a–3e – audio track 1.74 / Teacher’s Book p. 235 (photocopiable crossword)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Go back to Harry’s day in Tokyo from the previous lesson: what did he say about the noodles, the palace, the cherry blossom? Board the adjectives they give you, then ask for the opposite of each. The lesson is about pairs.

stages.name: Test
stages.todo: Ex 3a–3b on p. 41, alone and without help: opposites from the box for the three highlighted adjectives (crowded, huge, pretty), then six pairs matched. This is the diagnostic. They work from what they already know while you walk the room with the twelve words listed, marking which ones go wrong. No correcting, no hints, no comparing yet.
stages.avoid: The stage only works if you can see what they don’t know. A test done in pairs, or with you helping, tells you nothing.

stages.name: Teach
stages.todo: Now pairs compare and you take the answers — then teach only what your list shows went wrong. Likely candidates: magnificent and ordinary, ancient (for buildings and places, not people), narrow, and indoor and outdoor before a noun. Photos of your own town do the meaning. Add that huge, tiny and magnificent are already strong — really huge, not very huge. Then ex 3c–3d with track 1.74: they underline the stress, listen and repeat; magnificent, ordinary, ancient and peaceful are the ones to drill.
stages.avoid: The pull is to teach all twelve because you planned to. If the room got high and low right, say so and move on — that is the logic of the shape and the hardest part of it to hold.

stages.name: Second test
stages.todo: Teacher’s Book p. 235: a crossword split between Student A and Student B, each holding the words the other is missing. They take turns describing their words — an opposite, a place it fits — without saying them. Cut the page in half before class. It tests meaning and spelling together, which the first test did not.
stages.avoid: Pairs who just read out the answers to each other are filling in a crossword, not taking a test. Describing is the point — model one clue yourself before they start.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 3e: in groups, places they all know — the school, a street, a market — with one place for each adjective in 3b (the book prints 4b; it means 3b). Bring six or eight photos of local places to start the groups off, and ask each group for the one place the others will argue about.
stages.avoid: Groups will go for the easy pairs. If nobody uses magnificent or ancient, ask for them by name.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: The places the groups disagreed on, then three sentences you collected while monitoring, for the class to fix — a stress in the wrong place counts, and so does very huge.

slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 44 ex 1a–1b, 2a–2b / SB p. 45 ex 3a–3d, 4a–4c

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1a–1b on p. 44: how often they have a party, go out for a meal or invite people round, and which they would do for a birthday or the end of term. Leave out the listening in ex 1c–1e; this lesson goes straight to the emails.
stages.avoid: Four minutes, not ten. They will happily talk about parties all lesson, and the writing needs the time.

stages.name: Model text
stages.todo: Ex 2a: Barbara’s two invitations, to Martina and to Bill, and three questions — has she seen Martina recently, when is the barbecue, what does each need to bring? Then ex 2b: who does she see more often, and how do they know? The answer (Bill — she knows about his cycling trip) is the way into the difference in tone.
stages.avoid: Do not call Martina’s email formal. It is friendly but less close — We haven’t seen you for ages, Hope you’re enjoying your new job — and the book’s point is a difference of degree.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Ex 3a on p. 45: the table, four jobs with two versions of each — How are you? / How are things?, Would you like to come? / Can you come? Then ex 3b–3c: the two replies, who wrote which, and the phrases for thanking, saying yes, saying no, giving a reason and seeing each other again. Board them as two columns, a close friend and someone you see less. Ex 3d, five sentences to correct, is the check; pairs, at speed.
stages.avoid: I’m looking forward to seeing and Would you like to come? are the two forms that will go wrong in their own emails. Give those the board time, not the phrases they already use well.

stages.name: Writing the invitation
stages.todo: Ex 4a: pairs choose a weekend activity, decide where, when and what guests bring, then write the invitation to another pair together, one pen between them. Make a small checklist card with the four points from ex 4a — it is also what the other pair checks later. Tell each pair whether they are writing to a close friend or not, so the table has a job.

stages.name: Writing the reply
stages.todo: Ex 4b: invitations swap and each pair writes a reply — thanks, yes or no with a reason, and a comment or a question. Tell half the pairs to say no, or everyone accepts and the refusing phrases never get used.
stages.avoid: Bill signs off with xx and Martina with All the best. Point out that the ending follows the friendship as much as the greeting does.

stages.name: Feedback
stages.todo: Ex 4c: replies go back to the inviting pair, who check both emails against the card — where and when clear, the right phrases to invite and to reply. Then one invitation and one reply read aloud, and two phrases from your monitoring on the board.

5A.context: Work – finding a job, and the jobs of the future

slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 50 ex 1a–1b, 2a–2b, 3a–3b, 3d – audio track 2.09 / Grammar Focus 5B p. 150 – audio tracks 2.10, 2.11, p. 151 ex a / Communication 5B SB pp. 128, 130 / Workbook p. 29 ex 1b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Books closed. Ask the question in ex 1a — where do you go, and who do you talk to, when you need a job — and board what comes back: adverts, a CV, a friend who knows someone. If nobody offers careers fair, give it to them; the recording happens at one. Books open for ex 1b: three worries, three pictures, one minute in pairs to match them.
stages.avoid: Ex 1c asks whether they have ever had these worries. It is a good question and it costs four minutes your clarification needs. Skip it.

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Teach apply for a job in one line; all three speakers use it. Then ex 2a with track 2.09 (the book prints it 2.9): three people at the fair, two questions — where are they, and who sounds most and least positive. Play it once, let pairs compare, and ask what Marco said that made him the optimist and Sara the pessimist.
stages.avoid: This is the way in, not the lesson. One play, one task. The sentences you need are already printed in ex 2b, so there is no reason to play it again.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 2b prints the six predictions. Drop the book’s listen-again question about reasons and use the sentences instead: two columns on the board, sure and not sure, and pairs put each prediction in one. Then ex 3a: they underline more or less in the rule. Take the answers but hold back the explanation.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning on a line from certain to impossible: will at one end, won’t at the other, might and might not in between. Check it against the speakers — Is Marco certain he’ll make contacts? Is he certain he’ll get a job today? Form from the box on p.150: will or might plus the infinitive without to, the same for every person; won’t and might not, which stays in full. Add the frames people really use, I’m sure I’ll… and I don’t think I’ll…, and show that English says I don’t think I’ll get an interview, not I think I won’t. Then play 2.10 and 2.11 and drill the positive and negative lines: the contracted ’ll, and won’t, which they will say as want unless they hear the two side by side.
stages.avoid: 2.11 finishes with Do you think…? questions. Let them repeat them and move on; one structure with one meaning is the lesson, and the freer task hands them the question ready-made.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Focus p.151 ex a: Duncan’s chart for a year in China, seven sentences to finish with will, won’t, might or might not. The column he ticked decides the answer, so they cannot do it on form alone. Then Workbook p.29 ex 1b, eight sentences back in the world of interviews, salaries and contacts. A key on the board for the first, the second read aloud by the class — listen for might to.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 3d, Communication 5B. Student B interviews A about the future: p.130 if A has a job, p.128 if not; then swap. Every answer must commit — I’m sure I’ll…, I might…, I don’t think I’ll… — with a reason. Write two prompts of your own for anyone neither page fits, a retired volunteer or a full-time student, and model one exchange before they start. Close by boarding the will and might errors you heard most, and let the pairs who made them fix them first.
stages.avoid: Find out who in your class works before you plan this. If nobody does, everyone uses p.128 — decide that in your plan, not at minute thirty-seven.

slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 51 ex 4a, 5a–5c, 6a–6b (article: ‘Planning a safe future career’)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Three jobs on the board with every other letter missing — _c_o_n_a_t, _a_k_r, _l_c_r_c_a_ — and pairs race to fill them. Then one line back to the careers fair in the last lesson: Marco, Sara and Kate want jobs, but will those jobs still exist in twenty years? That is today’s text.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Ex 4a: pairs find five jobs in the photos — computer programmer, carer, shop assistant, postman, builder. Carer is the one most will not know; give it a situation and a concept question. Drill all five, with the stress on comPUter PROgrammer and asSIStant. Add predict or disappear only if you think they will block the gist question.
stages.avoid: Ex 4b–4e are a vocabulary lesson of their own — a Vocabulary Focus page and the /ʃ/ sound, with recordings — and none of it is on your card. Teach what blocks the text and stop.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 5a in pairs first: which jobs in the photos might disappear, and which will there be more of? Board the guesses in two lists. Then ex 5b: they read the article alone, fast, to check the board. Three minutes. Back to the board to tick and cross; shop assistants, postmen and builders are going, programmers and carers are staying.
stages.avoid: Photo processors and online education managers are in the article but not in the photos. They come up in ex 5c; don’t pre-teach them.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 5c: seven causes — online shopping, sending emails, digital photos, 3D printers, environmental problems, living longer, studying online — and what the article says each one will change. They read again and note an answer for each. Make the feedback yourself: a two-column handout, cause and result, that pairs fill, then check against a key you stick on the wall.
stages.avoid: Some answers are fewer jobs and some are new jobs. A pair who writes jobs disappear on every line has read the headings, not the sentences; send them back to the paragraph.

stages.name: Response task
stages.todo: Ex 6a in small groups: six predictions, from printed buildings to a four-day week. Will they happen in their lifetime, and why? Then ex 6b: each person writes three predictions of their own, using at least two of the jobs from ex 4a, and reads them to the group, who agree or disagree with a reason. Board a few topics — money, houses, travel, food — for anyone stuck.
stages.avoid: They will use will and might, because the last lesson taught them. Respond to what they predict, not how they built it; the grammar lesson came earlier today, and this one is reading.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Which prediction did a whole group agree on, and which one split it? Then board four predictions you overheard — one with a job word used well, one with it wrong — and let the class mend them before you do.

slots.pages: Empower B1 (1st ed.) SB p. 54 ex 1a–1e – audio track 2.20

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Describe a part-time or summer job you once had in three sentences without naming it, and let them guess. Then ex 1a in pairs: have they ever had a summer or part-time job, and did they enjoy it? Board the jobs that come up; you will want them again at the end.

stages.name: Pre-listening
stages.todo: Ex 1b: the four adverts. Headings first — what jobs do they expect? — then a proper read to decide which jobs each of the six sentences could describe. The adverts hold the words that would block the recording: barista, tips, training, pay and conditions. Clarify those as they come up, an example each, rather than as a list. Several sentences fit more than one job; accept any answer they can justify.
stages.avoid: Leave ex 1c until later. Asked now, it is a guess; asked after the recording, they have John’s opinion to agree or argue with.

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex 1d with track 2.20, Penny and John. Two questions: which jobs are they talking about, and do they like them? Play it once. The second answer is really two answers — John likes the café, Penny is tired of the supermarket — so check they have both.

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex 1e: five choices — has or hasn’t, likes or doesn’t, sometimes or always, is or isn’t. They try from memory, then hear 2.20 again to check. Then add three questions you write yourself from the audioscript, ones that ask why rather than what: why Penny finds the supermarket hard, what John says about training, what Penny will do before she applies. A third play only for the answer that splits the room, stopped at the line.
stages.avoid: Item 3 is the trap: John says he can sometimes make twenty pounds in a day, and some will hear always. Let the recording settle it, not you.

stages.name: Response task
stages.todo: Now ex 1c: which advert would they most like, least like, and be best at — and would they take John’s advice? Then new partners and a real choice: one summer, two of the four adverts, decide together, using what they now know about tips, pay, training and hours. Two minutes each way.
stages.avoid: The right-hand side of p.54, Penny’s application, is the start of the book’s writing lesson. It is not yours today, even if you finish early.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Content first: which job would the class take, by show of hands? Then write up what you heard people say about tips, training and pay, mistakes included, and let the room correct it.
