stages.todo: Groups of three: if you could be in Departures tomorrow, where to, and why – a plan you really have, and a dream you probably won’t. Give them a minute to think first. Listen in and note what you hear; you are listening for how they talk about the future, which is the next lesson’s grammar.

stages.name: Feedback and airport words again
stages.todo: One dream per group to the room. Then Workbook p. 17 ex 2, the airport gap text, in pairs as a two-minute race, to put the morning’s words to work. Check with an answer key.

3B.context: Plans and dreams – going to, the world’s top airports, and Lily meets Ben again

slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 21 Grammar ex 3a–3b – audio track 1.56; Pronunciation ex 4a – track 1.58; ex 4c / Grammar Bank p. 131 3A ex a / Communication 3A What are your plans? Student A p. 101, Student B p. 107

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Books closed: Olivia, Matthew and Lily from the airport interviews – where was each one going, and why? Write two answers on the board as they say them; they will contain going to. The interviews were heard last lesson, so do not play them again.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 3a on p. 21: five sentences from the interviews completed with be going to + verb, then track 1.56 to check. Then ex 3b in pairs: plan or prediction for each – PL, PL, PR, PL, PR. Take the answers; the reasons are the next stage.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Two meanings, one form. Plan: decided before now (I’m going to teach English – when did she decide? before the airport). Prediction: we think it will happen because of what we know or see (it’s winter, so it’s going to be cold). Concept-check both with their own examples. Form: be + going to + infinitive, with the negative and the question on the board. Pronunciation from ex 4a, track 1.58: the stressed words in What are you going to do tonight? – drill the five sentences for rhythm. Show them the gonna box for recognition only; they do not need to say it.
stages.avoid: Going to is not new, so do not present it from zero. The errors to watch are the dropped be (‘I going to’) and to going missing (‘I’m going study’).

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p. 131, 3A ex a: seven sentences with going to and a verb from the box – are you going to stay in a hotel, I’m not going to listen to you. Alone, then pairs, then the disputed ones aloud.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 4c: A on p. 101, B on p. 107, six prompts each – what / you / do after class?, / you / go anywhere next weekend? Two minutes to make the full questions first, checked. Then they interview each other and ask for more information after every answer. Plan a halfway swap or a mingle so each of them asks twice.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two plans from the room worth hearing, then four sentences from your monitoring on the board, not all of them wrong, for the class to correct.

slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 21 Reading ex 5a–5d (‘Top airports in the world’)

stages.name: Lead-in and prediction
stages.todo: Ex 5a in pairs: your nearest airport, what it is like, what you can do there while you wait. Then one question to the room: what would make an airport a place you actually enjoy? Three ideas on the board – they are the predictions the first read checks.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Three items the questions in 5b turn on: a queue, a pet, and a day room (a hotel room you rent for a few hours). Elicit each, check it with a question, and move on.
stages.avoid: Do not touch the six highlighted words – security, delayed, facilities, connecting flight, passengers, board. Ex 5c is built on guessing them.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Two minutes, alone: which of the three ideas on the board does the article mention, and which airport would you choose for a six-hour wait? A quick pair check, quick check.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 5b: the seven situations matched to the best airport – a medical problem, a film, sport, a dog for the weekend, getting lost, sleep, the city between flights. Alone, check with a neighbour, then check with the line that decided each: Osaka, Munich, Seoul, Osaka, Hong Kong, Zurich, Singapore.

stages.name: Vocabulary from the text
stages.todo: Ex 5c: the six highlighted words guessed from context in pairs, with six short definitions of your own to match them against. Check meaning, then drill security, delayed and passengers for stress.

stages.name: Response – roleplay
stages.todo: Ex 5d: A is at one of the six airports with a three-hour delay; B phones – where are you, what are you going to do? Two minutes to choose the airport and plan, then the call, then swap with a different airport. Monitor for the airport words and for going to from the last lesson.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Which airport did most people choose, and why? Then three things you heard on the board, good and bad together, for the class to sort.

slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 22 Reading & Listening ex 1b–1e – audio track 1.62 / SB p. 23 Grammar ex 2d–2e, 2g – tracks 1.65, 1.66 (the listening exercises only; the grammar in 2a–2c is not part of this lesson)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Do they remember Lily from the airport – where was she going, and who was she hoping to see? Then a question in pairs: do you keep in touch with old friends from school or university, and how? One minute, two answers from the room.

stages.name: Reading the messages
stages.todo: Ex 1b on p. 22: the seven Facebook messages between Lily and Ben, numbered into order in pairs; check. Then ex 1c: why does Lily get in touch, and what are they planning to do? Quick check. The messages are the way in to the recordings, so keep this to seven minutes.

stages.name: Vocabulary from the messages
stages.todo: Ex 1d: the six highlighted phrases matched to their meanings – for ages, arrangements, I’m still, perhaps, both, fix a day. Pairs, check, and drill for ages and fix a day as chunks.

stages.name: Listening 1 – the voicemail
stages.todo: Set up leave a message and reservation. Ex 1e, track 1.62: Lily’s voicemail, and they complete the flight details – the two dates, the arrival and departure times, the hotel. One play, compare in pairs, a second play if the dates split the room, then check.

stages.name: Listening 2 – the phone call
stages.todo: Ex 2d on p. 23, track 1.65: Lily phones Ben from the hotel – one question, what day do they arrange to meet? (Thursday.) Then ex 2e on a second play: Ben’s diary for the week, written as the book’s example – seeing Paul, meeting students, playing tennis. Check with a neighbour, check on the board, then ex 2f with the diary covered as a one-minute memory test.
stages.avoid: Ex 2a–2c in between are the grammar lesson and they are not on your card. Go from 1e straight to 2d.

stages.name: Listening 3 and response
stages.todo: Before ex 2g: in pairs, predict – is the meeting going to be a success? Then track 1.66 once: what happens when they meet? (Ben arrives with his girlfriend, Erika.) Then the response in groups of three: what is Lily thinking, what does she say to Ben the next day, and would you meet up with an ex? Five minutes of talk, monitored with a pen.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One answer per group, then two sentences from your monitoring on the board, one right and one not, and the room decides.

4A.context: Words and arrangements – an email to a host family, the game show What’s the word?, and where new words come from

slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 113 Writing 3 ‘An informal email’ ex a–d (Mrs Barnes’s email to Goran)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: You are going to study English abroad and stay with a family you have never met. In pairs: three things you would want to know before you go, and three things the family would want to know about you. Collect them on the board; the email is about to ask most of them.

stages.name: Model text
stages.todo: P. 113: Goran, from Croatia, is going to stay with the Barnes family. Ex a – read Mrs Barnes’s email and put the four expressions in the gaps (Dear Goran, Looking forward to hearing from you, Best wishes, PS). Then ex b, the seven questions, in pairs; 5, 6 and 7 are the ones that teach something. Check against the board: which of their questions does she ask?

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Two sets from the model, boarded. The frame of an informal email: Dear…, Thank you for your email, Looking forward to…, Best wishes, PS. And the arrangements language they will need to answer her: I’m arriving at… on…, my flight number is…, I’m going back on…, I’d prefer… Give the present continuous sentences as chunks for the writing; the grammar behind them is not today’s lesson.

stages.name: Preparing to write
stages.todo: Ex c: the three-paragraph plan – thank her and say when you are arriving; answer her other questions (going back, food, room, what you would like to do); a closing line. Notes only, with invented flight details if they like.

stages.name: Writing task
stages.todo: The reply to Mrs Barnes, three paragraphs, ending with Best wishes and their name. Alone and in silence, the plan and the board in front of them. Decide before the lesson how you will present it – an email template on paper does more than a blank sheet.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Ex d: swap with a partner, who checks two things – has every question in Mrs Barnes’s email been answered, and are there any mistakes of grammar, punctuation or spelling. Two minutes to read, two to talk. Then one sentence from the drafts on the board for the room to correct, and collect the emails.

slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 24 Listening ex 1a–1d – audio tracks 2.2, 2.3, 2.4; Grammar ex 2a–2b / Grammar Bank p. 131 3C ex a–b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1a on p. 24: do they like word games? Then the Scrabble letters on the page – pairs have three minutes to make as many words of four letters or more as they can. Take the longest.

stages.name: Listening – the game show
stages.todo: Ex 1b, track 2.2: how do you play What’s the word? Elicit the rules – six words, two minutes, you cannot use any part of the word. Then ex 1c, track 2.3: they write the six words Martin is defining; a pair check. Then ex 1d, track 2.4, to hear Lola’s answers and check: nurse, supermarket, mobile, blond, clever, turn off. Three recordings, one play each.
stages.avoid: Eight minutes is the budget. The show is the way in to who, which and where; the paraphrasing expressions it also carries are tomorrow’s vocabulary lesson, so leave section 3 alone.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 2a: three sentences from the show completed with who, which or where – something which, a place where, somebody who. Then ex 2b: when do we use each one? Pairs, then the rule in their words.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning: the clause says which person, thing or place we mean – it defines. Who for people, which for things, where for places; that can replace who and which. Form on the board: noun + who / which / where + a clause with its own verb (a nurse is somebody who works in a hospital). The book has no pronunciation here, so supply it: drill three definitions with the relative pronoun weak and the stress on the nouns.
stages.avoid: The error to plan for is ‘a place which you buy things’ – which for where. One concept question on the difference is worth more than the rule.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p. 131, 3C ex a: seven definitions completed with who, which or where. Alone, compare with a partner, then only the disputed ones.

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
stages.todo: P. 131 ex b: nine sentences built from prompts – that / the shop / I bought my wedding dress. Pairs, said aloud rather than written, with a check at the end.

stages.name: Freer practice and feedback
stages.todo: Each pair writes definitions for four words of their own choice – a person, a thing, a place and one more – with who, which or where, and reads them to another pair, who guess. Two minutes to write, three to play. Then two definitions from your monitoring on the board, one right and one wrong, which the class puts right.

slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 25 Reading ex 5a–5c (‘900 new words in 3 months’)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: In pairs: a word that came into your language in the last few years, and an English word you have started hearing recently. Two from each pair on the board.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Three items the gist task needs: combine, a brand and publish an update. Get them from the class, check each with a question, and move on. Leave the six highlighted words for ex 5b.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 5a: two minutes – how many ways of making new words does the article mention, and what are they? (Four: combining two words, nouns becoming verbs, adopting foreign words, names of brands.) Compare in pairs, check.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: The book has no detail task, so design one: eight words from the article on a handout – gastropub, text, barista, iPod, road rage, tweet, latte, google – to sort under the four ways the first task found. Alone, a quick pair check, check against the lines that decide them.

stages.name: Vocabulary from the text
stages.todo: Ex 5b: the six highlighted words matched to the definitions in pairs – toy boy, to text, barista, road rage, latte, gastropub. Then ex 5c: can they explain the other seven – emoticon, to tweet, iPod, to google, Wi-fi, ringtone, smartphone? Drill the stress on barista and emoticon.

stages.name: Response – invent a word
stages.todo: Groups of three invent a new English word by combining two words, the way the article does, and write a one-line definition for it. Then the words go round the room and the other groups guess what they mean. Give them a model first – brunch, breakfast and lunch. Walk round with your notebook; you will hear the relative clauses from the last lesson doing their job.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: A vote for the word the class would most like to see in the dictionary. Then two sentences from the definitions on the board, one right and one not, for the class to correct.

4B.context: Explaining words you don’t know, then parents and teenagers – annoying habits and the housework that hasn’t been done yet

slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 24 Vocabulary ex 3a–3c – audio track 2.6; Speaking 4 / Communication 3C What’s the word? Student A p. 101, Student B p. 107 / Workbook p. 21 ex 2

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 3a on p. 24: what do you do when you are speaking English and the word you need is missing – look it up on your phone, mime it, or explain it with other words? Pairs, then a show of hands. Then give them a word to explain to a partner without saying it – scissors – and watch what they reach for.

stages.name: Presentation
stages.todo: Ex 3b: the eight expressions completed from the list, then track 2.6 to check – it’s somebody who, it’s something which, it’s somewhere where, it’s a kind of, it’s the opposite of, it’s like … but, it’s similar to, for example you do this to. Meaning is mostly transparent; the work is form and sound. Board them as frames with the slot after each one, point back to yesterday’s who / which / where for the first three, and drill the whole chunks fast – it’s the OPposite of, it’s a KIND of – because they are only useful at speed.
stages.avoid: Eight frames is the set. Do not add the Teacher’s Book extras; the time goes to the game.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 3c: definitions completed for six words – a DJ, an art gallery, a camera, a lift, sunbathe, curly – each with the frame the book starts. Pairs, then two or three read aloud and the room says the word.

stages.name: Controlled practice 2
stages.todo: Workbook p. 21 ex 2: eight more words – mean, cardigan, hire, slim, souvenir, sunbathe, pilot, campsite – with the frame begun for them. Alone, then an answer key.

stages.name: Freer practice – the game
stages.todo: Speaking 4: Communication What’s the word?, A on p. 101, B on p. 107, six words each. A minute to plan, then two minutes each to define all six while the partner guesses and writes – no part of the word allowed. Then they compare lists. Play it as the TV show: time it, and keep a score on the board. Monitor for the frames.
stages.avoid: If a word on the card is unknown to the student, they put a hand up and you tell them quietly; otherwise the whole two minutes goes on one word.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Which pair got the most words, and which word nobody could define? Then three definitions you heard on the board, one of them correct – one with who for a thing – and the room decides before you confirm.

slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 28 Reading ex 1a–1e; Vocabulary ex 2a (‘Teenagers have annoying habits – but so do their parents!’)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book warm-up: MY FAMILY’S ANNOYING HABITS on the board, with one of yours as an example – my sister spends an hour in the bathroom. Pairs collect two each; three go on the board. Then ex 1a: teenager, its pronunciation, and whether their language has a word for that age.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Only what the first task needs: annoying, a habit and a mess. Elicit each one, check it with a question, and move on.
stages.avoid: The verbs and phrases in the posts – roll your eyes, carry on texting, the battery is dead – are ex 1d, guessed from context. Leave them.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 1b: the eight posts, three minutes – P if a parent is complaining about a teenager, T if a teenager about a parent. Then ex 1c, compare with a partner and argue the ones they disagree on; 1 and 3 could go either way. Check: T, P, T, P, P, T, T, P.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Design the task the book does not give: eight one-line summaries on a handout – they change the channel; they don’t listen while I’m talking; they never pick clothes up off the floor – to match to the eight names. Alone, check with a neighbour, check against the posts.

stages.name: Vocabulary from the text
stages.todo: Ex 1d: the highlighted verbs and phrases guessed in pairs; check, and drill the three that are hard to say. Then ex 2a: which three are about housework – tidy, pick up dirty clothes, do the washing-up. Then a practice task of your own, because guessing is not practice: a quick mime round, or five gapped sentences about your own house.

stages.name: Response – your post
stages.todo: Ex 1e first in groups of three: which of these habits annoy you, and whose side are you on? Then each student writes one post of their own, in the article’s style, about an annoying habit of someone they live with. Posts go round the group and each group picks the one to read to the class.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: The chosen post from each group, read aloud. Then two or three sentences from the posts on the board, one right, which the class puts right before you confirm.

slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 28 Grammar ex 3a – audio track 2.15 / SB p. 29 Grammar ex 3b–3d, 3f – track 2.18; ex 4d / Grammar Bank p. 133 4A ex b / Communication 4A Has he done it yet? p. 101 (the picture) and p. 102 (the task)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 3a on p. 28, dialogues covered: the four pictures of parents and teenagers – what are they arguing about? Pairs guess, two guesses on the board, nothing confirmed.

stages.name: Listening – the four arguments
stages.todo: Track 2.15 once to check the guesses – the jumper, the homework, the bathroom, the sandwich. Then ex 3b on p. 29: the four dialogues completed with the participles from the list – looked, done, finished, dried, cleaned – and a second play to check.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 3c: the first two questions of dialogue 1 – a specific time in the past, or sometime between then and now? (b.) Then ex 3d: underline just, yet and already in dialogues 2–4 and say in pairs what each one means.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning first: the present perfect for something that happened recently, no time said – have you seen my jumper? when? we don’t know and it doesn’t matter. Then the three words with a concept question each: just, a very short time ago; already, earlier than expected; yet, until now – only in questions and negatives, and at the end. Form on the board: have / has + past participle, with the contractions and the irregular participles done, seen. Pronunciation with ex 3f, track 2.18: the positive-to-negative drill – I’ve finished, I haven’t finished – which is where ’ve and ’s are heard.
stages.avoid: For many of this class the present perfect is new. Teach this one use and the three words, not the whole tense; yet and already in the wrong position is the error to expect, so make the position visible on the board.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p. 133, 4A ex b: eight sentences built with already, just or yet – I’ve just had breakfast; have you finished your homework yet? Alone, compare in pairs, then the disputed ones read aloud.
stages.avoid: Ex a on the same page is the plain present perfect without the three words; it is useful only if ex b fails.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 4d: Communication Has he done it yet? One minute to study Max’s room in the picture on p. 101, then p. 102: nine things Max does every morning – has he already done them, or not yet? Each writes nine sentences from memory, then a pair check, then they check against the picture. Monitor for yet at the end and already before the participle.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Who remembered the most? Then three sentences from your monitoring on the board – a misplaced yet, a past simple where the present perfect was needed, one right – and they find the wrong ones.

5A.context: Fashion and shopping – a designer’s interview, things you’ve bought and never worn

slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 30 Reading ex 1a–1d (‘The style interview’ with Lindka Cierach)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1a: in pairs, three fashion designers, their nationality, and whether they design for men or women. Two minutes, then names on the board.

stages.name: Pre-reading
stages.todo: Ex 1b: the introduction and the photos – do they like the clothes? Then three items the gapped sentences depend on: sewing, chic and a fancy dress party. Elicit, check and drill. The glossary covers bride and bridegroom.
stages.avoid: The highlighted fashion and shopping words are ex 1d. Do not pre-teach them.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Two minutes with the interview, pens down: which of the questions in capitals would they most like to ask a designer, and what is the one answer that surprises them? A pair check, two answers from the room.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 1c: the six sentences A–F put back in the gaps. Alone, then compare with a partner and point at the line before or after each gap that decides it. Check: E, B, F, A, D, C.

stages.name: Vocabulary from the text
stages.todo: Ex 1d: the highlighted words and phrases about fashion and shopping guessed from context in pairs, against short definitions of your own. Check meaning and drill the two or three that are hard to say.

stages.name: Response
stages.todo: Pairs take three of the interview questions and ask each other – have you ever been to a fancy dress party, have you ever met someone wearing exactly the same as you, have you ever fallen over in high heels or bad shoes – and get the story behind every yes. Then swap partners once. Collect errors and good sentences as you listen.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: The best story from the room, in a sentence. Then three things you heard on the board, some right and some not, which they correct together.

slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 31 Grammar ex 2a (the last four questions of the interview on p. 30); Listening ex 3a–3c – audio track 2.26 / Grammar Bank p. 133 4B ex b–c

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Books closed: what do they remember about Lindka – the fancy dress party, the shoes at the House of Lords, the men’s collection? Two sentences on the board as they say them. The interview was read last lesson; do not set it again.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 2a on p. 31 with the last four questions of the interview on p. 30: which questions are about experiences sometime in her life, which about a specific moment, and what ever means. Pairs, then check – and put the four questions on the board in two columns.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning from the two columns: Have you ever…? asks about any time in your life up to now, no time stated; when the answer is yes, the next question wants the details – when? what did you do? – and that is the past simple. Concept-check the switch with one exchange. Form: have / has + past participle against did + infinitive, and the participles that differ from the past – gone, been, worn. Pronunciation is yours to supply: the weak have in Have you ever…? and the contractions in the answers; drill the two pairs of questions from the board.
stages.avoid: The error that matters is staying in the present perfect for the detail – ‘When have you gone?’ Build the clarification around the switch, not around either tense alone.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p. 133, 4B ex b: the cinema dialogue, six gaps choosing present perfect or past simple – read aloud in pairs, A and B. Then ex c, been or gone, five sentences, fast.

stages.name: Listening – four shoppers
stages.todo: Ex 3a, track 2.26: four people answer Have you ever bought something you’ve never worn? Number the items – trousers, sports clothes, a shirt, a coat; one is not needed. Then ex 3b on a second play: what the problem was with each. Compare with a partner, check. It is the model for the next stage, so point at the shape: a present perfect question, then the past simple story.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 3c: have you ever bought something you’ve never worn – what was it, and what went wrong? Pairs, with at least two past simple questions after every yes, then swap partners. Monitor for the switch.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One unworn purchase from the room. Then three sentences from your monitoring on the board, not all of them wrong, and the pairs decide which is which.

slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 31 Vocabulary ex 4a – audio track 2.27; Speaking ex 6a–6b / Vocabulary Bank p. 155 section 1 ex a–c – track 2.28 / Workbook p. 26 ex 1a

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The last time you went clothes shopping: where, what, and did you try it on? A minute in pairs, two answers from the room.

stages.name: Test – what do they already have?
stages.todo: This is the diagnostic, so teach nothing during it. Ex 4a on p. 31: five sentences from the shoppers they heard last lesson, one word missing in each – changing room, sold, try on, take back, online – completed in pairs before track 2.27 confirms them. Then Vocabulary Bank p. 155, section 1 ex a: eight shop words matched to the pictures, and track 2.28 to check. Walk round and note which words the room does not have.
stages.avoid: Do not help while they match. A test they pass with your hints tells you nothing, and the next stage is built on what you saw.

stages.name: Teach – only what the test exposed
stages.todo: Take the words they got wrong – expect receipt, checkout, changing rooms, take something back, try something on – and clarify those: meaning through the pictures and a shopping situation, form for the two phrasal verbs (try it on, take it back – the pronoun goes in the middle), and the fit or suit box, which is where the real confusion sits. Pronunciation: the silent p in receipt, /tʃ/ in changing and checkout, and the stress on CUStomer; drill the ones that came out wrong. Ex 1c with the words covered to finish.
stages.avoid: Anything they matched correctly is not taught again. Section 2 of the Bank, shopping online, is nine more words and another lesson – leave it.

stages.name: Test 2 – controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 26 ex 1a: the shop text with nine gaps – try on, changing rooms, checkout, receipt, suit, size, fit, take back, shop assistants. Alone, then an answer key. It tells you whether what you taught went in.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Speaking ex 6a on p. 31: the eight Have you ever…? questions completed with the participles – bought, sold, had, tried, taken, got, lost – checked and drilled quickly. Then ex 6b as a mingle: find someone who says yes to each one and get the story with the follow-up questions. Give them a target – five yeses in eight minutes. Monitor for the shop words and the tense switch from the last lesson.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Who found a yes for question 5 – taking something without paying? One story. Then three things from your monitoring on the board, good and bad together, with at least one shop word, to be corrected in pairs.

5B.context: Lost weekend – a man stuck in a lift, and what people really did at the weekend

slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 32 Listening ex 1a–1b – audio track 2.32; Grammar ex 2a–2b – track 2.33; Pronunciation ex 3a–3b – track 2.35 / Grammar Bank p. 133 4C ex a

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book warm-up: MY WEEKEND STARTS ON FRIDAY AT … AND FINISHES ON SUNDAY AT … on the board, filled in for you. Pairs say when theirs starts and finishes, and who has the longest. Then the photo on p. 32: what do they think happened to Sven?

stages.name: Listening – Sven’s weekend
stages.todo: Ex 1a, track 2.32, once: how did he spend his weekend? (In the lift at his office, Friday evening to Monday morning.) Then ex 1b, the seven questions, on one more play; a quick pair check, quick check. Seven minutes and out – the story is the way in to the grammar.
stages.avoid: Do not run ex 1c or play the story a third time. The clarification needs the minutes.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 2a: three sentences from the story with a word missing – nothing happened, couldn’t find him anywhere, somebody came – from memory, then track 2.33 to check. Then ex 2b: complete the rule – things, people, places.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: The nine words in a three-by-three grid on the board: some-, any-, no- across; -thing, -body, -where down. Meaning and use together: some- in positive sentences, any- in questions and negatives, no- on its own or with a positive verb – nobody heard me, I didn’t see anybody, not ‘I didn’t see nobody’. One concept question on the double negative and one on the one-word answer. Pronunciation with ex 3a–3b, track 2.35: the three vowel sounds in nothing, nobody and anything, drilled in the six sentences.
stages.avoid: The two errors the Teacher’s Book names – the double negative, and ‘Who did you see?’ ‘Anybody.’ – are the whole stage. Teach those; do not lecture the grid.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p. 133, 4C ex a: ten gaps with something, anything, nothing and the rest. Alone, check with a neighbour, then only the disputed ones aloud. If they are fast, ex b and c on the same page – Nothing / I didn’t do anything – as a one-minute oral round.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: The speech bubble at the foot of p. 32 is the model: Did you do anything at the weekend? No, nothing. Pairs ask each other six questions about last weekend – what did you buy, where did you go, who did you see, did you eat anything special – and answer honestly, short answer first and then the full sentence. Then swap partners. Monitor for any- after didn’t.
stages.avoid: The weekend interview with an invented answer is the third lesson’s task. Keep this one short and honest.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Who did nothing at all at the weekend? Then three sentences from your monitoring on the board – a double negative, an any- in a positive sentence, one that was right – for the class to correct.

slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 32 Reading ex 4a–4c / SB p. 33 (the article ‘What did you really do at the weekend?’)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Did you have a good weekend? – the question everyone asks on a Monday. In pairs: what do you usually answer, and is it always the truth? A show of hands: who has ever made their weekend sound better than it was?

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Four items from the Teacher’s Book list: a survey, lie (not tell the truth), impress and jealous. Get them from the class, check each with a question, and move on.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 4a on p. 32: read the article on p. 33 once, two minutes, and choose the best summary of the three. (c – people sometimes don’t tell the truth about their weekend.) A quick pair check, check.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 4b: the four multiple-choice questions, read again and decided in pairs with the line that proves each – b, a, a, b. Check, and ask what the most common lie was.

stages.name: Language focus – the survey’s questions
stages.todo: What did the survey ask? Elicit the article’s questions onto the board – Did you have a good weekend? Did you go out on Saturday night? – and use them to revise past simple questions: did + subject + infinitive, was / were for be. Then pairs write a five-question weekend survey of their own, checked by you as you walk round.
stages.avoid: This is the sub aim, eight minutes: the form of the question and the survey written. The response is where the questions get used.

stages.name: Response – run the survey
stages.todo: Each student asks their five questions to three other people and notes the answers. Then back in pairs: what did they find, and does the class look like the article’s results – a third sleeping, a third working, and a few lies? Finish with ex 4c: would a survey in their country give the same answers?

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One finding from three pairs. Then two questions you heard on the board, one right and one with did missing, for the class to correct.

slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 33 Vocabulary ex 6a–6c – audio track 2.37; Speaking ex 5a–5b / Workbook p. 28 ex 2

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: How was your weekend, in one adjective? Go round fast and board what comes – boring, relaxing, tiring, great. Some will give you -ed where -ing was needed; say nothing yet.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 6a: tired in line 13 of the article and tiring in line 19 – which describes how you feel, and which describes a thing or a situation? Pairs, then the answer. The article was read last lesson; two minutes to find the lines is enough.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning with one pair on the board: I’m bored (how I feel) and the film is boring (what causes it); concept-check with ‘the teacher is boring’ against ‘the teacher is bored’, which is the mix-up they fear. Then the five pairs from ex 6b – bored / boring, depressed / depressing, relaxed / relaxing, interested / interesting, excited / exciting – with the preposition for the -ed ones: interested in, excited about, bored with. Pronunciation: the -ed is the past-simple ending, /t/ in relaxed, /ɪd/ in interested and excited; drill the pairs.
stages.avoid: Excited and exciting are a false friend in several languages. Check them separately.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 6b: the ten questions, circling the right adjective, then track 2.37 to check and repeat. Pairs, aloud.

stages.name: Controlled practice 2
stages.todo: Workbook p. 28 ex 2: ten sentences completed with the -ed or -ing form. Alone, then an answer key.

stages.name: Freer practice – last weekend, with one lie
stages.todo: Speaking ex 5a–5b: they plan truthful answers to the seven weekend questions but invent one to make the weekend sound more exciting, and must use at least three of today’s adjectives. Pairs interview each other and the listener guesses the lie. Then ex 6c, two or three of the ten questions, if time allows. Monitor for -ed against -ing.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: The best lie in the room. Then three sentences from your monitoring on the board, one right, one with the adjective the wrong way round, and they find the wrong ones.

6A.context: No time for anything – are we living faster? – and the superlative cities of Europe

slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 36 Reading & Vocabulary ex 1a–1f (‘We’re living faster, but are we living better?’ and the questionnaire) / Communication 5A How fast is your life? p. 101 (the results)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book warm-up: WORKING OR STUDYING, EATING, SLEEPING, RELAXING on the board; pairs say how long they spend on each in a normal day. Then one question: do you have enough free time?

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Three items: patient and impatient, an abbreviation, and the average. Check Snow White and Van Gogh are known, since two headings depend on them.
stages.avoid: The highlighted time expressions are ex 1c. Leave them for the text to teach.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 1a: the six headings matched to the six paragraphs, three minutes. Check with a neighbour, check.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 1b: one paragraph contains an invented fact – which? Read again and decide in pairs, with a reason. (Paragraph 4: the ten-word networking site.) Then ex 1d, books closed: the headings on the board and pairs rebuild what each paragraph said.

stages.name: Vocabulary from the text
stages.todo: Ex 1c: the highlighted time expressions guessed from context – save time, waste time, spend time, on time, in a hurry. Pairs, then check with a question for each (if you waste time, do you use it well?), and drill them as chunks.

stages.name: Response – how fast is your life?
stages.todo: Ex 1e: the six-question questionnaire in pairs, answered often, sometimes or never with a reason, the partner noting the answers. Then ex 1f on p. 101: add up the partner’s score and read the results – the slow lane, the medium pace, the fast lane. Do they agree? A show of hands for each lane.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Who is in the fast lane, and what gave them away? Then two sentences from your monitoring on the board, one right, and the room decides.

slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 37 Grammar ex 2b (as a check of the comparative forms); Pronunciation ex 3a–3b – audio track 2.41; Speaking ex 4a–4b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Three things about your own life five years ago against now – I slept more, I’m busier, I don’t see my friends as often. Say them, then ask the room which way their lives have gone. The article from the last lesson said we are all living faster; is it true of them?

stages.name: Useful language – comparing then and now
stages.todo: Ex 2b on p. 37: six sentences about the faster life, circling the right comparative – faster, worse, busier, more stressed, more quickly, as patient as. Pairs, check, and board the forms they will need: -er, more, worse, and not as … as. This is useful language, revised not taught: fix the two or three forms they got wrong and move on.
stages.avoid: This is a speaking lesson. If the whole class fails ex 2b, note it for the tutor; do not turn the stage into a grammar presentation.

stages.name: Pronunciation of the chunks
stages.todo: Ex 3a, track 2.41: five sentences – I’m busier than a year ago, I’m not as relaxed as I was – repeated for the rhythm, with the /ə/ in -er, than and as. Then ex 3b: which are true for you? One minute in pairs.

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Ex 4a: the questionnaire about the last three to five years – more or less time on sleeping, working, getting to work, cooking, shopping, talking to friends, being online; more or less free time; what there is no time for now. Alone, M or L against each item and a reason in note form.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Ex 4b: pairs go through the questionnaire together, each item a comparison with a reason, and decide whose life has changed more. Seven minutes, then change partners and compare again with someone new. Listen in and note what you hear for the comparatives and the time expressions.

stages.name: Feedback on content
stages.todo: Whose life has changed the most in the room, and in what? Two or three answers about a partner, not about themselves.

stages.name: Delayed error correction
stages.todo: Four things from your monitoring on the board, one of them correct, with at least one comparative that worked. Pairs sort them, you confirm.

slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 38 Grammar ex 1a–1d (the TripAdvisor survey); Pronunciation ex 2a–2c – audio track 2.44 / Grammar Bank p. 134 5B (rules) and p. 135 5B ex a–b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1a on p. 38: the five photos matched to the cities – Copenhagen, Venice, Barcelona, Dublin, Paris – and which country each is in. Has anyone been to any of them? One sentence each from two or three of them.

stages.name: Reading the survey
stages.todo: Ex 1b: the TripAdvisor survey with five gaps, each a city from 1a – the most romantic, the cleanest, the best-dressed people, the best architecture, the friendliest. Two minutes, compare in pairs, check: Venice, Copenhagen, Paris, Barcelona, Dublin. Then ex 1c for a minute: which cities in their own country would win each one?

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 1d: from the bold superlatives in the survey, how is the superlative made for a one-syllable adjective, a two-syllable one ending in -y, a three-syllable one, and good and bad? Pairs work out the four rules.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning: one against all the others in a group – the dirtiest city in Europe – with in after it for the place; concept-check against the comparative, which is two things only. Form from their rules: the + -est, -iest, the most, the best and the worst. Then the second use on p. 134, the one the pronunciation exercise runs on: the most beautiful city I’ve ever been to – superlative + present perfect + ever. Pronunciation with ex 2a–2b, track 2.44: the stressed syllables in the eight adjectives and the stress on the end preposition – been TO, bought; drill the questions.
stages.avoid: The errors the Teacher’s Book names are ‘the more expensive city in Europe’ and ‘the most beautiful city I’ve never been to’. Build one concept question for each.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p. 135, 5B ex a: ten superlatives – the most polite, the hottest, the worst, the friendliest. Then ex b: nine sentences with ever and the present perfect – it’s the hottest country I’ve ever been to. Alone, a pair check, the disputed ones aloud.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 2c: the eight questions – the most beautiful city you’ve ever been to, the most expensive thing you’ve ever bought, the most frightening film. A answers with a full sentence, B asks for more, then they swap each question. Monitor for the and for ever.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: The most surprising answer in the room. Then three sentences from your monitoring on the board – a comparative for a superlative, a missing the, one that was right – which they correct together.

6B.context: The friendliest city – Tim Moore’s three tests in four capitals, Istanbul’s turn, and how much is too much?

slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 39 Reading & Speaking ex 3a–3b (‘All capital cities are unfriendly – or are they?’) / Communication 5B The friendliest city: Student A p. 102 (New York), Student B p. 107 (Paris), Student C p. 110 (Rome)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book warm-up, made local: the biggest cities in Turkey on the board, then which has the friendliest people, and why. Is Istanbul friendly to tourists? Two opinions, left open.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Four items the tests depend on: inhabitants, polite, pretend and fall over. Elicit each one, check it with a question, and move on. The book gives you only two exercises, so the staging from here is yours.

stages.name: Reading for gist and prediction
stages.todo: Ex 3a: the article on p. 39, two minutes – what are the three tests? (Photo, shopping, accident.) Then questions 2 and 3 in pairs: are they good tests, and which of the four cities will be the friendliest? Predictions on the board; London’s result is the next lesson’s, so do not give it away.

stages.name: Reading for detail – jigsaw
stages.todo: Ex 3b: groups of three, A reads New York on p. 102, B Paris on p. 107, C Rome on p. 110. One task for all three: how did the city do in each test – well or badly – and one detail you will tell the others. Three minutes reading, then As check with As, Bs with Bs, Cs with Cs.
stages.avoid: Keep the three pages apart; if A reads Paris as well, the retelling has nothing to do.

stages.name: Retelling
stages.todo: Back in the A–B–C groups, books closed, each tells the other two what happened in their city, test by test, as the book models it – first he did the photo test… The listeners note well or badly for each test. Then the group decides which of the three is the friendliest so far, and a show of hands across the class.

stages.name: Response – the Istanbul test
stages.todo: Groups of three: Tim Moore arrives in Istanbul tomorrow and does the same three tests – in Taksim, in a shop in the Grand Bazaar, on a busy pavement in Kadıköy. What happens in each one? They write the three results in the style of the texts they read, four or five sentences in all, and one of them is a true story from their own experience. Then the groups read their results to the class and vote: is Istanbul friendlier than Rome?

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: The vote, and the best Istanbul story. Then three sentences from the groups’ texts on the board, some right and some not, which the class puts right.

slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 39 Listening ex 4a–4c – audio track 2.45; Vocabulary ex 5a / Vocabulary Bank p. 156 section 2 ex a–d – track 2.47

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Books closed: the three tests from the last lesson, and how New York, Paris and Rome did. Then the prediction: London – more friendly than the three, or less? A show of hands, and the number on the board.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Three items the detail questions turn on: a key ring, change (the money you get back) and the Tube. Elicit each, check it with a question, and move on.

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex 4a, track 2.45, once, pens down: how well does London do in each test? (Photo badly, shopping well, accident badly.) Compare in pairs, check, and settle the prediction – London is the most unfriendly of the four.

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex 4b: ten questions across the three tests – who he asked first, what the man said, where the tourist shop was, how much the bus and key ring cost, where the accident test was, what the man said. A minute to read them, a second play pausing after each test, compare with a partner, then check. A third play only for the part they missed.

stages.name: Language follow-up – describing a city
stages.todo: Vocabulary Bank p. 156, section 2: ex a, the six adjectives matched to the sentences – noisy, polluted, crowded, modern, boring, dangerous; ex b, their opposites – quiet, clean, empty, old, exciting or interesting, safe; track 2.47 to check. Drill the stress on polluted, dangerous and exciting, then ex d with the words covered. Twelve adjectives in six pairs, and they are the language the response needs.
stages.avoid: Sections 1 and 3 of the Bank are not for today. Section 2 only.

stages.name: Response – your city
stages.todo: Ex 4c and ex 5a together, groups of three: if Tim did the three tests in the nearest big city – Istanbul for most of them – what would happen, and is it a friendly city? Then describe it with the adjectives from the Bank: what it is like, and what it is not. Give them a minute to think first. Walk round with your notebook.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Three adjectives the room agrees describe Istanbul, and one it argues about. Then two sentences from your monitoring on the board, one right, and the pairs decide which is which.

slots.pages: English File Pre-int (3rd ed.) SB p. 40 Speaking ex 1a–1b (the diet and lifestyle questionnaire) / SB p. 41 Grammar ex 3a–3c; Pronunciation & Speaking ex 4a–4c – audio track 2.54 / Grammar Bank p. 135 5C ex a–b / Teacher’s Book p. 223 photocopiable ‘How old is your body?’ (instructions p. 202)

stages.name: Lead-in – the situation
stages.todo: Ex 1a on p. 40: the diet and lifestyle questionnaire in pairs – coffee, sun, computer games, chocolate, TV – with the amounts. Then ex 1b: are any of your habits unhealthy? The two speech bubbles are the target language in the room before you have taught it – I watch too much TV; I don’t spend enough time in the sun. Board them.

stages.name: Presentation
stages.todo: Ex 3a on p. 41 first, three minutes, as the revision it is: much, many, a lot of, a few, a little, with the reason for each. Then the new language in ex 3b: too much, too many, too long against not enough – more than is good for you, less than you need – matched to meanings A and B; and ex 3c, the position of enough, before a noun and after an adjective. Board the four frames with a countable and an uncountable example each, and concept-check too against very (it’s very big – a fact; it’s too big – a problem). Pronunciation with ex 4a–4b, track 2.54: /ʌ/ in enough, much, none, cups; drill the frames in the sentences from the questionnaire.
stages.avoid: The error the Teacher’s Book names is ‘too much tired’ – too much with an adjective. Make it the first concept question and the first drill.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p. 135, 5C ex a: eight sentences circling the right form – too much chocolate, too many crisps, enough water, too busy. Then ex b: eight gaps with too, too much, too many or enough. Alone, a quick pair check, the disputed ones aloud.

stages.name: Freer practice 1
stages.todo: Ex 4c: the twelve questions – do you read enough, eat enough fruit, spend too much time online, have too many clothes – in pairs, with a reason every time, as the speech bubble models it. Swap partners halfway.

stages.name: Freer practice 2 – how old is your body?
stages.todo: Teacher’s Book p. 223, one sheet each, folded: ten questions on exercise, diet and lifestyle, answered in pairs with a follow-up question each time, then unfolded to work out the partner’s body age. Demonstrate the first question yourself. Monitor for too much, too many and enough.
stages.avoid: Two freer stages is deliberate – this is the last practice of the course and the communicative task the source asked for. If the presentation overruns, cut this one, not the first.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Whose body is younger than their calendar age? Then three sentences from your monitoring on the board – a too much before an adjective, an enough in the wrong place, one that was right – to be corrected in pairs.

s8.name: Elementary · Speakout
s8.sources:
Eales, F. & Oakes, S. (2015) Speakout Elementary Students’ Book, 2nd edn. Pearson.
Eales, F. & Oakes, S. (2015) Speakout Elementary Teacher’s Book, 2nd edn. Pearson.
Eales, F. & Oakes, S. (2015) Speakout Elementary Workbook, 2nd edn. Pearson.

1A.context: Lifestyle – meeting people in a new city, daily routines and booking a tour (Unit 2)

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised the present simple with I/you/we/they – positive and negative statements and Do you …? questions – to say what they do regularly and to ask about other people’s activities.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency, interviewing another pair about what they do and choosing a group for them.
slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 18 ex 1A–1C (the three Group-meet extracts) / SB p. 19 ex 3A–3B, ex 4, ex 5A–5D – audio track 2.1 / Workbook p. 11 ex 4

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1A on p. 18, which is the book’s own way in: you arrive in a new city and know nobody – how do you meet people? Pairs, two minutes, then take four or five ideas onto the board. If the class is in one city, make it that city. Keep this to four minutes; the lesson is the grammar, not the discussion.

stages.name: Reading task
stages.todo: Ex 1B: the three people and the three Dublin groups. Read the three sentences aloud first so everyone knows who they are looking for, then they read the extracts once and match. Compare in pairs, check: 1 English Italian group, 2 film group, 3 Get fit group. Then thirty seconds on 1C – which group for you – as a quick open-class poll, no more.
stages.avoid: Do not pre-teach for this. The only word that could block the matching is get fit, and the extract explains it (you don’t do exercise … join our group, get fit). One reading, one task, and move on to the language.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 3A on p. 19: the table of positive, negative and question forms, completed from the extracts – watch, don’t eat, Do. Alone, with the texts open, then compare. Take the answers onto the board in the same table shape and leave it there; it is your board for the next stage.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex 3B gives you the three rules to elicit: regularly (not at this moment), don’t + verb, do you + verb. Spend your time where the errors will be – the positive they have, so one check question on meaning is enough (We watch films: today only, or every week?). Then don’t: show the negative beside the positive on the board and get them to tell you what changed and what did not (no -s, no change to the verb). Then Do you …? and the short answers Yes, I do / No, I don’t – an elementary class says Yes, I like, so drill the short answer as a pair with the question. Pronunciation is ex 5A with track 2.1: they listen and underline the stressed words in the two questions and answers, then 5B, do you as /dəjə/ – say it slowly, then faster, until it links, and drill the two questions that way.
stages.avoid: Three forms in twelve minutes is only possible because two of them are revision. If you present the positive from scratch, you will not reach the question form, and the question form is what the freer stage runs on.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 4 on p. 19 first: books closed on p. 18, they complete the text about the three groups with a positive or negative verb – speak, go, don’t eat, don’t like, do, don’t play, go. Four minutes alone, then they open p. 18 and check against the extracts themselves before you say a word. Then Workbook p. 11 ex 4 for the questions: ten prompts to turn into Do you …? questions with a short answer, as far as they get in three minutes. Check only the ones pairs disagreed on.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 5C and 5D: each pair writes three Do you …? questions for each of the three groups, using the extracts (Do you like films? Do you go running?). Then pairs join another pair and interview them, and decide which group suits the other two. Monitor with a pen for the question form and the short answers.
stages.avoid: Writing nine questions can eat the whole stage. Two per group is enough; the point is the interview, not the list.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One answer from two or three pairs: which group is right for the other pair and why. Then two sentences from your notes on the board, one right and one wrong, for the class to sort – make one of them a missing don’t or a Yes, I like.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have learned and practised nine daily-routine phrases – get up, have breakfast, leave home, start work/school, have lunch, finish work/school, get home, have dinner, go to bed – to describe a typical day.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency, asking and answering questions about their own daily routine.
slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 20 ex 1A–1C (Vocabulary: daily routines) / Workbook p. 12 ex 1A

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Write A typical day for your teacher on the board. In pairs they guess what you do and when – get up at six, have lunch at school – and you take six or seven guesses onto the board as a list. Do not confirm any of them: the list is the reading task in the next stage.

stages.name: Reading task
stages.todo: Hand out a short text you have written about your own day – eight to ten lines, with all nine phrases from the box in ex 1A on p. 20 in it, and clock times only on the hour. They read it once and tick or cross the guesses on the board. That is the whole task; the text is here so the phrases arrive in a day, not in a list.
stages.avoid: Keep the text plain. Every extra word you add is a word someone will ask about, and you have six minutes.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: They go back through your text and underline every phrase that says what you do, then match the nine phrases in the box in ex 1A to photos A–H on p. 20 and find the one that is not pictured (have dinner). Pairs, then the answers on the board under the photos: B leave home, C get home, D go to bed, E finish work, F have breakfast, G start work, H have lunch.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning is mostly done by the photos, so put the time into the two things that go wrong. First the verb that goes with each noun: have for the three meals, get for up and home, go to bed, leave home, start and finish work – board them as pairs so get home and leave home sit next to each other. Then the order of a day: get them to put the nine phrases in order on the board, which is also a check. Pronunciation: the stress falls on the noun (have BREAKfast, go to BED, get UP), and get up / get home / go to bed run together as one piece – drill them as whole phrases, not word by word. Quick check that early and late are known; ex 1B needs them.
stages.avoid: This is not a lesson on the present simple. If someone produces he get up, correct it and move on; the he/she form is tomorrow’s grammar lesson.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Two passes. Workbook p. 12 ex 1A first, the nine phrases with their letters jumbled, done from memory with the book closed on p. 20 – a spelling check, three minutes, then check in pairs and send two or three up to write the hardest ones on the board. Then SB p. 20 ex 1B: cover the box and complete the seven questions with the right verb – have, leave, start, have, get, go. Compare in pairs, then drill the questions: the yes/no ones rising, the wh- ones falling.
stages.avoid: Questions 3, 4 and 6 need clock times to answer. Do not stop to teach the time – lesson 2.3 does that properly; on the hour and half past is all they need today.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 1C: pairs ask and answer the seven questions and find three things they have in common. Model one exchange with a strong student first, using the book’s example (Do you get up early? Yes, I do. I get up at 6. How about you?). Change partners once at the halfway point. Monitor for the phrases and write down what you hear.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Ask three students for one thing they have in common with their partner. Then two phrases from your monitoring on the board – have a breakfast and go to the bed are the ones you will have heard – and let them fix them.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised listening for gist and for specific information to two tourists booking a tour at a tourist information centre in San Francisco.
slots.sub: To practise asking for information about a tour with What time does it start?, Where does it leave from?, When does it finish?, How much does it cost? and Do you take credit cards? in a role play.
slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 22 ex 2A–2B – audio track 2.8; ex 3A (the five questions, written out in order) – audio track 2.10 / SB p. 23 (the three tour leaflets; ex 5B table for the role play)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Books closed: where is San Francisco, what is it famous for – the bridge, the cable cars, Alcatraz. Then open at pp. 22–23 and ex 2A: pairs read the three leaflets and answer the three questions – what tours there are, which have eating or drinking, a famous bridge, shopping, and which tour they would choose. Check: all three have food or drink; the bridge is on the bus and boat tours; shopping on the bus and walking tours. Use the photos to check bus route, bay and hop-on-hop-off as you go.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Four items that the recording needs and the leaflets do not give: book a tour, leave from (the minibus leaves from the front gate), a pier and take credit cards. A situation for each and let them give you the word where they can – if the tour starts at Pier 43, is that a building or a place by the water. One concept question each and move on. The times – ten o’clock, nine forty-five, one p.m. – are in the recording; a thirty-second run over on the hour, half past and quarter to is worth it, because the detail task turns on them.
stages.avoid: Do not teach the language of the questions here. Students will meet it written out in the detail stage; the point of a listening lesson is that they understand it, not that they produce it yet.

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex 2B with track 2.8: three questions – which tour do they want, do they book it, what is the problem. Say before you play it that the first conversation goes wrong and they only need to know why. One play, compare in pairs, then check: the boat tour; no; he doesn’t understand the woman, she speaks too fast and he feels stupid.

stages.name: Listening for specific information
stages.todo: The tourists go back, and this time they ask the five questions of ex 3A – but give the questions to the class already in order, on the board or a slip, not as the jumbled words the book prints: What time does it start? Where does it leave from? When does the tour finish? How much does it cost? Do you take credit cards? Read them through together, then play track 2.10 and they write the answers. Check with a neighbour; play it once more for the ones they missed; check: ten o’clock, Pier 43 or the front gate, 1 p.m., 26 dollars each, yes. Leave the five questions on the board.
stages.avoid: Ex 3A as printed is a word-ordering exercise, and 3B–3D and 4A–4B are the pronunciation and functional work of a language lesson. None of that is yours: the questions are a listening task here, not a teaching point.

stages.name: Post-listening role play
stages.todo: The role play from ex 5B on p. 23, kept on that page. Student B is the tourist information officer and has the walking tour and rock concert information in the 5B table; Student A is a tourist, draws the empty table, and asks the five questions from the board for each one. Then swap: Student A invents a tour – a name, a start time, a place, a price – and B asks. Sit them facing each other with the book held up so A cannot read B’s table. Monitor and write down what you hear.
stages.avoid: Ex 5A sends Student A to p. 163 and that page is not on your card. Everyone works from p. 23 and from the questions on the board.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two or three tourists say which tour they would book and why. Then read out three things you heard – two with a slip, one asked well – and the class says which is which; the good one gets drilled once more.

1B.context: Lifestyle – high flyers: unusual jobs and routines; being a good guest (Unit 2)

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised listening for gist and for detail to a radio programme about two people with unusual jobs – a bridge painter and a pilot.
slots.sub: To develop students’ vocabulary for jobs and working routines – painter, pilot, tour guide, leave home, start work, get home, dangerous – and use it to talk about their own jobs.
slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 20 ex 2, ex 3A–3B – audio track 2.2 (Listening: high flyers) / SB p. 21 (the photos of Gonzales, Gagan and Emma for ex 2)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 2: the three photos on p. 21. Elicit where each person is and what the job is – Gonzales paints bridges, Gagan is a mountain guide, Emma is a pilot – and write the three jobs under the photos. Then the book’s question in pairs: one good thing and one bad thing about each job. Take one of each in open class. High flyer, the title, is worth thirty seconds: people who work high up, and people who are very successful.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Only what blocks the two tasks: dangerous (the wife thinks the job is dangerous), fresh air, fly between small towns, and a sandwich on the bridge is clear from the photo. Elicit each from a picture or a situation – the Gonzales photo gives you dangerous in one question – one concept question each and move on. Days of the week come up in 3B (Monday, Thursday): a ten-second check is enough.
stages.avoid: The routine phrases – leave home, start work, get home – were taught yesterday. Point at the board where they were, do not teach them again.

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex 3A with track 2.2: two questions only – do the people like their jobs, and do their families think the jobs are good. Tell them the programme is about two of the three people, not all three, so they listen for which two as well. One play, check with a neighbour, check: Gonzales and Emma; yes, both like their jobs; Gonzales’s wife thinks it is dangerous but loves the money, Emma’s daughter does not like her being away.

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex 3B: the true/false table, four statements for Gonzales and four for Emma. Give them a minute to read it first and to guess, then play the recording a second time and they mark T or F. A quick pair check and – the instruction that matters – tell each other why: he leaves home at four, not five. Check on the board: 1 Emma T; 2 Gonzales F, Emma F; 3 Gonzales T, Emma T; 4 Gonzales T, Emma F. If a line splits the room, play only that part again.
stages.avoid: Two full plays plus one short replay is the budget. A third play from the top takes the time from the speaking, which is where the lesson ends.

stages.name: Post-listening speaking
stages.todo: Their own jobs. Two minutes alone to note one good thing and one bad thing about their job, then groups of three tell each other and decide who has the best job in the group. For a student without a job: the job they want, or a job someone in their family does. Model it with your own job first – the good and the bad in two sentences – so they see the shape. Monitor with a pen; you want the job words and the routine phrases coming back.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One student from each group: who has the best job and why. Then a quick vocabulary check from your notes – say the wrong version you heard (he is pilot, a danger job) and let the student who said it put it right.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised present simple positive and negative statements with he/she/it – he works, she doesn’t like – including the third-person -s ending, to describe another person’s job and day.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken accuracy, telling a partner about a family member’s job and daily life.
slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 20 ex 4A–4C (Grammar: present simple he/she/it) – audio tracks 2.3, 2.4 / SB p. 169 (audio script 2.2 for ex 4A) / SB p. 21 ex 5 (Gagan text) / Workbook p. 12 ex 3A

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The three photos on p. 21 are back on the board. Ask what they remember about Gonzales and Emma from the last lesson and write three or four of their sentences up as they say them – He works on bridges. She flies. His wife doesn’t like it. Do not correct the -s yet; the sentences on the board are your evidence for the next stage.
stages.avoid: The recording was played twice in the previous lesson. Do not play it again – send them to the script.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 4A on p. 20: audio script 2.2 is on p. 169. They find the lines and complete the table – works, has, loves, watches, doesn’t like – and then the three rules under it. Alone, then compare in pairs. Take the answers and put the five verbs on the board beside the sentences from the lead-in.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning is the same as yesterday’s I/you/we/they – a routine, a fact – so one check question and move to form, which is the whole difficulty. Board the positive beside the I/you form and let them find the -s: works, loves; -es after -ch, -sh, -s: watches, finishes; has for have. Then the negative: doesn’t + the bare verb – She doesn’t like flying, and NOT doesn’t likes – which is the error that will follow this class for a year, so make the comparison with don’t explicit. Pronunciation: ex 4B, track 2.3 – the four verbs into /s/, /z/ and /ɪz/ – then ex 4C, track 2.4, eleven more verbs sorted into the three columns, and they repeat after the recording. Put a hand on the throat for /s/ against /z/ if they cannot hear it.
stages.avoid: Questions with does and the short answers are ex 7 on p. 21, and they are not in this lesson. If someone asks, say so and keep to statements; the freer stage needs none.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: SB p. 21 ex 5, the text about Gagan: twelve verbs in brackets, positive or negative, in the third person – doesn’t have, leaves, goes, meets, puts, walk, stop, makes, doesn’t eat, walk, doesn’t go. Look at the photo first and guess his day, then write. Alone, then pairs, then an answer answers on the board. Watch out for items 7, 8 and 11, where the subject is they and the -s must NOT appear. If that goes well, Workbook p. 12 ex 3A, Al the hot dog seller, is the same thing with fresh verbs; prepare it and use it only if there is time.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Each student picks a family member with an interesting job or an unusual day and writes four or five notes – not sentences: nurse, nights, home at 8. Then they tell a partner about the person, change partners and tell someone new. Model with one of your own relatives first. You are listening for the -s and for doesn’t, so stand where you can hear.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Four sentences from your monitoring on the board, two with the -s missing or doubled (she don’t work, he doesn’t works) and two correct. Pairs decide which are wrong and fix them; then you confirm and drill the corrected ones once.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have developed their spoken fluency, discussing what a good guest does and agreeing five top tips for guests in their country.
slots.sub: To practise the key phrases for giving and reacting to an opinion – What do you think?, I agree, I don’t agree, It depends, For example …, I think it’s important to … – in a group discussion.
slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 25 ex 4A–4B, ex 5A–5D (speakout: a good guest) – audio track 2.13

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Check guest first – draw a house, someone arriving with a bag, a week. Then ex 4A: the four questions in pairs – do you like having guests, what is good, what do you not like, three problems with bad guests. Take the problems in open class and board the new words as they come (noisy, late, dirty).

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Ex 4B: pairs finish the sentence A good guest … three different ways, choosing from the topics in the box – bring a small gift, arrive early or late, help with cooking, speak in your language. Check the box together first; most of it is transparent, give money and stay a short time are the two to check. Collect one ending from each pair and leave them on the board; they will compare them with the recording.

stages.name: Listening for a model
stages.todo: Ex 5A with track 2.13: two people doing exactly what the class has just done. Which topics from the box do they talk about – arrive early or late, give money, stay a short or long time, speak in your or their language. One play, pairs compare, check. Then 5B on a second play: tick the key phrases they hear – all of them except What do you mean?
stages.avoid: This recording is a model for speaking, not a listening lesson. Two plays, two quick tasks, and no detail questions of your own.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: The key phrases box, cut to the six that run a discussion: What do you think?, I agree / I don’t agree, It depends, For example …, I think it’s important to … Meaning they have from the recording; the work is saying them – mark the stress (I AGREE, it dePENDS) and drill them as you would want to hear them in the groups, fast and natural. Point out that For example and It depends buy thinking time. Board them and leave them up.
stages.avoid: Useful language is not target language. If a group does the task well without It depends, that is fine; the aim is the discussion.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Ex 5C in groups of three or four: five top tips for being a good guest in their country – or, in a mixed class, in a country they know. The book’s model (A good guest in Poland … brings flowers for the hostess) goes on the board. Eight minutes to argue and agree, one person writing. Then ex 5D, shortened: each group reads out its five tips, the others listen and ask one question. Keep the clock and monitor with a pen; you want the discussion phrases and the present simple with a good guest.
stages.avoid: Five tips in eight minutes means the group must disagree and decide, not list. If a group finishes in three minutes, they have listed – send them back to find the one tip they do not all agree on.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: A class vote on the best tip, which is the content feedback. Then four things from your notes on the board – one good use of a key phrase, one he bring, one a good guest don’t – for pairs to sort and correct before you confirm.

2A.context: People – big families and real friends (Unit 3)

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised reading for gist and for specific information in two short articles about very big families, the Bonells and the Radfords.
slots.sub: To develop students’ vocabulary for family life – parents, children, bedrooms, housework, neighbour, bakery – and use it to talk about their own family.
slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 28 ex 2A–2D (Reading: the Bonell family) / SB p. 167 (Student A text: the Radford family, for ex 2B)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 2A: big family or small family – what is good and what is bad about each. Write the two headings on the board, pairs talk for two minutes, then one good and one bad thing for each from the room. Have the photo on p. 28 visible: it is the Bonells, and someone will count the children.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Five items, two from each text and one shared: bakery and minibus from the Radford text, neighbour and housework from the Bonell text, and noisy. Elicit from a picture or a situation – the shop where you buy bread; the person who lives in the next house – with one concept question each, and move on. Check the list with your tutor at planning; the texts have more unknown words than this, and the task does not need them.
stages.avoid: Have got is all over both texts (they’ve got sixteen children, the house has got seven bedrooms). Leave it alone; it is the grammar of this lesson in the book and it is not on your card. If someone asks, give the meaning in one word – have – and move on.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Split the class: Student A reads the Radford text on p. 167, Student B the Bonell text on p. 28. One question on the board for both: How many children, and are the parents happy with a big family? Three minutes, alone, no dictionaries. Then A tells B and B tells A, in a sentence each. Check: sixteen children in both families, and yes, both sets of parents say they love it.

stages.name: Reading for specific information
stages.todo: Ex 2B: each student circles the numbers from their box that are in their text and notes what each number refers to – a two-column grid, number and meaning, that you give them on paper. Model one for each text first (A: 17 – a seventeen-seat minibus; B: 600 – food shopping costs $600 a week). Four minutes reading, then regroup A with A and B with B to compare. Then back into A/B pairs for ex 2C: tell your partner about your family using the numbers. Not every number in the box is in the text – say so.
stages.avoid: Keep the A/A and B/B check short, or the A/B exchange that follows it – the point of a jigsaw – gets squeezed out.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 2D: the six phrases joined to the right family. Now the pair has both texts between them, so they can check each other’s claims against the page. Answers: the Bonells don’t all live together, all do housework together, like their big family; the Radfords have got a bakery, sometimes make pizza, like their big family. Check in open class, and ask them to point at the line that proves each one.

stages.name: Post-reading speaking
stages.todo: Their own families. Ex 5A on p. 29 is not on your card, so build the prompts yourself from the texts – how many people, who lives in your house, who does the cooking and the housework, is it noisy. Two minutes alone to think, then groups of three with new partners talk and decide whose family is most like the Bonells. Model with your own family first. Monitor and write down what you hear.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One finding from each group – the biggest family, the noisiest house. Then a word check: say five of the pre-taught words in a sentence with a gap (the … lives in the next house) and the class fills them – that is the sub aim coming home.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised listening for gist and for detail to three people – Hakim, Bridget and Jane – talking about their friends.
slots.sub: To develop students’ vocabulary for talking about friends – close friend, best friend, online friends, visit / phone / text each other – and use it to say which speaker they are most like.
slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 30 ex 1A–1B, ex 2A–2C (Listening: real friends?) – audio track 3.2

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1A: the three photos on p. 30 – Hakim, Bridget, Jane – with the three labels online friends, have-fun friends and real friends.
