In pairs: what is each type of friend, and one example of each. Then 1B, the three questions, quickly – have you got a lot of online friends, friends you see every week, one real best friend. Take a show of hands on each; it tells you what the room will say later.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: From the script: close friends (Hakim hasn’t got many), personal things (he never talks about them), add someone as a friend (Mark adds people he meets at parties) and each other (we visit / email / text each other). Each one from a situation, with one concept question, and move on. Four items; you have five minutes.
stages.avoid: Usually, sometimes, often, hardly ever and never are in every speaker’s lines and they are the next lesson’s grammar. Do not board them, and do not explain them if asked – they are not needed for either task.

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex 2A with track 3.2: draw a line from each name to the topic – who talks about online friends, who about a friend they do things with, who about a best friend. One play, a quick pair check, check: Hakim b, Bridget a, Jane c.

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex 2B: six lines, each with three alternatives to tick. A minute to read them first; let them guess from the first play. Then play it again and they tick. Pairs compare, and play the part they disagree on once more. Check: 1 go running, 2 doesn’t want, 3 thirty-five, 4 doesn’t know, 5 talks to, 6 doesn’t see.
stages.avoid: Two plays and one short replay. If the whole room wants a third full play, the task was not read before the recording started – that is the thing to fix next time, not the number of plays.

stages.name: Post-listening speaking 1
stages.todo: Ex 2C: which of the four people – Hakim, Bridget, Mark or Jane – is most like you, and why. Pairs, then three or four answers in open class. It is a short stage; its job is to move the words from the recording into their own mouths.

stages.name: Post-listening speaking 2
stages.todo: New groups of three or four. Online friends: how many have you got, do you know them all, are they real friends, what is a real friend. Give them a minute to think before anyone speaks. Monitor and listen for the four pre-taught items coming back; note what you hear.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: The class answer to one question – what is a real friend – from two groups. Then two things you heard said well, repeated to the room as praise, and one error written up with a gap where the mistake was, for someone to fill.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised adverbs of frequency – always, usually, often, sometimes, hardly ever, never – and their position before a main verb and after be, to say how often they do things with their friends.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency, telling a partner what they do with a close friend and how often.
slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 30 ex 3A–3C (Grammar: adverbs of frequency) / SB p. 170 (audio script 3.2, to check the gapped sentences) / Workbook p. 17 ex 2

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The three photos again. Pairs: one thing you remember about Hakim, one about Bridget, one about Jane. Take a sentence for each on the board exactly as it comes – if someone says Hakim plays football with Tomi at the weekend, you have your first example waiting.
stages.avoid: Do not play the recording again. It has been heard twice this afternoon; the language is on p. 170 in print.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: The four sentences of ex 3A, on a handout with the adverbs taken out and the four adverbs in a box: At the weekends we ___ play football … Mark is ___ on his computer … We ___ visit each other … We ___ see each other … They fill the gaps from memory of the listening, then check against audio script 3.2 on p. 170. Then the line in ex 3A: they put usually, sometimes, often and hardly ever where they belong between never and always.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Draw the 0–100% line on the board and let them place the six adverbs – hardly ever at 10%, sometimes around 40%, often 60%, usually 80% – with a check question on the two they confuse: hardly ever, is that a lot or almost nothing. Then form, which is ex 3B: Mark IS sometimes on his computer, but we SOMETIMES play – the adverb goes after be and before every other verb. Board the two patterns one above the other with the adverb in a different colour, and get a second example of each from the class. Pronunciation: word stress on USually, HARDly ever, SOMEtimes, and the whole sentence drilled once so the adverb does not get its own stress.
stages.avoid: An elementary class puts the adverb at the end – I play football sometimes – and hears nothing wrong, because it is not wrong, only informal. Say that it is possible but that the middle position is what the book and the test want, and drill the middle.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 3C: six jumbled sentences about real friends to put in order, each with an adverb in it. Do the example together – A real friend often helps you with problems – then four minutes alone, compare in pairs, answer read the answers out. Items 3 and 6 have be in them; those are the two to watch.

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 17 ex 2: ten facts about colours where they choose the adverb that is true – apples are sometimes / hardly ever / never purple. It tests meaning, not position, which is why it comes second. Pairs, aloud, and let them argue about the eggs and the taxis.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: A grid you have made: six activities down the side (watch films, play sport, go to a café, text each other, talk about problems, visit each other) and the six adverbs along the top. Each student thinks of one close friend and ticks a box per line, then tells a new partner about that friend in full sentences – We often go to a café. We never talk about problems. Model it about a friend of yours first. Monitor for the position of the adverb and write down what you hear.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two students say one surprising thing about their partner’s friend. Then three sentences from your monitoring on the board, one correct, for the class to sort – make sure one has be in it.

2B.context: Places – unusual places around town, what you can do there, and shopping (Unit 4)

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised reading for gist, for specific information and for reference (what they, it and one refer to) in a short article about three unusual places – an underwater post office, a tiny free library and a solar-powered cinema.
slots.sub: To develop students’ vocabulary for places in a town – post office, library, cinema, supermarket, bank, school – found in the text.
slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 40 ex 1A–1E (Reading: around town); ex 2A (places in the text)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Books closed. Do you live in a village, a town or a city – has it got a cinema, a post office, a library? Then open at p. 40, ex 1A: the three photos only. In pairs: what are these places, and why are they unusual? Collect the guesses on the board and leave them there; the first reading checks them.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book names the four that block: plastic, maximum, for free and solar powered. Add underwater and borrow, which the tasks turn on. Six items, from a picture or a situation each – the sun gives the energy; you take the book and bring it back – with one concept question each, and move on. Check the list with your tutor at planning.
stages.avoid: Can is in every paragraph (you can send a postcard, you can borrow a book). It is the next lesson’s grammar: give the meaning in a word if someone asks and do not board it.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 1B: read once and check the guesses on the board. Two minutes, no dictionaries. Swap and compare, then tick or cross the board: an underwater post office in Vanuatu; a free library in Pakistan, one of 12,000; the smallest cinema in the world, in Wales.

stages.name: Reading for specific information
stages.todo: Ex 1C: six things someone might say, each matched to the post office, the library or the cinema. Do the example together (They’re plastic, not paper – PO). Four minutes alone with the text, check with a neighbour and point at the line that proves it, then check: 2 L, 3 C, 4 PO, 5 C, 6 L.

stages.name: Reading for reference
stages.todo: Ex 1D: what do they, one, it stand for in the six sentences. Explain in one line what you are doing – a word like it points back at something – and do number 1 with them (They = postcards). Pairs do the rest with the text open; then put the sentences on the board and send students up to draw the arrow to the word. Answers: 2 a book, 3 a film, 4 a postcard, 5 a library, 6 a book.

stages.name: Post-reading speaking
stages.todo: First ex 2A in pairs, two minutes: how many words for places in a town can you find in the text – post office, supermarket, school, bank, cinema, library – which is the vocabulary the text has given them. Then ex 1E in groups of three: which of the three places would you like to visit or use, and why. Then one more question of your own: is there an unusual place in your town? Monitor and write down what you hear.
stages.avoid: Ex 2B–2D are the vocabulary section proper, ten place words with can in every sentence. They are not on your card.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: A show of hands for each of the three places, then one reason from each camp. Then the vocabulary: cover the board, give the meaning of each of the six place words, and let them call the words back.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised can and can’t for possibility – You can send a postcard, you can’t borrow DVDs – to say what is and is not possible in the places in a town.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency, describing a place they often go to and what you can and can’t do there.
slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 41 ex 3A–3E (Grammar: can for possibility) – audio tracks 4.5, 4.6; ex 4A–4C / SB p. 40 (the article as the source of the examples; the list of places in ex 2B for ex 4A) / Workbook p. 26 ex 4A, 4B, 4D

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: A thirty-second quiz on the article they read last lesson, books closed: where is the underwater post office, how long is a film at the Sol Cinema, how much does a Little Free Library book cost. Three questions, hands up. The text is done; this only puts it back in the room.
stages.avoid: The text was read three times in the last lesson. Do not set it again – go straight from the quiz to the sentences.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 3B gives you two sentences about the library and the post office with can/can’t gapped; add four of your own from the article on p. 40 so that both forms appear – You ___ send a postcard from the beach. You ___ buy a paper postcard. You ___ take a book for free. You ___ watch a long film at the Sol Cinema. They complete them from the text, alone, then compare. Then ex 3A, the one-line meaning check: it’s possible or not possible.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning first, from their own sentences: can = it is possible, can’t = it is not possible – one check question on each (You can send a postcard from the beach: is it possible? Can you buy a paper one? No). Then form, which is where the errors live: can + verb without to, and the same word for every person – he can, they can, no -s, and the negative is can’t, not don’t can. Board a positive, a negative and a question (Can you …?) one under the other. Pronunciation is ex 3C with track 4.5 – can is weak /kən/, can’t is strong /kɑːnt/ – then ex 3D with track 4.6, six sentences to mark positive, negative or question by ear, and ex 3E, repeat after the recording. Drill the pairs: you can / you can’t.
stages.avoid: Do you can and You can to buy are the two errors the Teacher’s Book warns about. Put both on the board crossed out before the practice, not after.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 26: ex 4A, the five quiz questions completed with where, can and a verb from the box; then ex 4B, they answer the quiz in pairs; then ex 4D, can put into the five answer sentences (You can eat it in China …). Answer key on the board; take only the disputed ones.
stages.avoid: Ex 4C on the same page is the quiz’s answer key. Hold it back until 4B is done.

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 4A on p. 41: each student picks a place from the list in ex 2B on p. 40 and writes two sentences, one can and one can’t, without naming the place (You can buy stamps there. You can’t play tennis there). Then ex 4B: partners read their sentences and guess the place. Monitor the writing for to after can.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 4C with a new partner, turned into their own lives: think of a place you often go to in this town – a café, a gym, a library – and tell your partner what you can and can’t do there; the partner asks Can you …? questions to find out more. Model with a place of your own on the board first. Monitor and collect what you hear.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two sentences from your monitoring on the board, one right and one wrong, for the class to sort – make the wrong one a can to or a don’t can if you heard it. Confirm and stop.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised the language of buying something in a shop – Have you got it in large / in black?, It’s too small, How much is it / are they?, I’ll take it, and the polite refusals No, thanks, I’m just looking and I’m not sure, I need to think about it.
slots.sub: To give students practice in listening for specific information – the item, the price and whether the customer buys – in four short shop conversations.
slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 42 ex 1A (questions 1–2 only), ex 3A–3D (Function: shopping) – audio track 4.9 / SB p. 171 (audio script 4.9 for ex 3C) / SB p. 43 ex 4A–4B, ex 5A–5B – audio track 4.10, ex 6A–6B / Workbook p. 27 ex 2

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1A on p. 42, questions 1 and 2 only: do you enjoy shopping, and is there a big shopping centre in your town. Pairs, two minutes, hands up for the shoppers. Then the three photos: where are these people – a clothes shop, an electronics shop, a sports shop – which are the three shops in the recording.
stages.avoid: Ex 1B and ex 2A–2D are a twelve-item vocabulary section and not this lesson. The recording needs sweater, SIM card and trainers; check those three from the photos and leave the rest.

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Ex 3A with track 4.9: four customers; for each, the item and whether they buy it. One play, pairs compare, check: 1 a sweater, no; 2 a SIM card, yes; 3 trainers, no; 4 nothing, no. Then ex 3B on a second play: the prices – 19.99, 8.99, 120 euros, and nothing for the fourth. That is the listening done.
stages.avoid: This is the way in, not a listening lesson. Two plays, two quick tasks, no gist question of your own, and no third play – the clarification is where the minutes belong.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 3C: the four customer lines with a word gapped – It’s too small. Have you got it in large? How much is it? That’s fine, I’ll take it. They try from memory first, then open audio script 4.9 on p. 171 and check. Then ex 3D, the same four with different words in the gaps (too long, I’ll have, in medium, How much are they), which shows them the slots that change.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Six phrases on the board, customer’s side only: Have you got it in … ? / It’s too … / How much is it? – How much are they? / I’ll take it / No, thanks, I’m just looking / I’m not sure, I need to think about it. Meaning from the conversations they have just heard, with a role play for too – try to lift the table and say it’s too heavy, as the Teacher’s Book suggests. Form, briefly: too + adjective; it or them after take and in How much; a size or a colour after in. Then the pronunciation, which is ex 5A and 5B on p. 43 with track 4.10 – the three polite refusals, intonation high and friendly, because a flat No, it isn’t right is rude in English. Drill all six as whole lines, fast.
stages.avoid: Do not teach the shop assistant’s side as well. Can I help you? and Here you are are for the role play card; the aim is the customer.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 4A on p. 43: the flowchart, where they write the customer’s four lines from the prompts (Have you got this sweater in size forty-two? … That’s too small. I’ll have the grey one.). Then 4B, read it aloud in pairs, once each way. If a pair finishes early, Workbook p. 27 ex 2: two shop conversations with the missing words in a box.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 6A and 6B, kept on p. 43: Student A is the assistant in a sports shop and writes a price on a slip for each of the four things in 6A; Student B is the customer and tries to buy them, writing the price when they do. Then swap for 6B, the electronics shop. Tell the assistants to make one thing very expensive, so the customer has to say no politely. Model the first exchange with a strong student. Listen in and note what you hear.
stages.avoid: Ex 6A sends Student A to p. 164 and that page is not on your card. The assistant invents the prices; it works just as well.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Who bought the most, who said no best. Then two lines from your monitoring on the board, one a refusal that worked and one with a mistake, for the class to fix.

3A.context: A favourite place; you are what you eat – what is in your fridge (Units 4–5)

slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 45 ex 4A–4D (speakout: a favourite place) – audio track 4.12

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: A photo of your own favourite place on the board and two questions for the class to guess – where it is and what you do there – then tell them in three sentences. Do not use the questions in ex 4A here; they are the preparation stage.

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Ex 4A: each student chooses a place – countryside, town, building or room – and makes notes against the four questions. Notes, not sentences, and walk round feeding words.

stages.name: Listening for a model
stages.todo: Ex 4B with track 4.12, Lake Titicaca: they answer the same four questions about her place, then ex 4C on a second play, ticking the key phrases they hear (all but two). Decide your gist question before you play it – where is it – and nothing more; this is a model, not a listening lesson.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: The key phrases box: One of my favourite places is …, It’s near …, I go there every …, When I’m there I usually …, I like it because … Board them with the gaps and drill the three or four you most want to hear; they are help, not target language, so do not test them.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Ex 4D in groups of three or four: each student tells the others about their place from their notes, and the group decides which place they would all like to visit. Halfway through, regroup so everyone tells it a second time to new listeners – the second telling is where the fluency comes from. Stand where you can hear and write things down.
stages.avoid: Reading the notes aloud is not speaking. Notes stay on the desk, not in the hand.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Each group names the place it chose and why, then a class vote. Then two errors you heard, said aloud in their wrong form, and the class puts them right together – and one line that was good, said again for everyone to copy.

slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 49 ex 4A–4C (Listening: André’s fridge project) – audio track 5.2; ex 7A–7B (post-listening) / SB p. 48 (the photos of the two fridges, for the lead-in)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The two fridge photos across pp. 48–49, nothing else: in pairs, what kind of person owns fridge A and fridge B – age, job, personality. Then ex 4A, the four-line text: why does André photograph fridges, and who are the people in the project.
stages.avoid: Ex 1–3 on p. 48 are the food vocabulary and countable/uncountable grammar of another lesson. The photos are yours; the exercises are not.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Five words the two tasks turn on: healthy, takeaway (food), serious, visitors and cook (as a verb). Elicit each from a situation, with one concept question, and move on. Agree the list with your tutor.

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: One question of your own for the first play of track 5.2: which fridge belongs to one person and which to a couple – or whose fridge would André rather eat from. Compare in pairs, check, and keep it to one question.

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex 4B: they guess A, B or AB for the six phrases before the second play, then listen and check (2 A, 3 B, 4 B, 5 B, 6 A). Then ex 4C on a third play, cut down: which three foods does he name for each fridge. Play the part they miss again rather than the whole track.

stages.name: Post-listening speaking
stages.todo: Ex 7A and 7B: they complete the eight sentences about their own eating habits, then in groups find who has the most similar habits. Then the question that ties it to the recording – what would André say about your fridge? Walk round writing.
stages.avoid: The grammar lesson that follows starts at exercise 5 on this page – leave it. Do not board a, some or any, even if someone uses them.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One group reports the pair with the most in common. Then the five pre-taught words: point at each on the board, ask who used it, and get the sentence back from them, correcting anything in it as it comes.

slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 49 ex 5A–5B (Grammar: nouns with a/an, some, any) – audio track 5.3; ex 6A–6D / Workbook p. 29 ex 6–7

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The two fridges again: pairs recall three things André found in each one. Take them onto the board exactly as they come – some broccoli, an apple, no meat – because the target language is already in what they say.
stages.avoid: The recording was played three times in the last lesson. Do not play it again.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 5A: the three sentences about Vinnie’s fridge with a/an/some/any to choose, done from memory of the listening, then track 5.3 to check and to hear the weak forms of a, an and some. Then ex 5B, the table, alone and compared.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Three columns on the board – countable singular, countable plural, uncountable – and the five words placed in them from the table: a/an with one thing you can count, some with plurals and with things you cannot count in positives, any in the negative and the question. Plan your check questions on some against any and on an before a vowel sound. Pronunciation: /ə/, /ən/, /səm/ in the three sentences from 5A – drill them at speed so the articles disappear the way they do on the recording.
stages.avoid: Countable and uncountable is ex 2 on p. 48 and it is not on your card. If the room does not know that milk has no plural, give it in one example and keep going; the aim is a/an/some/any, not the noun system.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 6A–6B: Zoe’s meal, ten gaps for a/an/some/any after a thirty-second read for ex 6A’s question. Alone, pairs, put the key up. Then Workbook p. 29 ex 6, six more in dialogue form, for anyone who finishes.

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 6C–6D: each student draws a fridge with two fruits, two vegetables and two drinks in it, then pairs ask Have you got any …? and guess four items. The book’s example exchange goes on the board first.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: New partner: what is in your fridge at home right now, and what is not – a minute each way, then one thing you learned about your partner. Monitor for some and any.
stages.avoid: Ex 7A–7B belong to the listening lesson before yours and have been done. Keep the task to the fridge.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Write up two things you heard with the article or quantifier missing (I’ve got __ milk; Have you got __ eggs?) and the class fills the gaps; then drill both.

3B.context: A favourite dish; famous people when they were young (Units 5–6)

slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 55 ex 4A (notes on a favourite dish); ex 5A–5C (writeback: an email with a recipe)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Who cooks at home, and what is the one dish you can make well? Pairs, then a quick round of dish names onto the board – they are the raw material for the writing.

stages.name: Model text
stages.todo: Ex 5A: Sandra’s email to Pedro, read once for the two questions – why does he need a recipe, would you try it. Then ex 5B: the six underlined linkers, and which of them can swap places (Then, Next, After that; First and Finally cannot). Draw the shape of the email on the board: a greeting, why this dish, the steps in order, a joke to end.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Two sets from the model: the linkers First / Then / Next / After that / Finally, and the recipe verbs cook, cut up, heat, fry, add, stir, plus you need some … / a lot of … Board them in two columns and drill the verbs; the linkers they will copy.
stages.avoid: Do not re-teach a/an/some/any here – it was yesterday’s grammar lesson. Point at it in you need some onions and move on.

stages.name: Preparing to write
stages.todo: Ex 4A, used as a planning sheet: the name of the dish, the ingredients, how you make it, why you like it. Notes only, and walk round supplying the food words they ask for.

stages.name: Writing task
stages.todo: Ex 5C: an email to a friend who needs an easy recipe for five people, 80–100 words, in Sandra’s shape and with at least four of the linkers. Silence, the board and the model in front of them; answer questions by walking over.
stages.avoid: If the ingredients list is long, the steps never get written. Three or four ingredients is a recipe.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Emails swap with someone who chose a different dish, and the reader answers one question: could you cook this from the email? Then one thing from your monitoring on the board – a linker in the wrong place or a missing some – for the class to fix. Collect the drafts.

slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 58 ex 1A–1D (Listening: in their past) – audio track 6.1

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1A: the six photos – Messi, Oprah, Cumberbatch, Taylor Swift, Michelle Yeoh, Tarantino. Pairs: who are they, what are they famous for, where are they from. Say the names together once; the recording uses them.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Six items the sentences in ex 1B need: millionaire, chewing gum, hobbies, beauty contest, violence and opera singer (philanthropist is glossed on the page). A picture or a situation for each, one concept question, and move on.
stages.avoid: Was and were are in every line of ex 1B and they are the next lesson’s grammar. If someone asks, say past of is and are, and no more.

stages.name: Prediction
stages.todo: Ex 1B: for each person, tick two true facts and cross the false one – pure guessing in pairs, and let them argue. Collect a show of hands for one or two of the harder ones (Messi a good student? Tarantino hates violence?) before anyone hears the answer.

stages.name: Listening for specific information
stages.todo: Ex 1C with track 6.1: listen and check the eighteen guesses. One play, a quick pair check, then check on the board – the false ones are 1a, 2b, 3c, 4a, 5c, 6b – and ask what the recording actually said for two or three of them.

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex 1D: pairs pick three of the six people, listen again and write one extra fact about each (he always plays with his hair wet; her favourite number is thirteen). Second play, then each pair reads out its best fact.

stages.name: Post-listening speaking
stages.todo: Groups of three: which fact surprised you most, which of the six would you most like to meet and what would you ask them. Then one of your own: a famous person from your country – two true facts and one false, for the group to guess.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Pick one error you heard more than once, say it, ask whether it is right, and let the room repair it; then one good sentence from the groups, said again.

slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 58 ex 2A–2C (Grammar: was/were); ex 3A–3D – audio tracks 6.2, 6.3 / SB p. 59 ex 4A–4B (controlled); ex 5A–5B (freer, oral)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Pairs: two facts you remember from the recording about the six famous people. Take four onto the board as they say them – Oprah’s parents were poor, Yeoh was a dancer – and leave them up.
stages.avoid: The recording has been played twice. Do not play it again; the sentences you need are in ex 1B and 2A on the page.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 2A: the Oprah sentence – underline the verbs, present or past, singular or plural. Then ex 2B, the two tables, present beside past, completed from the Taylor Swift facts. Alone, then pairs, then the answers on the board.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex 2C does the form: from the two sentences they make the negative (weren’t) and the question (Was Messi …?) and complete the rules – was/were + not, verb before subject in the question, short answers Yes, he was / No, he wasn’t. Meaning is a timeline: is/are now, was/were then. Pronunciation is ex 3A–3D with tracks 6.2 and 6.3 – past or present by ear, then four sentences written down, the stress marked, and the weak forms /wəz/ and /wə/ drilled until was stops being /wɒz/.
stages.avoid: Plan the check questions on was against were (one person or more than one) and on the question form. Say was and were is one verb, not two; an elementary class hears two.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: p. 59 ex 4A: eight question prompts turned into Was/Were you …? questions, alone, then checked in pairs and drilled with the weak form.

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 4B: groups ask and answer the eight questions and count how many answers were the same. Model the first exchange with the book’s short answer.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 5A–5B, kept oral: favourite things when you were a child – a sport, a person, music, a food, a TV programme – a minute of notes, then compare in pairs using the book’s model (One of my favourite people was my uncle). Change partners once. Monitor for was/were and write down what you hear.
stages.avoid: Ex 5C–5D are writing and are not this lesson.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Three of their sentences on the board with was/were blanked out; they fill them in, and you drill the weak form once more.

4A.context: The past – time twins: two life stories; a profile of a special person (Unit 6)

slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 60 ex 1A–1D (Reading: time twins; Samiya’s story) – audio track 6.7 to check the order / SB p. 61 (Lidia’s story)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1A with the texts covered: the two pictures – why are the women time twins, and what can you guess about their lives? Check twins first.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Five or six items from the two stories – shy, information technology, got married, a company / apps, a fashion photographer, a professional model. Elicit each, with one concept question, and move on. Show your tutor the list before you teach it.
stages.avoid: The past simple is the next lesson. Do not board a verb table; the task is to order events, and the time words carry that.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 1B: Student A orders Samiya’s six paragraphs on p. 60, Student B orders Lidia’s on p. 61; then they tell each other the story in four or five sentences. Then ex 1C, track 6.7, to check the order (Samiya A C E B F D; Lidia A F D B E C).

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 1D: now with both texts, three things Samiya and Lidia have in common – the same birthday, both shy, a big change at fifteen, both bought their parents a house. Pairs, pointing at the lines.

stages.name: Post-reading speaking
stages.todo: Groups of three: whose life would you rather have, and why; then three things you have in common with one of the two women – I’m shy, I love sport, I’m good at maths. Collect what you hear for the end.
stages.avoid: From exercise 2 on, these pages belong to other lessons – the grammar, the vocabulary and the writing. Stay on ex 1 and the two texts.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: A show of hands – Samiya or Lidia – and one reason from each side. Then two sentences you heard with a word wrong, read aloud: hands up if it is right, and a volunteer fixes it.

slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 60 ex 2A–2D (Grammar: past simple, regular and irregular) – audio track 6.8; ex 3A–3B / SB p. 61 ex 4A–4C / SB p. 127 (irregular verbs list) / Teacher’s Book p. 169 photocopiable ‘Snapped!’ (past simple) for the freer stage

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: One sentence each about Samiya or Lidia from the last lesson, books closed, onto the board as they say it – she studied IT, she became a model. Four or five are enough.
stages.avoid: The stories have been read and ordered. Do not set them again; go to ex 2A.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 2A: circle the past forms of the eleven regular verbs in the two stories and complete the rule (-ed, -y to -ied). Then ex 2C: the eight irregular past forms found in the texts (went, had, made, knew, bought, took, became, thought).

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning on a timeline – finished, then – with one check question. Form in two halves: regular -ed (and the spelling rule) against irregular, which are vocabulary to learn, list on p. 127; then ex 2D, the negative with didn’t + infinitive and the question with did. Pronunciation is ex 2B with track 6.8: the five regular verbs into /t/, /d/ and /ɪd/, drilled, with the warning the Teacher’s Book gives – they will say every -ed as /ɪd/ unless you stop them.
stages.avoid: Positive and negative statements are the lesson. Questions are shown for the form, not practised; p. 61 ex 5A–5B is for another day.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 3A: eight sentences with the regular past form, then 3B, Samiya or Lidia. Then p. 61 ex 4A: eight sentences with irregular past forms, positive and negative, with p. 127 open. Alone, pairs, answers on the board.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 4B–4C: make the eight sentences true for you last year and find three in common with a partner. Then the Teacher’s Book photocopiable on p. 169, ‘Snapped!’: the twelve sentences about childhood (I had two pets, I hated weddings), true or false for each student, with the group asking follow-up questions. Monitor for the -ed sound and for didn’t + infinitive.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Four lines from your monitoring on the board – one with -ed said as /ɪd/ written phonetically, one didn’t went, two right – for pairs to sort before you confirm and drill.

slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 65 ex 3A (a person you admire); ex 4A–4B (writeback: a profile of a special person)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 3A: a hero or someone you admire – famous, a friend, family – and why. Pairs, then the names onto the board. Check admire and hero.

stages.name: Model text
stages.todo: Ex 4A: the profile of Fernanda Espinosa, read once to number the four paragraph topics (early life, a life-changing experience, her work, why I admire her). Then a second look for the past simple verbs that carry a life story – was born, was the fourth of eleven, met, got married, opened.
stages.avoid: Ex 3B–3E – the interview recording and the role play – are the speaking lesson on this page. The listening is not yours; the written profile is.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Board the four-paragraph plan with a phrase under each: X was born in … in …; When X was …, …; X met / opened / started …; X is a hero for me because … Drill the three past forms they will need most and leave the plan up.

stages.name: Preparing to write
stages.todo: Notes under the four headings for their own person – two facts a paragraph. Walk round with the irregular verbs they ask for.

stages.name: Writing task
stages.todo: Ex 4B: the profile, 80–120 words in four short paragraphs, model and plan in front of them. Silence; questions answered at the desk.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Profiles swap; the reader finds one fact and the reason for admiring the person, and tells the writer. Then one past-simple slip from your monitoring on the board for the class to fix. Collect the drafts.

4B.context: What did you do? – weekend activities and follow-up questions; travel partners (Units 6–7)

slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 62 ex 1, ex 2A–2E (Vocabulary: activities) / Workbook p. 37 ex 1

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1: your favourite day of the week, why, and what you do on it – the book’s model exchange on the board. Pairs, then two or three days from the room.

stages.name: Presentation
stages.todo: Ex 2A first, two minutes: how many activities can they still remember with read, listen to, have, play, watch, do, go from Unit 2 (the answers are on p. 18, not on your card – keep them yourself). Then ex 2B, the five new word webs – go, see, do, stay, write – where they cross out the one phrase that does not fit (see a book, do dinner, stay to a hotel, write my homework). Choose the ten collocations you will teach, check meaning with a question each (do nothing: are you busy?), mark the stress on the noun, and drill them as whole phrases.
stages.avoid: Twenty phrases are on the page. Ten is a lesson; name them in your plan.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 2C: tick the activities you sometimes do at the weekend and cross the ones you never do, then ex 2D, add one activity of your own to three of the webs. Then Workbook p. 37 ex 1: four short texts with the verbs gapped, as a written check. Check with a neighbour, read the answers out.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 2E: pairs ask about last weekend with the webs in front of them – Did you see your friends? Did you go for a walk? – and find three things they both did. Put Did you …? / Yes, I did / No, I didn’t on the board as a fixed frame before they start; the past simple question is tomorrow’s grammar, not today’s. Change partners once.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two pairs report their three things in common. Then a verb check: say the noun (my homework, for a walk, at home) and the class calls the verb back – it catches make my homework without a board.

slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 62 ex 3A–3E (Function: asking follow-up questions) – audio track 6.9; ex 4 – audio track 6.10 / SB p. 63 ex 5A–5B (role play), ex 7A–7B (speaking) / Workbook p. 37 ex 2A–2B

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ask three students How was your weekend? and accept whatever comes – good, OK, terrible – without correcting. Then: what do you say next? Leave the question hanging; the recording answers it.

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Ex 3A with track 6.9: whose weekend was most like yours – Isabel’s, Ahmed’s or Jane’s. Then ex 3B on a second play, the Saturday/Sunday table. A quick pair check; check. Two plays and no more – this is the way in.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 3C: the twelve phrases labelled question, answer or show interest, then ex 3E – which questions start a conversation (How was your weekend? Did you have a good weekend?) and which follow up (Where did you go? Who did you go with? Why was that?). Ex 3D, which they heard, can be done from memory in a minute.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Six phrases on the board in three rows: two openers, three follow-up questions, two ways to show interest (That sounds good / That’s a shame). Meaning: a follow-up question keeps the conversation going – show it by answering Good and stopping, then answering Good and asking back. Form: Wh- + did you + verb, no -ed after did. Pronunciation is ex 4 with track 6.10 – did you as /dɪdʒu/ – and the intonation of That sounds great, which falls from high. Drill the questions as a chain: How was your weekend? – What did you do? – Where did you go?
stages.avoid: The past simple itself was taught this morning. Teach the questions as chunks and do not re-open the tense.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 37 ex 2A, ten questions to unjumble, then 2B, matched to their answers – alone, then pairs. Then p. 63 ex 5A–5B: the prompts role play (How / weekend? – It / so-so – Why / that?) read through in pairs until it runs without the book.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: p. 63 ex 7A–7B: two minutes to invent a perfect or terrible weekend against the four questions, then groups of four talk about them, with every listener asking at least one follow-up question and one show-interest phrase. Who had the best and the worst weekend?

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two lines from your monitoring on the board – one follow-up question asked well, one with did you went – for the class to sort.

slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 68 ex 1A (the photos), ex 2A–2B (Speaking: the travel quiz) / SB p. 69 ex 3A–3C (Listening: two people do the quiz) – audio track 7.2

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1A, the first two questions only: do you enjoy travelling, do you ever go abroad – and the four photos, named in a word each. Pairs, then hands up for the travellers.
stages.avoid: Ex 1B–1D are the adjectives lesson; ex 4–6 on p. 69 are comparatives. Neither is yours. Do not teach than.

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Ex 2A: the seven-question travel quiz, answered alone and honestly. Check self-catering apartment, tent, sightseeing and local dishes before they start.

stages.name: Listening for a model
stages.todo: p. 69 ex 3A with track 7.2: two people doing the same quiz – how many answers are the same (four), are they good travel partners (yes). Then ex 3B on a second play, M and W against the answers. This is the model for the talk that follows, not a listening lesson.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: From the recording, the four lines that make it a conversation and not a quiz read aloud: I like travelling by …, And you? / What about you?, Me too, I don’t – I prefer … Board them, drill them, and leave them up.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Ex 2B: check with a neighbour answers and decide if they are good travel partners and why. Then stand up: find the best travel partner in the room – the person with the most answers the same – by asking, not by showing the book. Then ex 3C: is the man or the woman a better partner for you? Note down what you hear.
stages.avoid: A mingle this long needs a target. Say how many people they must talk to before they sit down.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Who found a perfect travel partner, and on which questions. Then two sentences you heard with the preposition or the -ing missing (I like travel by plane) for the room to repair, and finish.

5A.context: Now – the words people use online; what people are doing; actors who change their appearance (Unit 8)

slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 78 ex 1, ex 2A–2E (Reading: your words, your identity) / SB p. 168 (the answer to ex 2D, read out by you)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1: the four alternatives – camera or mobile, people or places, online or in a book, English or your language – true for you, in pairs. Then: do you use Facebook, and what do you write about?

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Five items the tasks need: researchers, messages, topics, swear words and an emoticon (draw <3 and ask). Elicit each, with one concept question, and move on. Teenagers comes up in ex 2B – check it there.
stages.avoid: Is cooking, ’m having, ’re relaxing in paragraph 6 are the next lesson’s grammar. Do not board them.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 2A: paragraph 1 only, one minute, and the best of three titles (Your words, your identity). Pairs, then check with a reason.

stages.name: Reading for specific information
stages.todo: Ex 2B as a prediction in pairs – who uses daughter, at work, homework, <3, YouTube – then ex 2C: read paragraphs 2–5 and check (1 d, 2 e, 3 c, 4 b, 5 a). Make them point at the line.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 2D: the two messages in paragraph 6 – who wrote each one, using what the article has just told them. Pairs decide, then you read the answer from p. 168 (a woman in her thirties; a man in his twenties) and they say which words gave it away.

stages.name: Post-reading speaking
stages.todo: Ex 2E in groups: do you agree with the research, is it true for you and your friends, what topics do the people you know write about. Keep a pen on what you hear.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: A show of hands – agree or disagree with the research – and one reason each way. Then recycle the five pre-taught words: say each one and ask for the line in the text it came from.

slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 78 ex 3A–3D (Grammar: present continuous) – audio track 8.1 / SB p. 79 ex 4A–4D / Workbook p. 46 ex 1, 2A / Teacher’s Book p. 176 photocopiable ‘I’m on the phone!’ (present continuous) for the freer stage

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The two messages from paragraph 6, books closed: what is Yuri doing, where is the second writer and what is he doing. Their answers go on the board as they say them – that is your exposure, already done in the last lesson.
stages.avoid: The article was read in the previous lesson. Do not set it again; go straight to the two messages.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 3A: the table completed from the messages – is cooking, ’m having, ’re relaxing – then ex 3B, the rule: at this moment, be + verb + -ing. Alone, then pairs.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning against the present simple they know – I teach English (every day) / I’m teaching you (now) – with one check question. Form: be is the piece they drop (she cooking), so board am/is/are in colour, the contractions, and the -ing spellings (having, swimming, relaxing). Then ex 3C–3D with track 8.1: the two questions completed with ’s or are, the stress marked, and drilled. Plan your check questions before the lesson.
stages.avoid: Positive statements and questions are enough for 45 minutes. Keep the present simple contrast to one example – it is lesson 8.2’s grammar, not yours.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: p. 79 ex 4A–4B: match the three comments to the photos, then complete them with the ten verbs in the box in the present continuous. Then Workbook p. 46 ex 1 (the -ing forms) and ex 2A (the street scene) for the ones who finish. Key on the board.

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 4C: one student picks a person in the three photos, the partner asks yes/no questions in the present continuous and guesses (Is he standing in a queue?). The book’s example first.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 4D: three people you know – what are they doing right now, with the book’s model (I think she’s getting up now). Or the Teacher’s Book photocopiable on p. 176, ‘I’m on the phone!’: pairs get a situation card, write what is happening, and other pairs guess where they are. Choose one; monitor for the missing be.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two sentences from your notes on the board, one with be missing, for the class to fix.

slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 80 ex 1A–1E (Listening: what a difference!) – audio track 8.3

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1A: the five photos – do you know the actors and the films, and for which films did they lose or put on weight? Guesses only; the recording decides.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Lose weight and put on weight from the lead-in, then kilos, appearance, doughnut and role. Elicit each, with one concept question, and move on. Check the list with your tutor.
stages.avoid: Ex 2 on this page is the appearance vocabulary of another lesson. Thin, slim, overweight are enough for the task; do not teach the set.

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex 1B with track 8.3: number the five photos in the order the two people talk about them (B, A, E, C, D). One play, pairs, check.

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex 1C: what the speakers say about coffee and an apple, 29 kg, 10 kg and doughnuts – guess first from the photos, then ex 1D, the second play to check. Pairs compare, replay the one line they argue about.

stages.name: Post-listening speaking 1
stages.todo: Ex 1E in groups: other actors who changed their appearance for a film, the good and bad things about doing it, would you do it for a job. Listen in and note what you hear.

stages.name: Post-listening speaking 2
stages.todo: Stand up: find someone who has changed their appearance – hair, beard, glasses, weight – and find out why. Two minutes, then sit with a new partner and report what you heard.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One finding from each group. Then one error from the mingle said aloud, hands up if it is right, and its owner corrects it; and lose weight / put on weight drilled a last time.

5B.context: Films and city bikes – types of film; Mexico City’s EcoBici and its rules (Units 8–9)

slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 82 ex 1A–1B (the film questionnaire); ex 2A–2E (Vocabulary: types of film) – audio track 8.6 / Workbook p. 50 ex 1A–1B

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1A–1B: the Moviewatch questionnaire – the last film you saw, your favourite film, actor and actress, where and how you watch – answered alone and compared in pairs. Take two or three film titles onto the board; you will sort them by type later.

stages.name: Presentation
stages.todo: Ex 2A: the eight posters matched to the eight types – a romantic film, a horror film, a drama, a comedy, an animated film, a musical, an action film, a sci-fi film. Meaning from the posters and from films the class knows (the titles on the board go into the types now); form – a + type, film after action/horror/sci-fi/animated/romantic but not after drama, comedy, musical; pronunciation is ex 2C–2D with track 8.6: the stress patterns, four of them Ooo. Drill them with the pattern hummed first.
stages.avoid: Eight is the set. The source document suggests adding genres; do not – eight items plus the stress patterns fills the stage.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 2B: eight definitions completed with the types (people fall in love in …, there’s a lot of singing and dancing in …). Then Workbook p. 50 ex 1A, the vowels missing, and ex 1B, seven review extracts matched to a type. Alone, pairs, key on the board.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 2E with the book’s model: do you like the same films, what kind do you not like and why. Then new pairs: three films for a long train journey, one each of three different types, agreed between you. Monitor for the eight words and their stress.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two pairs read out their three films and the types. Then three items from your notes on the board – a stress slip, a missing film, one right – for the class to sort and say again.

slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 88 ex 1 (lead-in); ex 3A–3D (Reading: Mexico’s bike revolution) / SB p. 89 (the last paragraph of the article – the taxi driver)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1: is there a lot of traffic where you live, when is the worst time, how do you prefer to get around – car, public transport, bike, on foot. Pairs, then a show of hands per transport.
stages.avoid: Ex 2A–2E, the adjectives, are another lesson. Pre-teach what the text needs and leave the set.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Five or six from the article: a bike-sharing system, a cycle station, a credit/debit card, a traffic jam, a scheme, (be) careful. Elicit each, with one concept question, and move on. Check the list with your tutor at planning.
stages.avoid: Can, can’t, have to and don’t have to run through the article and are the next lesson’s grammar. Do not board them.

stages.name: Prediction
stages.todo: Ex 3A: the photo of the EcoBici, and four questions in pairs with how much, how many, who and where (How much does it cost? How many bikes are there?). Write the best four on the board.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 3B: read once to find the answers to your own questions. Three minutes, then which questions were answered.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 3C: six statements true or false, and the false ones corrected (2, 4 and 5 are false). Alone, pairs with the line pointed at, check on the board.

stages.name: Post-reading speaking
stages.todo: Ex 3D in groups: is a bike-share system a good idea for your town, why or why not – then the taxi driver’s view at the top of p. 89: do you agree with Rafael? Stand where you can hear and write things down.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: A vote – bikes for your city or not – with a reason from each side. Then two sentences, one you really heard and one you invent, and the class guesses which is real and corrects it.

slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 89 ex 4A–4E (Grammar: can/can’t, have to/don’t have to) – audio track 9.2; ex 5A–5B; ex 6C / SB p. 88 (the article as the source of the examples)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Pairs: three rules of the EcoBici from the article they read last lesson, books closed – over sixteen, 300 pesos a year, free for forty-five minutes. Onto the board as they come.
stages.avoid: The article has been read twice. Do not set it again; ex 4A sends them to it only to check.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 4A: underline can/can’t, have to/don’t have to in the four sentences and check against the article. Then ex 4B: match them to the four meanings – it’s OK, it’s not OK, it’s necessary, it’s not necessary. Alone, then pairs.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning in a two-by-two on the board – allowed / not allowed, necessary / not necessary – with a check question on the pair they confuse: You don’t have to pay for the first 45 minutes – can you pay if you want? Form from ex 4C: all four take the verb without to (can’t to use, have to to pay are the errors to cross out), and have to changes with the person – has to. Pronunciation is ex 4D–4E with track 9.2: the weak /ə/ in /kən/ and /hæftə/, drilled against the strong /kɑːnt/. Can for possibility they met in Unit 4; have to is the new piece, so give it the time.
stages.avoid: Must is not on the page and should not be on the board.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 5A: eight sentences about getting around a town completed with can/can’t/have to/don’t have to. Alone, pairs, key, and a check question on 3 and 7.

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 5B: which of the eight are true for your town, and rewrite the ones that are not (You can’t drive on the left here – you have to drive on the right).

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 6C, with new partners: travelling in two or three towns you know – what you can do, what you have to do, what you don’t have to do – and which has the best transport system. The book’s example exchange on the board. Monitor for to after the modal.
stages.avoid: Ex 6A–6B needs pp. 162, 164 and 167 and those pages are not on your card. Ex 6C stands on its own.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two sentences from your monitoring on the board, one right and one with to after can or have to, for the class to sort.

6A.context: Plans and nature – surviving nature’s dangers; a day out in the city; wild weather (Unit 10)

slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 100 ex 1A (the four situations, lead-in); ex 2A–2D (Vocabulary: phrases with get) / Workbook p. 61 ex 1A–1B

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1A: the four photos – a storm on a hill, an earthquake, a bee, a forest at dusk. In pairs: how is each one dangerous or scary? Check survive in the title and scary in the question.
stages.avoid: Ex 1B–1D send them to the texts on pp. 161 and 168; that is the reading of this lesson and it is not on your card. The grammar on p. 101 is not either.

stages.name: Presentation
stages.todo: Ex 2A: the ten sentences completed with the words in the box – get hot, thirsty, tired, wet, warm, hungry, lost, stung, cold, sunburnt. Meaning: get = become, and each one checked with a question from the sentence that holds it (I forgot my umbrella – wet or dry?). Form: get + adjective, and the past got, which they will need to tell the story. Pronunciation: sunburnt and stung are the two to drill; then all ten as phrases. The Speakout tip on the other meanings of get is a minute, no more.
stages.avoid: Ten items plus one verb is the set. Do not add get up, get home, get a job here – they are the tip, not the lesson.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 61 ex 1A: ten sentences with the adjective’s vowels missing (Marco got sunburnt, so he …), then ex 1B, matched to their endings. Alone, pairs, put the key up.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 2C: each student writes one true situation with so and a get phrase (I didn’t have a map, so I got lost), then ex 2D in groups, books closed: read it aloud but stop after so, and the group guesses the phrase. Then the story behind the best one in each group – when, where, what happened. Monitor for got.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Each group tells the room its best story in two sentences. Then say three things you heard, one with get where got belongs, and the class puts a hand up for the wrong one; finish with the ten phrases drilled once more.

slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 102 ex 2A–2E (Function: making suggestions – the AlternativeCity website) – audio track 10.5 / SB p. 103 ex 3A–3E – audio track 10.6; ex 4A–4C – audio track 10.7; ex 5A–5C / Workbook p. 63 ex 2, 3A–3B / Teacher’s Book p. 186 photocopiable ‘What shall we do?’ (role cards) for the freer stage

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 2A–2B: the AlternativeCity website across pp. 102–103 – why the name, and what do you think you do at each of the four events (a silent disco, blind-date cinema, playback theatre, museum meditation). Pairs guess; do not confirm.
stages.avoid: Ex 1 on p. 102 is a ten-word vocabulary set and another lesson. Check exhibition and play from the website and leave the rest.

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Ex 2C with track 10.5: which two events do the couple decide to go to (the museum meditation and the playback theatre). Then ex 2D on a second play: were your guesses about the events right? Pairs, check, and stop – the recording has done its job.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: p. 103 ex 3A: underline the four ways of suggesting in the sentences – Let’s …, How about …?, Why don’t we …?, Shall we …? Then ex 3B, four gapped suggestions completed and checked with track 10.6.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: The four openers on the board with what follows each one in colour: Let’s + verb, Why don’t we + verb, Shall we + verb, How about + -ing. One check question on meaning (is it a question or an order?). Then the replies from ex 4A–4B with track 10.7, sorted positive and negative – That’s a good idea, I’d like to go, Brilliant! / I don’t feel like doing that, It’s not for me. Pronunciation is ex 3C–3D: a suggestion sounds positive when the voice starts high – play it, let them hear it, then drill the four so they start high. Six to eight phrases in all.
stages.avoid: How about to go and Why don’t we going are the two errors the Teacher’s Book predicts. Put them on the board crossed out before the practice.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 3E: Student A suggests, Student B says OK only if it sounded positive. Then Workbook p. 63 ex 2, the conversation completed with why / shall / how / let’s, and ex 3A, five suggestions and five replies with a mistake in each to correct. Pairs, answers on the board.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 5A–5B: three activities for next week with a place and a time, then the phone call in the flowchart – suggest, refuse with a reason, suggest again, agree a time – back to back. Then 5C, two more partners. The Teacher’s Book role cards on p. 186 (‘What shall we do?’ – a class party, a short holiday) are an alternative if your class needs a situation handed to them.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two suggestions from your monitoring on the board, one with the wrong verb form after it, for the class to fix and say with the high start.

slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 104 ex 1A–1B (the weather), ex 2A–2C – audio track 10.8 / SB p. 105 ex 4A–4C (speakout: a weather report) – audio track 10.9; ex 5A–5B

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1A: the six photos matched to It’s sunny / windy / snowing / raining / cloudy / stormy, then ex 1B in pairs – What’s the weather like? – pointing at a photo. Then today’s weather outside, and your favourite season.
stages.avoid: The DVD on p. 104 (ex 3) has no file on your card. Skip it; the lesson is the speaking on p. 105.

stages.name: Useful language 1
stages.todo: Ex 2A: the three pairs of opposites – hot/cold, warm/cool, wet/dry – then ex 2B, the Dublin forecast completed with them, and ex 2C, track 10.8, to check. Drill the six with the photos; this is the weather vocabulary the talk needs, taught as help, not tested.

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: p. 105 ex 4A: a time you had unusual weather – when, where, why you were there, what the weather was like, how you felt. Notes against the five questions; walk round feeding words.

stages.name: Listening for a model
stages.todo: Ex 4B with track 10.9: the sirocco in Pisa – her answers to the same five questions. Then ex 4C on a second play: tick the key phrases heard (five of the eight). Put the ones they will use on the board: This happened about … ago, But then one day the weather …, Everyone got very …, I was glad when it was over.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Ex 5A: pairs tell their story from the notes, the partner checking all five questions get answered. Then ex 5B in new groups of four: tell it again, listeners ask one follow-up question each, and the group picks the most unusual experience. Walk round writing.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Each group names its most unusual story in a sentence. Then two past-simple slips from the stories written up with the verb gapped, for the class to fill, and one key phrase used well, repeated.

6B.context: Health – feeling ill; one thing at a time; offering to help (Unit 11)

slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 108 ex 1A–1B (parts of the body, lead-in); ex 2A–2D (Vocabulary: health problems) – audio track 11.1 / SB p. 109 ex 6A (speaking) / Workbook p. 64 ex 2

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1A–1B: the five photos – how many parts of the body can you name, and what is wrong with each person? Pairs, then a quick point-and-name round. Do not teach the problems yet; collect what they already have.

stages.name: Presentation
stages.todo: Ex 2A: the eight health problems matched to the photos – a headache, stomachache, my leg hurts, a cold, a temperature, a cough, a sore throat, a runny nose – meaning by mime and photo, with a check question on the ones that overlap (a cold or flu? a cough or a sore throat?). Form: I’ve got a … / I have a … are the same; My leg hurts is a verb; and the two words that look wrong – stomachache /k/, cough /f/, which the Speakout tip flags. Pronunciation is ex 2B with track 11.1, the stressed syllables, then drilled as full sentences.
stages.avoid: Eight problems plus ex 2C’s arm / back / ear / finger is the set. Should and shouldn’t on p. 109 are another lesson; if someone gives advice, let it pass.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 2C: the five sentences completed from the box (I’ve got backache / earache, my arm hurts, I feel tired / better). Then Workbook p. 64 ex 2: eight problems with the letters jumbled. Alone, pairs, read the answers out.

stages.name: Freer practice 1
stages.todo: Ex 2D: Student A mimes a problem from 2A or 2C, Student B guesses with the full sentence (You’ve got a sore throat). Swap after three.

stages.name: Freer practice 2
stages.todo: p. 109 ex 6A in groups: for the six situations, a pharmacy, a doctor, a dentist or a hospital – and then question 2, the real one: a time you had one of these problems, where you were and what you did. Monitor for the eight phrases.
stages.avoid: Ex 6B–6D add the pharmacist’s side and should. Stop at 6A.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One story from each group in a sentence. Then two things you heard – I have headache, my leg is hurt – said aloud; the class says what is missing or wrong, and you drill the right forms.

slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 110 ex 1A–1D (Reading: are you a multi-tasker?)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1A: the photo and the title – what does a multi-tasker do, are you one, how many things can you do at once? Pairs, then hands up for the multi-taskers. Check task.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Five items from the three parts of the text: memory, a PIN number, loved ones, stress levels and make mistakes. Elicit each, with one concept question, and move on. Agree the list with your tutor.
stages.avoid: Quickly, slowly, carefully in part two belong to the adverbs lesson that follows and are not yours. Give the meaning in a word if asked.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 1B: the introduction only – how many different things did the writer’s friend do in one hour (seven). One minute, then a quick count together.

stages.name: Prediction and reading for specific information
stages.todo: Ex 1C: pairs write three ways multi-tasking is bad for you, then read part two – the six problems – and count how many of theirs are there. Check the six on the board in a word each: slow, memory, eating, people, mistakes, stress.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 1D: the last part – what is the writer’s plan, and is it a good idea? Pairs, then two opinions in open class.

stages.name: Post-reading speaking
stages.todo: Groups of three: which of the six problems is true for you, and one thing you will do differently this week – then agree the group’s three rules for one thing at a time. Collect what you hear for the end.
stages.avoid: Ex 2 (communication vocabulary) and ex 3 (adverbs) are other lessons. Stay on ex 1 and the text.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Each group reads its three rules; the class votes for one. Then one slip from the discussion written up with a gap where the mistake was, for someone to fill.

slots.pages: Speakout Elementary (2nd ed.) SB p. 112 ex 1A–1B (the seven situations); ex 3A–3B (Function: offering to help) – audio track 11.5; ex 3C – audio track 11.6; ex 3D – audio track 11.7 / SB p. 113 ex 4A–4B; ex 4C–4D – audio track 11.8; ex 5A–5B (thanking); ex 6A; ex 7 / SB p. 175 (audio script 11.5 for ex 5A) / Workbook p. 68 ex 2A–2B, ex 4 / Teacher’s Book p. 190 photocopiable ‘Let me help you!’ (role cards) for the freer stage

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Try to lift a pile of books and say Can you help me? Then ex 1A–1B: the seven situations and the photos – what is the problem in each, and do you help? Pairs, then a show of hands on two of them. Check carry, lift, drop and pick up from the situations as they come.
stages.avoid: Ex 2, the article on helpful cities, is the reading of this lesson and not yours. The situations are enough context.

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Ex 3A with track 11.5: three conversations matched to situations a–c in the article box (1 b, 2 a, 3 c). Then ex 3B on a second play: the four offers completed – Let me help, I’ll do it, Can I help you?, Shall I carry your bag?

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: p. 113 ex 5A–5B with audio script 11.5 on p. 175: the thanks and the replies gapped and found – Thank you very much, Thanks a lot, Thanks so much, That’s kind of you / No problem, That’s OK, You’re welcome. Pairs.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Four offers on the board – Let me …, I’ll …, Shall I …?, Can I …? – each with the verb without to after it, and the meaning: you offer before you are asked. Then three thanks and two replies. Pronunciation is ex 3C with track 11.6, which offer sounds more polite, and ex 3D with track 11.7 – the polite ones start high – drilled, with ’ll as one sound with the tongue behind the teeth. Keep it to the four offers and five responses.
stages.avoid: Let me to help and I’ll to carry are the predictable errors. Cross them out on the board before the practice.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 4A: five problems matched to five offers, then 4B, Student A says a problem and Student B offers with the book closed. Then Workbook p. 68 ex 2A–2B (four problems and four offers to unjumble) and ex 4 (circle the right thank-you reply) for the ones who finish.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 4C–4D with track 11.8: six sound-effect situations – a glass breaking, a man who can’t find his wallet – and pairs offer to help after each. Then ex 6A’s flowchart (ask about the problem, say it, offer, accept, reply) and the Teacher’s Book role cards on p. 190, ‘Let me help you!’: one card each, stand up, explain your problem to three people and accept the best offer. Note down what you hear.
stages.avoid: Ex 6B sends them to pp. 166 and 168 and those pages are not on your card. The role cards do the same job.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Who got the best offer of help. Then one offer you heard with to in it, said aloud for the room to repair, and one exchange that worked, said again by the pair who said it.

s9.name: Upper-intermediate · Language Hub
s9.sources:
Brinks Lockwood, R. et al. (2019) Language Hub Upper Intermediate Student’s Book. Macmillan Education.
Language Hub Upper Intermediate Teacher’s Book (2019). Macmillan Education.
Language Hub Upper Intermediate Workbook (2019). Macmillan Education.

1A.context: Connections – meet-up groups, and two people who took the long road to success

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised listening for the main ideas and for detail in three conversations at Get Together meet-up groups.
slots.sub: To develop students’ vocabulary for everyday conversation taken from the recording: sign in, how come, fair enough, get on with, give it a go and no rush.
slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 4 Listening ex A–D – audio track 1.1 (three conversations: ukulele group, running group, book club)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ask the room how they meet new people in a new city, then put up the logos of two or three meet-up sites they will know (meetup.com and a local one). In pairs: have you used one, and what happens on it? Two answers in open class, then Listening ex A on p. 4: they read the Get Together box in two minutes and answer the three questions with a partner. Take the answers quickly – the box exists to set up the recording, not to be read for its own sake.

stages.name: Listening for the main ideas
stages.todo: Ex B with track 1.1: three conversations matched to the three pictures a–c. Tell them before you press play that they only need to decide which group each conversation is at, nothing more. One play, a thirty-second pair check, then confirm in open class (1b, 2c, 3a).

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex C: six true-or-false statements, two per conversation. Give them a minute to read the statements first, then play the track again. Pair check with the instruction that they must also correct the false ones – it is the woman’s first meet-up, the flat is a long way from the station, and there is no rush to return the form. In feedback nominate someone for each statement and ask what the speaker actually said. If the room splits on one item, replay that conversation only.
stages.avoid: Do not play the whole track a third time. The recording is nearly six minutes and a third play costs you the vocabulary and the speaking.

stages.name: Vocabulary from the recording
stages.todo: Prepare a handout with six lines from the audioscript (it is in the Teacher’s Book, TB4) that carry the phrases: could you tell me where I sign in, how come, fair enough, I don’t really get on with my flatmates, I thought I’d give it a go, no rush to return it. Pairs match the phrases to six short definitions, working from the lines, not from memory. Check, then say each phrase at natural speed and have them repeat it – fair enough and how come only exist as whole chunks.

stages.name: Post-listening discussion
stages.todo: Ex D in groups of three: the benefits of joining a group like this, whether it is the best way to meet people here, and which Get Together group they would join and why. Add one question of your own about a group they have actually been part of. Listen with a pen for the phrases from the previous stage and for anything worth the whole room hearing.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One group’s choice of meet-up and why, then three sentences from your notes on the board, one of them correct, for the class to sort in pairs. Make one of the three a use of fair enough or how come so the vocabulary gets a second outing.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have reviewed and practised question forms – indirect questions, questions ending in a preposition, subject questions and negative questions – using the Get Together conversations as the model.
slots.sub: To give students spoken fluency practice asking and answering questions while planning a new meet-up group.
slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 4 Grammar ex A – audio track 1.2 (four extracts from the conversations) / SB p. 5 Grammar ex B, ex D; Pronunciation ex A–B – audio tracks 1.3, 1.4; Speaking Hub ex A–C / Grammar Hub p. 123 ex A–B (1.1 Question forms, controlled practice)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The three pictures from p. 4 on the screen. What do they remember about each conversation – who was new, who was moving flat, which book they talked about? Three minutes; the recording was taught in the previous lesson, so this is a reminder, not a listening stage.
stages.avoid: Do not set the gist or detail tasks again. Your lesson starts at the grammar.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Grammar ex A on p. 4 with track 1.2: four short extracts with the question gapped. A minute to read them first, one play, and they complete the questions – who’s leading the group tonight, why don’t you like them, who do you live with, could you tell me where I sign in. Pair check, then put the four questions on the board exactly as said; they are your examples for the whole lesson.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex B on p. 5: alone, then in pairs, they choose the options that complete the four rules – indirect questions keep statement order and drop do; the preposition goes at the end; a subject question keeps statement order with the question word as subject; negative wh-questions keep the auxiliary. Confirm each rule against the example on the board. Meaning is mostly known at this level, so the time goes on form and on the one meaning that is new: a negative question like who doesn’t want pizza expects the answer to be almost nobody – check it with a question, not an explanation. Then Pronunciation ex A and B (tracks 1.3, 1.4): they mark whether each question rises or falls, listen, and say how they decided. Drill the eight questions with the intonation; make the contraction in who’s and don’t audible.
stages.avoid: Four question types is a review, not four presentations. If the ex B answers show they already have one of them, say so and move on.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex D on p. 5: five jumbled questions to reorder, one of each type. Alone, pair check, then confirm with an answer key on screen rather than reading them out. If they finish early, Grammar Hub p. 123 ex A – eight questions with a mistake in each – is the second pass and catches the preposition and the subject-question errors.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Speaking Hub ex A–C on p. 5 as the base: groups brainstorm a meet-up group, choose one and plan what they would do, where, how often and what it costs. Then each group presents in two minutes and the listening groups must ask three questions – that is the stage’s purpose, so tell them before the presentations and keep a tally on the board of questions asked. Listen for the question forms, right and wrong.
stages.avoid: Without the three-questions rule this is a presentation lesson and the questions never happen. Set the rule when you set the task.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Which group would the class actually join? Then four questions from your notes on the board, two right and two wrong, for pairs to sort and correct before you confirm.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised reading for gist, scanning and reading for detail in an article about two people who overcame challenges to succeed.
slots.sub: To develop students’ vocabulary for talking about success and setbacks from the article: overcome, adversity, eccentric, gifted, groundbreaking, self-made.
slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 6 Reading ex A–C and the article The long road to success / SB p. 7 Reading ex D–E (top of the page only)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Photos of Stephen Hawking and Vera Wang on the screen, names covered. Ex A on p. 6 in groups: who are they and what do they know about them. Collect one fact for each on the board and leave the board up – the text will confirm or correct it.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Three items that the text does not explain: overcome, eccentric, groundbreaking. A situation for each and let them give you the word – a family that keeps bees in the basement and drives an old London taxi, is that normal or unusual; if you overcome a problem, does it still stop you. One concept question each and move on. Gifted, adversity and self-made come out of the text later; leave them.

stages.name: Reading for gist, then scanning
stages.todo: Ex B first: read the article once and choose the sentence that connects the two people – famous people who overcame challenges to succeed.
