Three minutes, no dictionaries, a quick pair check, confirm. Then ex C: six statements ticked against Hawking or Wang. Say what scanning is and give them four minutes, because the task is to find, not to read everything again. Pair check with the rule that they point at the line that proves each tick, then check in open class. A variation if the room is strong: give the text with its five question-headings removed and have them put the headings back before ex B.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex D on p. 7: eight sentences completed with no more than two words from the article – lazy, an hour, two, awards, figure skater, sales assistant, 17 years, $600 million. Do the first one together so they see the two-word limit means the words as printed, not a paraphrase. Alone, then pairs, then take only the ones that split the room.
stages.avoid: The Grammar section at the bottom of p. 7 belongs to tomorrow’s first lesson. Do not touch the highlighted sentences or the tense review.

stages.name: Post-reading task
stages.todo: Ex E widened into a task: groups of three choose a well-known person, from here or anywhere, who overcame a serious setback and succeeded, make notes for three minutes and present the person to the class in one minute each. Every other group asks one follow-up question. Put overcome, gifted, self-made and groundbreaking on the board as words they could use.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Which story did the room find most surprising? Then two or three sentences from the presentations on the board, one of them correct, for pairs to sort before you confirm.

1B.context: Connections – who we are: tenses from the success article, the six friends everyone needs, and what runs in the family

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have reviewed six tenses – present simple and continuous, past simple and continuous, present perfect and past perfect – and practised choosing between them to tell a short biography.
slots.sub: To give students spoken fluency practice summarising a biography to a partner and comparing the two people.
slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 6 the six highlighted sentences in The long road to success / SB p. 7 Grammar ex A, B, D; Speaking ex A–C (bottom of the page) / Grammar Hub p. 123 ex A–C (1.2 Tense review, controlled practice) / Communication Hub p. 149 (Student A – Emily Blunt) and p. 152 (Student B – Jean-Dominique Bauby)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Hawking and Wang on the board, a column each. Groups of three have two minutes to write down everything they remember from yesterday’s article – include anyone who was absent in a group that was there. Collect four or five facts under each name. The text has been read; your lesson starts with the sentences in it.
stages.avoid: Do not set a reading task. The article was taught yesterday and the time is needed for the clarification.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Grammar ex A on p. 7 with the article open at p. 6: the six highlighted sentences matched to the six tense names. Name the first one together – while each of them read a book, past continuous – then they do the rest alone and compare. Put the six sentences on the board under their tense names; they are the examples for the next stage.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex B: they complete the six rules with the tense names, alone and then in pairs, and you confirm each rule against its sentence on the board. It is a review, so teach where the matching showed gaps and pass quickly over what they had – at this level the pairs that still go wrong are present perfect against past simple with a finished time, and past perfect for the earlier of two past events; build a concept question for each of those. Form on the board for the two perfect tenses only. Pronunciation is yours to supply: the weak and contracted auxiliaries – she’d completed, he’s admitted, she’s built – said at speed and drilled, because the contraction is what hides the tense when they listen.
stages.avoid: Six tenses is the book’s review, not six presentations. If you present each from scratch you will not reach the practice.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex D on p. 7, the Saroo Brierley text: ten verbs in the right tense across one continuous story. Alone, pair check, answer key on screen; take only the ones they disagreed on and make them say which rule decides it. Grammar Hub p. 123 ex A (1.2 Tense review) is a second pass for anyone who finishes early.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Speaking ex A–C on p. 7. A/B pairs: Student A reads about Emily Blunt on p. 149, Student B about Jean-Dominique Bauby on p. 152, and each makes notes under the three bullet points – notes, not sentences, four minutes. Books closed, they tell their partner the story from the notes; the partner notes the tenses they hear. Then ex C: what the two people have in common and who faced the bigger challenge. Monitor for the tenses, especially the past perfect where one event came before another.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two pairs say who faced the bigger challenge and why. Then three sentences from your monitoring on the board, right and wrong mixed, for pairs to sort before you confirm.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised listening for the main ideas and for detail in a radio interview about the six types of friend successful people have.
slots.sub: To develop students’ vocabulary of personality adjectives from the interview: loyal, open-minded, easy-going, arrogant, self-centred, stubborn, down-to-earth, witty.
slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 8 Listening ex A–D – audio track 1.5 (interview with the psychologist Richard Bonnel); Vocabulary ex A – audio track 1.6 (listen and check) / SB p. 9 Vocabulary ex B (top of the page only)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Describe one close friend of yours in three sentences – how you met, how you are alike, how you are different. Then Listening ex A on p. 8 in pairs: their closest friends, and whether it matters to have different types of friend. Ask two people what their partner said, not what they said themselves.

stages.name: Listening for the main ideas
stages.todo: Read the skills box on listening for the main ideas with them first – the next is, another one is, the last is are the signposts – then ex B with track 1.5: six friend types numbered in the order the psychologist mentions them. Say it is a number, not a tick, and that there are six to find. One play, pair check, confirm.

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex C: five three-option questions. A minute to read them and underline the key words, then play the track again. Pair check; in feedback ask what else the speaker said that supports each answer – 50 people, new situations do not stress them, brutally honest, neighbours, feeling part of a group. Replay a short section if an answer splits the room, not the whole interview.

stages.name: Vocabulary from the recording
stages.todo: Vocabulary ex A on p. 8: eight extracts from the interview gapped with the eight personality adjectives in the box. Pairs complete them from what they remember and from the sense of the sentence, then track 1.6 to check. Meaning they can mostly work out from the extracts, so the time goes on the three that look alike and are not: self-centred against arrogant, stubborn against determined, and easy-going against open-minded. Drill the stress – ARRogant, self-CENtred, down-to-EARTH, open-MINDed – then ex B at the top of p. 9, eight sentences choosing between two adjectives, alone and compared.
stages.avoid: Stop at ex B. Ex C sends them to the Vocabulary Hub and ex D is the personality quiz; neither is on your card and the lesson is the listening.

stages.name: Post-listening task
stages.todo: The six friend types on the board: loyal best friend, open-minded adventurer, honest friend, complete opposite, dependable neighbour, witty colleague. Two minutes alone to think of a real person for as many of the six as they can and a word on why. Groups of three tell each other, using the adjectives from the previous stage. Then ex D question 2 if a group finishes early.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two people describe one of their partner’s friends to the room. Then two sentences from your notes on the board, one right and one wrong, with an adjective in each, for the class to sort.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised developing a topic and changing the subject in conversation using speaking of which, talking of …, actually, that reminds me of …, strange you should mention that and anyway.
slots.sub: To give students spoken fluency practice in a role play about the things that run in their families.
slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 11 Family matters ex A; Speaking Skill ex A (the printed extract, completed and used as the text), ex B and the box Developing and introducing new topics, ex C

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Tell them one thing that runs in your family – a talent, a habit, a flaw – in two sentences. Then ex A on p. 11 in pairs: the job they have or want and what makes them suited to it. One or two answers, then ask whether that suitability came from their parents; the extract they are about to read is two friends having exactly that conversation.

stages.name: Text
stages.todo: The Café Hub video is not in our files, so the Speaking Skill ex A extract is your text. Prepare it with the three gaps filled – speaking of which, strange you should mention that, talking of – and give it out as a handout. Two questions on the board before they read: what is Sam busy with (opening a new café) and what runs in Harry’s family (untidiness). Two minutes, pair check, confirm. That is all the reading the lesson needs.
stages.avoid: This is a language lesson. Keep the text stage to its two questions and do not turn the extract into a reading lesson.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex B in pairs: what the three phrases are doing, and what is different about anyway. Elicit the answers and board the exponents under two headings – developing the topic: speaking of which, talking of which, talking of [topic], actually, that reminds me of …, strange you should mention that (because) …; changing the topic completely: anyway. Then the box to confirm.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Check meaning with the extract: when Sam says speaking of which, is the hand soap connected to the paper towels (yes); when he says anyway, is Harry’s progress connected to the café delivery (no). Form: talking of takes a noun or -ing, that reminds me of takes a noun. Pronunciation is yours: the phrases are said fast and low before the new topic, with the stress on the topic that follows – drill all five as chunks.
stages.avoid: One function, five exponents. Do not add the idioms from the Café Hub page opposite; they are a different lesson.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex C: Student A talks about one of the six topics – a film, a news item, a restaurant – and Student B has to either develop it with one of the developing phrases or change it with anyway. Swap after each topic. Keep the board up and listen for the phrases; stop the room once to correct a phrase that is not landing before you continue.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: A role play in pairs about things that run in their families: one partner keeps developing the subject, the other keeps trying to move off it. Three minutes to plan, four to run it twice with roles swapped, and a sentence of brief each time on who they are – two colleagues at work, two cousins at a wedding. If the group is small, two pairs perform for the room; otherwise monitor and collect what you hear.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Which pair managed the most topic changes? Then three lines from your monitoring on the board, one of them right, for pairs to sort before you confirm – the one worth time is a developing phrase used where anyway was needed, or the reverse.

2A.context: Lifestyles – a full life: health and fitness, six ways to live longer, and what people give up for the new year

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have learned and practised six health and fitness nouns – calorie, cholesterol, obesity, depression, stress, anxiety – and used them to argue about health.
slots.sub: To give students spoken fluency practice agreeing and disagreeing with statements about health.
slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 14 Vocabulary ex A–C, ex E (the Vocabulary section only) / Workbook p. 11 Vocabulary ex A (controlled practice)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Tell the room two things you do to stay healthy and one you know you should. Then Vocabulary ex A on p. 14: pairs brainstorm things with a positive or a negative effect on our health. Two columns on the board, healthy and unhealthy, and collect their ideas; if any of the six target nouns come up, leave them on the board and say nothing yet.

stages.name: Presentation
stages.todo: The six sentences in ex B carry the words in context, so present from them rather than from a list. Read sentence 1 together and let the clue – a lack of healthy lunch options, worrying levels – give them definition c, obesity. Then they match the other five alone and compare. Meaning is settled by the definitions, so your time goes on what the definitions cannot give them: the two that overlap, stress against anxiety (pressure from outside against worry from inside – ask which one a deadline causes and which one keeps you awake with no reason); the collocations the words live in – suffer from depression, under stress, high cholesterol, levels of obesity; and the sounds – cholesterol has four syllables with the stress on the second, anxiety is /æŋˈzaɪəti/, obesity /əʊˈbiːsəti/. Drill the six, board them with the stress marked and the collocation beside each.
stages.avoid: Six items and their collocations is the lesson. The Vocabulary Hub (ex D) adds seven more phrases – that is a second lesson, not an extension of this one.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex C: six gapped sentences, one word each. Alone, pair check, then answers on screen. Then Workbook p. 11 Vocabulary ex A, the Staying healthy as a student article with the same six nouns to place across one continuous text – harder than ex C because the clues are spread out. Pair check and take only the disputed ones.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Four or five provocative statements about health on the board, each built around one of the words – eating meat causes obesity; meditation should be taught in schools to cut students’ stress; most anxiety is caused by phones; a diet is more important than exercise. Groups of three agree or disagree with each and must give a reason. Then ex E as the last round: the effects of junk food, smoking, lack of exercise and a poor work-life balance. Listen for the nouns and their collocations.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Which statement did the room disagree about most? Hear both sides for a minute. Then four sentences from your monitoring on the board, two right and two wrong – make one of them a collocation error, such as suffer depression or in stress – for pairs to sort, then confirm.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised predicting, scanning and reading for detail in an article about six ways to live longer.
slots.sub: To develop students’ vocabulary for talking about health from the article – life expectancy, processed foods, mental health, physical activity, reduce the risk, slow the ageing process.
slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 14 Reading ex A–D (the Reading section only) / SB p. 15 the article Six ways to live longer / Vocabulary Hub p. 143 (2.1 Health and fitness – vocabulary from the text)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: One question on the board: how can we live longer? Collect six or seven ideas from the room fast and leave them up – the article will agree with some and surprise them with others. The health words from the previous lesson are fresh; use them yourself as you write.
stages.avoid: The source document opened with a six-minute taboo game. Leave it out: it spends the pre-reading time on the last lesson’s aim, not yours.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Three items only, because they block the gist and the text does not explain them: life expectancy, sedentary and immune system. A context for each and let them give you the word – the average age people live to in a country; a job where you sit all day; the part of your body that fights illness. One concept question each and move on.
stages.avoid: Do not pre-teach processed foods, optimist or pessimist – the text makes them clear and they come back in the vocabulary stage.

stages.name: Prediction and scanning
stages.todo: Ex A on p. 14 with the six pictures and sub-headings on p. 15: pairs say how a pet, moving to Japan, thinking of the details, helping others, singing and not moaning could each lengthen a life. Board one guess per heading. Then ex B: scan the article in three minutes to check the guesses – a scan, so they are looking for their guess, not reading every line. Pairs compare what they found before you give the answers.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex C: six questions, one per section, with the instruction to underline the part of the text that answers each. Alone, then compared in pairs pointing at the lines. Check in open class and ask for the evidence – less risk of heart disease from walking the dog, less fat and smaller plates, better sleep and less comfort eating, volunteering, stress, their own physical health.

stages.name: Vocabulary from the text
stages.todo: Vocabulary Hub p. 143, the 2.1 exercise: seven gapped sentences with the box – level of fitness, life expectancy, mental health, physical activity, processed foods, reduce the risk, slow the ageing process. All of them are in the article they have just read, so pairs do it with the text open and find each phrase in it. Check, then drill the stress on the longer chunks – slow the AGEing process, reDUCE the risk.

stages.name: Post-reading discussion
stages.todo: Ex D questions 3 and 4 in groups: which of the six changes they would actually make and what else they could change. Then the source’s find-someone-who, if there is time: six lines on a handout – find someone who exercises every day, who never eats processed food, who sings – and they mingle to fill it. Close with the question who is the healthiest person in the room.
stages.avoid: Do not open the Speaking section at the foot of p. 15. The discussion in ex D is the response this lesson needs.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised listening for gist, for the main ideas and for reasons in a radio programme about people who gave something up for the new year.
slots.sub: To develop students’ language for giving and recognising reasons – because of, as, since, that’s why, due to the fact that, in order to, and the infinitive of purpose – from the skills box and the interviews.
slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 16 Listening ex A–E and the box Listening for reasons – audio tracks 2.1 (first part of the programme) and 2.2 (the five interviews)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Write New Year’s resolutions on the board and elicit what one is. Tell them something you once gave up and whether it lasted. Then Listening ex A on p. 16 with the six pictures a–f: pairs pick the one they would find hardest to give up and say why. Two answers in open class.

stages.name: Prediction and listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex B: pairs guess what percentage of people break their resolution within a month and within a year. Put three or four pairs’ figures on the board. Then ex C with track 2.1, under a minute long: they listen for the two numbers and check – 43% and 86%. Whose guess was closest?

stages.name: Listening for the main ideas
stages.todo: Ex D with track 2.2: five speakers matched to the things they gave up, with one picture left over. Tell them there is one extra before you play. One play, pair check, confirm – smartphones, coffee, sugar, shampoo, meat.

stages.name: Listening for reasons
stages.todo: Before the second play, the box Listening for reasons: ask how a speaker signals a reason and collect the signals on the board – because (of), as, since, that’s why, due to the fact that, in order to, and the infinitive of purpose (I stopped … to help …) – then the box’s point that a reason is often implied and has to be inferred. Then ex E: track 2.2 again, notes on each speaker’s reason. Pair check, then open class – more family time, better sleep, sugar’s health effects, a friend’s advice about hair, carbon footprint and health. Replay one speaker if the room missed the reason, not all five.
stages.avoid: Two plays of the interviews is the budget. The recording is long; a third full play eats the discussion.

stages.name: Post-listening discussion
stages.todo: The five things given up back on the board. Groups of three or four decide which of the five they could give up and which they could not, and must give a reason for each using the language from the box. Each group agrees on one thing they could all give up and tells the room why.
stages.avoid: Stop before the Grammar section on the right of p. 16. The present perfect extracts are tomorrow’s first lesson.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Each group’s choice in one sentence. Then three reasons from your monitoring on the board, one of them correct – look for in order to with -ing, or because of followed by a clause – for pairs to sort before you settle it.

2B.context: Lifestyles – change: advice for a new year, a family that moved from London to a remote island, and what they used to do

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have written a short article giving advice on a lifestyle change – reducing stress, improving their diet or getting fit – organised under headings with bullet points.
slots.sub: To practise the structures for giving advice from the model article: why not …?, don’t forget to, make sure you, remember to, try to, avoid + -ing, and if + present simple + imperative.
slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 155 Unit 2 Writing ex A–D (the model article Clear the mess and clear your mind and the box Using different structures to give advice); Writing ex A–D

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The five things given up in yesterday’s radio programme on the board – smartphones, coffee, sugar, shampoo, meat. Which worked, and what advice would they give someone trying one of them? A minute in pairs, two answers, and the word advice stays on the board; the day is still about changing how you live.

stages.name: Model text
stages.todo: Ex A on p. 155 in pairs: the title Clear the mess and clear your mind – what advice will the article give? Then ex B, read it quickly to see which of their ideas it has. Now the shape of the thing, because that is what they will copy: an introduction that says why, three headings, and bullet points under each. Ask them to count the headings and the bullets and to say what the introduction does. Keep it to ten minutes – the model is there to be copied, not studied.
stages.avoid: Do not turn the article into a reading lesson. Two quick tasks and the structure, then the language.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Ex C: the table completed with examples from the text – if + present simple + imperative (if you don’t watch it, sell it), negative imperatives (don’t keep broken things), positive imperatives (make sure you …, remember to …) – plus why not …?, try to and avoid + -ing from the bullets. Board the seven structures in two columns, soft and strong, and the form that trips them: avoid takes -ing, try to and remember to take the infinitive, why not takes the bare verb. Then ex D, six sentences rewritten with the word in bold, in pairs, as the controlled check. Drill the three that run together in speech: don’t forget to, make sure you, why not.
stages.avoid: This is the sub aim, not a grammar lesson. Ten minutes and the structures are on the board for the writing; the writing is the lesson.

stages.name: Preparing to write
stages.todo: Writing ex A: pairs choose one of the three topics – reducing stress, improving your diet, getting fit – and brainstorm six to eight pieces of advice as notes. Then ex B: they sort the notes under three headings of their own. Notes and headings only; the sentences get written in the next stage.
stages.avoid: If they start writing full sentences here, the writing stage becomes a copying stage. Notes only, and say so.

stages.name: Writing task
stages.todo: Ex C: each student writes the article alone – an introduction of two or three lines, three headings, two or three bullet points under each, and at least five of the seven structures from the board. Around 150 words. Silence, the model and the board in front of them, and answer questions by walking over, not by speaking to the room.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Ex D: articles swap with someone who chose a different topic, and the reader checks three things from the book’s list – spelling and punctuation, the advice structures, and whether the advice is clear and good. One line on the board from what you saw while they wrote – it will be -ing after try to or avoid – and let them correct it. Collect the drafts and write on them before the next lesson.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised listening for gist and for detail in an interview with a family that moved from London to a remote island.
slots.sub: To develop students’ vocabulary for talking about a change of life from the interview: the rat race, take the plunge, a midlife crisis, out of the question, better off, homeschooled.
slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 18 Listening ex A–D – audio track 2.5 (interview with Frank and Katie Gerrard)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Where do they live now, and would they move to a small island or somewhere remote near here? Then Listening ex A on p. 18 in groups of three: the advantages and disadvantages of a family moving from a city to a remote island. Two columns on the board and collect four ideas in each. Keep it to six minutes – the source gave this ten and paid for it later.

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex B with track 2.5: which members of the family are happy with the move and which are not. One play, notes only, check together, confirm – Frank and the young son are happy, Katie is not, and the mother is not clear. Make them say what they heard that told them.

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex C: six three-option questions. A minute to read them and underline the key words, then play the interview again. Pair check, then open class with the reason for each answer – the demanding job, growing and catching food, the money, the internet, UK exams, playing outside all day. If one question splits the room, replay just that part.
stages.avoid: Two plays. A third full play of a long interview costs the vocabulary and the response.

stages.name: Vocabulary from the recording
stages.todo: A handout with six lines from the audioscript (it is in the Teacher’s Book notes for the lesson) that carry the phrases – escaping the rat race, taken the plunge, a midlife crisis, out of the question, better off, homeschooled – and six definitions to match. Pairs, from the lines. Check, then drill the ones that are chunks: the RAT race, take the PLUNGE, out of the QUEStion.

stages.name: Post-listening discussion
stages.todo: Ex D in pairs: imagine moving to a small island far from here – what would you miss, and what would you be glad to leave behind? Push for the vocabulary from the previous stage; put it on the board again if it has gone.
stages.avoid: Stop before the Grammar section at the foot of p. 18. The used to extracts are the next lesson’s.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Three people say what their partner would miss most. Then two sentences from your notes on the board, one right and one wrong, for the class to sort.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised used to and would for finished habits, and be used to and get used to for familiarity, to talk about how their own lives have changed.
slots.sub: To give students spoken fluency practice explaining the biggest changes in their lives over the last ten years.
slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 18 Grammar ex A–B (extracts from the interview) / SB p. 19 Grammar ex D; Pronunciation ex A–B – audio tracks 2.6, 2.7; Speaking ex A–C / Workbook p. 13 Grammar ex A (controlled practice)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Frank and Katie on the board. What was Frank’s life like before the move, and what is it like now? Collect two sentences for each and write them as they come – if anyone produces used to or is used to, leave it on the board untouched. The interview was taught last lesson; this is a reminder of the context only.
stages.avoid: Do not replay the interview. The listening tasks were done in the previous lesson.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Grammar ex A on p. 18: four extracts from the interview matched to four meanings. Pairs, then confirm – used to work: true in the past, not now; I’m used to getting up at six: strange at first, normal now; we’re getting used to it: still strange, becoming familiar; he’d complain: a past habit. Board the four extracts under their meanings.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex B: they complete the four rules with the box, alone, then pairs; confirm against the extracts. The meaning split that matters is past habit against familiarity, and it is the form that carries it: used to + infinitive against be/get used to + -ing or a noun. Concept-check the dangerous pair on the board – I used to get up early (do I now? no) against I’m used to getting up early (do I now? yes, and it is easy). Would takes habits but not states – they would complain, not they would live in London – say it once with an example. Then Pronunciation ex A with track 2.6: is the /d/ in used to heard, strong or weak to – no, and weak, /ˈjuːstə/ – board it in phonemics, then ex B with track 2.7 and drill the five sentences.
stages.avoid: Four forms with two meanings is what 45 minutes holds. Do not add didn’t use to and the question forms as separate teaching points; mention the form once and let the practice carry it.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex D on p. 19: eight sentences with used to, would, be used to or get used to and the verb in brackets. Alone, a quick comparison in pairs, answer key on screen; take only the ones they disagreed on and make them say whether it is a past habit or a familiarity. Workbook p. 13 Grammar ex A – ten sentences, some wrong, to correct – is the second pass for the fast finishers and catches didn’t used to and get use to.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Speaking ex A–C on p. 19: a minute to list changes in their lives in the six areas, then notes on the three biggest using the book’s questions – what prompted it, how it affected them, whether they are used to it yet. Groups of three take turns explaining their changes and ask each other follow-up questions. Monitor for the target forms and write down what you hear.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One change from each group that surprised the others. Then three sentences from your notes on the board, right and wrong mixed – the one to expect is I’m used to get up – for the class to correct, then confirm.

3A.context: Change – changing environment: how wolves changed Yellowstone’s rivers, the passive, and an eco-friendly home

slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 50 Reading ex A–B and the article How wolves change rivers / SB p. 51 Reading ex C–D and the box Identifying cause and effect (the Reading section only)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book’s way in is a good one: a predator on the board, what it eats, what eats it, and the words predator, prey and food chain come out of the drawing; groups then write the longest food chain they can. Then ex A on p. 50 with the diagram, question 3 left open.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: This is a hard text, so pick the three or four words that block the gist and are not in the glossary – reintroduce, explode (of a population), riverbank, overlook – and teach them in context; the passive forms in the text are the next lesson’s, so leave them alone.

stages.name: Scanning to check predictions
stages.todo: Ex B: three minutes to scan the article and check their answers to ex A, especially what happened when the wolves were removed. Pair check, then feedback through the three questions.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex C on p. 51: read the box on cause and effect first and model one relationship from the text on the board (wolves hunted → elk population grew), then the six true-or-false sentences, corrected where false and justified with the line that proves it.
stages.avoid: The Grammar section on p. 51 belongs to the next lesson. Do not underline the passives.

stages.name: Post-reading discussion
stages.todo: Ex D in groups: which animals are in danger in their country and what is being done, with a second question of your own about whether a predator should ever be reintroduced near people.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One animal per group, then two or three sentences you heard during the task on the board and let the room find the errors.

slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 50 the article (ten passives to find) / SB p. 51 Grammar ex A–D; Speaking ex A–B / Grammar Hub p. 131 ex A (5.1 The passive, controlled practice) / Communication Hub p. 151 (5.1 – the Borneo cause-and-effect pictures)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Rebuild the Yellowstone story in four lines on the board from what the class remembers – wolves hunted, elk exploded, wolves reintroduced, rivers changed – and write at least one of them in the passive without comment; the article has been read, so go straight on.
stages.avoid: Do not set the reading again.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Grammar ex A on p. 51 with the article open: ten passives underlined in the text, then ex B in pairs – what tense each one is, which has a modal, which is an infinitive. This is also your test of what they already know, so listen to how they name the tenses.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex C, the rules, alone and then confirmed against their underlined examples: be + past participle, any tense, and the three reasons for choosing it – agent unknown, agent unimportant, focus on the receiver. It is a review, so clarify only what ex B exposed; the form that usually needs work is the passive with modals and infinitives (can’t be changed, to be used), and the pronunciation point is the weak been and were in were hunted, have been identified – drill the examples from the text.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex D on p. 51: eight sentences in the right passive form, then Grammar Hub p. 131 ex A, six active sentences to rewrite, for anyone who finishes; a thirty-second check with a neighbour and an answer key.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Speaking ex A: Communication Hub p. 151 (5.1), the Borneo story in ten pictures – pairs work out the chain of cause and effect in the passive (a chemical was sprayed, the lizards were caught by cats, more cats were parachuted in), then compare with another pair; ex B if there is time.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Tell the real ending in two lines, then three sentences you wrote down while they spoke on the board, right and wrong mixed, to be corrected in pairs.

slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 52 Vocabulary ex A–C; Listening ex A–B – audio track 5.1 (radio interview about an eco-friendly home) / Workbook p. 33 Vocabulary ex B (controlled practice)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: A photo of a house with solar panels and a wind turbine, or your own home’s energy bill: what makes a home eco-friendly, two minutes in pairs, ideas on the board.

stages.name: Presentation
stages.todo: Vocabulary ex A on p. 52, the labelled house: ten items – compost heap, double glazing, energy-efficient lightbulb, insulation, smart meter, solar panels, thermostat, underfloor heating, water butt, wind turbine – meaning from the picture and from what each one does, then the stress in the compounds (SOlar panels, WAter butt, WIND turbine, THERmostat) drilled before you board them.
stages.avoid: Ten items is the top of what 45 minutes holds. If the room is slow, drop thermostat and insulation and teach them from the listening.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex B, ten gapped sentences, alone and pair-checked; Workbook p. 33 Vocabulary ex B is the second pass if they finish.

stages.name: Listening
stages.todo: Listening ex A with track 5.1: which of the ten features Harry does not mention, one play; then ex B, eight gaps of up to four words, on a second play with compare answers in pairs – the recording is where the words come back in use, so keep feedback to the answers.
stages.avoid: Two plays. This is the sub aim; the speaking still needs its seven minutes.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex C widened: which of the ten they have at home, which they would install with the money, and which one they think is a waste – groups of three, a reason each time.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: The most popular choice in the room, then two items you wrote down while they spoke on the board to sort.

3B.context: Change – changing places: the rise of the megacities, words for the parts of a city, and how to make where you work greener

slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 54 Reading ex A–D and the article Rise of the megacities

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book’s warm-up: the five most populated cities in the world on the board as a title, pairs guess the five in three minutes, then the list (Tokyo, Delhi, Shanghai, São Paulo, Mumbai).

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Three blockers that are not in bold – swell, prosperous, deter – each from a context, with one concept question; the eight words in bold are the next lesson’s vocabulary, so do not touch them.
stages.avoid: Leave suburbs, industrial, urban, slum, residential, housing, commercial and rural for the next teacher.

stages.name: Prediction and scanning
stages.todo: Ex A with the two photos of Dubai: what makes a city grow so fast and what the effects are, guesses on the board, then ex B – three minutes to scan the article and check them.

stages.name: Reading for organisation and detail
stages.todo: Ex C, six sentences a–f back into the six gaps, with a word first on how to do it (read before and after the gap, look for the words the sentence picks up); then, since the book has no detailed-reading task here, five questions of your own on Seoul, Abu Dhabi and the push-and-pull reasons, answered with the line that proves each.

stages.name: Post-reading discussion
stages.todo: Ex D in groups of three – the advantages and disadvantages of living in a major city – and whether they would rather live in the centre or outside it.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One advantage and one disadvantage the room agrees on, then two sentences you heard during the task on the board to sort.

slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 54 the article (the eight words in bold) / SB p. 55 Vocabulary ex A–C (Describing areas of a city) and Speaking ex A–C (the first Vocabulary section and the Speaking section only)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Two photos of your own city, one of the centre and one of the edge, and the question what the difference is – the article was read last lesson, so recall Seoul and Abu Dhabi in a line each and move on.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: The article open at p. 54: find the eight words in bold and say what kind of word each is and what it goes with in the text – commercial area, residential areas, housing projects.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Vocabulary ex A on p. 55, the eight definitions, then your clarification: noun or adjective (housing, slum and suburbs are the nouns), the pairs that get confused – urban against rural, industrial against commercial, residential against suburban – and the stress on comMERcial, inDUStrial, resiDENtial; drill and board with a collocation beside each.
stages.avoid: Stay in the first Vocabulary section. The Pronunciation and Prefixes sections lower on p. 55 are different lessons.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex B, eight three-option sentences, alone and pair-checked, with an answer key; make them say why the other two options fail on the ones they argue about.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex C, then Speaking ex A–C at the foot of p. 55: notes on how their town has changed in transport, shopping, housing and cost of living, told to a partner with the eight words in front of them, then whether the changes were good.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One change per pair, then three items collected while monitoring on the board, some correct, some not, to sort.

slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 58 Comprehension ex A; Authentic English ex B–D and the box Conditional counterarguments / SB p. 59 Speaking Hub ex A–C

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Comprehension ex A on p. 58 with the picture of the disposable cups: are they environmentally friendly, and what does their own workplace or school do about waste – two minutes in pairs, ideas on the board.
stages.avoid: The two Café Hub videos on these pages are not in our files. Nothing in this lesson needs them.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: The box Conditional counterarguments and the model exchange under it (nobody wants to carry a cup – but they might if coffee shops offered bigger discounts): the pattern is but + modal + if + past, with the stress on the modal; drill the model, then ex D, three arguments answered with a conditional in pairs.
stages.avoid: This is useful language, not the main aim. Twelve minutes, then the task.

stages.name: Preparation
stages.todo: Speaking Hub ex A–B on p. 59: groups list five ways to be greener in the six areas and rank them, with the rule that any objection has to be answered with a conditional.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Groups regroup so each new group has one member from each old one, and must agree a single ranked list of five; then ex C, each group presents its list and takes one objection from the floor.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: The room’s top suggestion, then four lines overheard in the groups on the board, at least one a conditional counterargument that worked, and they fix the wrong ones.

4A.context: Change – Mars One: three candidates for a one-way trip, the verb forms they use, and which of them to send

slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 56 Listening ex A–E and the FAQs page – audio track 5.7 (three radio interviews with Mars One candidates)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: What do they know about Mars, and would they go if the ticket was one-way? Then ex A on p. 56: the FAQs page read in two minutes and the four questions discussed in pairs – who would qualify, who would apply.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Only what blocks the gist: candidate, mission, legacy, and leave your mark – the last one is in ex D, so teach the words around it and let the recording carry it.

stages.name: Listening for the main idea
stages.todo: Ex B with track 5.7: six questions answered A, T or B. It is a long recording, so decide beforehand whether you pause after each interview; compare with a partner, confirm.

stages.name: Listening for rhetorical questions
stages.todo: The box first – a question asked for effect, not for an answer – then ex C on a second play: seven questions from the interviews, tick the rhetorical ones; feedback asks what each speaker meant by it.
stages.avoid: The Grammar section on p. 57 is not on your card: it takes extracts from this recording, and the -ing and infinitive forms are the next teacher’s.

stages.name: Post-listening discussion
stages.todo: Ex D and E together in small groups: what leave their mark behind means and how they want to make theirs, then which candidate they would choose for the mission and why.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: A class vote on the candidate, then three sentences overheard in the groups on the board – which are right?

slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 57 Grammar ex A – audio track 5.8 (nine extracts from the interviews); ex B–C, E–F / Grammar Hub p. 131 ex A (5.2 -ing and infinitive forms, controlled practice)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Agatha, Tim and Bernie on the board: one thing each would miss on Mars, from memory. The interviews were taught last lesson; this is a reminder, then straight to the extracts.
stages.avoid: Do not replay the interviews. The listening tasks were done.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Grammar ex A on p. 57: nine extracts, the verb in brackets put into -ing, to + infinitive or the bare infinitive, then track 5.8 to check; ex B on forget in sentences 5 and 8 is the meaning question, so take it before you teach.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex C: the nine examples matched to the seven rules in the box – -ing after prepositions, as subject and after certain verbs; to + infinitive after adjectives, for purpose and after certain verbs; bare infinitive after modals – plus the verbs that take both with a change of meaning. Clarify the patterns the matching exposed, and give the meaning pair forget doing against forget to do a concept question each; pronunciation is the weak to /tə/ in the infinitives, drilled in the extracts.
stages.avoid: Seven rules is a review of patterns, not seven presentations. The one new meaning is the forget / remember / try pair.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex E, eight sentences about teamwork with the verbs in the box, then Grammar Hub p. 131 ex A (5.2) for the fast finishers; check together and an answer key.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex F: do they agree with the eight sentences about teams, in pairs, with a reason each – then a quick round of their own: three things they will never forget doing, and three they must remember to do this week.
stages.avoid: The Speaking Hub at the foot of p. 57 is the next lesson’s task.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One sentence the room disagreed with, then three you wrote down while they spoke on the board – expect a to after a preposition – and they decide which is which.

slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 57 Speaking Hub ex A–B / Communication Hub p. 147 (5.2 – six candidate profiles, ex A–B)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Four qualities of a good astronaut on the board, from the room, ranked by show of hands – the Mars One context was set in the first lesson, so a line is enough to bring it back.

stages.name: Preparation
stages.todo: Communication Hub p. 147, ex A: six candidate profiles – leadership, personality, qualifications, unique skills – read alone, with notes on the three they would select and one reason each.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: The language of a selection meeting, yours to choose and board: putting a case (the main thing in her favour is …), conceding (I take your point, but …), ruling out (we can’t send someone who …); drill the three or four you want to hear.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Ex B: groups of four compare their choices and must agree on two candidates for the mission – a deadline on the board, and a rule that every rejection needs a reason from the profile.

stages.name: Presenting
stages.todo: Speaking Hub ex B on p. 57: each group tells the class who they chose, who they rejected and why, in a minute; a class vote on the final two.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Four lines collected while monitoring on the board, not all of them wrong, at least one of them a phrase from the useful language used well, for the class to correct.

4B.context: Coming of age – education: a governess in Agnes Grey, the articles in Coming of age, and the words for schooling

slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 64 Reading ex A–B – audio track 6.5 (interview with the actress Jane Nash, as the way in); ex C–D and the extract from Agnes Grey (the Reading section only) / SB p. 65 Reading ex E–F and the box Pronoun referencing

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Who taught them before they went to school, and what would it be like to be taught at home by a stranger? Two minutes in pairs, then the word governess on the board.
stages.avoid: The Vocabulary section at the top of p. 64 is the third lesson’s. Start at the Reading section.

stages.name: Listening as the way in
stages.todo: Reading ex A with track 6.5: when the film is set and who the actress plays, one play; then ex B, the summary of school life in the period with no more than three words per gap, on a second play. Keep it to eight minutes – it sets the text up, it is not the lesson.

stages.name: Prediction and scanning
stages.todo: Ex C: what might be hard for Agnes as governess to two rich children, guesses on the board; then ex D, three minutes to scan the extract and check them.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex E on p. 65 with the box: the eight pronouns traced back to what they refer to, with the line numbers – model them (line 2) on the board first, then alone, pairs, and feedback by nominating.

stages.name: Post-reading discussion
stages.todo: Ex F in groups: what making faces means here, what Agnes could have done differently, and whether children should choose when they study.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One idea for Agnes from each group, then two sentences you heard during the task on the board to sort.

slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 66 Reading ex A–B and the article Coming of age (as the way in); Grammar ex A / SB p. 67 Grammar ex B, D–E / Grammar Hub p. 133 ex A–B (6.2 Articles, controlled practice) / Communication Hub p. 151 (6.2 Student A – the Maasai) and p. 152 (6.2 Student B – the fiesta de quince años)

stages.name: Lead-in and text
stages.todo: Reading ex A on p. 66 in pairs – when does someone become an adult, and what marks it in their country – then ex B, a two-minute scan of Coming of age to match the three ages to what they mean. That is all the reading this lesson takes; the article is here for its articles.
stages.avoid: A language lesson: do not set ex C or D. Seven minutes on the text, then the grammar.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Grammar ex A: six extracts from the article with a, an, the or nothing to fill from memory, then the text to check – the Teacher’s Book is right to say no explanation yet.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex B on p. 67: the three rule blocks labelled a/an, the or zero, alone and then confirmed against the extracts. Teach what the gaps exposed – at this level it is usually the zero article for general ideas (childhood is over) and the in the Pacific Ocean, Vanuatu without it; the pronunciation point is weak /ə/ and /ðə/, with /ði/ before a vowel, drilled in the extracts.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Hub p. 133 ex A and B (6.2), sixteen sentences in all, alone and pair-checked; make them name the rule on the ones they argue about.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex D: Student A completes the Maasai text on p. 151, Student B the quinceañera text on p. 152, then ex E – each explains their ceremony to the other from notes, with the articles in it.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Which ceremony would they rather attend, then three lines collected while monitoring on the board, including one that is right, to sort.

slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 64 Vocabulary ex A and ex C and the infographic Education around the globe (the Vocabulary section only) / Workbook p. 40 Vocabulary ex A (controlled practice)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Two or three facts about your own schooling on the board – uniform or not, hours, what was compulsory – and pairs compare theirs; the day’s context is education, so a line is enough.
stages.avoid: Stay in the Vocabulary section. The Reading section below it was taught in the first lesson.

stages.name: Presentation
stages.todo: Vocabulary ex A on p. 64: the infographic carries the six items in bold – private school, compulsory, state school, curriculum, boarding school, higher education – so they meet them there and complete the definitions, then your clarification: the three school types against each other, the stress on comPULsory and curRICulum, and the collocations (go into higher education, on the curriculum).
stages.avoid: Six items. Ex B sends them to the Vocabulary Hub for nine more – that is another lesson.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 40 Vocabulary ex A, six sentence halves matched, then a second pass of your own – the six words gapped out of three or four sentences about schooling here; a quick comparison in pairs, answer key.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex C in groups of three: the five questions on starting age, private schools, compulsory subjects, free higher education and lectures, with the rule that each answer uses one of the six.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: The question the room disagreed on most, then four lines you heard during the task on the board, good and bad together, and let the room find the errors.

5A.context: Community – how we live: a moneyless community, the phrasal verbs its founder uses, and a phone call about shared housing

slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 80 Listening ex A–D and the article How We Live returns – audio track 7.5 (interview with Callum Castling)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Could they live for a month without money? Pairs list what they would need and how they would get it; three ideas on the board. A short, concrete way into the moneyless man.

stages.name: Pre-listening
stages.todo: Ex A on p. 80: the article about Mark Boyle read in four minutes for the four questions, underlining the answers; then pre-teach three blockers from the audioscript – renovate, abandoned, scout around – and nothing else, because the three-part phrasal verbs belong to the next lesson.
stages.avoid: Leave come up with, get around to, cut down on, come up against, get on with and look up to for the next teacher.

stages.name: Listening for organisation
stages.todo: Ex B with track 7.5: five topics numbered in the order Callum talks about them; one play of a five-minute recording, a thirty-second check with a neighbour, confirm.

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex C, six gaps of up to three words, on a second play. Decide beforehand how you will support them – pause after each answer on the second play, or play a third time only the part that beat them – and confirm with the words as said.

stages.name: Post-listening discussion
stages.todo: Ex D in groups: how well they know their neighbours, what community events exist where they live, and whether they would join a moneyless community.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One answer from each group to the third question, then two sentences overheard in the groups on the board to sort.

slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 80 Vocabulary ex A – audio track 7.6 (six sentences from the interview, listen and check) / SB p. 81 Vocabulary ex C–D (Three-part phrasal verbs); Pronunciation ex A–B – audio tracks 7.7, 7.8 / Vocabulary Hub p. 146 ex A (7.2 – two more verbs: keep up with, run out of) / Workbook p. 49 Vocabulary ex A (controlled practice)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Callum’s community centre on the board: what they remember he set up and who helped – a minute of recall, because the interview was taught last lesson and the verbs come out of it.
stages.avoid: Do not replay the interview for its tasks. The sentences in ex A are the exposure.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Vocabulary ex A on p. 80: six sentences from the interview gapped with the six three-part phrasal verbs, the definitions in brackets as the clue; pairs, then track 7.6 to check.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning is largely done by the brackets, so the time goes on form and sound: three parts, never separated, the object after the last particle (come up with a plan, not come a plan up with); add keep up with and run out of from Vocabulary Hub p. 146 ex A so ex C can be done in full – eight verbs; then Pronunciation ex A with track 7.7 (main stress on the verb, secondary on the first particle: COME up with) and ex B with track 7.8, drilled as whole chunks.
stages.avoid: Eight verbs is the lesson. The other four in the Hub exercise are passive items; do not teach all twelve.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex C on p. 81, six questions completed with the verbs, then Workbook p. 49 Vocabulary ex A, eight sentences where the words in bold are replaced by the phrasal verb; compare answers in pairs, answer key.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex D: the six questions from ex C asked and answered in pairs, swapping partners halfway; listen for the verbs and for the stress.
stages.avoid: The Speaking Hub on p. 81 is a project-planning task that does not need the verbs. Stay with ex D.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One thing learned about a partner, then three sentences you wrote down while they spoke on the board, one with the stress marked wrong, to sort and say aloud.

slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 83 Living together ex A; Speaking Skill ex A (the box Talking on the telephone, completed from the list of phrases – without the video) and ex B; Speaking Hub ex A–C

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex A on p. 83 in pairs: who they tell first when they have big news, and whether they would ever tell someone something important over the phone; two answers in open class.
stages.avoid: The Café Hub video is not in our files. The box and the list of phrases on the page are enough for the lesson.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Speaking Skill ex A without the video: pairs put the eleven phrases in the list into the box by function – checking who it is (is that you? / yes, it’s me), asking what they are doing and if it is a good time, giving the reason for calling (that brings me to what I was calling about), ending (I need to go, got to go, I’d better be going), and not hearing (what was that? you’re breaking up, I didn’t catch that); confirm, then drill them as fast, friendly chunks.
stages.avoid: Useful language, not target language. Twelve minutes and then the task.

stages.name: Preparation
stages.todo: Speaking Hub ex A–B: pairs brainstorm the pros and cons of shared housing, then Student A plans how to talk their partner out of moving into a shared housing project and Student B plans how to argue for it – notes only, and a reminder that the call has to open and close like a real one.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Ex C: the phone call, back to back so they cannot see each other; then ex B from the Speaking Skill section for a second call with new partners and a topic from its list. Monitor with the phrases in front of you.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Who was persuaded? Then four lines you wrote down while they spoke on the board, some correct, some not, at least one a phone phrase used well, to be corrected in pairs.

5B.context: Mystery – myths and legends: two unexplained incidents, guessing what must have happened, and three famous myths

slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 86 Reading ex A–B and the article How do you explain that? / SB p. 87 Reading ex C–F and the box Decoding: similes and metaphors (the Reading section only)

stages.name: Lead-in and pre-teaching
stages.todo: Ex A and B on p. 86: how far they believe in ghosts, aliens and monsters on a scale of 1–5, compared in groups; then the three or four words that block the stories – lighthouse, hikers, avalanche, hypothermia – taught fast in context.
stages.avoid: The highlighted sentences are the next lesson’s past modals. Do not explain must have or can’t have here.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: The source’s jigsaw: half the room reads only the first paragraph of the lighthouse story, half only the first paragraph of Dyatlov Pass, two minutes, then new pairs tell each other their mystery with the book closed.

stages.name: Prediction and scanning
stages.todo: Pairs predict the explanation for each mystery, then ex C: scan the rest of both stories for the explanations that were first given – murder, a sea monster, a ghost ship; wild animals, a yeti – and compare with their own.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex D on p. 87, six questions on the two stories, answered alone with the line that proves each and compared in pairs before you give the answers.

stages.name: Similes and metaphors
stages.todo: The box, checked with two examples on the board – is Tom really a lion, was the snow really a blanket – then ex E: three questions answered by finding the simile or metaphor (like a ghost town, as quick as a flash, white as a sheet).

stages.name: Post-reading discussion
stages.todo: Ex F in groups: why people prefer the unusual explanation when the obvious one is there; one answer per group and a sentence you heard during the task to correct.

slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 86 the highlighted sentences in the article / SB p. 87 Grammar ex A–B, D; Speaking ex A–B / Grammar Hub p. 137 ex A–B (8.1 Past modals of deduction, controlled practice) / Communication Hub p. 151 (8.1 – the answer to the Hopkinsville goblin case)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The two mysteries in a line each from the class, and the explanation the writer settles on for each; the stories were read last lesson, so go straight to the sentences.
stages.avoid: Do not set the reading again.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Grammar ex A on p. 87 with the article open: the highlighted sentences sorted into almost certain, possible and impossible; pairs, then the sentences on the board under the three headings.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex B, the three structures completed – must have, may/might/could have, can’t/couldn’t have + past participle – and confirmed against the board. Concept-check certainty, not grammar: for the men must have been blown into the sea, is the writer sure, does he have evidence; and the trap, can’t have for the impossible past, where learners reach for mustn’t have. Pronunciation is the sub aim and it is the weak have – /məstəv/, /maɪtəv/, /kɑːntəv/ – modelled, boarded in phonemics and drilled in the sentences from the text.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Hub p. 137, 8.1 ex A (ten choices) and ex B (six conversations) – pick one, or ex A for everyone and ex B for the fast finishers; compare with a partner, answer key.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex D, the three situations, discussed in pairs with the modals; then Speaking ex A, the Hopkinsville goblin case in groups, and ex B – the likely answer on p. 151 to compare with their theory.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Which group came nearest to the owl, then three deductions collected while monitoring on the board, not all of them wrong, said aloud with the weak have, and they fix the wrong ones.

slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 88 Listening ex A–D – audio track 8.1 (interview with Phillip Norris on myths and legends); Vocabulary ex A (Word families – the table)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: One myth or legend from your own country in three sentences, then the question whether every country has one about a monster; hands up for yes.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: From the audioscript, only what blocks the gist – voyage, giant, turn to stone, cubicle – each from a context, with one concept question, and move on.

stages.name: Prediction and listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex A on p. 88: the three illustrations, what happens in each story and where it comes from, guessed in pairs and put on the board; then ex B with track 8.1, one play to check – Hanako-San, Sinbad, Perseus and Medusa.

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex C, seven three-option questions, key words underlined before a second play; it is a long interview, so plan how you check – check together, then nominate, and replay only the part that beat them.

stages.name: Vocabulary from the recording
stages.todo: Vocabulary ex A, the word-family table – transform, myth, believe, hero, represent, tradition across verb, noun, adjective, adverb – completed in pairs with the box, then the stress shifts drilled: MYTH, MYTHical; HEro, heROic; TRAdition, traDItional.
stages.avoid: Stop at ex A. Ex B on the next page is a different lesson’s practice.

stages.name: Post-listening discussion
stages.todo: Ex D in groups: why myths are still told and new ones still made – and the source’s question, a myth from their own country told to the group; one each in open class if there is time.

6A.context: Mystery – who did it? The curse of the Black Falcon, the adjectives that describe it, and the crime words to solve a murder

slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 90 Reading ex A–C and the story The curse of the Black Falcon / SB p. 91 Reading ex D; Vocabulary ex A–C (Easily confused verbs) – NOT the Grammar section

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book suggests old detective-story covers; two or three on the screen, and the genre, the characters and what happens come out of them. Then ex A on p. 90 with the title and the picture: what is the Black Falcon and what happens.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex B: three minutes to skim the story and check their guesses – a necklace, a burglar in the professor’s study during the party. Pair check, confirm, and clarify two or three words that stopped them, but not like a million dollars, which is ex D.

stages.name: Reading for the main ideas
stages.todo: Ex C: eight true-or-false sentences, the false ones corrected – he never liked parties, the historical value mattered more, the safe was behind the painting, the burglar waited two minutes. Alone, pairs, then nominate with the evidence.

stages.name: Inferring meaning
stages.todo: Ex D on p. 91 in pairs: what like a million dollars means, why the figure waits for the thunder, and how the burglar finds the safe – answers from the text, and the word simile if it comes up.
stages.avoid: The Grammar section on p. 91 is the next lesson’s. Do not underline the adjectives.

stages.name: Vocabulary from the text
stages.todo: Vocabulary ex A: six pairs of sense verbs – see/watch, feel/touch, hear/listen, look/see – chosen and checked against the story, then the difference in each pair elicited (intention against perception), and ex B, eight gaps, as the practice.

stages.name: Post-reading discussion
stages.todo: Ex C, the five questions about news, films and listening to other people, in groups of three – the verbs have to come out – and one line overheard in the groups corrected at the end.

slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 90 the story (adjective pairs to find) / SB p. 91 Grammar ex A–B, D–E (the Grammar section only) / Grammar Hub p. 137 ex A–B (8.2 Order of adjectives, controlled practice) / Communication Hub p. 150 (8.2 Student A) and p. 153 (8.2 Student B)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The study on the board: the desk, the painting, the safe, the vase, the necklace – what does the class remember about each? Write one of their descriptions with two adjectives and leave it; the story was read last lesson.
stages.avoid: Do not set the reading again.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Grammar ex A on p. 91 with the story open: find the sentences where two or more adjectives describe one noun – a beautiful blue dress, the large rectangular painting, the antique gold clock, a small Chinese vase – and put them on the board.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex B: a specific order, opinion before description; elicit the full order from the examples and the Grammar Hub table – opinion, size, shape, age, colour, origin, material – and check it with one wrong sentence on the board for them to fix. Pronunciation: the stress falls on the noun, with the adjectives run together before it, drilled in the four examples.
stages.avoid: Three adjectives is the usual limit in real speech; say so, and do not build sentences with five.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex D, eight sentences rewritten with the adjectives in brackets, then Grammar Hub p. 137, 8.2 ex A (add the adjective in the right place) or ex B (correct five mistakes in the extract) for the fast finishers; a quick comparison in pairs, answer key.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex E: Student A describes the picture on p. 150 and Student B the one on p. 153, each using adjectives in order, and they find the similarities without looking at each other’s page.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: The similarities the pairs found, then three descriptions you wrote down while they spoke on the board, one of them in the right order, to sort.

slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 92 Vocabulary ex A–B, D (Crime) / SB p. 93 Speaking Hub ex A–C (the murder at the dinner party) / Vocabulary Hub p. 146 (8.2 Crime vocabulary, controlled practice) / Communication Hub p. 148 (8.2 Speaking Hub ex B – the suspects’ profiles)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Vocabulary ex A on p. 92 with the two pictures – a DNA sample and a witness in court – what they show and which is more reliable; the day’s context is the Black Falcon, so a crime is already in the room.
stages.avoid: The Listening section on pp. 92–93 is not on your card. Stay with the Vocabulary section and the Speaking Hub.

stages.name: Presentation
stages.todo: Ex B: six sentences with the crime words in bold matched to definitions – burglary, bribe, identity theft, robbery, fraud, blackmail; then your clarification of the pairs that blur (burglary against robbery, fraud against identity theft), the word families (burglar, rob, blackmailer) and the stress – BURglary, ROBbery, BLACKmail – drilled and boarded.
stages.avoid: Six items and their families. Ex C sends them to the Vocabulary Hub for ten more; take only the exercise, not its word list, as practice.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Vocabulary Hub p. 146, the 8.2 exercise, where the six crimes sit inside a story of arrest, charge and sentence – alone, a thirty-second check with a neighbour, answer key; glossary the verbs from the box that are new.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex D for three minutes, then Speaking Hub ex A–C on p. 93: the murder of Sofia Baldursson, the suspects’ profiles on p. 148 read in groups for where they were, their motive and their alibi, and the group must agree who did it – the crime words and the past modals from yesterday both come out.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: A class vote, then the answer (Linus, the only one with no confirmed alibi), then four lines overheard in the groups on the board – which are right?

6B.context: Fact or fiction – testing urban legends; then Customers – who we trust online, and the relative clauses that describe them

slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 94 Comprehension ex A (three urban legends); Authentic English ex B–C and the box Understatement / SB p. 95 Speaking Skill ex A, C–D; Speaking Hub ex A–D

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Comprehension ex A on p. 94: the three claims – the penny from the skyscraper, the shark and the drop of blood, the phone at the petrol station – true or urban legend, in groups, with a show of hands for each.
stages.avoid: The two videos on these pages are not in our files. Nothing in this lesson needs them.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Two short pieces of language for the task: the box Understatement on p. 94 with ex B (five situations matched to their understated descriptions) and ex C in pairs; then Speaking Skill ex A on p. 95 – why Harry asks does that sound like a plan, and what else they could say – and three phrases of yours for keeping a group discussion going (what do you think of that? shall we go with that? would that work?), drilled.
stages.avoid: Useful language, not target language. Twelve minutes, then the task.

stages.name: Preparation
stages.todo: Speaking Hub ex A–B: pairs brainstorm how to test each of the three legends and choose their best test, with notes on equipment, why it works, how many runs and what could go wrong.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Ex C: pairs join into groups of four or six and must agree one test per legend, using the phrases to keep the discussion moving; then ex D, each group presents one test and takes questions. If time is short, ex C–D on p. 95 (the car that breaks down at night) is a shorter task with the same language.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: The test the room would most like to watch, then four lines collected while monitoring on the board, including one that is right, and they decide which is which.

slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 98 Reading ex A–B and the article Who would you trust? / SB p. 99 Reading ex C–D (the Reading section only – NOT the Grammar section)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex A on p. 98 in groups: would they trust a stranger to drive them, advise them, stay in their house, rate their skills – and the apps that already ask them to.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Three items the text does not explain – reputation, endorsement, go viral – each from a context, with one concept question, and move on.

stages.name: Reading for the main idea
stages.todo: Ex B: the five headings read first and any unknown word in them cleared, then the article in five minutes to put a heading on each section; compare answers in pairs and feedback with the sentence that gave each away.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex C on p. 99: eight sentences completed with no more than two words from the article, alone and compared in pairs with the line that proves each; take only the disputed ones in open class.
stages.avoid: Stop before the Grammar section on p. 99. The highlighted sentences are the next lesson’s.

stages.name: Post-reading discussion
stages.todo: Ex D in groups: whether they read reviews before buying, whether they have ever complained on social media, and how to protect an online reputation.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One tip for an online reputation from each group, then two sentences you heard during the task on the board to sort.

slots.pages: Language Hub Upper Intermediate (1st ed.) SB p. 98 the highlighted sentences in Who would you trust? / SB p. 99 Grammar ex A–C, E; Pronunciation ex A–B – audio tracks 9.1, 9.2 (the Grammar and Pronunciation sections only – NOT the reading tasks) / Grammar Hub p. 139 ex A–B (9.1 Relative clauses, controlled practice)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The question that opens the article on the board – who are the people in your life that you place your trust in? – answered in a line by three people; the text was read last lesson, so go straight to the sentence.
stages.avoid: Do not set the reading tasks again.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Grammar ex A with the article open at p. 98: the relative clause underlined in each highlighted sentence, then ex B in pairs – defining or non-defining, and how they know; the six sentences go on the board.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex C: the six sentences matched to the six rules – that for who/which only in defining clauses, the pronoun dropped only when it is the object, commas round a non-defining clause, where and whose never dropped, the preposition first in formal English; confirm against the board and concept-check the one that changes meaning (my sister, who lives in Leeds – how many sisters?). Then Pronunciation ex A with track 9.1 – the pitch steps down on the non-defining clause – and ex B with track 9.2, drilled.
stages.avoid: It is a review with one new point for most: the comma and pitch of the non-defining clause. Do not re-teach who, which and where from scratch.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Hub p. 139, 9.1 ex A (eight choices) and ex B (six pairs of sentences joined, pronoun omitted where possible); compare with a partner, answer key, and the rule named on the disputed ones.

stages.name: Freer practice: the review rewritten
stages.todo: Ex E: the Meal Maker review rewritten in pairs with relative clauses that add information to each feature – the Teacher’s Book has a model version – then a second short review of an app they actually use, written together; the source suggested writing as the sub aim, and this is where it happens.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two reviews read out, then three sentences from the writing on the board, one with the comma missing, for the class to correct.

s10.sources:
Roberts, R., Clare, A. & Wilson, J.J. (2011) New Total English Intermediate Students’ Book. Pearson.

1A.context: Unit 1 Friends and family – cultural misunderstandings, best friends and how many friends you should have

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have improved their fluency telling the story of a cultural misunderstanding, their own or one they saw happen, after reading and retelling the two stories in the book.
slots.sub: To practise using five phrases from the texts for telling that kind of story: at first I thought…, I was on my best behaviour, I’d had enough, I turned bright red, I wanted to make a good impression.
slots.pages: New Total English Intermediate SB p. 10 ex 9, 10a–10c (Student A’s text ‘Not in my culture…’) / SB p. 147 (Student B’s text and questions, Unit 1 Lesson 1.1 ex 10a)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 9 on p. 10: the five photos (the dancer, the bow, the mint tea, the two men greeting, the café) and the three questions — what aspects of culture do they show, what is typical of your culture, how is yours different from the others. Pairs, three minutes, then take one typical feature of their culture from two or three pairs and board them. That board is where the stories will come from, so leave it up.

stages.name: Blocking words
