stages.todo: Four items only, the ones the two texts do not make clear on their own: a term of endearment, to insult somebody, to be on your best behaviour, to throw up. A sentence of context for each, let them give you the word where they can, then a quick drill of endearment and insult with the stress marked. Four minutes, because the texts are the way in to the speaking, not the lesson.
stages.avoid: Do not pre-teach gordita, wrinkly or sultani. The texts explain all three themselves, and the explaining is part of what the reader has to retell.

stages.name: Model texts – jigsaw reading
stages.todo: Ex 10a. Halve the room: A reads Kyle’s story on p. 10 and answers its four questions; B reads François’s story on p. 147 and answers the four questions printed there. Alone, six minutes, then A checks with another A and B with another B. Walk round and confirm answers at the desks — there is no open-class check here, because the other half of the room must not hear the story yet.
stages.avoid: This is ten minutes and no more. It is a jigsaw, so each half only reads one text: if you run both texts past everybody there is nothing left to tell in the next stage.

stages.name: Retelling
stages.todo: Ex 10b. Re-pair every A with a B, books closed. A tells Kyle’s story, B asks about anything unclear; then they swap. Give them the two questions the listener must be able to answer afterwards — what went wrong, and what the explanation was. In open class, ask a B to tell you A’s story and an A to tell you B’s, which is how you find out whether the retelling worked.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Five phrases, all lifted from the two stories, on the board: at first I thought…, I was on my best behaviour, I’d had enough, I turned bright red, I wanted to make a good impression. Elicit which part of a misunderstanding story each one belongs to (the start, the breaking point, the embarrassment, the reason). Drill them as whole phrases, fast, with the stress on enough, red and impression. Leave the board up through the task.
stages.avoid: It is useful language, not a target: nobody fails the task for not using it. What you want is the phrases available to them when they reach that point in their own story.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Ex 10c in groups of three: a cultural misunderstanding of their own, or one they have watched a visitor to their country fall into. Anyone who has neither tells a misunderstanding between generations or between two towns — the shape of the story is the same. Two minutes each, listeners ask one question per story, and the group picks the best one to tell the room. Listen with a pen for the feedback.
stages.avoid: Give them a minute of silence to choose their story before the groups start. Without it the first speaker tells a long story while the other two are still thinking of theirs.

stages.name: Feedback on content and language
stages.todo: Each group’s chosen story in one sentence, told by someone other than its owner. Then three or four sentences from your monitoring on the board, right and wrong mixed, one of them a good use of a phrase from the board; pairs sort them, you confirm.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised reading for gist and for detail in the context of how many friends a person should have.
slots.sub: To develop students’ vocabulary for talking about friendship from the article — acquaintance, close friend, inner group, worth, generation, social skills.
slots.pages: New Total English Intermediate SB p. 12 ex 5a–5b, 6 (the article ‘How many friends should you have?’) / SB p. 13 ex 7, 8

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The book gives no way in, so make one: the article’s title on the board — How many friends should you have? — and in pairs they agree on a number and on how many of those are friends they could ring at four in the morning. Board three or four pairs’ numbers. They will check them against the article later, which is what makes the numbers worth boarding.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Three items, because the tasks need them and the text does not explain them: acquaintance (someone you know a little, not a friend — check it against close friend), worth (how much is each friend ‘worth’ is question 1 of ex 6) and generation. Elicit from a context sentence each, with one concept question, and move on.
stages.avoid: Leave inner group and social skills alone. The article defines the first and the second is transparent; they belong to the vocabulary you pick up after reading.

stages.name: Prediction
stages.todo: Ex 5a: four statements, true or false, decided in pairs before anyone reads — more friends means more money, most people have about 150 friends, the Facebook average is 700, most people have one or two close friends. Take a show of hands on each and do not confirm anything.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 5b: they read the article once to check the four statements. Three minutes — the Teacher’s Book says no more, and the limit is what makes it a gist read. Pair check, then confirm: T, T (though not all close), F (130), F (about five), and make them correct the false ones. Then back to the board: whose number from the lead-in was closest to the article’s 150 and five?

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 6, five questions that need the text — two percent of salary, better social skills do better at work, 100 acquaintances, more than 300 million Facebook users, and the writer’s view that technology changes nothing about close friends. Four minutes alone, then pairs point at the line that gave them each answer. Check in open class and ask the Teacher’s Book’s follow-up: which answer surprised you?
stages.avoid: Ex 9–12 at the bottom of p. 13 are the grammar section, and the Active grammar box takes its five sentences from this article. That is tomorrow’s first lesson, not yours — do not touch the box, and do not draw attention to the tenses.

stages.name: Post-reading discussion
stages.todo: Ex 7 on p. 13: the three website comments (Sylwia would never accept an online friend she has not met, Jon reads Facebook at work, Rui thinks hundreds of online friends means attention-seeking). Pairs read and decide who they agree with and why — four minutes. Then ex 8 in groups of three or four: what is the right number of friends, and why. Give them the article’s figures to argue with. Stay out and listen with a pen.

stages.name: Feedback on content and language
stages.todo: One number and one reason from each group. Then three sentences from your monitoring on the board, one correct — make one of them a use of acquaintance or close friend so the vocabulary gets a second outing — and pairs decide which to fix before you confirm.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised using ten adjectives for describing personality — dependable, encouraging, generous, jealous, kind-hearted, mean, pleasant, selfish, sulky, upbeat — to talk about the people they are friends with.
slots.sub: To give students practice in listening for specific information: Pete answering four questions about his best friend Rob.
slots.pages: New Total English Intermediate SB p. 11 ex 1a–1b – audio track 1.5 (Pete on his best friend) / SB p. 11 ex 2a–2c / SB p. 11 ex 3a–3b – audio tracks 1.6, 1.7 (the four sounds of ‘ea’) / Workbook p. 6 ex 1, 2

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1a on p. 11, the four questions about a best friend: who, where and when you met, what you like about them, how they differ from you. Pairs, then the Teacher’s Book’s own twist — change partners and ask again, so each person tells it twice. Take two answers to question 3 in open class and board the adjectives you hear; some of the target set may already be in the room.

stages.name: Listening
stages.todo: Ex 1b with track 1.5: Pete answers the same four questions about Rob, and they note his answers. One play, compare with a neighbour, then confirm — Rob, met about three years ago working at the same school, he seems younger than he is and they share a sense of humour, he likes cricket. The recording is six minutes of the lesson, no more: it is the context the adjectives come out of, not a listening lesson.
stages.avoid: Cricket comes up. If nobody knows what it is, one sentence — a bat-and-ball game played in England and its former colonies — and move on; it is not what the lesson is about.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ask what words Pete used for Rob — sincere, funny, kind — and board them. Then ex 2a: ten definitions completed with the adjectives in the box. Pairs, with the box visible, and when they finish let two pairs join to compare before you take answers. The answers are the meanings; the teaching is next.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning first: which five are things you want in a friend and which five are not (ex 2a has just told them), then concept questions on the three that cause trouble — mean (does a mean person spend money on you?), jealous (is a jealous person happy when you do well?), sulky (does a sulky person shout, or go quiet?). Form: all adjectives, so a/an + adjective + person, and kind-hearted as a hyphenated compound. Pronunciation is where ‘ea’ bites, and the book has it ready: ex 3a with track 1.6 sorts fearful, jealous, kind-hearted, mean, pleasant, upbeat into /iː/ /e/ /ɪə/ /ɑː/, and 3b with 1.7 checks it. Drill all ten with the stress marked — dePENdable, enCOURaging, GENerous.
stages.avoid: Mean here is the opposite of generous. One learner will offer ‘cruel’; take it as a second meaning and park it, because the Workbook practice (p. 6 ex 1 item 6) tests the money one.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 6 ex 1: eight sentences choosing between two adjectives — kind-hearted or sulky, dependable or jealous, encouraging or mean. Alone, then compare with a neighbour, take only the ones they argued about. Then ex 2 on the same page, five meaning questions, as a quick second pass; question 3 (the pair of opposites) is the one to check in open class.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 2b: the three adjectives that matter most in a good friend, with reasons, agreed in pairs. Then ex 2c with a new partner: a friend who one of the adjectives describes, and why — the book’s model about Lucia the encouraging friend is worth putting up, because it shows the adjective followed by a story, not just a label.
stages.avoid: Ex 2b can swallow the stage if it becomes a debate. Three minutes for the ranking, four for ex 2c, and the second half is the one where the words actually get used.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One friend described by two or three students, in a sentence each. Then two items from your monitoring on the board, one right and one wrong, for the class to sort.

1B.context: Unit 1 Friends and family – how many friends, falling out, and the Dassler brothers

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised using the present simple and present continuous accurately, including state verbs, to ask and answer questions about their routines and about what is going on in their lives at the moment.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency, finding things they have in common with other people in the room.
slots.pages: New Total English Intermediate SB p. 13 ex 9a–9b (Active grammar box – the five sentences come from yesterday’s article), 10, 11, 12 / Workbook p. 7 ex 6 / SB p. 19 Reference (present simple and present continuous)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book’s own lead-in: two sentences on the board — I am a teacher, and I’m wearing… with whatever you have on today. Pairs decide what is different about them, then write two of their own, one of each kind, and read them to each other. Elicit the two names, present simple and present continuous. Keep it to four minutes: the sentences from yesterday’s article do the real work next.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 9a on p. 13: the five sentences in the Active grammar box all come from yesterday’s article (people with better social skills do better, I have more than 700 Facebook friends, I’m studying as well as working, I see them once a week, I’m reading this at work), and they match each to a rule A–E. Alone, then compared. Do not re-read the article; remind them who said each line and move on.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Take the matching (1 B, 2 C, 3 E, 4 A, 5 D) and use it to board the meaning split: present simple for routines, permanent facts and states; present continuous for now and for temporary situations around now. Then the point the box is built for — ex 9b, the twelve verbs sorted into action, state and both. The Teacher’s Book’s pair for it is I hate cheese / I’m hating cheese: which is wrong and why. Concept-check live and have, which sit in both columns, with the Reference on p. 19 (we’re having a holiday / we have a room). Form: this is a review, so board positive, negative and question for both tenses in two lines each, and spend the time on the questions and negatives, which is where the errors will come. Pronunciation: the weak do you /dəjə/ and are you /əjə/ at the start of a question — drill What do you do? and Are you reading a good book? until they come out as one piece.
stages.avoid: Twelve minutes is for the state verbs and the question forms. Do not re-teach the two tenses from scratch: the room has met them before, and the test of this lesson is whether anyone says ‘I’m knowing’ or ‘Do you reading?’ in the mingle at the end.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 10 on p. 13: ten gaps, present simple or continuous — Are you reading that book?, Sasha doesn’t work on Tuesdays, I need a holiday, I don’t want to leave too late because I hate driving in the dark. Alone, then pairs check against the box, then open class on the ones they disagreed on, with the reason each time. Then Workbook p. 7 ex 6: eight sentences, four of them wrong, all of them state verbs in the continuous (I’m not understanding, Are you wanting, He’s having a very good job, I’m knowing). Find and correct, quick check.

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 11: ten questions built from prompts — What/you/do?, How often/you/go out with friends?, You/read/a good book/at the moment? Pairs, and make them say the whole question aloud rather than write it, because the question form is what the clarification was for. Check the ten in open class, fast, one question each round the room.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 12 turned into a mingle rather than one partner: they move round the room asking the ex 11 questions and must find two people they have something non-obvious in common with — not that you both live here or both study English. Model it yourself first: ask a student three questions and say Me too! when you hit one. Two minutes a partner, you call the change, and they note the name and the thing in common.
stages.avoid: If you let them stay with one partner the whole time, the questions get asked once and the stage is over in three minutes. The partner change is what makes the ten questions get used.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Three students report one thing they found in common with someone. Then two sentences from your monitoring on the board, one right and one wrong, for the class to sort.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised listening for gist and for specific information in the context of three people describing someone they fell out with.
slots.sub: To develop students’ vocabulary for arguing from the recording — have an argument, get angry, lose your temper, have a huge row, fall out over something, see red.
slots.pages: New Total English Intermediate SB p. 14 ex 1a–1c – audio track 1.8 (three speakers: a father, Romina, Sarah) / SB p. 14 ex 2 (vocabulary – arguing), 3

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book’s warmer, because the topic is new: fight, argue, discuss, fall out with on the board, and pairs decide which is the odd one out (discuss — the only one with no disagreement in it). Then the three photos A–C on p. 14: who are the people and what is the relationship between them? Take guesses and confirm nothing; the recording settles it.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Three items from the recording that the table in ex 1b depends on: a colleague (speaker 3 talks about one), to be a big influence on someone (speaker 1 on his father) and to be in touch with someone (speaker 2 and Romina are not). Context sentence, elicit, one concept question each, and move on.
stages.avoid: Do not pre-teach lose your temper, fall out or have a row. They are the vocabulary of ex 2, which the students pull out of the recording themselves after the listening — teaching them now empties that stage.

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex 1a with track 1.8: three people on someone they fell out with, matched to the photos A–C. One play straight through, check in pairs, confirm (1 B, 2 A, 3 C) and ask what word told them — father, best friend, supermarket.

stages.name: Listening for specific information
stages.todo: Ex 1b, the table: who they talk about, how long they have known each other, why and when they fell out, how the relationship is now. Give them a minute with the table first. Play again, pausing after each speaker so they can write; then ex 1c, pairs compare. Check against a completed table on the board rather than reading twelve answers out — his father, all his life, came home at five in the morning aged fifteen, fine now; Romina, twelve years, fell out over money on holiday last year, no contact; Sarah, a colleague for one year, said bad things about her, still not speaking.
stages.avoid: Two plays and that is the budget. If the table is half empty after the second, fill it from the board, not with a third play — the vocabulary stage needs the recording once more.

stages.name: Vocabulary from the recording
stages.todo: Ex 2: the table of arguing phrases with gaps — have an argument, get angry, lose your temper, have a huge row, fall out over something, see red. Check argument first (the Teacher’s Book flags it). Pairs guess the missing words, then one more play to check — the phrases are in the recording, which is the point. Then drill the six as whole phrases: row rhymes with now, and the stress is on temper and red.

stages.name: Post-listening discussion
stages.todo: Ex 3 in new groups of three: do you argue with friends, have you ever fallen out with a close friend and what happened, what do friends and family usually argue about. Tell them to use at least two phrases from the table. Walk round and note what you hear; the Teacher’s Book’s own suggestion is to collect the errors for the board.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One answer to question 3 from each group. Then three or four sentences from your monitoring on the board, right and wrong mixed, at least one of them a phrase from ex 2 used well, and the room votes on each one before anyone corrects anything.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised reading for gist and for detail in the context of a true story about two brothers who fell out, the founders of Adidas and Puma.
slots.sub: To develop students’ ability to work out the meaning of new words from context — supplied, founded, relocated, market leaders — and to use them to retell the story.
slots.pages: New Total English Intermediate SB p. 14 ex 4a–4b, 5, 6 (Lifelong learning box), 7 / SB p. 15 (the article ‘Brotherly love?’)

stages.name: Lead-in and prediction
stages.todo: The photos on p. 15 — the Adidas and Puma logos and the statue of a man with the footballer Messi. Pairs: what connects them? Take ideas. Then ex 4a, the box of six items (a business, an argument, a nickname, a shoemaker, a wild cat, the 1932 Olympic Games): in pairs they guess how each one fits into a story about two brothers. Board three or four of the guesses and confirm nothing — the gist read checks them.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Two items only: nickname (the brothers’ story turns on one — Adi) and a split (the noun in paragraph 6, which the true-or-false in ex 5 needs). Elicit each from a sentence, with one concept question, and move on. Everything else either explains itself or is the job of ex 6.
stages.avoid: Do not touch supplied, founded, relocated or market leaders. Guessing those from context is the lesson’s sub aim, and it only works if nobody has told them first.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 4b: they read the article on p. 15 once, three minutes, to find out what the six items in the box have to do with the story. Pair check, then back to the board — which predictions were right? Confirm quickly: the brothers argued and founded Adidas and Puma, their father was a shoemaker, Puma is named after the wild cat, their first company shod Germany’s athletes in 1932.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 5: six statements, true or false — the father was a sportsman, they first made shoes at home, they argued about the shoes, they started their own companies, Puma sells more, the town has forgotten. Four minutes alone, pairs compare and point at the line, then check in open class (F, T, F, T, F, F) and make them correct every false one, which is where the detail is.

stages.name: Guessing meaning from context
stages.todo: Ex 6 and the Lifelong learning box beside it. Ask first what they do when they meet a word they do not know — dictionary, ignore it, work it out — and get a show of hands. Then the four definitions, each with its paragraph number: provided a product (supplied), created a company (founded), moved permanently (relocated), the most successful companies (market leaders). Pairs, text open. Check, and ask how the paragraph told them.

stages.name: Retelling the story
stages.todo: Ex 7 in new pairs, books closed: they retell the story in turns, one taking it up to the argument and the other from there. The book asks for the arguing phrases from ex 2 — have a row, fall out over something, lose your temper, taught in the lesson before this one — and the four verbs from ex 6, so put both lists on the board before they start and tell them the target is to use three.
stages.avoid: Ex 2 is the listening lesson’s vocabulary table, not something in your part of the page. Check with the teacher before you that it was taught; if it was not, give the six phrases yourself in one minute, because the retelling is built on them.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One pair retells the whole story to the room, one sentence each, round the class. Then three sentences from your monitoring on the board, right and wrong mixed, one of them with founded or relocated used well, and they rewrite the faulty one alone, then compare.

2A.context: Unit 1 into Unit 2 Media – famous siblings, then films: a review of Man on Wire, and dubbing or subtitles

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised choosing between the present perfect simple and the past simple to talk about what has happened in their lives — finished time against time that reaches up to now — with for, since and ago.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency, telling a partner true and false things about their past and recent lives.
slots.pages: New Total English Intermediate SB p. 16 ex 8a–8b (Active grammar box – the eight extracts come from yesterday’s article on p. 15), 9, 10 / Workbook p. 8 ex 4 / SB p. 19 Reference (present perfect simple and past simple)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book’s lead-in: two wrong sentences on the board — I lived here since 2001 and I have seen him yesterday. Pairs fix them, you board the corrections with the verbs underlined and elicit the two names. One question to the room: what did the brothers in yesterday’s story do in 1948, and what has happened since? That re-opens the text without re-reading it.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 8a on p. 16: eight extracts from the Dassler story, each marked present perfect or past simple. Since 1928 they have supplied shoes…, On 1st July 1924 they formed a shoe company…, They worked together for many years, The companies have now been in competition for over sixty years. Alone, then pairs, and the Teacher’s Book asks pairs to try a rule for the difference before you give one.
stages.avoid: The story was yesterday’s reading. Do not hand the article out again or set a reading task — the extracts are on p. 16 and that is all the text this lesson needs.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex 8b, the rules in the box, done from their own matching. The contrast is the lesson: past simple for a finished time with no link to now (in 1948, in 1924, for many years — the working-together is over), present perfect for a period that runs up to now (since 1928, for over sixty years — the competition is still on). Draw the two on a timeline and concept-check with the Dasslers: are the companies still competing? Did the brothers stop working together? Then for and since: a period against a point, and ago only with the past simple. Form: have/has + past participle, contracted in speech. Pronunciation: the weak ’ve and ’s — they’ve supplied, it’s been — drilled in two of the extracts so the auxiliary does not disappear. The Reference on p. 19 is the check.
stages.avoid: The box runs to six rules and brings in just, yet and already. Leave those for ex 10 to introduce in practice; if you try to clarify all six, the contrast — the one thing this lesson is for — gets three minutes.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 9: three short texts about famous siblings — the Williams sisters, the Gyllenhaals, the Cruz family — with five choices between have played and played, starred and have starred, hasn’t learnt and didn’t learn. Alone, compare with a neighbour against the box, and in open class they say why for each one, not just which.

stages.name: Controlled practice 2
stages.todo: Ex 10: six sentences about the Minogue sisters with the time words from the box — since, ago, already, yet, for, just. Pairs. Then Workbook p. 8 ex 4: seven sentences, some right and some wrong (I haven’t had a cigarette since three weeks, I’ve lived here since ten years), to tick or correct. Take the ones they disagreed on and elicit where since and for went wrong.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: The book gives no speaking for this grammar, so this is yours: each student writes four sentences about their own life, two in the present perfect (I’ve lived…, I’ve never…) and two in the past simple with a time (… ago, in 20…), and one of the four is false. Partners guess the false one and ask two follow-up questions, which pull the past simple out of them (When did you…? Why?). Model it with four sentences of your own before they write, and give them two minutes of silence to write.
stages.avoid: The follow-up questions are the real practice. Without them the stage is four sentences read aloud and a guess; say it when you set it up and hold them to it.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two or three students report one thing their partner has done and one thing they did. Then three sentences from your monitoring on the board, some correct and some not; pairs decide which, then fix the faulty ones — expect a since with a period or a present perfect with a finished time.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised giving opinions and agreeing or disagreeing politely — I think…, What do you think?, I agree actually, That’s true, but…, I’m not sure about that, It depends on… — in the context of foreign-language films.
slots.sub: To give students practice in listening for specific information: three people on dubbing against subtitles.
slots.pages: New Total English Intermediate SB p. 24 ex 7, 8a–8c – audio track 1.10 (Sue, Ekaterina and Ben on dubbing and subtitling) / SB p. 24 ex 9 (How to… box), 10a–10c – audio track 1.11 (five statements) / Workbook p. 13 ex 5

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The context was set by the reading before this lesson, so one touch is enough: ex 7, the two posters (Le Hérisson, Red Cliff) and the two questions — do you watch foreign-language films, and what kind do you like or avoid. Pairs, two minutes, then two answers in open class.

stages.name: Listening
stages.todo: Ex 8a as one quick open-class question: dubbing or subtitles, and board the popular answer. Then ex 8b with track 1.10, three people on the same question, and they note who prefers which — Sue and Ekaterina subtitles, Ben dubbing. Second play for ex 8c, the six who-thinks-what questions; pairs compare, quick check. Seven minutes: the recording is where the phrases come from, not a listening lesson.
stages.avoid: Two plays is the budget. The clarification and the practice are the lesson; if the six questions in 8c are not all answered after the second play, give the answers and move on.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 9: the How to… box, with its five headings to put in place — giving an opinion, asking for an opinion, agreeing, disagreeing, saying it may change. Pairs, then check (A giving, B asking, C agreeing, D disagreeing, E it depends). Ask which phrases they heard the three speakers use.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Six exponents to carry out of the room: I think…, What do you think?, I agree actually, That’s true, but…, I’m not sure about that, It depends on…. Meaning: which two disagree without saying no — That’s true, but… and I’m not sure about that — and why a learner who says ‘You are wrong’ sounds rude in English. Form: I think + a clause, What do you think of + a noun, it depends on + a noun or it depends who/when with no on. Pronunciation is what makes them polite: the fall-rise on I’m not SURE about that and That’s TRUE, but…, and the stress on actually in I agree actually. Drill all six as whole phrases, fast, then individually.
stages.avoid: The box holds nine phrases. Six are the target; I guess, What’s your opinion? and That makes sense stay on the page as extras for the strong students. Trying to drill nine leaves no time for the practice.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 13 ex 5 first: a dialogue about animated films with eight gaps for the phrases (I reckon, What’s your opinion, I’m not sure, That’s true, it depends on, What do you think, makes sense). On their own first, then in pairs, three minutes. Then ex 10a with track 1.11: five statements, tick agree or cross disagree; and ex 10b on a second play, pausing after each, they write a one-line response using a phrase from the box. Walk round and read what they write.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 10c: pairs discuss their responses to the five statements, agreeing and disagreeing with the phrases on the board. Then the Teacher’s Book’s extension for the last three minutes: each student names a famous person, the partner gives an opinion of them for one minute and the other agrees or disagrees, and they tick each phrase from the box as they use it. Monitor for the feedback.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Which statement split the room most, and one line from each side. Then three sentences from your monitoring on the board, right and wrong mixed — a flat I’m not sure about that counts as wrong here — and the room votes on each one before anyone corrects anything.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised reading for gist and for detail in the context of a film review: Man on Wire, the story of Philippe Petit’s walk between the twin towers.
slots.sub: To develop students’ vocabulary for describing a film from the review — gripping, poignant, fascinating, inspiring — and to use it to tell a partner about a film.
slots.pages: New Total English Intermediate SB p. 22 ex 1, 2a–2b (the review ‘Man on Wire’) / SB p. 23 ex 6 (speaking: a film you have seen)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: A new unit and a new topic, so start where the Teacher’s Book does: silver screen on the board — which medium, and why that name. Then ex 1, the photos from Man on Wire: a man on a wire between two towers. Pairs: what do you think the film is about, and is it fiction? Take guesses and board two; the review settles it.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Three items the tasks depend on and the text does not explain: a high wire, the twin towers (of the World Trade Center in New York, built in the early 1970s) and to forge documents. A quick elicit from a sentence each, with one concept question, and move on.
stages.avoid: Leave gripping, poignant, fascinating and inspiring in the text. They are the sub aim and they come out after reading, when the room has seen what each one was describing.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 2a, questions 1–3 only: what type of film (a docu-drama), what it is about, and whether the critic liked it and why (fascinating and inspiring). Three minutes, alone. Pairs compare and add question 4 — would you enjoy it? Check 1–3 in open class and ask, as the Teacher’s Book does, which words told them the critic’s opinion.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 2b: seven statements, true or false — the towers were already built when Petit decided, he walked six years later, he was already experienced, they got permission, they used a bow and arrow, his team filmed the walk, he came off the wire as soon as he saw the police. Four minutes alone, pairs compare and point at the line, check in open class and correct the false ones: F (going to be built), T, T, F (forged documents), T, F (only photos), F (he stayed 45 minutes).
stages.avoid: Ex 3–5 on p. 23 are the grammar section, defining relative clauses, and this set does not teach them. Do not stray onto them, and do not pick out who, which and whose in the review — it is a reading lesson.

stages.name: Vocabulary from the text
stages.todo: The four adjectives the review uses for the film: gripping (the story), poignant (the photos of the towers), fascinating and inspiring (the adventure). Pairs find each in the text and decide what it was describing and whether it is positive. Then meaning in open class — gripping is a story you cannot put down, poignant is sad in a way that stays with you — and pronunciation: the silent g in poignant /ˈpɔɪnjənt/, stress on the first syllable of all four except inspiring. Drill and board.

stages.name: Post-reading speaking
stages.todo: Ex 6 on p. 23: a film they have seen, told to a partner under the four headings — the type, the main characters, what happens, scenes they remember — and with at least one of the four adjectives. Two minutes to make notes, then tell it; then the Teacher’s Book’s variation, which is better: new pairs, and the listener has to guess the film from the description. Listen with a pen.
stages.avoid: Give the two minutes of notes before anyone speaks. A film plot told without notes becomes a ten-minute monologue from one student while the other waits.

stages.name: Feedback on content and language
stages.todo: Which film described in the room sounded the most worth seeing — one vote. Then three sentences from your monitoring on the board, right and wrong mixed, one with an adjective from the review used well, and pairs decide which to fix before you confirm.

2B.context: Unit 2 Media – eco-gadgets, television, and Britain’s oldest working TV set

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised forming and using the passive — be + past participle — to say what happens to things when who did it is unknown or does not matter, in the context of the history of television.
slots.sub: To give students practice in reading for specific information: the article about Britain’s oldest working television.
slots.pages: New Total English Intermediate SB p. 26 ex 8, 9 (the article ‘Completely reliable… and built to last’) / SB p. 27 ex 11 (Active grammar box), 12, 13a–13b – audio track 1.15 / Workbook p. 14 ex 2

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 8: the photos of old televisions on p. 26 and the two questions — when were they made, and how are they different from a TV today. Pairs, two minutes, two answers in open class. Television is yesterday’s context and the unit’s, so that is all the setting the lesson needs.

stages.name: Reading
stages.todo: Ex 9: the article about the Marconiphone 702, read once to find what the five numbers in the box refer to — 1948, 3,000, 1936, 11,000, 12. Three minutes, compare with a neighbour, confirm (the London Olympics, TVs lost in the bombing, the year it was made, 60 guineas in today’s money, the screen in inches). Check converted and broadcast as you go if anyone stops on them. That is the whole reading: six minutes, because the text is here to supply the grammar.
stages.avoid: Ex 10, the true/false/not-given task, is a reading lesson’s detail stage and it is not yours. The source document listed it; the lesson does not need it. Six minutes on the text, then the language.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 11: the four gapped sentences in the Active grammar box, completed from the article — it is thought to be, it was made, the set has been converted, it can be used — and then the three rules A–C matched to the three example sentences. Alone, then pairs. Board the four sentences as they give them to you; they are the model for the next stage.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning from the four sentences on the board: who made the set? who converted it? — nobody says, because it does not matter; the thing it happened to is the subject. The Teacher’s Book’s lead-in is a good concept check here — John Logie Baird invented the TV against The TV was invented by John Logie Baird: same fact, different focus, and by when the doer matters. Form: be + past participle, and the be carries the tense — is, was, has been, can be — which is what the four sentences show. Pronunciation: the weak forms, was /wəz/ and been /bɪn/, and the past participle endings in converted and made; drill It was made over seven decades ago and It’s thought to be the oldest. The unit’s Reference section at the back of the unit is there if they ask for more.
stages.avoid: One structure, one meaning: the passive to shift the focus onto the thing affected. Do not spend the stage on passive forms of every tense in the language; the four in the box are enough, and the practice tests exactly those.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 12: six active sentences rewritten in the passive — could be received, is replaced, are made, could be watched. Do the first in open class as the Teacher’s Book does (active or passive? which verb?), then pairs, with the box as the check. Workbook p. 14 ex 2, eight more of the same, is there for the pair that finishes first.

stages.name: Controlled practice 2
stages.todo: Ex 13a: eight sentences of a news story about fake DVDs, each with one word missing — have been jailed, were produced by, were sold, is estimated by the police. Alone, no check in pairs yet; then 13b with track 1.15, which reads the story correctly, and they listen to check. The recording is the answer key, so hold your feedback until after it.

stages.name: Freer practice and feedback
stages.todo: The book gives no freer stage and the Teacher’s Resource Disc is not on the card, so this is yours: pairs pick an object everyone knows — a phone, a bicycle, a newspaper — and write four passive sentences about it without naming it (it was invented in…, it is made of…, it is used for…, it can be found…). Read them to another pair, who guess the object. Two sentences from your monitoring on the board at the end for the class to correct.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised listening for gist and for detail in the context of a radio programme about four eco-gadgets.
slots.sub: To give students practice in using yesterday’s phrases for giving opinions and agreeing or disagreeing — I think…, I’m not sure about that, That’s true, but… — to decide which gadget they would want.
slots.pages: New Total English Intermediate SB p. 25 ex 1a–1c – audio track 1.12 (radio programme: Julian, Anna, Chris, Joe) / SB p. 25 ex 2, 3 / SB p. 24 How to… box (the opinion phrases from the previous day, for ex 3)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: A new context, so use the Teacher’s Book’s warmer: gadget on the board and three definitions to choose from — a machine for cleaning the house, a mechanical or electronic device with a practical use, something different or unusual. Then one question round the room: the most important gadget in use today, and why. Finish with the Teacher’s Book’s own: is a TV a gadget, and could you live without it?

stages.name: Prediction
stages.todo: Ex 1a: the four gadgets A–D in the pictures. Pairs guess what each one is and what they all have in common. Take guesses and confirm nothing — the recording answers it.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Three items the detail task needs: wind-up (the radio and the torch — mime the handle), a solar panel, and to be powered by (petrol, the sun). Context sentence, elicit, one concept question each, and move on. Eco-friendly can be left: the room will meet it in ex 1c and the word explains itself.

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex 1b with track 1.12: four speakers, matched to the gadgets A–D. One play, check in pairs, confirm (1 A, 2 D, 3 B, 4 C) and ask which words told them. Then ex 1c without another play: what do they all have in common? They are eco-gadgets, environmentally friendly — now the lead-in guesses can be checked.

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex 2: a good point and a bad point for each gadget, noted on a second play. Give them a grid of four rows before you press play. Pairs compare, then two pairs compare, then check on the board — the bike fast and easy but petrol-powered, the wind-up radio works and looks nicer than plastic but unprofessional, the torch easy to wind but a weak solar panel, the speakers clear and cheap but ugly.
stages.avoid: Exercise 4 and exercise 5 at the bottom of the page are a language lesson — the How to… box for describing an object — and there is no room for it in a listening lesson. Stop at ex 3.

stages.name: Post-listening discussion
stages.todo: Ex 3 in groups of three: which gadget they would most like, which least, and why — and the group must agree on one to buy. Before they start, board five of yesterday’s phrases from the How to… box on p. 24 (I think…, What do you think?, I agree actually, That’s true, but…, I’m not sure about that) and tell them to use at least three. The Teacher’s Book adds: any other eco-gadgets they know of. Walk round and note what you hear.

stages.name: Feedback on content and language
stages.todo: Each group’s choice and one reason. Then three or four sentences from your monitoring on the board, right and wrong mixed, one of them an opinion phrase used well, and they rewrite the faulty one alone, then compare.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised using ten adjectives for describing television programmes — annoying, boring, entertaining, exciting, gripping, incredible, inspiring, moving, unrealistic, unwatchable — with the /n/ and /ŋ/ endings pronounced right.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency, talking about programmes they have watched.
slots.pages: New Total English Intermediate SB p. 26 ex 6a–6c, 7a–7d – audio tracks 1.13, 1.14 (/n/ and /ŋ/) / Workbook p. 14 ex 1

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book’s lead-in: television on the board and a one-minute brainstorm of words that go with it. Keep the board, because ex 6a is next and the room will have half the answers up already.

stages.name: Television collocations
stages.todo: Ex 6a: twelve words that go before or after television — channel, commercials, digital, live, on (the), presenter, producer, programme, satellite, screen, set, viewers. Pairs sort them; check fast and board the two columns. These are mostly words they know in new company, so seven minutes is enough. Then Workbook p. 14 ex 1, six sentence halves to match (a new TV set, anything good on TV, a TV producer), as a one-minute check.
stages.avoid: Do not turn the collocations into a second clarification. They are a warm-up to the adjectives, which are the lesson; if you teach both sets properly you will reach the speaking with five minutes left.

stages.name: Presentation
stages.todo: Ex 6c: the adjectives in the box sorted into positive and negative — pairs first, then check. Meaning on the ones that are not transparent: moving (makes you feel, not makes you move), gripping (you cannot stop watching), unrealistic, unwatchable (so bad you switch off). Form: nearly all -ing adjectives, and un- on two. Then the pronunciation the book built in — ex 7a with track 1.13, how the last n of entertaining sounds; 7b, every n in the box underlined and sorted /n/ or /ŋ/; 7c with track 1.14 to check and repeat. Drill the ten with the /ŋ/ ending held — boring, gripping, moving — and board them with the stress marked.
stages.avoid: Nonsense and nauseating are in the box but not in the ten: one is a noun doing adjective work and the other will not get used. Leave them as passive items and keep the drilling for the -ing words.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 6b: the word in brackets put in the right place and the sentence finished with their own idea — the best television channel is…, my favourite television presenter is…, the most exciting programme I’ve ever seen is…. Alone, then read to a partner. Then the Teacher’s Book’s variation: number the students 1–5 and each finds the most popular answer to their sentence round the room.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 7d: programmes they have seen that each adjective fits, told to a partner with the book’s frames — I thought it was…, I found it…. Then change partners and the Teacher’s Book’s extension: each student reports what the first partner said about a programme, and the new partner says whether they agree. Monitor for the /ŋ/ endings and for the adjectives.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One programme that two people in the room disagreed about, and why. Then three sentences from your monitoring on the board, right and wrong mixed, one of them an adjective with the ending said properly, and pairs decide which to fix before you confirm.

3A.context: Unit 2 Media – strange stories in the news, and telling a story of your own

slots.pages: New Total English Intermediate SB p. 28 ex 2a–2b, 3a (the six news stories A–F) / SB p. 29 ex 4, 5a–5c

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 2a on p. 28: six headlines completed with the verbs in the box (delivers, takes, escapes, saves, survives, inherits), then ex 2b — matched to the pictures A–F, and pairs guess what happened in each. The guessing is the prediction for the reading, so take two or three and board them.
stages.avoid: Ex 1 and its recording (Eben and Rachel on the news) are not on your card. The headlines are the way in.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Three items the stories do not explain: a refugee, to flood (the restaurant), a circus. Elicit from a sentence each, with one concept question, and move on.
stages.avoid: Leave take a wrong turn, get lost, move in with and the rest of ex 5a alone — they are the vocabulary stage after reading.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 3a: the six stories read quickly and matched to the six headlines. Three minutes, check in pairs, confirm, and back to the board to see whose guesses were right.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 4 on p. 29: the seven questions across the six stories — where Mrs Bright wanted to go, why the chef did not cook the lobster, who looks after Pooker, what Lala did, what Parn Hung Kuk ate. Five minutes alone, pairs point at the line, check in open class.
stages.avoid: Ex 3b–3c (the topics list) is a second task over the same stories; one detail task is enough in 45 minutes.

stages.name: Vocabulary from the text
stages.todo: Ex 5a: seven collocations from the stories completed with the verbs in the box and matched to their definitions — take a wrong turn, get lost, move in with, return to, cause damage, give first aid, take a break. Pairs, text open. Check, then drill the stress on the noun and board them.

stages.name: Retelling and discussion
stages.todo: Ex 5b, books closed: pairs retell the stories in turns with the seven phrases on the board, three stories each. Then ex 5c: which stories were the most unbelievable or funny, and what strange story have they heard recently.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One recent story from the room, then three sentences from your monitoring on the board, some correct and some not, and pairs decide which. Tell them the next lesson’s grammar comes straight out of these stories.

slots.pages: New Total English Intermediate SB p. 30 ex 7a–7b (Active grammar box; the examples are in the stories on pp. 28–29, read in the previous lesson), 8, 9 / Workbook p. 16 ex 3

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book’s lead-in: pairs recall Mrs Bright’s story from p. 28, then answer one question in a full written sentence — when did she lose her way? (as she was driving round Calais). They underline the verbs and name the two tenses. Do not set the stories again; they were read in the lesson before.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 7a: the two underlined examples in the Active grammar box and question 1 (complete, or temporary and in progress?). Then 7b: find more past continuous in the stories on pp. 28–29 and read them out — the chef was planning, he was eating a seagull, I was drinking a coffee.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Rules A and B from the box: a longer action in progress, interrupted by a shorter complete one; and setting the scene at the start of a story. Timeline on the board for I was drinking a coffee when a taxi driver shouted. Question 2, the state verbs that do not take the continuous. Form: was/were + -ing, questions and negatives. Pronunciation: the weak was /wəz/ and were /wə/, drilled in two sentences from the stories.
stages.avoid: One meaning: the long action and the short one that interrupts it. The past simple itself is not new; do not re-teach it.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 8: eight sentences, past simple or past continuous — I was working in Prague when I met my boyfriend, he didn’t break his arm while he was playing rugby. Alone, then a quick compare in pairs, reasons in open class.

stages.name: Controlled practice 2
stages.todo: Workbook p. 16 ex 3: six picture prompts (someone stole my wallet while I wasn’t looking, Josie met Clyde while they were skiing). Pairs say them aloud before writing. Ex 9 on p. 30, the little sister story, is the fast finishers’ extra.
stages.avoid: Ex 9 is also the next teacher’s model text, so take it as a gap-fill only and say nothing about the stages of a story.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Your own task, because ex 10 and 11 belong to the next lesson: three moments on the board — 8 p.m. last night, the last time the phone rang, when you heard a piece of big news — and pairs ask what were you doing and what happened next. Model one yourself first.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Three sentences from your monitoring on the board, and the room votes right or wrong on each before anyone corrects anything.

slots.pages: New Total English Intermediate SB p. 30 ex 10, 11a–11b (the story in ex 9 as the model) / SB p. 154 Writing bank – Narrative ex 1a–1b, 2 (How to… sequence a narrative), 3a–3b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Books closed, the Teacher’s Book’s question: what are the ingredients of a story? Board what they give you, then ex 10 on p. 30, the four stages — setting the scene, the main events, the big event, the result — against the board.

stages.name: Model texts
stages.todo: Ex 10: pairs mark the four stages in the little-sister story in ex 9, completed in the previous lesson. Then p. 154 ex 1a–1b, the Rio 2016 story — how the photos connect — read once, and ex 2: tick the How to… phrases used in each paragraph.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: The How to… box on p. 154 — I remember when…, A few years ago…, then / after that, Suddenly…, To my surprise…, In the end…, and I’ve never forgotten that day — sorted by the four stages. Remind them the scene is set in the past continuous and the events run in the past simple; drill the four openers.

stages.name: Preparing to write
stages.todo: Ex 11a on p. 30: choose an event — someone was born, good news, exam results, something important in the country — and ex 11b / p. 154 ex 3a: notes under the four paragraph headings. Notes only, in silence; walk round and check everyone has a big event.

stages.name: Writing task
stages.todo: P. 154 ex 3b: the story in four paragraphs, 120–150 words, with at least four phrases from the box. Plan and board in front of them; answer questions at the desk, not to the room.
stages.avoid: Fifteen minutes is the writing. If the preparation overruns, cut the lead-in next time, not this.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Drafts swap: the reader names the big event and underlines one phrase from the box. Then two sentences from the drafts on the board, one with the two tenses together done right, for the class to check. Collect the drafts.

3B.context: Unit 2 into Unit 3 Lifestyle – news collocations and gossip, describing a film, and where you live

slots.pages: New Total English Intermediate SB p. 31 ex 1a–1b, 2, 4, 5a–5b, 6a–6c / Workbook p. 17 ex 4a–4b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book’s warmer: take a ____ on the board, and pairs have a minute to complete it as many ways as they can. Board their ideas and name the thing — a collocation.

stages.name: Presentation
stages.todo: Ex 1a: nine verbs with three nouns each, one of which does not fit — make a profit / a discovery / a job. Pairs find the odd one out. Meaning on the ones that are not literal: come into money, break up with someone, cause trouble. Form: ex 2, which take a/an and which take no article (go on strike, commit suicide). Pronunciation: the stress sits on the noun — make a PROfit, comMIT a CRIME — drill the nine with their nouns and board them.
stages.avoid: Ex 3 (which newspaper page) is skipped, as the source did. Nine verbs with two nouns each is the set; do not add the Reference list.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 4: seven sentences completed with a collocation in the right tense — the Rolling Stones performed the song, Paul Getty came into billions, Marie Curie made a discovery. Then Workbook p. 17 ex 4a–4b, five sentence halves and their replies. Alone, then compare with a neighbour, disputed ones in open class.

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 5a: a famous person for each of the six prompts — has had plastic surgery, won a race recently, committed a crime, has broken a record. Then 5b, compare in pairs, and the Teacher’s Book’s twist: show the list in a different order and the partner guesses who is who with a full collocation.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 6a–6c: groups of three or four, a piece of gossip each about a famous person — made up if they like — ending with an opinion, and the group reacts with the book’s opinion lines (That’s a terrible way to behave, I feel quite sorry for her) and the agreeing and disagreeing phrases taught on day two. The Teacher’s Book’s variation: one true story and one invented, and the group decides which is which.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: The best piece of gossip from each group in a sentence. Then three sentences from your monitoring on the board, right and wrong mixed, one with the article wrong, and pairs decide which need fixing.

slots.pages: New Total English Intermediate SB p. 32 ex 1, 2a–2b – audio track 1.18 (a description of The Orphanage) / SB p. 32 ex 3 – audio track 1.19 / SB p. 32 ex 4a–4b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1 on p. 32: what makes you want to see a film — advertising, the director, friends, reviews, the stars — and the three posters A–C: which would you see, and why. Pairs, then two answers in open class.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Three items the notes in ex 2b need: an orphanage, a ghost, spooky. Elicit from a sentence each, with one concept question, and move on. Plot is a heading in the table — check it as you set the task.

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex 2a with track 1.18: one question — which of the three films is being described (A, The Orphanage). One play, compare with a neighbour, and ask what gave it away.

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex 2b: the notes table — type of film, the plot, the characters. The Teacher’s Book has pairs fill what they can from memory first; then play again and complete. Check on the board: a horror film; a woman who buys the house where she lived as a child, her son starts to see ghosts and disappears; the woman and her husband, and a spooky old woman.
stages.avoid: Two plays for ex 2. Ex 3 has its own track; do not spend a third play of 1.18 rescuing the notes.

stages.name: Listening for more detail
stages.todo: Ex 3 with track 1.19: more about the same film, notes while listening, compared in pairs and added to the table on the board.

stages.name: Post-listening speaking
stages.todo: Ex 4a: pairs choose a film they have both seen and make notes under the ex 2b headings; board the frames the recording used — It’s a … film, It’s about … who …, The main characters are …. Then 4b: pairs join into fours and describe their film without naming it; the other pair guesses. Listen with a pen.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: The film that took longest to guess, described once more to the room. Then three sentences from your monitoring on the board, one of them a frame used well, and the room votes on each one.

slots.pages: New Total English Intermediate SB p. 35 ex 1a–1b, 2a–2b (house and neighbourhood words), 3a–3b / Workbook p. 20 ex 1a

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: A new unit, so the Teacher’s Book’s warmer: you are going to tell them about your home, and pairs have two minutes to write questions to ask you. Answer them, and let them follow up. They have just heard the model for the task.

stages.name: What home means
stages.todo: Ex 1a: notes on what home means to them — favourite rooms, smells, views, special objects, feelings. Then 1b, compared in groups of three. One idea from each group in open class.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Ex 2a: the box words sorted into the table — I live in… / It’s got… for the house, and the same two for the area. Check the ones that need it (semi-detached, terraced, a cottage, an attic, a cellar, the suburbs, the outskirts), drill the stress, and 2b: one more word per column from the room. Workbook p. 20 ex 1a, seven definitions, is a two-minute check at the end.
stages.avoid: This is useful language, not a target: the task is judged on fluency. If the table runs over ten minutes, stop and move on.

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Ex 3a: pairs describe the four houses in the photos with the table’s phrases — a rehearsal of the frames before they talk about their own home.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Ex 3b: describe where you live — the place, what it has got, the area — and the listener asks two follow-up questions. Then the Teacher’s Book’s repeat with a new partner, and a third round in new pairs on the home they would most like to have. Keep the clock and monitor with a pen.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book’s feedback: one thing about the first partner’s home and one about the second. Then four sentences from your monitoring on the board, without saying which are wrong — they find out in pairs and rewrite those.

4A.context: Unit 3 Lifestyle – a home exchange: the properties, the families’ plans, and what went wrong

slots.pages: New Total English Intermediate SB p. 36 ex 1, 2 (the two property descriptions, Yourhome – My home) / SB p. 37 ex 3a–3b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1 on p. 36: the four photos, two outsides and two insides, matched in pairs, and how each place compares with where they live. Then one question to the room: would you swap your home with a stranger’s for a month? Hands up, and keep the count for the end.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Three items the texts lean on: refurbished, ensuite (bathroom) and a patio. Elicit from a sentence each, with one concept question, and move on. Victorian can wait until it comes up.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 2: the two descriptions read quickly and matched to the photos — Property 1 is the Seville apartment (A and 2), Property 2 the London house (B and 1). Two minutes. Pairs compare, and the Teacher’s Book asks for the words that decided it.
stages.avoid: The Teacher’s Book offers a jigsaw variation (A reads one, B the other). Do not take it here: the detail task needs everyone to have read both.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 3a on p. 37: seven which-property questions — near the centre, outside space, more than one bathroom, near public transport, near somewhere for children, a balcony, redecorated. Four minutes alone, pairs point at the line, check in open class with the line read out each time.
stages.avoid: Ex 4 onwards on p. 37 is the listening and the grammar — the next two lessons. Stop at ex 3b.

stages.name: Post-reading speaking
stages.todo: Ex 3b in groups of three: which of the two would they live in for a month, and why — the group has to agree on one. Then a step beyond the book: each student describes their own home in three sentences as if it were Property 3 on the website, and the group decides whose would attract the most swaps. Walk round and note what you hear.

stages.name: Feedback on content and language
stages.todo: Each group’s choice, then a second show of hands on the lead-in question to see who changed their mind. Three sentences from your monitoring on the board, and the room votes right or wrong on each one.

stages.name: Vocabulary from the texts
stages.todo: If there is time: pairs find in the two texts the words for a noisy street, a place with plants and sunlight, the floor a flat is on, and the little bars that serve tapas (heavy traffic, decorated with plenty of plants, on the third floor, local bars). Two minutes, quick check.

slots.pages: New Total English Intermediate SB p. 37 ex 4a–4b – audio track 1.20 (the Armitage and Dos Santos families’ plans) / SB p. 37 ex 5 (Active grammar box), 6 / SB p. 38 ex 7a–7c / Workbook p. 20 ex 2, 3 / SB p. 47 Reference (future plans)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book’s lead-in: three sentence halves on the board — I’m going to… / I think I’ll… / I’m meeting… — matched to buy a new car, buy my own house one day, the owner tomorrow evening. Pairs match, then write one true sentence of their own with each opener. The home exchange is the morning’s context, so one line links it: the two families are about to swap, and they have plans.

stages.name: Listening
stages.todo: Ex 4a with track 1.20: six activities marked D (Dos Santos) or A (Armitage). One play, quick check. Then ex 4b: the six extracts with a choice of forms — ’ll spend or ’re spending, going to do or doing — predicted in pairs first, then a second play to check. The extracts are the examples for the grammar, so board the six as they confirm them.
stages.avoid: Eight minutes is the whole listening. It is a way in to the forms, not a listening lesson.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 5: the six sentences from 4b matched to the three rules in the Active grammar box — be going to for something decided (2, 4, 5), will for a decision made now or an offer (3, 6), the present continuous for an arrangement with a date (1). Pairs, then check.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: The three meanings from the board: decided earlier (going to), decided this second or offered (will), arranged with someone (present continuous). Concept questions on the pair that overlaps: I’m going to see the villages against I’m meeting the owner tomorrow — which one has a time fixed with another person? Form: going to + infinitive, ’ll + infinitive, be + -ing. Pronunciation: ’ll and won’t, and going to at speed. Drill two of the extracts. The Reference on p. 47 is the check.
stages.avoid: Three forms is the book’s lesson, but the contrast to teach is decided-earlier against decided-now; the present continuous for arrangements is the third and gets the least time.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 6: the two family texts with eight gaps filled from the box (’m starting, ’re going to, ’s moving, ’ll). On their own first, then in pairs, reasons in open class. Then Workbook p. 20 ex 2 and 3 (will or going to in four mini-dialogues; one word added to five sentences) for the pair that finishes first.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 7a–7c on p. 38: ten things to do before a month abroad, listed alone; then pairs guess each other’s lists with yes/no questions (Are you going to get a passport?); then they look at each other’s lists and offer to help (I’ll get you some suntan lotion…). The offer is where will comes out, so make the third step happen.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Three sentences from your monitoring on the board, and each pair rewrites the faulty ones before you show the correct versions.

slots.pages: New Total English Intermediate SB p. 38 ex 9, 10a–10b – audio track 1.21 (Miriam and Jeremy on their problems) / SB p. 38 ex 10c, 11 (How to… complain politely) – audio track 1.22 (Miriam phones the company) / SB p. 38 ex 12a–12b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 9 on p. 38: the four pictures of the two families during the exchange. Pairs predict what went wrong in each; board the predictions, as the Teacher’s Book does, because the first listening checks them.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Three items the tasks need: in the middle of nowhere, mosquitoes, compensation (what the company offers Miriam). Elicit from a sentence each, with one concept question, and move on.

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex 10a with track 1.21: the two interviews, listened to once to check the predictions on the board. Pair check, then confirm which guesses were right.

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex 10b: a second play, notes on four problems each — Miriam’s old dark house in the middle of nowhere with no heating or hot water; Jeremy’s tiny hot flat, the mosquitoes, the bar downstairs until four in the morning. Pairs compare, check on the board.

stages.name: Listening for detail – the complaint
stages.todo: Ex 10c with track 1.22, Miriam phoning the company: six questions — how long the journey took, the bathroom, why the house was a mess, what she had to buy, the heating, what compensation she was offered. Pairs compare, check. Then ex 11 on one more play: the How to… box, marking M for Miriam’s phrases and R for the representative’s. Drill the four she uses (I don’t like to complain, but…, I’m sorry, but…, it just isn’t good enough, I’d like you to…) — they are the roleplay’s language.
stages.avoid: Three plays across the two tracks is the budget. If ex 11 is thin after the third, give the answers and drill; do not play it a fourth time.

stages.name: Post-listening roleplay
stages.todo: Ex 12a: from their notes, what should Jeremy ask for? Brainstorm compensation on the board for one minute. Then 12b: A is Jeremy ringing to complain, B the representative explaining and apologising, with the How to… box open. Swap roles and partners once. Listen with a pen.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Which pair got the best compensation. Then three lines from your monitoring on the board, one a complaint phrase used well, and pairs decide which need fixing.

4B.context: Unit 3 Lifestyle – city life: a poem about the city, adjectives for places, and the best cities to live in

slots.pages: New Total English Intermediate SB p. 39 ex 1a–1c – audio track 1.23 (city sounds) / SB p. 39 ex 2a–2b – audio track 1.24 (the poem ‘In the city’) / SB p. 39 ex 3a–3c, 4

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1a with track 1.23: a minute of sounds — are they in the city or the country, and which of the box they heard (car horns, engines, sirens, people talking). Then 1b–1c: the sounds where they live, morning to night, compared in pairs. Say the box words aloud as you check them; the lesson is about sound.

stages.name: Listening to the poem
stages.todo: Ex 2a with track 1.24: they listen and read the poem and match the four verses to the photos A–D. Then 2b on a second read: what the poet hears and sees in each verse, and whether he enjoys it (he does). Pairs, then check, and only then the glossary — swish, swash, sputter, swoosh, scurrying, shimmer, lull.
stages.avoid: Nine minutes. The poem is the text the sound features come out of; it is not a reading lesson.

stages.name: Highlighting the sound features
stages.todo: Ex 3a–3c in pairs: the rhymes (hurrying/scurrying, races/faces/places, nights/lights/heights, creep/sleep), the words that sound like what they describe (swash, swoosh, sputter), and the words close together that start with the same sound (sweepers/swooshing, pacing/places, city/senses/sleep). Take the answers; the teaching is next.

stages.name: Clarifying the sound features
stages.todo: Three things, named and drilled: rhyme (the same final sound, so lights and heights, not lights and lives), onomatopoeia (the Teacher’s Book’s hiss for a snake), and alliteration (phone and fun — the same first sound, not the same first letter). Model and drill the lines that carry them — the /sw/ cluster in swishes, swashes, swooshing, the /s/ run in city, senses, sleep — and the rhythm of a verse, with the stressed words beaten out.
stages.avoid: The terms are a tool, not the aim. One minute each on what they are; the rest of the stage is the room saying the lines.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Pairs read the poem aloud, a verse each, marking the rhymes and the stressed beats as they go; then swap verses. Listen for the clusters and the rhythm and correct at the desk.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book’s extension: groups of three write a four-line poem about city or country life with at least one rhyme, one sound-word and one alliteration, then perform it; the room guesses town or country. Ex 4 — city or a smaller place, and why — is the one-minute way in to choosing.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: The best line from the room, said twice. Then two words from your monitoring on the board for the class to say right.

slots.pages: New Total English Intermediate SB p. 40 ex 5a–5b, 6a–6b – audio track 1.25 (Heather on Kyoto), 7a–7b / Workbook p. 22 ex 1a–1b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book’s lead-in: what adjectives did the room use for city life in the poem lesson? Board them and ask for more. Half the target set may arrive by itself.

stages.name: Presentation
stages.todo: Ex 5a: the sixteen adjectives paired as opposites — bustling/quiet, clean/polluted, dull/lively, enormous/tiny, friendly/unwelcoming, modern/traditional, picturesque/ugly, unspoilt/touristy. Pairs first, then the eight that are new carry the teaching: bustling, polluted, dull, lively, picturesque, unwelcoming, unspoilt, touristy. Meaning through the opposite and a city each; form: adjectives, unspoilt and unwelcoming with un-; pronunciation: picturesque /ˌpɪktʃəˈresk/ with the stress at the end, bustling as two syllables. Drill and board with the stress marked.
stages.avoid: Sixteen words is the page, eight is the lesson. The other eight — clean, modern, quiet, tiny and so on — the room already has; confirm them in the pairing and spend nothing more.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 22 ex 1a: eight adjectives matched to definitions; then 1b, eight sentences with the adjectives in gaps (an absolutely enormous city, a tiny village with three houses, Seatown is pretty but very touristy). Alone, then a quick compare in pairs, disputed ones in open class.

stages.name: Practice in listening
stages.todo: Ex 6a with track 1.25: Heather on Kyoto — which adjectives from 5a does she use (lively, bustling, traditional, quiet, modern, friendly)? Predict in pairs first, as the Teacher’s Book does. Then 6b on a second play: what she liked and did not (the climate). Check.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 5b and 7a–7b together: a city for each adjective, then a list of what makes a city good or bad to live in, compared in pairs and settled on one city each would move to. Change pairs and repeat. Monitor for the adjectives.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: The most popular city in the room and one reason. Then three sentences from your monitoring on the board, without saying which are wrong; pairs find out and rewrite those.

slots.pages: New Total English Intermediate SB p. 40 ex 8, 9 (the article ‘Why not move to…?’ on p. 41) / SB p. 41 ex 11 (Active grammar box), 12, 13a–13b, 14a–14b / Workbook p. 22 ex 2, 3

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book’s lead-in: two gapped sentences on the board — … is taller than … / … is the tallest person in the class — completed with names from the room. Elicit the two forms’ names. Cities were the morning’s context, so say the article is about where to move to.

stages.name: Reading
stages.todo: Ex 8: skim the article on p. 41 for the four cities (Santiago, Sydney, Vancouver, Krakow). Then ex 9: which city has the old university, the skiing, the subway, thirty-seven beaches, the pollution, the ring of gardens, beaches within reach. Four minutes, check in pairs, confirm. That is the whole reading.
stages.avoid: Ex 10 (would you move there?) is a reading lesson’s response and this is a grammar lesson: eight minutes on the text, then the language.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 11: the nine rules A–I in the Active grammar box matched to the underlined examples in the article — higher than, more relaxed than, sunnier than, better than, not as good as, cleanest, the most expensive, leafiest, the best. Pairs, then check on the board.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Form is the lesson, because the meaning is known: -er and -est for one syllable, more and the most for longer adjectives, -y to -ier, the irregulars (good, bad, far), and not as … as for the negative. Spelling on the board: bigger, sunnier. Pronunciation: weak than /ðən/ and the /ə/ in -er, drilled in two sentences from the text. Board a table and leave it up.
stages.avoid: One structure: comparing. Do not spend the stage on the superlative’s one of the … constructions in rules H and I beyond the examples — ex 13b practises them.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 12: the Russia-trip text with eight comparatives and superlatives (the biggest, more comfortable, better than, as cold as). Alone, compare with a neighbour against the table. Workbook p. 22 ex 2 and 3 for the pair that finishes first.

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 13a–13b: the three comparative sentences and five superlative sentences completed about cities they know (probably the … in …, one of the most …). Read to a partner, who agrees or not.

stages.name: Freer practice and feedback
stages.todo: Ex 14a–14b: groups choose the three best places to live in the country and tell the other groups why; a vote at the end. Two sentences from your monitoring on the board for the class to correct.

5A.context: Unit 3 Lifestyle – eco-homes: the home of the future, compound nouns, and small ads

slots.pages: New Total English Intermediate SB p. 42 ex 1, 2a–2b (the article ‘What does the future hold?’) / SB p. 43 ex 5 (Active grammar box), 6, 8a–8b / Workbook p. 24 ex 1 / SB p. 47 Reference (future possibility)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1 on p. 42: the definition of eco-friendly and the two questions — have you changed how you live to be greener, and what. Pairs, two answers in open class.

stages.name: Reading
stages.todo: Ex 2a: the title, the introduction and the box of words (adaptable, climate, flooding, fuel, household waste, insulated, recycling, self-sufficient, sound waves) — pairs guess how each will matter. Then 2b, read once to check. Three minutes, confirm the guesses, and stop: the text is here for the underlined phrases.
stages.avoid: Ex 3 (the detail questions) and ex 4 (the listening) are a receptive lesson’s stages, not this one’s. Six minutes on the article, then the grammar.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 5 on p. 43: the Active grammar box completed from the underlined phrases in the article under certain, probable and possible — will definitely have to, will probably become, probably won’t be, may/might/could change, might not all have. Then the two questions under the box: where the adverb goes, and which modal has no negative.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Three degrees on a line on the board: certain (will definitely / definitely won’t), probable (will probably / probably won’t), possible (may, might, could). Concept-check with the article’s own predictions. Form: the adverb after will and before won’t; may, might and could with the infinitive and no to; could not in the negative for possibility. Pronunciation: won’t /wəʊnt/ against want, and the weak ’ll; drill three sentences from the box. The Reference on p. 47 is the check.
stages.avoid: The one structure is will + adverb for how likely something is, with may/might/could as the lower end. Do not re-teach going to and the present continuous from the earlier lesson.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 6: four sentences choosing the right order (will probably, will definitely, probably won’t, might not). Then Workbook p. 24 ex 1: eight jumbled sentences to put in order (We’ll probably see you at the party, I definitely won’t go to that restaurant again). Alone, then compare with a neighbour, disputed ones on the board.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 8a–8b: seven predictions about people in the class, written without names (She’ll probably move to the USA, He might become a famous musician), swapped with a partner who guesses who each is about; change partners once. Ex 7 (twenty-five years ago, twenty-five years ahead) is the fast finishers’ extra.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: The prediction the room found most likely, read aloud. Then three sentences from your monitoring on the board, right and wrong mixed — expect probably in the wrong place — and the room votes on each one.

slots.pages: New Total English Intermediate SB p. 44 ex 9 (the four home descriptions), 10a–10b, 11a–11c – audio track 1.27 (word stress in compound nouns), 12 / Workbook p. 24 ex 2a–2b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book’s lead-in: the four photos on p. 44 — a treehouse, a bike-powered motorhome, a house dug into a hill, a yurt. Pairs: which would be the best place to live, and why. Two answers in open class.
