Then ex 2c: eight sentences with one mistake each, mostly the preposition – a talent to it, exceptional for their field, skilled for the game, brilliant on ball sports. Alone, then compared, then confirm, with the reason each time.
stages.avoid: Ex 2b in the Workbook plays the Workbook’s recording to check 2a. Use a paper key; there is no track on your card.

stages.name: Freer practice and feedback
stages.todo: Ex 3d: five people – someone skilled at a sport or an art, someone with a talent for an instrument, someone famous they think is brilliant, someone exceptional in their field, the most successful person they know – two minutes of notes. Then ex 3e in pairs: tell each other, with a reason for each, and the listener asks one question back. Five minutes while you listen with a pen. Then two minutes: one person the room should hear about, and a preposition error from your notes written up with the preposition missing – pairs fill the gap, and you say whether the speaker had it right.

3A.context: Talent – what makes a top athlete, and learning something new

slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 35 Reading ex 1a–1f (Born to be the best) / SB p. 36 Vocabulary ex 2a / Workbook p. 17 Vocabulary ex 2b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1a on p.35: the photos, the sports and the people – who do they recognise? Then the Teacher’s Book’s own game if you want more: pairs write five clues for a famous sportsperson, hardest first, and the room guesses.

stages.name: Prediction and pre-teaching
stages.todo: Ex 1b–1c: the nine things in the box, and groups choose the five that matter most for a top athlete; pre-teach genetic make-up before they start, and gene, cell and tribe with a sentence each. Compare the groups’ five in open class and leave them on the board.
stages.avoid: Five words is the budget. Champion, competitor and victory are the vocabulary stage, not the pre-teach.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 1d: read the four texts once, quickly, for one question – what do the four sportspeople have in common? A natural, genetic advantage. Pairs, then confirm.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 1e: four questions for each sport – the sport, the example, the unusual feature, the result – in a grid on the board or a handout. Alone, then pairs, then check against the texts.

stages.name: Vocabulary from the text
stages.todo: Ex 2a on p.36: seven words in the texts with the same meaning as the italics – champion, performed, competitor, championships, training, victory, athletes, professional. Pairs with the text open, then the stress on each (CHAMpion, comPETitor, VICtory, proFESSional) and a drill. Then Workbook p.17 Vocabulary ex 2b: the same word family in a gapped text, alone, pair check.
stages.avoid: The Workbook’s ex 2a on p.17 is the Vocabulary Focus set – referee, spectators, pitch – not yours. 2b only.

stages.name: Response
stages.todo: Ex 1f in groups: which of their five things did the text mention, and does genetic make-up matter in every sport or only at the top? Six minutes, with the seven words on the board. Then one view from each group, and two sentences you heard with a sport word in them, one right and one wrong, for pairs to judge.

slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 36 Listening ex 3a, 3c – audio tracks 1.48, 1.49 (The Sports Gene on the radio) / SB p. 37 Grammar ex 4a, 4c–4e / Workbook p. 17 Grammar ex 1a

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The book cover on p.36, The Sports Gene – the texts the class read this morning came from it. What would a runner and a tennis player say about the idea that champions are born, not made?

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Ex 3a with track 1.48: who is Barbara and what does she think of the book – a runner and trainer, and she mostly agrees. Then ex 3c with track 1.49: the same two questions for Marta – a tennis professional, who agrees completely. One play each, pair check, confirm.
stages.avoid: Ex 3b and 3d are the detail tasks and a second play each. They belong to a listening lesson; yours is the grammar, so one play of each part and on.

stages.name: Highlighting target language
stages.todo: Ex 4a on p.37: four sentences from the programme – you’ve been playing tennis since you were a child, I’ve also read the book, I’ve been thinking a lot about this, I’ve lived in Kenya myself – matched to the four uses. Pairs, confirm (1b, 2a, 3d, 4c).

stages.name: Clarifying target language
stages.todo: The four on a timeline, in two columns: simple for a completed action or a life experience, continuous for an activity still going or recently going on. Concept-check with the Teacher’s Book’s pair – I’ve met Jessica Ennis-Hill (when? we don’t know) and I’ve been training for six weeks (still? yes) – and watch for the present simple for a continuing state (I live here for three years). Pronunciation: ’ve been is /vbɪn/ and the main verb carries the stress; drill the four sentences.
stages.avoid: The lesson is the contrast. If you find yourself presenting the present perfect simple from the beginning you have left the level behind.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p.17 Grammar ex 1a: ten sentences, choosing between the two forms (and in some the past simple), alone, pair check, disputed ones only. Then SB p.37 ex 4c: add a second sentence to the four prompts in whichever form fits – I haven’t played it for years, she’s been running since she was ten.

stages.name: Freer practice and feedback
stages.todo: Ex 4d–4e: a sport or activity they have been doing for some time, notes against the four questions – how good, how long and why, what made them good, does the book apply – then told to a partner who asks two questions. Six minutes, then three present perfect sentences dictated onto the board by the people who said them, for the class to check the form.
stages.avoid: Section 5 Reading and Speaking on p.37, the two baseball case studies, is a different lesson. Not on your card.

slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 34 Listening ex 4a–4b – audio track 1.44 (Seamus, Fiona and Henry) / Grammar ex 5a / Grammar Focus SB p. 139 ex a–b / Workbook p. 16 Grammar ex 1a, 1c / SB p. 34 Speaking ex 6a–6c

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The three photos on p.34 – a chemist, a comic-book writer, a saxophonist: what does each have to learn and remember to do the job?

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Ex 4a with track 1.44: who talks about the best time to learn, learning hours, the strength of memory, and do their ideas work for them? One play. Then ex 4b, notes only, on a second play paused after each speaker; pairs compare notes. Ten minutes and stop – the lesson is the verbs.
stages.avoid: Ex 4c is a discussion. Not yours.

stages.name: Highlighting target language
stages.todo: Ex 5a: be into, come up with, try out in the two sentences from the listening – what do they mean, and which is closest to the verb on its own? Then four more lines from the recording on the board with the particle gapped – making … my own stories, figure … all those symbols, look … on this kind of thing, look … these techniques – for pairs to complete from memory.

stages.name: Clarifying target language
stages.todo: Meaning is mostly done, so the stage is form: Grammar Focus p.139 (3A) ex a as the discovery task – which of the four sentences are correct – and from it the three patterns on the board: no object (take off), object either side of the particle but a pronoun always in the middle (try it out, make it up), object always after (believe in, look into, fall out with). Stress on the particle, and drill the pronoun versions, which is where it goes wrong.
stages.avoid: Ten or so verbs is the cap for one lesson; the ones in ex a and b on p.139 are the set. Do not add the whole Grammar Focus list.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p.16 Grammar ex 1a, the garage story, ten particle choices, alone with a pair check; then ex 1c cut up – ten jumbled sentences in envelopes, one set a group, ordered on the wall as a race. Grammar Focus p.139 ex b for anyone who finishes.
stages.avoid: The Workbook’s 1b plays its own recording. Paper key.

stages.name: Freer practice and feedback
stages.todo: Speaking ex 6a–6c on p.34: something they have put real effort into, notes against the five questions, then told to a group of three with at least three of the verbs – take off, give up, figure out, come up with, be into. Five minutes of talk, then who in the group has put in the most, and a particle check: say three verbs you heard without their particle and the class supplies it, pronoun in its place.

3B.context: Talent – planning a wedding carefully, and sport in Britain by the numbers

slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 39 Listening ex 4a–4b – audio track 1.55 (Part 3: who should we invite?) / Useful language ex 5a – audio track 1.56, ex 5b–5d / Speaking ex 6a–6b / Workbook p. 18 Useful language ex 1a

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: A wedding you have been to, and the one decision the couple got wrong – guests, venue, food. Pairs, two minutes, two answers for the room. Then the photo on p.39: Becky and Tom are planning theirs.

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Ex 4a with track 1.55 (Part 3 of the video, as audio): the main topic – the guests. Then ex 4b, notes on the five items, on a second play with a pause after each; pairs compare. Eight minutes and move to the language.
stages.avoid: Parts 1 and 2 on p.38 are not on your card. One sentence of back-story is enough: they are getting married in June.

stages.name: Highlighting target language
stages.todo: Ex 5a: the two gapped suggestions from the conversation – We could always invite them…, Don’t you agree that it’d be easier not to…? – completed from memory and checked with track 1.56. Ex 5b: why so careful? The subject is sensitive and neither wants to offend.

stages.name: Clarifying target language
stages.todo: Ex 5c: five exponents sorted into putting an idea forward (another idea might be to…, I think maybe we should…, I thought maybe we could…) and asking the other person (don’t you think it’s a good idea to…?, how does it sound if we…?). Form on the board: what follows each – to + verb, if + clause, a bare verb after should and could. Then pronunciation, which is what makes them careful: the fall-rise, the softening maybe, the stress off the verb. Drill all five, tentative, chorally and then one each.
stages.avoid: The same page teaches keeping to the topic (anyway, as I was saying…). It is a second function and not yours; if a student produces it, fine, but do not teach it.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 5d: four careful suggestions with a mistake each – might to be booking, maybe I thought, how does it sound we – corrected alone, pair check. Then Workbook p.18 Useful language ex 1a: six jumbled sentences put in order, skipping item 2, which is not one of yours.
stages.avoid: Ex 5e sends A to p.131 and B to p.129 for a role-play. It is not on your card; the party in section 6 is the freer practice.

stages.name: Freer practice and feedback
stages.todo: Ex 6a: two minutes alone on a class party – when, where, theme and music, food and drink. Then ex 6b in groups of four: agree a plan, every suggestion made carefully with one of the five exponents, and the group has to reach one decision on each point. Eight minutes while you listen for the exponents and the tone. Then one plan for the room, a vote, and two suggestions you heard made too bluntly, for pairs to make careful again.

slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 40 Reading ex 2a–2c (the bar chart) / SB p. 41 (A nation of armchair athletes?)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Pairs list the five sports most people in their country actually do – not watch – in two minutes, then compare with another pair. Board the class’s five.
stages.avoid: Section 1 Speaking and Listening on p.40 is a listening about three people at a sports centre. It is not on your card.

stages.name: Prediction from the chart
stages.todo: Pre-teach participation, statistics and glued to with a sentence each. Then ex 2a: the bar chart – five UK sports, two periods – and four true-or-false sentences about what it shows, in pairs. Confirm (3 and 4 are false), and ask them to guess what the article will say about the drop in swimming.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 2b: read A nation of armchair athletes? once, three minutes – does it say the same as the chart? Yes. Pair check, then the one extra thing they noticed.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 2c: five questions – did the big event get people playing, is it only five sports, what surprised the writer, why cycling, what change in the last paragraph. Alone, pairs, then confirm with the line that answers each.

stages.name: Language from the text
stages.todo: Paragraph d: pairs underline every verb about change – there has been no sudden increase, participation hasn’t decreased, interest has increased slightly, has increased noticeably – and say why the present perfect. The change runs from then to now; the tense from yesterday’s lesson in its natural home. Board the pattern: there has been a + adjective + increase / decrease; the number has increased + adverb.
stages.avoid: Seven minutes of noticing, not a grammar lesson. The next slot writes with this language; you only need them to see it.

stages.name: Response
stages.todo: Groups: do they believe the writer’s reasons – athletics because it is on TV and cheap, cycling because of BMX – and which of the five sports has changed most at home? Seven minutes, then one view a group, and correction of the present perfect only – one line each, as you heard it, reformulated by the room.

slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 40 Writing Skills ex 3a / SB p. 41 ex 3b–3d, Writing ex 4a–4c

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Straight on from the last lesson: which of the article’s five sports are popular at home, and which has grown? Pairs, then two answers.

stages.name: Preparing to write – the organisation
stages.todo: Ex 3a on p.40: the five summaries matched to paragraphs a–e of the article they read last lesson – what the chart shows, the issue, the main conclusion, the detail, the extra information. Pairs, confirm, and board the five-paragraph shape: it is their plan.
stages.avoid: Do not set the article again. They read it an hour ago; the matching is enough to bring it back.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Ex 3b on p.41: the table from paragraph d – noticeable / change / slight / significant as adjective and noun, slightly / noticeably / significantly as adverb, has increased / hasn’t decreased as verb. Pairs fill it, confirm, drill the stress (sigNIFicant, NOticeably). Ex 3c: This points back, and the paragraph runs data then comment. Then ex 3d: four sentences about the British city from the figures – tennis 18% to 22%, football teams 53 to 39 – written alone and compared.

stages.name: Writing task
stages.todo: Ex 4a: the Market Street Sports Complex chart and the three notes – what does it show? Then ex 4b: pairs plan the five paragraphs in four minutes, then each writes the article alone, to the plan, with at least four phrases from the table. Twelve minutes of writing; walk round and answer at the desk.
stages.avoid: Pairs plan, individuals write – or the stronger one writes and the other watches. Say so when you set it.

stages.name: Feedback
stages.todo: Ex 4c: swap with another pair and check against the book’s four questions – the language from 3b, verbs and nouns, the organisation of 3a, easy to understand – one comment each. Then books closed, groups note what they learned about describing data and where they might use it. Collect the articles and mark them before next time.

4A.context: Life events – two lottery winners, how the money changed them, and what money does to happiness

slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 44 Speaking ex 1a–1b, Reading ex 2a–2c / SB p. 45 ex 2d–2f / Communication 4A: SB p. 128 (Sharon Tirabassi, Student A) and p. 130 (Ihsan Khan, Student B)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1a on p.44: $10,000, $100,000, a million – how would you spend each? Pairs, then the most common and the most unusual answer. Ex 1b: the three headlines – what happened to these people?
stages.avoid: A warmer, not a grammar check. They will reach for the second conditional and get it wrong; leave it.

stages.name: Prediction and pre-teaching
stages.todo: Ex 2a: the first paragraph of each story – Sharon back on the bus, Ihsan taking the money home to Pakistan. Then ex 2b, the book’s own vocabulary task: eight meanings matched to words in the two boxes (pay day, mansions, earthquake, parliament, mayor…). Then ex 2c: from the keywords, pairs guess each story.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 2d, a jigsaw: A reads Sharon on p.128, B reads Ihsan on p.130, each with six or seven questions and keywords to answer. Alone, then A checks with another A and B with another B before the stories cross.
stages.avoid: Make sure nobody reads both. The exchange in the next stage only works if each half is missing.

stages.name: Information exchange
stages.todo: Ex 2e: back in A–B pairs, each tells the other their story, keywords from 2b in front of them, and the listener asks what they do not understand. Then both pairs answer one question from the board: who spent it more wisely?

stages.name: Response
stages.todo: Ex 2f in groups: the sensible and the poor decisions each made, why, and the moral – written down in one line and compared with the three on the page. Then two morals for the room, and the language errors kept for the written feedback – content is the point of this stage.
stages.avoid: Section 3 Grammar on p.45 is the next lesson, and it builds on these two stories. Do not go near used to and would.

slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 45 Grammar ex 3a–3c (used to and would), the stories on SB p. 128 and p. 130 read in the previous lesson / Grammar Focus SB p. 140 (4A, the rules) and p. 141 ex a / Workbook p. 22 Grammar ex 1a (items 1–7)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book’s way in: how you earned money as a child – I used to wash my dad’s car, my mum would pay me for housework – and what they did. Then one line back to Sharon and Ihsan: the class read both stories last lesson, so go straight to the language.
stages.avoid: Do not set the texts again. The exposure was the previous slot; your lesson starts at highlighting.

stages.name: Highlighting target language
stages.todo: Ex 3a on p.45: three sentences from the stories and the rules completed with past, now, used to, would. Then ex 3b: pairs underline every other used to and would in their story on p.128 or p.130 – about five in each – and read two to the room.

stages.name: Clarifying target language
stages.todo: Meaning: both for the past that is no longer true; used to for states and habits, would for habits only – I would live in the city is the error to kill. Neither for a single event: she won $10.5 million, not she used to win. Form: didn’t use to, did you use to. Ex 3c: no longer before the verb, not… any more at the end. Pronunciation: /ˈjuːstə/ with the d silent; drill the sentences from 3a and two of their own.
stages.avoid: Be used to and get used to are on p.140 too and in Grammar Focus ex b. A different structure; not today.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Focus p.141 (4A) ex a: six sentences, tick the forms that work – both, one, or the past simple only. Then Workbook p.22 Grammar ex 1a, items 1–7: came or used to come, wouldn’t or couldn’t snow, didn’t use to be. Alone, pair check, disputed ones only.
stages.avoid: Items 8–10 in the Workbook exercise and ex b on p.141 are be / get used to. Stop at seven and at a.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book’s extra activity: group A lists what Sharon used to do and would do when she was rich, group B the same for Ihsan, from memory; one notes, one presents. Then the real thing: three ways their own life has changed in ten years, told to a partner with used to, would and no longer.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two changes the room should hear, then four sentences from your notes on the board, one right, for pairs to sort – a would with a state verb among them.

slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 45 Listening ex 4a–4c – audio track 2.5 (Monica Sharpe on money and happiness) / SB p. 46 Vocabulary ex 5a – audio track 2.6, ex 5b–5e / Workbook p. 22 Vocabulary ex 2a–2b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 4a on p.45: a researcher into the psychology of money is about to answer three questions – does winning make you behave badly, does money make you happy, does buying things. Pairs predict her three answers.

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Ex 4b with track 2.5: check the predictions – no, no but it won’t stop you, no. Then ex 4c: six points, tick the ones she makes (2, 4, 5), on a second play. Pair check, confirm, and one minute on ex 4d – which do they agree with?
stages.avoid: Two plays. The lesson is the six expressions; the interview is where they come from.

stages.name: Highlighting target language
stages.todo: Ex 5a on p.46: six sentences from the interview, each with a choice – leads into / to, causes / is caused by, effect on / to, as a result from / of, effect / affect, results in / on. Alone, then track 2.6 to check. Board the six correct expressions.

stages.name: Clarifying target language
stages.todo: Ex 5b in pairs, then confirmed: lead to and result in mean cause; as a result of means caused by; affect is the verb and effect the noun; result is a noun in 4 and a verb in 6. Then the form on the board as chunks – lead TO, result IN, have an effect ON, as a result OF – because the preposition is the whole difficulty, and the stress: afFECT against EFfect. Drill the six sentences from 5a.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 5c: six gaps from the box – effect, lead, affect, cause, result, result. Then Workbook p.22 Vocabulary ex 2a, eight sentences with one mistake each (lead in, the affect, as a result from, resulted of), and ex 2b, the gapped text on unhappiness, if there is time. Alone, pair check, disputed ones only.

stages.name: Freer practice and feedback
stages.todo: Ex 5d: an important event in their life and something that happened as a result – three sentences with three different expressions. Ex 5e: read to a partner, who asks two questions. Then three sentences with the expressions, written up by the students who said them, and the class checks the prepositions.
stages.avoid: Section 6 Listening on p.46 belongs to tomorrow’s first lesson. Stop at 5e.

4B.context: Life events – a baby, a year abroad, and training that is harder than it looks

slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 46 Listening ex 6a–6c – audio track 2.7 (Alphonso and Dragana: life-changing events) / Speaking ex 7a–7b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Five life events on the board – first job, children, university, leaving home, marriage – and pairs choose the three that change a life most. One vote in open class.

stages.name: Prediction and pre-teaching
stages.todo: Ex 6a on p.46: the blog box – Alphonso and Carmen have just had a baby, Dragana studied abroad for a year – and the six topics. Pairs predict how each life changed, topic by topic. Then four words the recording needs: cautious, adventurous, adapt to, a steady job.

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex 6b with track 2.7: which of the six topics does each speaker talk about? One play, pair check, confirm – Alphonso most of them, Dragana only attitude to life.

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex 6c: six sentences, true or false, and the false ones corrected – they answer from the first hearing, then listen again to check. Pair check, confirm (2, 3, 4, 5 are false), with the line that proves each.

stages.name: Response
stages.todo: Ex 7a: how they themselves have changed in ten years, notes against the six topics. Ex 7b: told to a partner, and the recording hands them the language for it – used to, would, no longer, more cautious than I used to be – which the class met yesterday. Eight minutes of talk, a change of partner halfway. Then two changes for the room, and one line of correction: the used to or would error you heard most, reformulated for the room.
stages.avoid: Sixteen minutes is long for one exchange. Plan the halfway change – a new partner, or one topic they must add – before you stand up.

slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 48 Reading ex 3a–3c (Training to be the best) / SB p. 49 ex 3d, Vocabulary ex 4a–4c

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 3a on p.48: photos a–d – what are the jobs, and what training might each need? Pairs guess; do not confirm.

stages.name: Reading task
stages.todo: Ex 3b: read the two texts once to check – a Peking Opera School, the Swiss Guard. Then ex 3c: eight statements, who would say each, P or S; alone, pairs, confirm. Ex 3d for one minute: which training is harder, and which would they choose?
stages.avoid: Nine minutes, and this is a vocabulary lesson. The texts are long; set the gist read to two minutes with the clock showing.

stages.name: Highlighting target language
stages.todo: Ex 4a: seven lines from the texts with an adjective in bold – punishing, strict, tough, arduous, gruelling, rigorous, tricky – and one question: which is not as strong as the others? Tricky. Pairs, then board the seven.

stages.name: Clarifying target language
stages.todo: Ex 4b first: which means hard to the point of hurting (punishing), hard because so thorough (rigorous), hard because of rules (strict). Then what the matching leaves: arduous and gruelling as the near-synonyms for long, exhausting effort; tough as the everyday one; tricky as difficult because complicated, never because hard work. Collocations on the board – a strict teacher, rigorous training, a gruelling schedule, a tricky situation – and the stress: ARduous, GRUelling, RIGorous, PUNishing. Drill the collocations.
stages.avoid: Seven adjectives plus their collocations is the lesson. Vocabulary Focus on p.157 has eight more; it is not on your card.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Your own material: eight sentences, each with a gap and a context that allows only one of the seven – a journey through the mountains, a teacher who allowed no talking, a schedule of 5 am starts, a question with no easy answer. Alone, pair check, disputed ones only.
stages.avoid: The Workbook page for 4B mixes in the Vocabulary Focus adjectives (demanding, testing, straightforward). Write your own eight; it is assessed from this practice on.

stages.name: Freer practice and feedback
stages.todo: Ex 4c: four questions in pairs with extra detail – a marathon, tough or punishing? a strict teacher? a job with rigorous training? a tricky situation? – then swap partners for two of them. Then one answer for the room and a collocation check – you give the noun, they give the adjective they used with it, and the room judges the fit.

slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 49 Listening ex 5a, 5c – audio track 2.10 (Miranda and Fred on their training) / Grammar ex 6a, Speaking ex 7a–7b / Grammar Focus SB p. 140 (4B, the rules) and p. 141 ex a–b / Workbook p. 23 Grammar ex 1b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: One line from the last lesson – the Peking Opera students, up at five, ten hours a day – and one question: what were you made to do at school that you hated, and what were you not allowed to do?

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Ex 5a with track 2.10: Miranda at drama school, Fred at a football academy – which of the three sentences fits both? One play, pair check, confirm (1). Then ex 5c for a minute: was the sacrifice worth it? That is the way in; the language is next.
stages.avoid: Ex 5b is eight true-or-false sentences and a second play. It belongs to a listening lesson. One play.

stages.name: Highlighting target language
stages.todo: Ex 6a: six sentences from the recording with the phrases in bold – was supposed to, made us work, weren’t allowed to, let me do it, were allowed to, were forced to – sorted into obligation and permission. Pairs, confirm (O, O, P, P, P, O).

stages.name: Clarifying target language
stages.todo: Six phrases, past, on the board in two columns. Meaning with the Teacher’s Book’s concept questions: the trainer made us do more – did you have a choice? who decided? the boss let us go home – was it an obligation? Supposed to is the odd one: a rule or plan that was not kept. Form, which is the error: make and let take an object and the bare verb (made us work, let me do it, never let me to do), be allowed / forced / supposed take to. Pronunciation: the weak to /tə/ and the contracted weren’t; drill the six sentences. Grammar Focus p.140 (4B) is the reference afterwards.
stages.avoid: The page is a modality review and p.140 lists everything from must to needn’t. Your lesson is the six phrases the recording exposed, in the past. Leave the present-tense table alone.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Focus p.141 (4B) ex a: eight sentences rewritten with the word in brackets – forced, allowed, let, made, supposed. Then Workbook p.23 Grammar ex 1b: ten choices, including made me run / to run and were let / allowed / forced to. Alone, pair check, the disputed ones only.
stages.avoid: Ex b on p.141, Andy’s computer course, is all present-tense rules. Not today.

stages.name: Freer practice and feedback
stages.todo: Ex 7a: a time at school, university or work when they had to train and follow rules – notes on the situation, the strictest rules, how they felt. Ex 7b in pairs: tell it, with at least three of the six, and compare. Then the strictest story for the room, and two sentences with make or let in them from your notes, one right, for pairs to judge.

5A.context: Chance – why we expect the best, what the odds really are, and a job in Antarctica

slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 56 Reading ex 1a–1b (the quiz), 1d (Why we think we’re going to have a long and happy life) / SB p. 57 ex 1e–1f, Vocabulary ex 2a–2b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1a on p.56: the optimist-or-pessimist quiz, seven questions, answered honestly and alone. Then ex 1b in pairs: compare, and count the a’s and b’s. Mostly a is the optimist; that is all the scoring you need.
stages.avoid: Ex 1c sends them to p.131 for the results. Not on your card – the count does the job.

stages.name: Pre-teaching and prediction
stages.todo: Three items the article does not explain: life expectancy, be diagnosed with, take out insurance. Then the title – why we think we’re going to have a long and happy life – and one prediction from each pair: is that a good thing or a bad thing?

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 1d: read the article once, quickly, and choose the words that complete the summary – optimistic, an advantage, more successful. Three minutes, pair check, confirm.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 1e on p.57: eight statements, tick the five the article makes. Alone, then pairs pointing at the line that proves each, then confirm (2, 3, 5, 6, 8).

stages.name: Vocabulary from the text
stages.todo: Ex 2a: six adjectives found in the article from their meanings – optimistic, realistic, unrealistic, adventurous, cautious, ambitious. Pairs with the text, confirm, then the stress (OPtimistic? no – optiMIStic, reaLIStic, adVENturous, amBItious, CAUtious) and a drill. Ex 2b for a minute: which describe you?
stages.avoid: Ex 2c sends them to Vocabulary Focus on p.158 for eight more. Six is the set.

stages.name: Response
stages.todo: Ex 1f in groups of three: do they have the Optimism Bias, is optimistic better than realistic, where will they be in twenty years? Seven minutes with the six adjectives on the board, then one answer a group, and the adjectives that were used well read back to the class with the speaker’s name.

slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 58 Listening ex 3a–3c – audio track 2.23 (What are your chances?) / Grammar ex 4a – audio track 2.24, ex 4b–4d / Grammar Focus SB p. 143 ex b / Workbook p. 28 Grammar ex 1c / SB p. 58 Speaking ex 5a–5c

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 3a on p.58: five statistics – living to 100, a road accident, the lottery, a plane crash – and the numbers in the box to guess from. Pairs guess, and the room votes on the lottery.

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Ex 3b with track 2.23: check the numbers (1 in 6, 1 in 4, 1 in 8,000, 1 in 18 million, 1 in a million). Then ex 3c from memory – how to improve your chances of surviving a crash, getting to the airport, living to 100 – and the track again to check. Pairs, confirm.
stages.avoid: Two plays. The lesson is the language of probability, and the recording is three minutes long.

stages.name: Highlighting target language
stages.todo: Ex 4a: eight sentences from the recording gapped with likely, unlikely, could, may, probably, certainly, chance – pairs complete, then track 2.24 to check. Ex 4b: which phrases mean certain, probable, possible, not probable? Board them on a line from 100% to 0%.

stages.name: Clarifying target language
stages.todo: Ex 4c gives the form: will probably / certainly + verb, probably / certainly won’t + verb, is likely / unlikely to + verb, it’s unlikely that…, there’s a chance that…. The error is word order – probably after will, before won’t, never Probably I will. May well and could well sit at ‘quite possible’. Concept-check with the line: is ‘you almost certainly won’t win’ nearer 0% or 50%? Pronunciation: ’ll and the weak will, the stress on the adverb – you’ll PROBably, you almost CERtainly won’t. Drill four of the sentences from 4a.
stages.avoid: The Grammar Focus rules page has the whole cline including I doubt if, I shouldn’t think, bound to. Teach the seven in the box; the rest is reference.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 4d: six predictions with a percentage – I’ll meet someone famous, 70% – rewritten with the right phrase; alone, compared. Then Workbook p.28 Grammar ex 1c, ten three-way choices (could / will / shall, probably will / will probably), or Grammar Focus p.143 (5A) ex b, six rewrites, for a stronger group. Disputed ones only.

stages.name: Freer practice and feedback
stages.todo: Ex 5a–5c: six questions about their lifetime – a cure for cancer, people on Mars, another world war – each decided as certain, probable, possible, unlikely or certainly not, plus one question of their own. Then a mingle: each student asks two questions round the room and notes the answers. Six minutes, then ex 5c for the room – is the class optimistic? – and two probability sentences you heard with the adverb in the wrong place, for pairs to reorder.

slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 59 Reading ex 1a, 1d–1e / SB p. 60 ex 1f (Cooking in Antarctica), Vocabulary ex 2a–2e / Workbook p. 29 Vocabulary ex 2a–2b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1a on p.59: the photos of Antarctica – what can they see, what do they know, would they go? Pairs, two answers for the room.
stages.avoid: The quiz in ex 1b–1c and its answers on p.132 are a lesson on their own. Not on your card.

stages.name: Reading task
stages.todo: Ex 1d: the job conditions – six months indoors, six days a week, only your colleagues – would they apply? Ex 1e in pairs for a minute: why do people go, what jobs, what do they do all winter? Then ex 1f on p.60: read Cooking in Antarctica once, quickly, to see which of their ideas are in it. Pair check, confirm. Eight minutes, then the language.
stages.avoid: Ex 1g–1h are the detail notes and the discussion. They belong to a reading lesson; this is a vocabulary lesson and the text is the way in.

stages.name: Highlighting target language
stages.todo: Ex 2a: article covered, pairs match A and B into nine collocations – rough weather, global warming, environmentally friendly, carbon footprint, solar energy, climate change, fragile environment, the Earth’s atmosphere, ecological impact. Then ex 2b: uncover and check against the text.

stages.name: Clarifying target language
stages.todo: Meaning where it is needed: global warming is the cause and climate change the result; a carbon footprint belongs to a person or a company; fragile means easily damaged, not small. Form: these are fixed pairs – weather is rough, not hard; the environment is fragile – and environmentally friendly is adverb plus adjective. Stress on the first word of most of them – CARbon footprint, SOlar energy, CLImate change, GLObal warming – and drill them with the Teacher’s Book’s device: you say global, they say warming, then reversed.
stages.avoid: Nine collocations is the set and the cap. Resist adding the ones the Workbook brings in.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 2c on p.60: seven sentences completed with the collocations – solar energy and a carbon footprint, the ecological impact of coal, a boat trip cancelled by rough weather. Then Workbook p.29 Vocabulary ex 2a, eight sentence halves to match, and 2b, nine picture sentences with the words half-given. Alone, pair check, disputed ones only.

stages.name: Freer practice and feedback
stages.todo: Ex 2d: notes on three questions – a fragile environment in their country, inventions with a negative ecological impact, how they could cut their own carbon footprint. Ex 2e in groups of three, six minutes, with the nine on the board. Then one idea a group, and a last drill of the two collocations that came out wrong most often.

5B.context: Chance – a scientist off to count penguins, a café that needs more money, and whether the weather is changing

slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 61 Listening ex 3a–3b – audio track 2.27 (Martha and Joe on the penguins) / Grammar ex 4a, 4c–4d / Grammar Focus SB p. 143 (5B) ex a–b / Workbook p. 29 Grammar ex 1a

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: One line back to Fleur the Antarctic chef from yesterday, then: what is she doing right now, what will she be doing this time tomorrow, what will she have done by an hour from now? Take the answers without correcting – that is the Teacher’s Book’s way in, and the lesson will fix the forms.

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Ex 3a on p.61 with track 2.27: Martha is off to count Adelie penguins – four questions: how well Joe understands, is he serious, what are the penguins like, why the research matters. One play, pairs, confirm. Then ex 3b: five events numbered in order – pairs from memory, then the track again to check.
stages.avoid: The grammar is in the second half of the recording. Two plays, and no third.

stages.name: Highlighting target language
stages.todo: Ex 4a: three lines from the conversation – this time next week I’ll be settling in, I’ll be doing similar things every day, by the time I arrive the penguins will already have got into pairs – matched to uses a–c. Pairs, confirm (1a, 2c, 3b), board the three.

stages.name: Clarifying target language
stages.todo: Two forms on a timeline with a point in the future marked: will be + -ing for what is in progress around that point (and for what is already planned), will have + past participle for what is finished before it, usually with by. The Teacher’s Book’s concept questions do the meaning: this time next week I’ll be travelling to Spain – will I be in Spain? and this time tomorrow I’ll have marked your homework – will the marking be finished? Form is the error: will have went, will be + infinitive. Pronunciation: ’ll have is /əl həv/ and ’ll be /əl bi/, both swallowed before the stressed verb – drill the three sentences from 4a.
stages.avoid: Future continuous and future perfect are two forms, but they are one lesson because the book contrasts them around one point in time. Keep the contrast; do not add the future simple as a third column.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Focus p.143 (5B) ex a: eight sentences, tick the correct and fix the rest – I’ll have attended a meeting at that time, I’ll have carried a sign. Then ex b, Christina’s calendar, seven gaps, or Workbook p.29 Grammar ex 1a, ten choices, for a stronger group. Alone, pair check, disputed ones only.

stages.name: Freer practice and feedback
stages.todo: Ex 4c: notes on two questions – where will you be living this time next year, what will you have achieved in five years? Ex 4d in pairs, with two follow-up questions each. Then the most ambitious plan for the room, and two future forms you heard – one right, one with the wrong auxiliary – for pairs to judge.
stages.avoid: Section 5 Speaking on p.61, the job interview role-play, is a different lesson and not on your card.

slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 62 Listening ex 2a–2b – audio track 2.31 (Part 2: Sam and Emma) / Useful language ex 3a–3b – audio track 2.32, ex 3c–3d – audio track 2.33, ex 3e / SB p. 63 Pronunciation ex 4a–4b – audio tracks 2.34, 2.35 / Workbook p. 30 Useful language ex 1a

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Running your own café on the board: pairs list two advantages and two disadvantages in two minutes, then four for the room. Then photo b on p.62 – Sam and Emma, and Sam’s café is not making enough money.
stages.avoid: Part 1 (ex 1b–1c, track 2.30) is Phil’s idea in the café. Not on your card – one sentence of back-story is enough: a customer suggested opening in the evenings.

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Ex 2a with track 2.31 (Part 2 of the video, as audio): five topics, which four do Sam and Emma discuss? One play, confirm (not Sam’s birthday). Then ex 2b, a second play: the idea, the points for and the points against, in notes. Pairs compare, confirm.

stages.name: Highlighting target language
stages.todo: Ex 3a: two gapped lines from the conversation – Of course, the … is we’d have to invest even more money / Yes, but the … is, it might be a way to get more business – completed from memory, then track 2.32 to check (trouble, good thing about it). Ex 3c: which other words fit – problem, disadvantage, drawback in the first; advantage, best thing in the second. Board the six.

stages.name: Clarifying target language
stages.todo: Six exponents: the trouble with… is, the good thing about… is, the advantage / disadvantage of… is, the only drawback of… is, another problem with… is. Ex 3d with track 2.33 gives the prepositions – about, of, of, with, with – and that is the form, with a noun or -ing after the preposition and a clause after is. Then p.63 ex 4a with track 2.34, which is where the meaning lives in the voice: a slight pause after is, the stress on good and trouble, the voice up on is. Ex 4b with track 2.35: drill the four sentences with the pause, then two of your own.
stages.avoid: Section 6 on p.63, responding to an idea, is the page’s second function. One function, six exponents, forty-five minutes; leave that’s a great idea and I don’t know about that alone.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p.30 Useful language ex 1a: Magda and Roman on a job in Paris, nine preposition choices – thinking of, one good thing about, the trouble with, a big disadvantage of. Alone, pair check, paper key. Then SB p.62 ex 3e: three people’s plans – sell the car, live in London, work in China – and a second sentence for each with an expression from 3d, said aloud with the pause.
stages.avoid: The Workbook’s 1b plays its own recording. Paper key.

stages.name: Freer practice and feedback
stages.todo: Four ideas on the board – live in a hot country, be part of a big family, learn a language on your own, work from home – the Teacher’s Book’s set. Pairs take two each and argue the advantages and disadvantages with the six exponents, then swap partners and do the other two. Seven minutes while you listen for the preposition and the pause. Then one exchange for the room, and three expressions you heard with the preposition missing, written up with the gap, for pairs to fill.

slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 64 Speaking and Listening ex 1a (the photos only), ex 1d, the essay Are extreme weather events a sign of climate change? / SB p. 65 Reading ex 2a–2b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1a on p.64: photos a–d – what extreme weather is each (snow, flooding, drought, a hurricane), which could hit their region, and what can people do? Pairs, then two answers for the room. Board the four weather words.
stages.avoid: Ex 1b–1c is a listening, four news reports. Not on your card. The photos are your lead-in and the essay is your text.

stages.name: Pre-teaching and prediction
stages.todo: Three words the essay needs: unstable (weather that keeps changing), take action, invest in. Then the title – are extreme weather events a sign of climate change? – and each pair predicts whether the writer will say yes, no, or both.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 2a on p.65: read Leon’s essay once for two questions – which sentence summarises it (he weighs both sides and concludes) and what his conclusion is (act now or it will be too late). Three minutes, pair check, confirm.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 2b: notes in two columns, the points for and the points against extreme weather being a sign of climate change. Alone with the text, then pairs compare, then the columns on the board from them.

stages.name: Language from the text
stages.todo: Pairs underline every phrase in the essay that says how sure the writer is: will almost certainly get worse, it’s not certain that, is probably linked, we can’t be completely sure, by then it will be too late. That is yesterday’s probability language in a text that argues – board the cline from certain to not certain and ask where each phrase sits. Five minutes of noticing; the next lesson is where it gets practised.
stages.avoid: Noticing, not a grammar lesson. The class did the forms in 5A.

stages.name: Response
stages.todo: Ex 1d on p.64, questions 2 and 3, in groups of three: which of the two statements do they agree with – natural process, or man-made – and what should governments do? Eight minutes, with the probability phrases on the board to argue with. Then one position a group, and the probability phrases that were used well read back to the room, with one error reformulated.
stages.avoid: Section 3 Writing Skills and the essay task on p.65 are a writing lesson. Stop at 2b and the discussion.

6A.context: Around the globe – famous sights, two tourists who did it differently, and places nobody has heard of

slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 68–69 Reading and Listening ex 1a–1c (four attractions and eight tourist comments), ex 1d–1e – audio track 2.39 (Di and Bernie), ex 1f

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1a: the four attractions across pp.68–69 – the Louvre, the Tower of London, Schönbrunn, Topkapi – and their facts. Have they been to any, which would they choose? Pairs, then a vote.

stages.name: Pre-listening – the comments
stages.todo: Ex 1b: eight tourist comments, positive or negative, alone; then ex 1c, each matched to its attraction, in pairs. Confirm. Then two words the recording needs: maze and hedge, from the Schönbrunn gardens. The comments have set up the question the listening answers – is organised sightseeing worth it?

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex 1d with track 2.39: which of the four places do Di and Bernie mention, and do they agree about tours? One play, pairs, confirm – Schönbrunn and the Louvre, and no: she left her tour, he wishes he had been on one.

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex 1e: four questions on Di, four on Bernie. Read them first, then a second play paused after Di so they can write. Pairs compare, then confirm with the words from the recording where they disagreed.

stages.name: Response
stages.todo: Ex 1f in groups of three: similar experiences, how they prefer to go sightseeing, the downsides of tourism the comments and the speakers mention – and do those downsides put them off? Ten minutes, then one view a group, and the two most useful things said, dictated back to the room by the people who said them.
stages.avoid: Section 2 Grammar on p.69 takes its sentences from this recording and is the next lesson. Do not touch gerunds and infinitives.

slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 69 Grammar ex 2a – audio track 2.40, ex 2b–2c, 2f–2g / Grammar Focus SB p. 144 (6A, the rules) and p. 145 ex a–b / Workbook p. 34 Grammar ex 1a

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Two lines back to Di and Bernie from the last lesson – she left the coach tour, he drove on the wrong side of the road in Paris. The class heard the recording an hour ago, so the lesson starts at the language.
stages.avoid: Do not replay track 2.39. The exposure was the previous slot.

stages.name: Highlighting target language
stages.todo: Ex 2a: four lines from the recording with a choice in each – to meet or meeting, travel or to travel, Drive or Driving, arriving or to arrive – chosen in pairs and checked with track 2.40. Then ex 2b: the four rules matched to the four sentences – gerund after a preposition and as a subject, to-infinitive after an adjective and for purpose.

stages.name: Clarifying target language
stages.todo: The four rules from 2b on the board with their example, then ex 2c, the two verbs that take both with a change of meaning: try to include (an attempt) against try going on a tour (an experiment); remember visiting (a memory) against remember to be back (a job not to forget). Concept-check each pair – did he manage it? is it in the past or the future? Form: the gerund after every preposition, including to in looking forward to. Pronunciation: to is weak /tə/ and the -ing never carries stress; drill the four from 2a and the four from 2c.
stages.avoid: Ex 2d, sense verbs with an object and -ing, is a third pattern and the lesson already holds four rules and two meaning changes. Leave it, and leave Grammar Focus ex c, which needs it.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Focus p.145 (6A) ex a, five choices, then ex b, ten sentence halves that turn on try, remember, forget, stop and go on. Alone, pair check, disputed ones only. Then Workbook p.34 Grammar ex 1a, Helen and Max, fifteen choices, for whoever finishes.
stages.avoid: SB p.69 ex 2f mixes the sense-verb pattern into its ten gaps (items 6 and 9). If you use it, drop those two.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 2g in groups of three: why do we all visit the same attractions, do you have to see the famous sights, how will tourism change? Each answer must use at least one of the patterns – it’s easy to…, without seeing…, I remember visiting…, we went there to…. Seven minutes while you listen with a pen.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One opinion the room should hear, then four sentences from your notes on the board, one right, for pairs to sort – an enjoy to do among them if you heard one.

slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 70 Reading ex 3a, 3c (Where to go? – Uruapan, Ha Long Bay, Kizhi Island) / Vocabulary ex 4a–4b, 4c – audio track 2.45, ex 4d / Workbook p. 34 Vocabulary ex 2a

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: A place in their country tourists never go to but should. Pairs, one each, then three for the room. Then the website on p.70: three readers answered that question.

stages.name: Reading task
stages.todo: Ex 3a: three questions over three texts – which countries, are the places well known, nature or man-made? Three minutes, pair check, confirm (Mexico, Vietnam, Russia; no; nature, nature, man-made). Then ex 3c for a minute: which sounds most interesting? That is the way in; the adjectives are next.
stages.avoid: Ex 3b, the six true-or-false sentences, is the detail read of a reading lesson. Not in this one.

stages.name: Highlighting target language
stages.todo: Ex 4a: the adjectives in bold in the three texts – spectacular, impressive, remarkable, superb, exotic, astonishing, breathtaking, dramatic, stunning, memorable, unique – positive or negative? All positive. Then ex 4b: ten questions, one per adjective, in pairs, confirm.

stages.name: Clarifying target language
stages.todo: Ten adjectives in groups on the board: very beautiful (stunning, breathtaking, superb), admired (impressive, remarkable), surprising (astonishing), unusual (exotic, unique, dramatic), stays with you (memorable). The ones to separate: unique – only one, so no very unique; exotic – foreign and attractive, not strange; dramatic – scenery, not a person. Ex 4c with track 2.45: the stress – imPRESSive, STUNNing, BREATHtaking, reMARKable, draMATic, MEMorable, suPERB, exOTic, asTONishing, uNIQUE – and drill them inside a noun phrase: breathtaking views, a unique experience.
stages.avoid: Ten adjectives is the cap. Vocabulary Focus on p.159 (ex 4e) adds outskirts, feature, setting and more; not on your card.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p.34 Vocabulary ex 2a: eight definitions and the letters jumbled – not easily forgotten, odd and strange, the only one of its kind. Alone, pair check. Then four sentences of your own with a gap and a context that allows one adjective only, read aloud for the stress.
stages.avoid: Workbook ex 2b on the same page is the Vocabulary Focus set – lobby, terrace, trails. Not yours.

stages.name: Freer practice and feedback
stages.todo: Ex 4d: three interesting or beautiful things they have seen as a tourist, with an adjective from 4c for each, told to a partner who asks two questions. Then new pairs and the best one again. Seven minutes, then one place for the room, and the adjectives that came out listed on the board as they were said – the room decides which went with the right noun.
stages.avoid: Section 5 Reading and Speaking, the destinations on pp.128 and 130, is a lesson on its own. Not on your card.

6B.context: Around the globe – languages that are dying out, and a travel blog from the Grand Canyon

slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 71 Reading and Listening ex 1a–1b – audio track 2.49 (the languages quiz and Professor Barnett) / Vocabulary ex 2a–2b, 2c – audio track 2.50, 2d – audio track 2.51, ex 2e–2f / Workbook p. 35 Vocabulary ex 2a–2b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1a on p.71: the languages-of-the-world quiz, five questions, done in groups of three with guesses allowed. Do not confirm anything.

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Ex 1b with track 2.49: the professor answers the quiz – groups check their score – and two questions: which languages are most in danger, and what is a language hotspot? One play, pairs, confirm. He uses the verbs of the lesson as he goes, which is the point of hearing him.
stages.avoid: One play. The verbs come next, and the second half of the interview belongs to the last lesson of the day.

stages.name: Highlighting target language
stages.todo: Ex 2a: nine verbs in the box – be lost, decline, decrease, deteriorate, die out, disappear, increase, preserve, revive – matched to six meanings; some meanings take more than one verb. Pairs, confirm. Then ex 2b: four sentences about the quiz figures completed with the right verb in the right form.

stages.name: Clarifying target language
stages.todo: Three groups on the board: going down (decrease, decline), gone (be lost, die out, disappear), and the pair of opposites preserve and revive – keep alive against bring back. Concept-check revive against preserve: was the language dead first? Deteriorate is get worse, not get smaller. Then ex 2c with track 2.50, the form that matters: INcrease and DEcrease as nouns, inCREASE and deCREASE as verbs – and ex 2d with track 2.51 to say the four sentences. Ex 2e: the nouns – disappearance, deterioration, revival, preservation. Drill the noun and verb of increase and decrease until the stress moves on its own.
stages.avoid: Nine verbs plus four nouns is the lesson. Section 3 Reading, over the page, is the next slot; do not open the Dying languages text.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p.35 Vocabulary ex 2a: six pictures and graphs, two verbs to choose from in each – decline or disappear, deteriorated or died out, decreased or increased. Then ex 2b: the professor conversation with eight noun forms to make – survival, preservation, disappearance, revival. Alone, pair check, disputed ones only.

stages.name: Freer practice and feedback
stages.todo: Ex 2f: three things that have increased or decreased in their country recently – a noun sentence and a verb sentence for each – told to a partner, who asks whether it will continue. Then new pairs for one of them. Six minutes, then one change for the room, and a stress check: say three of the nouns and verbs and the class marks the syllable, then one error from the pairs said the wrong way and the right way.

slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 72 Reading ex 3a (Danger! Dying languages) / SB p. 73 ex 3b–3c

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Do they know a language that has died out, or a dialect their grandparents spoke that they do not? Pairs, then two for the room, and why it happens – young people do not want it, a bigger language takes over. The verbs from the last lesson will come out; let them.

stages.name: Pre-teaching and prediction
stages.todo: Four items with a sentence each: mother tongue, ancestor, fluent, a click (the sound in N|u – make it). Then the title and the introduction on p.72: one dead language, one dying, one being brought back – pairs guess which of Bo, N|u and Wampanoag is which.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 3a: read the three texts once, four minutes, for two questions – how are the languages similar, how are they different? Old and small; one gone, one going, one coming back. Pairs, confirm, and check the guesses.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 3b on p.73: a grid for each language – number of speakers, increasing or decreasing, other important facts. Alone with the text, then pairs, then the grid on the board from them: Bo none, N|u eight and falling, Wampanoag about fifty and rising.

stages.name: Response
stages.todo: Ex 3c first, in pairs: one question for each of the three people – Boa Sr, Hannah Cooper, Jessie Little Doe – and the answer they imagine. Then groups of three on one question of your own: should a language with eight speakers be saved, and who should pay? Ten minutes, then one answer a group, and feedback on content only – the change vocabulary from the first lesson that came out well, read back to the room.
stages.avoid: Section 4 Grammar on p.73 takes the passive out of this text, and section 5 plays the rest of the interview. Neither is yours; the text is.

slots.pages: Empower B2 (1st ed.) SB p. 76 Speaking and Listening ex 1a (the photos), 1d–1e / SB p. 77 Reading ex 2a (Kirsten’s travel blog), Writing Skills ex 3a–3f, Writing ex 4a–4c

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1a on p.76: the top five US attractions in the photos – what do they know, why do people go, which would they choose? Then ex 1d–1e: their own country’s top three, compared in pairs.
stages.avoid: Ex 1b–1c is a listening about the same trip. Not on your card: the photos and the blog are your material.

stages.name: Preparing to write – the model
stages.todo: Ex 2a on p.77, Kirsten’s Grand Canyon blog, with the question changed because the class has not heard the recording: what did they see on each of the three days? Four minutes alone, pairs compare, confirm – the salt desert and the cowboys, the sunset, the sunrise and the condor. Then one question for the room: what makes it a blog and not a report?

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Ex 3a: five adjectives in the blog meaning very beautiful or very big – breathtaking, superb, impressive, fantastic, huge. Ex 3b: the box sorted into positive and negative. Then ex 3c, the point of the stage: absolutely goes with the strong ones (absolutely mind-blowing) and very with the normal ones (very disappointing), never very awesome; totally and really as the alternatives. Ex 3d: three flat sentences made stronger. Ex 3e: the three experience expressions – an experience in itself, the experience of a lifetime, a whole different experience. Drill four of the strong adjectives with absolutely in front, stress on both.
stages.avoid: Ex 3f is a speaking task. Skip it; the writing needs its time.

stages.name: Writing task
stages.todo: Ex 4a: one of the photos on p.76, or a trip of their own, and notes on where, what they saw, what they did, what it was like. Ex 4b: the blog, alone, in three short paragraphs like Kirsten’s, with at least four strong adjectives and one experience expression. Eleven minutes of writing; walk round and answer at the desk.
stages.avoid: Set a length – 120 to 150 words – or the writing runs past the feedback.

stages.name: Feedback
stages.todo: Ex 4c: swap with a partner who chose a different place, read, ask two questions, and answer one: does it make you want to go, and why? Then one blog read to the room and one thing from your monitoring on the board – an intensifier with the wrong adjective, which is what you will have seen – for them to fix. Collect the blogs and write on them before next time.

s12.name: Upper-intermediate · English File
s12.sources:
Latham-Koenig, C. & Oxenden, C. (2014) English File Upper-intermediate Student’s Book, 3rd edn. Oxford University Press.
Latham-Koenig, C. & Oxenden, C. (2014) English File Upper-intermediate Teacher’s Book, 3rd edn. Oxford University Press.
Latham-Koenig, C. & Oxenden, C. (2014) English File Upper-intermediate Workbook, 3rd edn. Oxford University Press.

1A.context: Questions and answers – extreme job interviews, then making conversation with someone you have just met (File 1A)

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised reading for gist and for detail in the context of ‘extreme’ job interview questions.
slots.sub: To develop students’ ability to work out the meaning of unknown words from context, using the ten highlighted items in the article (demanding, flustered, bizarre, think on your feet, approach …).
slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 6 ex 4a–4b (photo and article ‘Extreme interviews’) / SB p. 7 ex 4c–4d, ex 4e – audio track 1.8, ex 4f–4g

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Project the photo on p. 6 with the article covered: an interviewer asking ‘So, what sort of dinosaur would you be?’ Ex 4a in pairs — what is happening here, and would anyone really ask this in a job interview? Take two or three guesses, write the vote on the board (real or not) and leave it there; the gist reading settles it.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Three items the text does not explain: merely (line 11), pioneer (line 19) and stranded (line 16). Elicit each from a short situation — if you are stranded on an island, can you leave? — one concept question each and move on. Headhunter and Silicon Valley are in the glossary, so point at it rather than teaching them.
stages.avoid: Leave the ten highlighted words alone. Guessing them from context is ex 4c–4d and the sub aim of the lesson; if you pre-teach them there is nothing left to guess.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 4b: read the article once to answer the question from the lead-in — is the dinosaur question real — and decide how you would answer it. Three minutes, alone, no dictionaries. Quick pair check, then settle the board vote (yes, it is a real interview question) and hear two or three of their dinosaurs.

stages.name: Reading for detail: words from context
stages.todo: Go through the Guessing the meaning box on p. 6 with them: the words around it, the part of speech, a similar word they know. Demonstrate with flustered (line 26): what has just happened to the candidate, is it an adjective, a good feeling or a bad one. Then pairs read again and guess the other nine highlighted items, and do ex 4d, matching them to definitions 1–10. Play track 1.8 (ex 4e) to check, and they underline the stressed syllable. Drill demanding, bizarre, flustered and recruitment agency.

stages.name: Reading for detail: the questions
stages.todo: Ex 4f: the three questions — what extreme interviews are, which companies started them, why some people think they are better — answered in their own words, not read out from the text. Pairs, then check in open class. Push them to use the words from ex 4d in their answers (candidates have to think on their feet, the approach comes from Silicon Valley).

stages.name: Discussion and feedback
stages.todo: Ex 4g in groups of three or four: are extreme interviews a good way to choose people, and which of the real questions in the circles would work — room, desk or car, which TV character, does life fascinate you. Give them a job to decide for: each group picks the most and the least useful question and says why. Eight minutes talking while you listen and note what to correct. Then three minutes of content feedback — one group’s choice and the room’s reaction — and two or three sentences from your notes on the board, one right and one wrong, corrected in pairs before you confirm.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have developed their spoken fluency, interviewing a partner with ‘extreme’ questions and answering under pressure with reasons.
slots.sub: To practise listening for detail: five people describing the strangest question they were asked at an interview, as the model for the interviews.
slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 7 ex 5a–5d – audio track 1.9 (played twice), ex 6a–6d / Communication Extreme interviews: p. 104 (Student A) and p. 108 (Student B)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Point back at the dinosaur question from the last lesson, then ex 5a in pairs: have you ever been for a job interview, what did they ask, did you get the job. Two minutes, then two answers in open class. If the class is young and has not been interviewed, ask about any interview — university, a visa, a flat.

stages.name: Listening as a model
stages.todo: The chart on p. 7 is too small to write in, so give them an enlarged copy or project it. Pre-teach reincarnated (the Teacher’s Book flags it; nothing else in the recordings blocks the task). Ex 5b, track 1.9: five speakers, and they complete the five gapped questions in the first column — Do you still practise philosophy? What would make you kick a dog? How tall are you, how much do you weigh? Pause after each speaker. Pairs compare, then show the five questions. Ex 5c, the same track again: notes on how each person answered and what happened in the end. Pairs compare, check. Ex 5d as one open-class question: which were good or bad questions to ask.
stages.avoid: Two plays is the whole budget. The listening is the model for the interviews, not the lesson; a third play comes straight out of the speaking task.

stages.name: Preparation and useful language
stages.todo: Pairs A and B. A reads the eight questions on p. 104, B the eight on p. 108, silently, and marks anything unclear — the Teacher’s Book expects aspect and deserted on A’s list, lead role and financial limitations on B’s. Clear those in open class. Then board the interviewer’s follow-ups they heard in the recordings and will need: Why? Can you give me an example? Tell me more about that. The task is answers with reasons, so the interviewer has to push.

stages.name: Speaking task: the interviews
stages.todo: Seat the pairs face to face like an interview. Demonstrate with one student: ask question 1 from p. 104, push for a reason, react. Then A interviews B with the p. 104 questions, B answers quickly and gives reasons, and A ends by saying whether B gets the job and why. Swap: B interviews A from p. 108. Five minutes each way; you keep the clock. Monitor with a pen for question forms — the Teacher’s Book says to correct those — and for good answers to use in feedback.
stages.avoid: Do not let the As read all eight questions in a row and the Bs answer in one word each. Say before they start that every answer needs a reason, and that the interviewer asks a follow-up before moving on.

stages.name: Second task: their own questions
stages.todo: Ex 6b: each student writes three extreme questions of their own that would tell them something about a person — elicit one or two first so they have the idea. Then ex 6c: stand up, mingle, ask as many people as possible and answer theirs. Four minutes of mingling is enough.

stages.name: Feedback
stages.todo: Ex 6d: which questions were the most interesting and how did people answer them — two or three answers worth the whole room hearing, and a quick vote for who got the job. Then three questions from your monitoring on the board, right and wrong mixed, and the class decides which is which.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised forming questions accurately — auxiliary word order, negative questions, questions ending in a preposition and subject questions — to keep a conversation going with someone they have just met.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency, keeping a conversation on one topic going with follow-up questions.
slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) Teacher’s Book p. 188, photocopiable Communicative 1A ‘Ask me a question’ (one copy per student) / Grammar Bank 1A, SB p. 132, rules 1–4 and ex a

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The photocopiable has no context of its own, so give it one: a dinner party. Show a picture of two guests at a table, one of them plainly bored. Elicit what is wrong and how you keep a stranger talking — you ask them things. Then in pairs: which topics are safe with someone you have just met and which you would avoid. Board the safe ones; the sheet’s eight topics (home, getting around, free time, lifestyle, travel, family, childhood, a relative) will mostly come up.

stages.name: Test
stages.todo: Give out p. 188: eight topics, five gapped questions each, with the question words and auxiliaries missing. In pairs they work out the missing words — saying them, not writing them in, as the Teacher’s Book insists, so the sheet stays usable for the speaking. Five minutes. Walk round and note which questions go wrong; the sheet is built to catch the preposition at the end (Who do you live with? What did you want to be?), the negative question (Is there anything you don’t like …?), the indirect form (Do you think it’s better to travel alone?) and the subject-free How long does it take? Confirm nothing yet.
stages.avoid: Do not correct while they work and do not let them check with another pair. The test only tells you something if it is theirs.

stages.name: Teach
stages.todo: Teach only what the test exposed, against the four rules of Grammar Bank 1A on p. 132: inversion with an auxiliary or modal and do/does/did for the simple tenses; negative questions for surprise or when you expect agreement; the preposition at the end, never at the front; who/what as the subject with no auxiliary (Who lives there?). Board three or four of the sheet’s questions as the models, elicit the pattern under each, then drill the ones with a preposition at the end and the negative question, because the rhythm is what goes wrong in speech — what do you, who do you, isn’t there. Then confirm the full questions on screen.
stages.avoid: At B2 they can form most questions, so do not present question formation from scratch. If the test showed only the preposition and the negative question, those two are the lesson.

stages.name: Second test: controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p. 132 ex a: ten jumbled questions to put in order. On their own first, then compare; open class only for what split them. Items 3, 8 and 10 are indirect questions (Could you tell me when …?), which the sheet only touches; take them if the test showed a need, otherwise skip them and say so.

stages.name: Freer practice: dinner-party conversation
stages.todo: Groups of three; each group takes one or two topics from the sheet. Model with the Family questions: ask one student, then a follow-up, then another, and show that the aim is to stay on the topic as long as possible, not to get through the five questions. Then each student finds someone from another group and interviews them on their topic; on your signal they swap roles, on the next they change partner. Three or four rounds. Monitor for question forms.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Which topic was easiest to keep going and which died — one answer each. Then three or four questions you heard, on the board, right and wrong mixed; pairs sort them, you confirm.

1B.context: Do you believe in it? – what your signature says about you, true stories of the paranormal, and reacting to strange news (File 1B)

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised listening for gist and for detail, taking notes from a graphologist explaining what a signature reveals about personality.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency, interpreting a partner’s signature from the notes they have taken.
slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 10 ex 6a–6c, ex 6d – audio tracks 1.17, 1.18, 1.19, 1.20 (the notes on the right of the page), ex 6e–6g

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 6a is the book’s own way in and it does the work: everyone writes I look forward to hearing from you on a slip of paper, signs underneath as they would a formal letter, and swaps slips with a partner, who keeps it safe for later. Then ex 6b: the ten famous signatures — pairs identify any (Tolstoy, Obama, Paris Hilton, Usain Bolt, Dickens, McCartney, Connery among them) and say what they know of the person. Ex 6c, the short extract: read it and answer one question in open class — can a signature say something about personality?

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Graphology itself and three words the notes need: initials, legible/illegible and self-esteem. Elicit each from an example — write your name on the board as initials, write something unreadable — one concept question each and move on. Everything else in the four recordings is either on the page already or can be guessed.

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: The book has no gist task, so make one from the page: notes covered, one question — which four features of a signature does the expert talk about? Play tracks 1.17 to 1.20 straight through (about four minutes). Pairs compare their four, then uncover the notes and check against the four headings on the right of p. 10: what is in it, its size, its legibility, its angle.

stages.name: Listening for detail: taking notes
stages.todo: Go through the Taking notes box first: key words, not sentences. Then ex 6d one part at a time, the way the Teacher’s Book does it — read the notes for that section, play the track, pause for them to write, play again if they ask. Track 1.17 (what is in your signature), 1.18 (size), 1.19 (legibility), 1.20 (angle). Pairs compare after 1.18 and again after 1.20. Check on screen; the answers are short — your surname = your public self, capital letters = big-headed, illegible = you may be disorganized or secretive, rising = determined and optimistic.
stages.avoid: Two plays of each part is the budget and the notes are key words. If a pair wants a third play of 1.19 to get the full sentence, they have missed the box — point at it rather than pressing play.

stages.name: Response: interpreting signatures
stages.todo: Ex 6e: pairs go back to the famous signatures and interpret two or three from their notes — do the readings match what they thought of the person? Then ex 6f, the real task: take out the partner’s slip from the lead-in and read their signature to them, feature by feature; the partner says whether they agree. Sign your own name on the board first and let the class read you — it shows the language they need (your surname is bigger, so …). Monitor and collect.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two people say one thing their partner’s signature revealed and whether it was true. Then two or three sentences from your monitoring on the board, one of them right, and the class decides which is which.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised reading for gist and for detail, in the context of three true stories about the paranormal, and retelling one of them.
slots.sub: To give students practice in writing a short narrative collaboratively, continuing a spooky story one sentence at a time.
slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 8 ex 1a–1c (the quote, the story beginnings, The Coffee Cup Reading) / Communication Hard to believe?: p. 104 Noises in the Night (Student A) and p. 109 The Strange Object on the Hill (Student B) / SB p. 9 ex 1d (the rest of The Coffee Cup Reading, read aloud by you from the script on p. 120 — recording 1.10 is not in our audio set), ex 1e – audio track 1.11

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book’s own lead-in: the Stuart Chase quote on p. 8 on the board, books closed — for those who believe, no proof is necessary; for those who don’t, no proof is possible. What does it mean, and do they agree? Then the lesson title, Do you believe in it? — elicit paranormal, and hands up: believers and sceptics. Ex 1a: the two story beginnings — what might they have in common.
stages.avoid: Keep religion out of it. If it comes up, steer back to ghosts and UFOs — the stories are about unexplained happenings, nothing more.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Three items only: fortune-teller, clairvoyant and spooky. Elicit from a situation — who reads your palm at a fair — one concept question each and move on.
stages.avoid: The highlighted words in the two Communication stories — curtains, estate agent, dragging, dome, gliding, hallucinating — are not for pre-teaching. Guessing them and filling the glossary is the reading task on those pages.

stages.name: Reading for detail: the jigsaw
stages.todo: Ex 1b: pairs A and B, face to face. A reads Noises in the Night on p. 104, B reads The Strange Object on the Hill on p. 109 — ex a on each page: read, guess the highlighted words, complete the glossary. Five minutes, time limit on the board. Then the stories get covered and A retells from the bullet questions on the page (when, what happened, how they feel now) while B listens and asks; then B retells. Finish with one open-class question: what do they think the noises and the object really were.

stages.name: The third story: reading, then listening
stages.todo: Ex 1c on p. 8: everyone reads the beginning of The Coffee Cup Reading and answers the question — would you have let Fatos read your cup, and why. Then ex 1d on p. 9: they read the nine questions, and you read the rest of the story aloud from the script on p. 120, at a storyteller’s pace, pausing twice to let them write. The recording for this part (1.10) is not in our audio set, so this is a live listening — rehearse it. Pairs compare, then check the nine answers.

stages.name: Vocabulary from the story
stages.todo: Ex 1e with track 1.11: five short extracts from what they have just heard, one word missing in each — spot on, laid-back, weird, spooky (coincidence), sceptical. They fill the gaps on the first play, and in pairs work out the meaning from the extract. Check, then drill sceptical and laid-back.

stages.name: Response: a story in a chain
stages.todo: Groups of four, and one sheet per group with the first line of a strange story already on it — write your own, something like It was nearly midnight when I heard the knock.
