Each student adds one sentence and passes the sheet on; four rounds, a minute each, then the sheets go back to the group that started them, who read theirs out. Two minutes for the reading. Do not open the discussion of the three stories — the next teacher starts with it.
stages.avoid: Ex 2 on p. 9 (which story is spookiest, any explanation) is the next lesson’s lead-in. Leave it.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised using auxiliary verbs to react to what someone says — reply questions (Did you?), So / Neither do I, and a stressed auxiliary for emphasis (I did see one) — in conversations about strange experiences.
slots.sub: To practise the sentence stress and intonation of reply questions and emphatic auxiliaries, copying the recordings.
slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 9 ex 2 (the Reacting box and the first two questions, as the lead-in), ex 3a, ex 3b – audio track 1.12 / Grammar Bank 1B, SB p. 133, rules 2–6 and ex a / SB p. 9 ex 4a – audio track 1.14, ex 4b, ex 4e – audio track 1.15, ex 4c–4d

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Reacting to a story box on p. 9: elicit How strange / That’s bizarre, odd, weird, spooky and model them with the wide intonation they need, because flat they sound bored. Then the first two questions of ex 2 in groups of three or four: which of yesterday’s three stories was the spookiest, and is there an explanation for any of them. Four minutes; they react to each other with the phrases.

stages.name: Test
stages.todo: Ex 3a: four short dialogues with five gaps, each needing a positive or negative auxiliary — Did you?, do you?, I did see one, Neither have I, I have. Pairs complete them, then track 1.12 (ex 3b) to check. Then the second half of ex 3b: match auxiliaries 1–5 to what they do — add emphasis, say you are different, check information, show surprise, say you are the same. Monitor: the Teacher’s Book expects 1, 2 and 4 to be revision and the emphatic did in 3 to be new. Note who stumbles on which.
stages.avoid: Give nothing away while they work — the matching is the diagnosis, and it tells you what the next stage is.

stages.name: Teach
stages.todo: Work from their matching and Grammar Bank 1B on p. 133 (rules 2–6), teaching only what the test exposed — usually emphasis (rule 5: do/does/did before the main verb, or the auxiliary stressed and uncontracted) and reply questions (rule 4). Concept check the emphatic one: I did see one — is B contradicting A? Is did there for the past? Then the form on the board. Pronunciation sits here: track 1.14, the two dialogues in ex 4a — they notice the stressed auxiliaries (Did you? rising; So did I with the weight on So and I), then ex 4b, pairs repeat them copying the rhythm. Track 1.15 (ex 4e): is do stressed in I do like them? Yes. Drill those five lines, the whole class and then individuals.
stages.avoid: Six rules are on p. 133 and five uses on p. 9. The test tells you which two or three to teach; do not walk them through all six.

stages.name: Second test: controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p. 133 ex a: ten mini-dialogues, one auxiliary or modal each. Alone, then pairs, and take only the disputed ones — read them aloud with the stress, not just the word.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 4c: they complete the eight sentences about themselves — I’m not very good at …, I’ve never read …, I didn’t … last night. Then ex 4d: A reads a sentence, B answers with a reply question and then says whether they are the same or different (Aren’t you? Neither am I. / I am.), then swap. Demonstrate with your own first two sentences before they start, as the Teacher’s Book suggests. Monitor for the auxiliary and the intonation.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two or three exchanges you heard on the board — a reply question with the wrong auxiliary, one that was right — and the class decides which is which. Re-drill the one that was flat.

2A.context: Call the doctor? – first aid, illness and injury, and a patient who has been reading the internet (File 2A)

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised reading for specific information and for detail, checking a first-aid quiz against the Red Cross answers and explaining them to a partner.
slots.sub: To develop students’ vocabulary for injuries and first aid — the ten highlighted words in the quiz: choke, lean, burn, bleed, press, wound, treat, pinch, collapse, bandage.
slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 14 ex 1a–1c (the quiz ‘Help save lives!’) / Communication First aid quiz: p. 105 (Student A, answers 1–3) and p. 109 (Student B, answers 4–6)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: You are first today and you set the context for the two lessons after you. Elicit first aid from the Red Cross logo or a picture of a first-aid kit, then two questions in pairs: has anyone had any first-aid training, and what would you do if someone next to you collapsed. Two minutes, two answers in open class. Board any illness or injury words that come up — they are the day’s lexis.

stages.name: Vocabulary for the quiz
stages.todo: Ex 1a: the ten highlighted words in the six quiz questions — choke, lean, burn, bleed, press, wound, treat, pinch, collapse, bandage. Pairs work out the meaning from the questions and the pictures. Check by miming or with the pictures, and drill the ones that will come out wrong: wound (the vowel), choke, bandage. This is the pre-teaching; the answers on pp. 105 and 109 reuse all ten.

stages.name: Prediction: the quiz
stages.todo: Ex 1b: the six questions, a, b or c, in pairs. Get a quick vote for each question so the room has committed itself, and confirm nothing — the reading is where they find out.

stages.name: Reading for specific information, then for detail
stages.todo: Pairs A and B. A reads the answers to questions 1–3 on p. 105, B the answers to 4–6 on p. 109. First read, two minutes: find the correct letter for each of your three and compare it with what the pair guessed. Second read, five minutes: the steps and the reason behind each — why cold water, why lean forward, why not straighten the leg. Then ex 1c: books covered, A tells B the right answer to 1–3 and why, B does the same for 4–6, using the quiz pictures as prompts. Finish with hands up: who had all six right.
stages.avoid: Do not let them read all six answers. Half each is what makes the telling necessary, and the telling is where the vocabulary gets used.

stages.name: Response: what would you do
stages.todo: Groups of three or four: which of the six emergencies would you feel confident dealing with now, which still frightens you, and has anyone in the group ever seen one happen — what did people do? Six minutes of talking while you collect what you hear; push them to use the words from the quiz.
stages.avoid: Ex 2f on p. 15 is not on your card — it is the next lesson’s discussion. Keep yours to the six emergencies in the quiz.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One story from the groups that the room should hear. Then three sentences from your notes on the board, one of them right, and they correct them in pairs — make one of them a use of wound, choke or press so the vocabulary gets a second outing.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised pronouncing medical words containing the sounds /ʃ/, /dʒ/, /tʃ/ and /k/, with the correct word stress.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency, talking about illness, injury and first aid in their own lives.
slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 15 ex 2a, ex 2b – audio track 1.33, ex 2d, ex 2e – audio track 1.34, ex 2f / Workbook p. 13 ex 4a and 4c

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The four sound pictures at the top of ex 2a: shower, jazz, chess, key. Elicit the sound each one stands for and have the class say it. Then ask for one word from the first-aid lesson for each sound — rash, bandage, choke, ache will do — and leave the four columns on the board.

stages.name: Presentation
stages.todo: Ex 2a: the nine words sorted into the four columns, in pairs, saying them aloud as they go. Track 1.33 (ex 2b) to check. Then the teaching: /ʃ/ and /tʃ/ — the same place in the mouth, one continuous and one with a stop; /tʃ/ and /dʒ/ — the voicing; and the spelling trap the book points out, that ch is usually /tʃ/ (choking) but /k/ in ache and stomach. Drill the four columns, then across them: pressure, choking, allergy, ache. Then ex 2d–2e: the twelve longer words with their phonemics — track 1.34, they underline the stress, and you drill the ones that fall wrongly in most languages: antibiotics, paracetamol, cholesterol, emergency, injection.
stages.avoid: This is the one lesson of the day where pronunciation is the main aim, so the drilling is not a minute at the end: the whole class, then rows, then individuals, and go back to anyone who has the stop in the wrong place.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 13 ex 4a: six rows of four words, circle the one with the different sound. Then ex 4c: underline the stress in ten words — antibiotic, allergic, diarrhoea, dizzy, headache, medicine, swollen, temperature, vomit, unconscious. Alone, pairs, and check by having them say the rows aloud, not by reading out letters.

stages.name: Practice in sentences
stages.todo: Pairs write three sentences about a patient, each using two words from today’s lists — I’ve got a rash on my stomach and a temperature; she needs an injection and some antibiotics. They read them to another pair, who write down which sounds they heard. Monitor for /ʃ/ against /tʃ/ and the stress on the long words.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 2f in groups: what injuries or illnesses you might get cooking, doing sport or eating out; whether any has happened to you; whether you have ever given or been given first aid; what you should do for a high temperature, a wasp sting with an allergic reaction, bad sunburn. Eight minutes; a secretary in each group keeps the questions moving. Listen for the target sounds and for anything good.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One story from the groups. Then four or five words you heard mispronounced on the board, say them wrongly and rightly, let them tell you which was which, and re-drill the wrong ones.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised using the present perfect simple and continuous to talk about illness and habits — the continuous for an unfinished or repeated action, the simple for a completed one or a number of times.
slots.sub: To practise listening for detail: a doctor and a patient who has been reading too much on the internet.
slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 15 ex 3a–3b – audio track 1.35, ex 3c – audio track 1.36, ex 3d / Grammar Bank 2A, SB p. 134, rules and ex b / SB p. 15 ex 3f

stages.name: Lead-in and listening task
stages.todo: The context is set; one line is enough — after this morning’s first aid, who would you rather have treating you, a doctor or your friend who did the course? Then ex 3a, track 1.35, books closed or the dialogue covered: what symptoms does Mr Blaine have and what does the doctor suggest? Headaches, a cough, a temperature; wait a few days. Ex 3b, second play: complete the six gaps with the verb forms they hear. Pairs compare, check on screen. Then track 1.36 (ex 3c), twenty seconds: what do the doctor and nurse think of him — a hypochondriac, which is the word the next lesson needs.
stages.avoid: This is a grammar lesson with a short listening in front of it, not a listening lesson. Two plays of 1.35 and one of 1.36, and you are at the language by minute eleven.

stages.name: Highlighting the target language
stages.todo: Ex 3d: the two sentences — Have you been taking / taken anything for the headaches? and How many tablets have you been taking / taken so far today? Circle the right form or tick both, in pairs, and say why. The first takes both; the second only the simple, because it asks how many. Take the answers; the teaching is the next stage.

stages.name: Clarifying the target language
stages.todo: Board two of the gapped sentences from the dialogue: I’ve been coughing a lot and I’ve taken it five or six times. Meaning first: the continuous for an action still going on, repeated, or just stopped with a result (I haven’t been feeling well for a few days); the simple when it is finished or counted (how many tablets, five or six times) and with non-action verbs (I haven’t had one for two months). Concept check with the Grammar Bank’s own pair — I’ve painted the kitchen / I’ve been painting the kitchen: which one is finished? Then the form on the board: have/has + been + -ing against have/has + past participle. Pronunciation: the weak ’ve been /əv bɪn/ — drill I’ve been coughing a lot and Have you been taking anything? as whole sentences. Grammar Bank 2A on p. 134 is the reference; have your concept questions ready before the lesson.
stages.avoid: One contrast, not two. The simple with just / yet / already / ever is on p. 134 too, but it is not what the dialogue is about and it will not fit in thirteen minutes.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p. 134 ex b: eight sentences, present perfect simple or continuous — we’ve known Jack and Ann, have you been working out, Emily hasn’t done her homework yet, we’ve been walking for hours. Individually, then compare; deal only with what they argued about; make them say which rule decided it.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 3f: eight pairs of prompts — the first question in the present simple or continuous, the second in the present perfect simple or continuous: Do you often get colds? How many colds have you had in the last three months? Elicit the first two questions from the class so they have the shape, then pairs ask and answer from the prompts without writing the questions out. Monitor for the choice of form.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Three sentences from your monitoring on the board, one right, for the class to sort. The wrong one will be a counted action in the continuous — I’ve been having three colds — so have that one ready.

2B.context: Call the doctor? (continued) – cyberchondriacs, writing to a friend about being ill, and medical myths (File 2A)

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised using medical vocabulary from an article about cyberchondria — life-threatening, mouth ulcer, alternative remedies, under the weather, cancer, infection, heart rate, surgery, pulse, tumour, miracle cures — to talk about health worries.
slots.sub: To practise reading for gist, in the context of a journalist who diagnoses herself online.
slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 16 ex 5a–5b (‘Confessions of a cyberchondriac’) / SB p. 17 ex 5c, ex 5d – audio track 1.40 (ex 5e is a detailed-reading task and is not part of this lesson)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Yesterday’s Mr Blaine, the patient who had read about brain tumours online — what did the nurse call him? Ex 5a: how would you define a hypochondriac, and what might a cyberchondriac be? Drill both words; the stress is on -chon-. Two guesses on the board and no confirmation — the first read gives it.

stages.name: Reading task
stages.todo: Ex 5b in two passes, both quick. First: read the article once to check what a cyberchondriac is — two minutes, one answer. Then go through the Topic sentences box, and pairs fit sentences A–E to the five paragraph gaps, with a four-minute limit. Check: 1 B, 2 E, 3 D, 4 C, 5 A. The text has done its job; from here on it is a vocabulary lesson.
stages.avoid: No pre-teaching before the reading and no comprehension questions after it. Ex 5e is detailed reading and is not on your card; the text is here to carry the eleven phrases, nothing else.

stages.name: Highlighting the target language
stages.todo: Ex 5c: the eleven highlighted words and phrases matched to definitions 1–11, in pairs with the article open, because the context decides most of them. Take no answers yet.

stages.name: Clarifying the target language
stages.todo: Track 1.40 (ex 5d) to check the matching, then the teaching. Meaning the definitions have mostly done, so check the two that confuse: pulse against heart rate (you take a pulse; a rate is a number per minute), and infection against tumour. Then form and pronunciation while each is on the board: life-threatening is a compound adjective, stress on life; under the weather goes with be or feel; surgery is uncountable (have surgery, not a surgery); infection gives infected and infectious; and the sounds in tumour /ˈtjuːmə/ and ulcer /ˈʌlsə/. Drill the lot in short phrases — a life-threatening illness, feeling under the weather, take your pulse, a miracle cure.
stages.avoid: Eleven items is the top of what forty-five minutes holds. If you are running late, let cancer and alternative remedies go as passive items; the practice needs under the weather, pulse, heart rate, infection, surgery and life-threatening.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: The book gives no practice exercise for this set, so bring one: eight sentences about a patient with one phrase missing from each, first letter given — She was feeling u___ the weather, so she googled her symptoms; The doctor took his p___ and said it was normal. Alone, pairs, and check only the disputed ones.

stages.name: Freer practice and feedback
stages.todo: Pairs write a short exchange between a doctor and a cyberchondriac who has diagnosed himself online, using at least four of the phrases; three minutes to write, then they perform it to another pair, who count the phrases they hear. Two pairs perform to the room if there is time. Then two lines from your monitoring on the board, one right and one wrong, for the class to sort.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised writing an informal email to a friend, explaining that they have not been well and saying what they have been doing recently.
slots.sub: To practise the expressions used to open, respond and close an informal email — Sorry for not writing earlier, Hope you feel better soon, That’s all for now, Take care.
slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 15 ex 4 (the task) / Writing Bank, SB p. 113, An informal email: ex a–f (Anna’s email, the Useful language box, the plan)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Two questions in pairs: when did you last write to a friend to say you had been ill, and what did you tell them? Then set the task from ex 4 on p. 15 before anyone reads a model: today they write to a friend, saying they have not been well and what they have been doing. Point out that the grammar from yesterday — I haven’t been feeling well, I’ve been catching up on my emails — is exactly what this email needs.

stages.name: Model text
stages.todo: Writing Bank p. 113, Anna’s email to Sue. Read it once for content: what has happened to Anna, and what does she want from Sue? Then ex a in pairs: the twelve highlighted mistakes — four grammar or vocabulary, four punctuation, four spelling — decide which kind each is and correct it. Check on screen. Then ex b: find the three sentences that mean I haven’t written or phoned, I’ve been reading and replying to my emails, Have you been doing anything exciting? Elicit the shape of the email while you are there: an apology, news, questions, a request, a sign-off.
stages.avoid: Ex a is a proofreading exercise and it can eat the lesson. Six minutes, then the answers on screen; the point is to see what a good email looks like, not to teach spelling.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Ex c: the Useful language box with fourteen gaps — Thanks for your email, It was great to hear from you, Sorry for not writing earlier, Glad to hear that you’re all well, Hope you feel better soon, That’s all for now, Looking forward to hearing from you, Give my regards to, Take care. Pairs complete it, then check. Board the three groups — opening, responding to news, closing — and the form that trips them: for + -ing (Sorry for not writing), to + -ing after looking forward to. Drill three or four as whole phrases.

stages.name: Preparing to write
stages.todo: Ex d: they plan. Decide who the friend is and what the illness was (invented is fine), then notes under three headings — the apology and what was wrong, what you have been doing since, a question or two for the friend. Notes only, silence.

stages.name: Writing task
stages.todo: Ex e: 120–180 words in two or three paragraphs, informal, with contractions, at least three expressions from the box and the present perfect simple and continuous where the content calls for it. Plan and board in front of them, in silence. Answer questions by walking over, not by talking to the room. Give a two-minute warning for ex f: check it yourself before you hand it over.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Swap emails with someone else. The reader answers one question — what has your friend been doing? — and underlines one phrase from the box they used well. Then one thing from your monitoring on the board for the class to correct: make it the -ing after for or looking forward to, because that is what you will have seen. Collect the emails and write on them before the next lesson.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised reading for gist and for detail, in the context of four medical myths examined by the British Medical Journal.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency, discussing medical myths and home remedies in their own country.
slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) Workbook p. 11, 2A Reading ‘Medical myths’: ex 1a (missing sentences), ex 1b (true or false), ex 1c (highlighted words)

stages.name: Lead-in and pre-teaching
stages.todo: Three myths on the board — we only use ten per cent of our brains; reading in dim light ruins your eyesight; shaving makes hair grow back thicker. True or false, in pairs, with a reason. A quick vote, nothing confirmed. Then three words the text needs and does not explain: blink, drowsy, short-sighted. Elicit each, with one concept question, and move on.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: One question over the whole text: which of the three myths on the board are in it, and does the British Medical Journal say any of them is true? Three minutes, alone. Pair check, then settle the board — all three are in it (and a fourth, about turkey), and none is true.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 1a: four sentences A–E to fit into the gaps in the four myths, one sentence not needed. Alone, then pairs justify each choice by pointing at the line before and after the gap. Then ex 1b: five statements true or false — doctors spend a lot of time on myths, unshaven hair is the same colour, turkey contains less tryptophan than cheese. Pairs compare, then check both exercises on screen, with the line that gave each answer.

stages.name: Vocabulary from the text
stages.todo: Ex 1c: the highlighted words and phrases — guess them from the sentence they sit in, pairs, then a quick check. Spend the time on the two or three the discussion will want, not on all of them.

stages.name: Response: myths and remedies at home
stages.todo: Groups of four: what medical myths and home remedies do people in your country swear by, and who taught you them; do people trust doctors; why do so many people now look for a diagnosis online, and how reliable is it? Give each group a secretary to keep the questions moving and ask them to agree on one remedy that actually works. Nine minutes while you listen and note what to correct.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Each group’s one remedy that works, and the room’s reaction. Then two or three sentences from your notes on the board, one right, and let them find the wrong one before you say anything.

3A.context: Older and wiser? – two journalists live as old people for a month; dressing your age; clothes and fashion (File 2B)

slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 18 ex 1a–1b (lead-in), ex 2a–2b / SB p. 19 ex 2c–2g (‘Trading ages’)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1a–1b on p. 18 is the book’s own way in and it is a good one: fifteen adjectives sorted into teenagers or elderly people, then whether they are stereotypes. Keep it to six minutes and one question from 1b.

stages.name: Prediction and reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 2a, the photos of Karoline and Nick: what has been done to them and why. Then ex 2b, the first paragraph only, to check, and the highlighted body phrases guessed in pairs — wrinkled skin, false teeth, wigs, contact lenses.

stages.name: Prediction, then reading to check
stages.todo: Ex 2c: the three questions predicted in pairs before they read — how people treated them, what they learnt, how they felt afterwards. Then ex 2d, the rest of the article against a time limit, to see who was right.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 2e: nine statements, K, N or B, over the whole article. Alone, then pairs pointing at the line, then check.

stages.name: Vocabulary from the text
stages.todo: Ex 2f: the five highlighted verb phrases matched to their meanings — treat you, breaks down, been through, deal with, be ready. Check, then text covered and definitions only: can they remember the phrases?

stages.name: Response and feedback
stages.todo: Ex 2g in groups: how much contact do you have with elderly people, and are they treated well in your country? Seven minutes, then one view from each group and two or three sentences from your notes on the board, right and wrong mixed.

slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 20 ex 4a, ex 4b – audio track 1.45, ex 4c (the same track again), ex 4d

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 4a: the four photos — Adele, Jane Fonda, Gareth Malone, Mick Jagger. How old are they, and do you like the way they dress? Pairs, then two opinions in open class.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: The clothes the notes in ex 4c depend on: cardigan, slippers, blazer, chinos — pictures do it in a minute each. Nothing else in the script blocks the tasks.

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex 4b, track 1.45: do the two journalists agree that people should dress their age, and complete each one’s fashion rule. They do not agree; Liza says wear what suits you, Adrian says dress for the age you are. One play, pair check, confirm.

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex 4c, the same track: notes on why each journalist mentions the seven things — the warm cardigan and slippers, Jane Fonda’s leather miniskirt, teenagers, women over thirty, very short shorts, men in their twenties in blazers, men in their thirties. Read the list first, play once with a pause in the middle, pairs compare, and play again only for what they missed. Check on screen.

stages.name: Response
stages.todo: Ex 4d in groups of three or four: who do you agree with, Liza or Adrian, and why — then push it to themselves: has anyone ever told you to dress your age? Eight minutes while you collect what you hear.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Hands up for Liza or Adrian and one reason each way, then two or three sentences from your notes on the board and they correct them in pairs.

slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 20 ex 5a, ex 5c (the clothes quiz) / Vocabulary Bank Clothes and fashion, SB p. 153, ex 2a, 2b – audio track 1.48, ex 3a, 3b – audio track 1.49 / SB p. 21 ex 7

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 5a as a race: two minutes to list everything you can wear on your hands and arms, round your neck, on your feet, on your head. Pairs, then the longest list reads out.

stages.name: Test
stages.todo: The clothes quiz, ex 5c, in pairs against a time limit: opposites (smart, tight, trendy, get dressed, short-sleeved), what things are made of, it doesn’t fit / suit / match, and when you try on, dress up, hang up, get changed. Monitor and note which of the verb phrases and adjectives they cannot produce — that is what you teach.
stages.avoid: Do not confirm answers as you go round; the quiz is the diagnosis.

stages.name: Teach
stages.todo: Clarify only what the quiz exposed, from the two sets on p. 153: the adjectives in 2 (fashionable, trendy, stylish, smart, scruffy, old-fashioned — the box explains trendy, stylish and fashionable) and the verb phrases in 3, where the confusion is fit, suit, match and go with: fit is size, suit is you, match and go with are two things together. Form while each is up: dress up and hang up take an object between the two words, get changed / dressed / undressed is get + past participle. Drill the phrases with the stress on the particle — get CHANGED, hang it UP.
stages.avoid: Fifteen items are on the page; teach the ones the quiz showed they lack, not the whole bank. The materials and the describing-clothes set in section 1 are not on your card.

stages.name: Second test: controlled practice
stages.todo: P. 153 ex 2a: six sentences completed with the adjectives, track 1.48 to check. Then ex 3a: nine sentences matched to responses A–I, track 1.49 to check. On their own, then compare, and open class only for what they disagreed on.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: P. 21 ex 7, questions 1 and 2 in small groups: at what age is it OK to have a tattoo, pink streaked hair, an earring in one ear; in what situations is it not OK to wear torn jeans, a baseball cap backwards, very short shorts. Give them a target — one item the group agrees is never OK — and listen for the day’s phrases.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Each group’s never-OK item, then two sentences from your notes on the board — one with fit or suit used well, one wrong — and let the room find the wrong one.

3B.context: The truth about air travel – the inside story of flying, an emergency over the Atlantic, and telling a travel anecdote (File 3A)

slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 24 ex 2a–2d (the extract from ‘Air Babylon’) / SB p. 25 ex 4 (the flying questionnaire)

stages.name: Lead-in and prediction
stages.todo: A quick vote for who has flown this year, then ex 2a: the back cover of Air Babylon and its four questions — pairs guess the answers. Take a guess for each and board them; confirm nothing.
stages.avoid: Ex 1 at the top of p. 24 is a listening and is not on your card. Start at ex 2.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Four items the text does not give away and the tasks need: inflate, smuggle, shortage and sarcastic. Elicit each, with one concept question, and move on.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 2b: read the extract once to find the book’s answers to the four cover questions, against a time limit. Pair check, then settle the guesses on the board.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 2c: eight statements, true or false, and they underline the line that decides each one. Alone, then pairs defend their answers with the line, then check.

stages.name: Response
stages.todo: Ex 2d as the bridge — which fact surprised you, do you believe it — then p. 25 ex 4, the flying questionnaire, in pairs: how you feel about flying, your last flight, and the Have you ever list. Put anyone who has never flown with a pair who has, as the Teacher’s Book suggests. Listen in and note what to correct later.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: The best flight story in the room, told once more to everyone, then two or three sentences from your notes on the board corrected in pairs before you confirm.

slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 26 ex 6a–6c, 6e (‘Nightmare over the Atlantic!’) / Grammar Bank 3A, SB p. 136, rules 1–4 and ex b / Communication Flight stories: p. 105 (Student A) and p. 110 (Student B)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The headline Nightmare over the Atlantic! and one question: what could go wrong three hours into a flight? Two guesses and straight into the text.

stages.name: Reading task
stages.todo: Ex 6a: read the story once to answer one question — what exactly happened — ignoring the numbered verb choices. Pair check, confirm: a recorded emergency announcement played by mistake.
stages.avoid: This is a grammar lesson with a text in front of it, not a reading lesson. Six minutes here, no comprehension questions, and no pre-teaching for the gist task.

stages.name: Highlighting the target language
stages.todo: Ex 6b: circle the right verb form in 1–9, in pairs. Then ex 6c: the two highlighted verbs — had flown and had been flying — what is the difference? Take their answers without teaching yet.

stages.name: Clarifying the target language
stages.todo: The four narrative tenses on one timeline from the story: took off (main events), was screaming (in progress), had been played (earlier past), had been flying for three hours (earlier and continuing). The past perfect continuous is the new one — the Teacher’s Book says the other three are revision — so spend the time there: form (had been + -ing), the contrast with the past perfect simple from Grammar Bank 3A on p. 136 (she’d been reading / she’d read), and the pronunciation of the contraction ’d been, which disappears at speed. Drill two sentences from the story.
stages.avoid: Do not present the four tenses one by one from scratch. They know three; the lesson is the fourth and how it sits against the past perfect simple.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p. 136 ex b: ten sentences, past perfect simple or continuous. Individually, then a pair check; take the ones that split them — make them say why.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 6e as a warm-up, one minute: finish the two sentences four ways. Then Communication Flight stories: A reads the Hudson River landing on p. 105, B the story on p. 110, each imagines being a passenger and tells the partner the story in the first person. Monitor for the narrative tenses and keep two minutes for correction at the end.

slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 27 ex 7d – audio track 2.11 (the extract, as a model), ex 7e, ex 8b–8c (telling an anecdote)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Tell them a one-minute travel anecdote of your own, true or invented, and let them vote on which it was. That is the task they are about to do, shown before it is explained.

stages.name: Model
stages.todo: Ex 7d, track 2.11: a six-line story opening about a flight to Tokyo — they listen and notice the stressed words; then ex 7e, pairs read it with the rhythm. Point out what the opening does: scene, background, then the event.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: The Telling an anecdote box: setting the scene (This happened when I was …, I was …-ing when …), the main events (So then I …, Suddenly …), the end (In the end …, I felt …). Board them in three groups with the tense each one carries, and add the listener’s side — Really? How big was it? — which the task needs just as much.

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Ex 8b: choose one of the three topics — a frightening travel experience, getting ill or having an accident while travelling, a surprise on arriving home — true or invented, and plan it in notes under the three headings from the box. Walk round and feed in vocabulary.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Ex 8c: A tells, B shows interest and asks for details, then guesses true or invented; swap. Then change partners and tell it again — the second telling is where the fluency comes. Monitor for the narrative tenses.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Who fooled their partner, and one story the room should hear. Then three or four sentences from your notes on the board, right and wrong mixed, and the class decides which is which.

4A.context: Incredibly short stories – fifty-word stories, adverbs that are easy to confuse, and reading habits (File 3B)

slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 28 ex 1a (four fifty-word stories) / SB p. 29 ex 1b–1c, ex 4a–4c (writing a fifty-word story) / Grammar Bank 3B, SB p. 137, rules 1–5 and ex b

stages.name: Lead-in and reading task
stages.todo: The website name fiftywordstories.com and the Orson Welles quote on p. 28 set it up in a minute. Then ex 1a: the four stories matched to their titles, with the glossary, against a time limit; pairs retell one story each in their own words. Keep it to nine minutes — the stories carry the adverbs, and the adverbs are the lesson.

stages.name: Highlighting the target language
stages.todo: Ex 1b: the highlighted adverbs sorted into the chart — time, manner, degree, comment — and pairs notice where each sits in its sentence.

stages.name: Clarifying the target language
stages.todo: Ex 1c first — pairs place the five bold adverbs — then the rules from Grammar Bank 3B on p. 137 as they come up: manner after the verb, frequency in mid-position, time and place at the end, degree before the adjective, comment adverbs at the front. The Teacher’s Book tip is worth boarding: if in doubt, mid-position. Drill two of the sentences for the rhythm of a front-placed comment adverb (Unfortunately, …).

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p. 137 ex b: ten sentences with one or two adverbs to put in the normal position. On their own first, then compare; take only what they disagreed on.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 4a–4c on p. 29: pairs pick one of the titles offered, draft a story, then edit it to exactly fifty words with at least two adverbs in the right place. Swap with another pair and read.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One story read to the room, then two misplaced adverbs from the drafts on the board for the class to move.

slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 29 ex 2a–2c (‘Exam nerves’) / Vocabulary Bank Adverbs and adverbial phrases, SB p. 155, ex 1a, 1b – audio track 2.15 / Workbook p. 21 ex 3

stages.name: Lead-in and reading task
stages.todo: Ex 2a: the fifty-word story Exam nerves, read once for one question — who is it about? A teacher, not a student, which is the twist. One minute to enjoy it and move on.

stages.name: Highlighting the target language
stages.todo: Ex 2b: the highlighted pairs — hard and hardly, near and nearly — what is the difference? Pairs decide from the story, then p. 155 ex 1a: the eight confusing pairs matched to their sentences. Take no answers yet.

stages.name: Clarifying the target language
stages.todo: Track 2.15 (ex 1b) to check, then the teaching, pair by pair, on the four the Teacher’s Book flags as the real confusions: actually is not now; especially is above all and specially goes with a participle (specially made); at the end of something, but in the end after a wait; yet at the end of the phrase, still in mid-position. Concept questions for each, and the stress while they are up — ACtually, eSPEcially, eVENtually. Drill in the book’s sentences.
stages.avoid: Eight pairs is sixteen words. Half of each pair they know; teach the contrast, not the word, and give the time to the four pairs above.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 21 ex 3: twelve sentences, circle the right adverb. On their own, then compare, and open class only for what they disagreed on, with the reason.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Six questions of your own on the board, each with one of the day’s adverbs — Have you heard from an old friend lately? What do you still do that you did at ten? Is there a cinema near here? Pairs ask and answer with a follow-up each, then swap partners for three of them.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two things learned about a partner, then two sentences from your notes on the board, one right and one wrong, and they correct them in pairs.

slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 30 ex 5a–5b (the Reading habits questionnaire)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: What have you read today — a message, a menu, a novel, a sign? Hands up for each, and the point that everyone reads, just not the same things.
stages.avoid: Ex 6, the short story Lazy Susan, shares p. 30 with you. Leave it to the next session; the questionnaire is your material.

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: The questionnaire on p. 30: they read it through, check the text types they do not know (comics, classics, manuals, chat forums), decide their Yes or No route at Do you read books for pleasure?, and note their own answers so the interview is not the first time they think.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: The frequency language the answers need and the follow-ups the interviewer needs: every day, now and then, hardly ever, I used to … but …; and What kind? Why did you stop? What did you think of it? Board and drill a few.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Ex 5a: A interviews B through the questionnaire, asking for more each time, then swap. Then ex 5b in new pairs: how similar were you and your first partner? Give the interviewer a job — find the one thing your partner reads that you never would.

stages.name: Feedback on content
stages.todo: How many in the room read for pleasure, and the most surprising reading habit found. Plan how you collect it so it is not twelve people reading a list out.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Four or five sentences from your notes on the board, right and wrong mixed, with at least one frequency phrase used well, and they fix them in pairs, then you confirm.

4B.context: Stories and reading – a short story with a twist, an expert on children’s books, and people’s favourite books as children (File 3B, Colloquial English 2&3)

slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 30 ex 6a – audio track 2.19 (‘Lazy Susan’, Part 1) / SB p. 31 ex 6b – audio track 2.20, ex 6c – audio track 2.21, ex 6d – audio track 2.22

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The title Lazy Susan and the first line — a woman asks her husband to teach her to shoot. Pairs: why might she want that? Two guesses and start.
stages.avoid: Ex 5, the reading questionnaire, shares p. 30 with you and belongs to the other group’s session. Start at ex 6.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Three words the first two parts turn on: mugging, shooting range and purse (American for handbag — the glossary gives it). The p. 31 glossary covers the rest for Part 2; point at it before you play.

stages.name: Part 1: reading and listening
stages.todo: Ex 6a, track 2.19: they read and listen to Part 1 on p. 30 at the same time, then answer the four questions in pairs — where she wants to go, why Stan is surprised, what happened the week before, why ‘hard-earned’ is an exaggeration. Check.

stages.name: Part 2: listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex 6b, track 2.20 — this part is audio only. Read the eight questions and the glossary first, play once, pairs pool what they have, play again with a pause in the middle. Check; the self-defence instructor’s advice is the detail that matters for the ending.

stages.name: Part 3 and the ending
stages.todo: Ex 6c, track 2.21: read and listen to Part 3 on p. 31, answer questions 1–3 and predict in pairs what happens next (5). Then ex 6d, track 2.22, the ending: what happened, what Susan will do now, and did it end the way they expected. Let the prediction stand for a minute before you play — the twist is the point of the story.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Hands up: who saw the twist coming, and who liked the ending. Then two or three sentences from the predictions on the board and let the room find the wrong one.

slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 32 The interview: Part 1 ex a–c – audio track 2.23, Part 2 ex a–b – audio track 2.24 / SB p. 33 Part 3 ex a–b – audio track 2.25

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book’s own lead-in: six characters on the board — Christopher Robin, Captain Hook, Hermione, Lyra, the four Pevensie children, Laura Ingalls — and pairs name the books. Then Part 1 ex a: the biography of Julia Eccleshare and the book covers — has anyone read them?

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: The glossaries on p. 32 give warrior and teen anthem; add stamina and trilogy. A minute each.

stages.name: Part 1: gist, then detail
stages.todo: Ex b, track 2.23: why does she mention the four books — Warrior Scarlet, Little House on the Prairie, Mouse House, Northern Lights? One play, pair check. Then ex c on a second play: five statements true or false, and they correct the false ones. Check.

stages.name: Part 2: gist, then detail
stages.todo: Part 2 ex a, track 2.24: number the three photos in the order she mentions them. Then ex b, second play: circle the right answer in the five sentences — what makes a child a reader, films and books, Jacqueline Wilson, JK Rowling. Pairs compare, check.

stages.name: Part 3 and response
stages.todo: P. 33 Part 3 ex a, track 2.25: the three questions — print or e-books, will people read less, does she still read for pleasure. Then ex b on a second play: what she means by the five quoted lines. Then two minutes in pairs: do you agree with her about films, e-books and ‘the right book’?
stages.avoid: Looking at the language, In the street and the Speaking on p. 33 are the next lesson’s. Stop after Part 3.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One opinion from the pairs, then two sentences from your notes on the board for the class to sort.

slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 33 In the street ex a–b – audio track 2.27, ex c – audio track 2.28; Looking at the language – audio track 2.26 (fillers: well, actually, I mean, all right, sort of, you know); Speaking ex 1–4 / Workbook p. 23 ex 1

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ask one student a hard question — what was your favourite book as a child, and why — and let the room hear the um, the well, the pause. That is the lesson: what you say while you think.

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: In the street ex a, track 2.27: three people and five book titles — who mentions which. Then ex b, second play: the six statements matched to Charlie, Sean or Lucy. Pairs compare, check. Nine minutes; the recording is the vehicle, not the lesson.
stages.avoid: No pre-teaching before this and no third play. The language stage is where the time goes.

stages.name: Highlighting the target language
stages.todo: Looking at the language, track 2.26: six extracts from the interview with the filler missing — well, actually, I mean, all right, sort of, you know. They complete them, then go through the Ways of giving yourself time to think box in pairs: which fillers change the meaning (none) and what they do instead.

stages.name: Clarifying the target language
stages.todo: The six fillers on the board with what each buys you: well and I mean to start or restart an answer, actually to correct or surprise, sort of and you know to soften, all right to concede a point. Form is position — most sit at the start or before the word they soften — and the pronunciation is the whole point: unstressed, run together, with the voice held up so the turn is not over. Model the gapped extracts at speed and drill them; then ex c with track 2.28, the five colloquial phrases from the street interviews, as a quick extra.
stages.avoid: This is not a vocabulary lesson about six words. If they say well with full stress and a pause after it, it is not a filler; the drilling decides whether the lesson worked.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 23 ex 1: six mini-dialogues about books with the fillers gapped. Pairs complete them and then read them aloud as fast exchanges, swapping roles.

stages.name: Freer practice and feedback
stages.todo: Speaking ex 1–4 on p. 33: favourite childhood book, a character you identified with, whether your parents read to you, print or e-books — with the instruction the book gives, use fillers to give yourself time to think. Six minutes in pairs, then two things from your notes on the board, one of them a filler used well.

5A.context: Eco-guilt – how green are you, and how we will be living in twenty years’ time (File 4A)

slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 34 ex 1a–1c (‘How eco-guilty are you?’)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1a: the title Eco-guilt — what might it mean? Pairs guess, then the Alan Eddison quote at the top of the page if you want a second minute. Board one guess and leave it.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Four items the questionnaire needs and does not explain: reusable, recycle, organic, pollute. Elicit each, with one concept question, and move on; the rest can be guessed.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 1b, first half: read the introduction only to check the guess — eco-guilt is what you feel when you do something you know is bad for the environment. One question, two minutes, pair check.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 1b, second half: the questionnaire — six sections, three options each, tick the one that is true for you and add up the eco-points. Alone and honestly. Then they read what their score means at the bottom of the page.
stages.avoid: A questionnaire is a detail-reading task only if they have to read every option to choose. Set it so — true for you, not the greenest answer — or the reading collapses into skimming for the plus points.

stages.name: Response
stages.todo: Ex 1c in pairs: compare answers section by section and explain why you do or do not do these things; then do you agree with what your score says? A quick vote for the three score bands. Walk round and collect what you hear.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: The greenest person in the room and their secret, then three sentences from your notes on the board corrected in pairs before you confirm.

slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 35 ex 2a–2c (‘How we will be living in 20 years’ time’) / Grammar Bank 4A, SB p. 138, rules and ex a / Workbook p. 25 ex 3a

stages.name: Lead-in and reading task
stages.todo: The photo on p. 35 — wind turbines, solar panels, an electric car — and one question: what will be different in twenty years? Then ex 2a: the ten predictions sorted in pairs into already happening, likely, and probably not; ex 2b, the two you would most and least like to come true. Nine minutes and stop — the text is here for its verbs.
stages.avoid: Do not turn the predictions into a reading lesson. No pre-teaching, no comprehension questions; the sorting is the reading.

stages.name: Highlighting the target language
stages.todo: Ex 2c: the highlighted verbs — will have installed, will be recycling, will have been banned, will be driving — sorted into finished by then and in progress then. Pairs, then take the two lists.

stages.name: Clarifying the target language
stages.todo: Two sentences from the text on a timeline with a point marked twenty years ahead: temperatures will have risen (finished before that point) and we will be having more extreme weather (in progress at it). Concept check with the Grammar Bank’s pair — we’ll have dinner at 8.00 / we’ll be having dinner at 8.00 — and by as ‘at the latest’. Form: will have + past participle, will be + -ing. Pronunciation: the contractions ’ll have /əl əv/ and ’ll be, which vanish at speed — drill two sentences as whole sentences. Grammar Bank 4A on p. 138 is the reference.
stages.avoid: Two tenses is the top of what fits; keep both to one meaning each and do not open the future continuous for plans (Will you be going out?), which the Grammar Bank mentions and the lesson does not need.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p. 138 ex a: nine situations, each needing the future perfect or the future continuous. Individually, then a pair check, and open class only for the ones that split them.

stages.name: Further practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 25 ex 3a: six sentences, choose between three future forms. Pairs, aloud, and they say why for each.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two or three sentences from your monitoring on the board, right and wrong mixed, and the class decides which is which. Ex 2e, the oral practice, is the next lesson’s — leave it.

slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 35 ex 2e and the definitely / probably / likely box / Teacher’s Book p. 194, photocopiable Communicative 4A ‘In 20 years’ time’ (one copy per group of three)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: One prediction of your own about the class in twenty years — in twenty years’ time you’ll all be speaking better English than me — and a vote: will it happen? The task in a minute.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: The box on p. 35: it’ll definitely happen, it probably won’t, it’s (very) likely / unlikely to — board them on a scale from certain to impossible, note that unlikely replaces not likely and that improbably does not exist, and drill them with the two tenses from the last lesson underneath: it’s unlikely that cars will have been banned.

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Ex 2e: the six predictions — working from home, swimming pools banned, retiring at 70, handwriting gone — pairs decide what they think of each and why, with the phrases from the box. This is the rehearsal for the group task.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Groups of three with the p. 194 sheet: twelve predictions, and for each one the group decides whether it will happen and whether it would be a good thing, then votes before moving on. Do the first one with the whole class so they hear the shape. Keep the clock; stop them when most groups are past number nine.
stages.avoid: Twelve predictions in nineteen minutes is a pace. Tell them to vote and move, or one group will still be on self-driving cars at the end.

stages.name: Feedback on content
stages.todo: Each group’s most positive and most negative prediction, and one disagreement that did not get settled.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Four sentences from your notes on the board — at least one future perfect or continuous used well and one wrong — corrected in pairs before you confirm.

5B.context: Are you a risk taker? – risk in everyday life, safety rules, and expressions with take (File 4B)

slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 38 ex 1a, ex 1b – audio track 2.38, ex 1c–1d (the same track again), ex 1e–1f (the interview circles run on to p. 39)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Ahn Jun photo on p. 38 — real or a trick? (Real.) Then ex 1a in pairs: the dream on the edge of a precipice, and what the answer says about your attitude to risk. Drill precipice.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Three items from the recording that the detail task turns on: self-conscious, speeding ticket and set up a company. Quick.

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex 1b, track 2.38: six people answer Are you a risk taker? — how many say yes? One play, pair check, confirm: three.

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex 1c, second play: six statements matched to speakers. Pairs compare. Then ex 1d on a third play, pausing after each speaker: the risks they would take and would not. Check, then one minute in pairs — which speaker do you identify with?
stages.avoid: Three plays is the budget and the third is paused per speaker. Read the questions for 1c and 1d before the second play so it does double duty.

stages.name: Response: the risk interview
stages.todo: Ex 1e: A interviews B with the red circles (sports, appearance, health, on the road, shopping), writing R where B takes risks; then B interviews A with the blue circles on p. 39. Ex 1f: who is the bigger risk taker, and does the partner agree? Listen in and note what to correct later.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: The biggest risk taker in the room and the evidence, then three sentences from your notes on the board and they correct them in pairs.

slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 39 ex 2a–2c, ex 3a – audio track 2.42, ex 3b – audio track 2.43, ex 3c, ex 2e / Grammar Bank 4B, SB p. 139, rules and ex b

stages.name: Lead-in and text
stages.todo: One line back to the risk interviews, then ex 2a: eight sentence halves to match — If my dad finds out I’ve been hitchhiking, he’ll be furious; As soon as I’ve passed my driving test, I’m going to buy a car. Pairs, check. The eight sentences are the text; there is nothing else to read.

stages.name: Highlighting the target language
stages.todo: Ex 2b: from the highlighted verbs, which forms can go after if / when / as soon as, and which in the main clause? Then ex 2c: the two extra sentences — a possible consequence or an always-true one? Pairs; take their answers.

stages.name: Clarifying the target language
stages.todo: One rule carries the lesson: after if, when, as soon as, until, unless, before, after and in case, a present form — simple, continuous or perfect — never will, and the main clause takes any future form or an imperative. Board the error the Teacher’s Book predicts, I’ll be ready as soon as I’ll have had a shower, and let them fix it. Concept check in case against if with the umbrella pair in Grammar Bank 4B on p. 139. Then the pronunciation, which is the sub aim: ex 3a, track 2.42, six sentences dictated into the two dialogues; ex 3b, track 2.43, underline the stressed words — the content words carry the stress, if and ’ll go weak. Drill the six, then ex 3c, pairs say the dialogues smoothly.
stages.avoid: The zero conditional is one open-class question (ex 2c), not a second lesson. The time belongs to the time clauses and the rhythm.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p. 139 ex b: ten sentences completed with before, as soon as, in case, unless, until, when, after, if. In silence, then with a neighbour; deal with the two or three they argue about, read aloud with the rhythm.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 2e: eight safety tips to finish in your own words — don’t let children play near a pool unless …, keep a first aid kit in case …, unplug appliances as soon as …. Pairs, then a vote on the best tips as the Teacher’s Book suggests.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Three tips from the pairs on the board, one with will after when, for the class to find and fix.

slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 41 ex 5a, ex 5b – audio track 2.44 (as the way in), ex 6a–6c (expressions with take) / Workbook p. 28 ex 2

stages.name: Lead-in and listening task
stages.todo: Ex 5a: eight statements about the risks of driving, a, b or c — pairs choose and give reasons. Then ex 5b, track 2.44, once: listen and check. Ten minutes, and the recording has done its job: the expert says we need to take the risks involved in driving very seriously, which is the first of the day’s expressions.
stages.avoid: Ex 5c (a second play for detail) and 5d (the discussion) are a listening lesson. Not here.

stages.name: Highlighting the target language
stages.todo: Ex 6a: the three sentences from the lesson — take out insurance, taking risks, take the risks very seriously — what do the phrases mean and which is a phrasal verb? Then ex 6b: nine more expressions and phrasal verbs with take matched to meanings A–I. Pairs, no answers yet.

stages.name: Clarifying the target language
stages.todo: Check the matching, then the teaching on the nine: meaning where it is not transparent (take after, take into account, take advantage of), the form — which take an object and where it goes (take it into account, take your time), which are phrasal verbs (take after, take off, take up) — and the pronunciation, which is the weak take in the fixed phrases: take CARE of, take PART in, take PLACE. Drill them inside the ex 6c questions.
stages.avoid: Twelve expressions with take are on the page. Nine is the set; take out insurance, take risks and take seriously were the way in and need no more than a minute.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 28 ex 2: ten sentences, complete the expression with take. On their own first, then compare; take only what they disagreed on.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 6c: complete the eight questions with the right expression, then interview a partner — who do you take after, have you taken up a new hobby, what would you take into account buying a phone — with the Giving examples box (for example, for instance) to push for more.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One answer worth hearing, then two sentences from your notes on the board, one right and one with the wrong preposition, and let the room find the wrong one.

6A.context: The survivors’ club – how people react in an emergency, feelings, and what you would have done lost in the jungle (File 5A)

slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 44 ex 1a (the questionnaire), ex 1b–1c / SB p. 45 ‘How to eat an elephant’ (the article)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1a: four emergency situations, three reactions each — pairs choose and give reasons. Hands up per question; confirm nothing, the article and the end of the lesson settle it.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Three items that block and are not highlighted: cadet, avalanche and survival rate. Quick.
stages.avoid: The eight highlighted words — overwhelmed, stunned, challenge, bewildered, rational, overcome, keep calm, manageable tasks — are ex 1c. Do not pre-teach them.

stages.name: Reading for gist and detail
stages.todo: Ex 1b in two passes: first, two minutes, what is the answer to ‘How would you eat an elephant?’ and why does the Air Force teach it. Then the three questions — the key to survival, the 10-80-10 principle, the other factor — with a line reference for each. Pairs compare, check.

stages.name: Vocabulary from the text
stages.todo: Ex 1c: the eight highlighted words guessed from the sentence they sit in and matched to definitions 1–8. Check, drill the stress on overwhelmed, bewildered and rational — the next lesson builds on them.

stages.name: Response
stages.todo: Groups of three go back to ex 1a: which of the three groups in the 10-80-10 principle would each of you be, honestly, and what is the best answer to questions 2–4 now you have read the article? Then give the answers from the Teacher’s Book (2 c, 3 a, 4 c) and a quick vote for who had them.
stages.avoid: Ex 1d sends them to three Communication pages that are not on your card. The response is the discussion above, not the jigsaw.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two or three sentences from the groups on the board, one right, corrected in pairs before you confirm.

slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 45 ex 2a, ex 3a, ex 3b – audio track 3.5, ex 3c / Vocabulary Bank Feelings, SB p. 157, ex 2a, 2b – audio track 3.3 (the strong adjectives) / Workbook p. 31 ex 2b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The text has been read in the last lesson, so one line brings it back: the 10-80-10 principle — and ex 2a, which three of the four adjectives in 1c describe feelings? Overwhelmed, stunned, bewildered. Those three are the way into the set; do not set the article again.

stages.name: Highlighting the target language
stages.todo: P. 157 section 2: nine strong adjectives matched to their definitions — stunned, devastated, delighted, thrilled, astonished, desperate, overwhelmed, bewildered, horrified. Pairs, then track 3.3 to check.

stages.name: Clarifying the target language
stages.todo: Meaning the definitions have done; sort the nine onto a line from very happy to very unhappy and check the two that overlap (stunned against astonished — both surprise, but stunned cannot react). Then the two things the set needs: the Modifiers box — absolutely, really, totally with strong adjectives, never very or a bit — and the pronunciation, which is the lesson’s own point: ex 3a on p. 45, underline the stress in the nine bold adjectives in the dialogues, track 3.5 to check, then drill the dialogues in pairs copying the stress and the intonation.
stages.avoid: Sections 1 and 3 on p. 157 (the ordinary adjectives, the slang) are not on your card. Nine strong adjectives with their stress is a full lesson.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 31 ex 2b: seven sentences, replace the underlined words with the right strong adjective. Alone, pairs, disputed ones aloud with the stress.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 3c: choose two of the adjectives and tell your partner about a time you felt like that, with the modifier in front — I was absolutely devastated when …. The partner asks for details. Swap, then change partners for one more.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One story worth the room, then three sentences from your notes on the board — one with very before a strong adjective — and the class decides which is which.

slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 46 ex 4b (the beginning of ‘Lost in the jungle’), the ending – audio track 3.11, ex 4d / SB p. 47 ex 5a–5b, 5d / Grammar Bank 5A, SB p. 140, rules / Workbook p. 32 ex 3b

stages.name: Lead-in and text
stages.todo: Ex 4b: the beginning of the true story on pp. 46–47 — four men, a guide, the Amazon — read once for questions 1–3 (the plan, the tensions, why they split). Then jump to the end: track 3.11, the last part, with one question — how was Yossi found? Ten minutes; the story is here so that the conditional sentences in ex 5a have something to be about.
stages.avoid: Parts 1–5 of the listening (ex 4c) are a listening lesson of their own and are not on your card. The beginning and the ending are enough for the grammar.

stages.name: Highlighting the target language
stages.todo: Ex 5a: the four gapped sentences — what would you do if you were lost, if I thought someone was in my house I’d call the police, what would you have done if you had been in Yossi’s situation, if Kevin hadn’t looked for his friend Yossi would have died. Then ex 5b: which two are about the past? Pairs, then take the answers.

stages.name: Clarifying the target language
stages.todo: The contrast is the lesson: second conditional for an imagined present or future (if + past simple, would + infinitive), third for an imagined past that did not happen (if + past perfect, would have + past participle). Concept check with the Grammar Bank’s own pair on p. 140 — if you came to class more often / if you had come to class more often — which one still has a chance? Form on the board, then the pronunciation: would’ve and hadn’t at speed, drilled in the two Yossi sentences. The Teacher’s Book says both are known separately; the third conditional is what still breaks down in speech, so that is where the drilling goes.
stages.avoid: Mixed conditionals are in the Grammar Bank for recognition only. Leave them.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 32 ex 3b: eight pairs of facts rewritten as second or third conditionals. Individually, then a pair check; take the ones that split them, said aloud with the contractions.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 4d on p. 46 — would you have survived in Yossi’s situation, what would you have done differently — then ex 5d, the two stems about the city centre and the phone bill. Groups of three, and they push each other for the reason.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two sentences from your notes on the board, one a third conditional that worked and one with would in the if-clause, for the class to sort.

6B.context: It drives me mad! – things that annoy us, how we talk about feelings, and the regrets people have (File 5B)

slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 48 ex 1a–1b (the #iwishtheywouldn’t thread), ex 1d–1e / Grammar Bank 5B, SB p. 141, wish + would and ex a / Workbook p. 33 ex 1b

stages.name: Lead-in and text
stages.todo: One thing that drives you mad, told to the class in a sentence. Then ex 1a: the fourteen tweets — tick the ones that annoy you too — and ex 1b, compare your top three in pairs with the Useful language box (It really annoys me when …, It drives me mad when …). Nine minutes; the tweets are the text and every one of them carries the structure.
stages.avoid: No reading tasks beyond the ticking. The thread is there for its fourteen examples of wish + would, nothing else.

stages.name: Highlighting the target language
stages.todo: Two tweets on the board — I wish people would turn up when they say they’re going to; I wish my boss wouldn’t arrange meetings in my lunch hour — and two questions for pairs: who does the wishing, and who has to change? Is the thing happening now?

stages.name: Clarifying the target language
stages.todo: Meaning: wish + someone or something + would / wouldn’t for a habit or situation that annoys you and that you want to change — other people, the bus, the rain, never yourself (Grammar Bank 5B on p. 141 says so: not I wish I would). Concept check: is the person doing it now? Do you want them to stop? Form: wish + subject + would / wouldn’t + infinitive; ’d in speech. Pronunciation: the contracted ’d and the stress on the annoyance — I wish you’d PUT your shoes away — drilled in three tweets with real exasperation in the voice.
stages.avoid: Wish + past simple and past perfect (regrets) is the second half of the unit and another lesson. One structure today.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p. 141 ex a: ten annoyances rewritten as I wish … would / wouldn’t. Individually, then a pair check, and open class only for the ones that split them. Workbook p. 33 ex 1b as a second pass for anyone who finishes.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 1d: three tweets of their own for the thread, things they want people to change; then ex 1e, compared in groups of four — who shares the same annoyance? Collect the best for the board.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Three tweets from the groups on the board, one of them with a wish about the writer themselves, for the class to spot and fix.

slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 49 ex 2a, ex 2b – audio track 3.16, ex 2c–2e / Workbook p. 33 ex 2

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Back to the last lesson’s thread: one tweet, and three ways to say how you feel about it — it annoys me, it’s annoying, I’m annoyed. Board the three; they are the shape of the lesson.

stages.name: Test
stages.todo: Ex 2a: ten sentences, each completed with the right form of the bold word — infuriate, frustrate, embarrass, exhaust, disappoint, amaze, terrify, inspire, confuse, thrill — a verb, an -ing adjective or an -ed one. Alone, no help. Walk round and note what goes wrong: it is usually the -ed/-ing choice (I’m exhausting) and the verb pattern (it amazes me that).
stages.avoid: Give nothing away while they work; the gaps are the diagnosis.

stages.name: Teach
stages.todo: Track 3.16 (ex 2b) to check, then teach what the test exposed with the Ways of talking about feelings box: the verb takes the person as its object (it frustrates me), -ing describes the cause, -ed describes the person. Concept check with one pair — a confusing manual, a confused reader. Then ex 2c, the five that have no -ing form — impressive, stressful, scary, delightful, offensive. Pronunciation sits here: the -ed endings /d/, /t/, /ɪd/ (annoyed, depressed, irritated), as the box says; drill the ten sentences.
stages.avoid: Ten verbs with three forms each is the cap. Do not add the Vocabulary Bank adjectives from the last session; this lesson is the system, not more words.

stages.name: Second test: controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 33 ex 2: twelve sentences, an adjective or a verb made from the word in bold. In silence, then with a neighbour; deal with the two or three they argue about, and make them give the reason.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 2d: choose three of the circles — an embarrassing mistake, something that stresses you daily, a film that was disappointing — and tell your partner, starting I’m going to tell you about …. Then ex 2e: anything you feel exactly the same way about? Monitor for the -ed/-ing choice.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One shared feeling from the pairs, then three sentences from your notes on the board, one with the wrong ending, and they correct them in pairs.

slots.pages: English File Upper-intermediate (3rd ed.) SB p. 50 ex 3a–3d (‘Regrets, we’ve had a few’), ex 3e – audio track 3.17

stages.name: Lead-in and prediction
stages.todo: The Sinatra line in the glossary — Regrets, I’ve had a few — and one question: what do people in this country regret most? Then ex 3a: the five statements about regret, true or not, decided in pairs before they read. A quick vote on each, nothing confirmed.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Three items the text turns on and the glossary does not cover: dwell on, survey and fall out with (which is in the top-twenty list). Quick.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 3b: the first part of the article, to line 16, read once to check the five predictions. Pair check, then settle the board; make them point at the line.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 3c, text covered: another way of saying 75%, 66.6%, 25% — and what each one referred to. Then ex 3d: the twenty regrets, and pairs number what they think the top five were. Ex 3e, track 3.17, gives the answer in reverse order; who got all five?

stages.name: Response
stages.todo: The last question of ex 3e in groups of four — which would be the top regrets for your age group — then one regret of their own from the list, or one that is not on it, with the regret doing / having done box in front of them. Nine minutes while you listen and note what to correct.
stages.avoid: Ex 4 on p. 51 is not on your card: it teaches wish + past simple and past perfect, and the grammar of regret is another lesson.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Each group’s number-one regret for their age, and whether the room agrees. Then three sentences from your notes on the board — one with regret + -ing used well — and let the room find the wrong one.

s13.name: Pre-intermediate · New Total English
s13.sources:
Crace, A. & Acklam, R. (2011) New Total English Pre-intermediate Students’ Book. Pearson.
New Total English Pre-intermediate Teacher’s Book (2011). Pearson.
New Total English Pre-intermediate Workbook (2011). Pearson.

1A.context: 24 hours – Are you a culture vulture? What people do with their day and their weekend, and what they like doing

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised reading for gist and for detail in the context of three people describing what they like doing at the weekend.
slots.sub: To clarify the lifestyle labels party animal, workaholic, couch potato and culture vulture, and the going-out phrases the texts use (go clubbing, go to an exhibition, go bowling, go on a guided walk).
slots.pages: New Total English Pre-int SB p. 10 ex 1a–1b (gist), ex 2 (detail), ex 3 (response)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book warmer: party, work, couch and culture on the board. Elicit what each one means (couch is the one they will not know — it is a sofa). Pairs write five words they connect with each of the four, two minutes. Then pairs read out words at random and the room guesses which of the four it belongs to. Board a few of them and stop — this is a way in, not a vocabulary lesson.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Ex 1a: match photos A–D to descriptions 1–4. The four descriptions define the four labels for you, so after the answers (A 3, B 1, C 2, D 4) check each label with one question — a couch potato: does he go out much; a culture vulture: where does she spend Saturday. Be ready to draw a vulture. Then ask the room which one they are, hands up, thirty seconds.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 1b: read the three texts once and decide which type Marek, Lola and Henry are. Two minutes, books open to p. 10 or a photocopy, on their own, no dictionaries — tell them they only need the type, not every word. Quick check with a partner, then open class with one piece of evidence each: Marek the workaholic, Lola the culture vulture, Henry the couch potato. Deal with one or two words they ask about in a sentence each.
stages.avoid: The texts are full of like / don’t mind / can’t stand. If someone asks about them, give the meaning in a word and move on — the third lesson today takes those expressions apart, and that is not your aim.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 2: eight sentences to complete with Marek, Lola or Henry. Individually, five minutes, and tell them to underline the line in the text that proves each one. Pairs compare by pointing at the line, then nominate round the room: 1 Henry, 2 Lola, 3 Marek, 4 Lola, 5 Henry, 6 Marek, 7 Lola, 8 Henry. Have two harder questions ready on a slip for anyone who finishes early — what Marek does on Sundays, what Lola does on Saturday evenings.

stages.name: Vocabulary from the text
stages.todo: The going-out phrases the three texts use, which are the sub aim: go ice skating, go bowling, go to an exhibition, go to a concert, go to the theatre, go to a musical, go on a guided walk, go clubbing. Pairs find them in the texts and say who does each. Board them under go / go to / go on, so the preposition is visible, and drill the ones with linking — go to an exhibition, go on a guided walk.

stages.name: Post-reading writing
stages.todo: Ex 3 asks them to think of a friend or someone in their family whose weekend is like one of the three. Turn that into writing: on a handout that looks like a profile page, they write five or six sentences about that person’s typical weekend, using the texts as a model and at least two of the going-out phrases from the board. The person can be invented. Six minutes writing, in silence, you walking round. Then groups of three: read each other’s profile and say which of the four types the person is, and whether the writer agrees.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two groups say which type they found most of. Then three sentences from the profiles on the board, one of them right, for the room to sort — make one of them a go / go to / go on slip, because that is what you will have seen.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised using everyday-action verb phrases (have a lie-in, go for a swim, have a take-away, stay in for the evening, chat on the phone, do nothing) to say what they do on a normal day and at the weekend.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency comparing their day and their weekend with a partner’s.
slots.pages: New Total English Pre-int SB p. 9 ex 2 (diagnostic), ex 3a–3b / Workbook p. 4 ex 2 (ex 1 for fast finishers)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book warmer for this page: everyone stands up. Write a sentence about a normal day on the board — On Mondays I get up after 8 a.m. — and anyone it is true for sits down. Ask two of the ones still standing what time they do get up. Next sentence, same again, until one person is left standing. Four sentences is enough, and make them the kind of thing ex 2 is about: breakfast, the bus, the phone, the evening.

stages.name: Test
