stages.todo: Ex 2 on p. 9 as a cut-up: the verbs from box A on one colour of card, the endings from box B on another, one set per pair. They match as many as they can in five minutes, books closed, no help from you. Show one match on the board first (get up + early) and check with two questions that they know they are making phrases, not sentences. While they work, walk round with a list of the twenty phrases and tick the ones pairs get wrong or leave out — that list is your next stage. Then the photos: which phrases can they see.
stages.avoid: Do not confirm or correct while they match, and do not let a pair that finishes early tell the others. The stage exists to show you what they already have; a test the room passes together tells you nothing.

stages.name: Teach
stages.todo: Give the full key (it is in the Teacher’s Book notes for this page) and then teach only what your list says they missed. Expect it to be the ones with no translation-friendly verb: have a lie-in, have a take-away, stay in for the evening, do nothing, have a nap, chat on the phone, go for a swim. Meaning with a question each — a lie-in: is it sleeping, and is it on a work day; a take-away: do you cook it. Form is the verb that goes with the noun, so put four headings on the board — do, have, go / go for, and the rest — and have pairs sort the phrases they got wrong under them; point out the ones the book does not give but they will try (make breakfast and have breakfast both work; take a take-away does not). Then say the phrases as chunks and drill the ones they stumble on, with the weak a and for: have a lie-in, go for a walk. Leave the sorted board up.
stages.avoid: Twenty phrases is the test, not the teaching. If you present all twenty from scratch you have thrown the shape away and there is no time for the second test. Teach six to eight, the ones your list shows.

stages.name: Test
stages.todo: Workbook p. 4 ex 2: ten sentences with the verb missing — checks her emails, stay in on Saturday nights, take the train, have a lie-in, go for a swim, take a nap, read, have friends over, listen to the radio, do the shopping. On their own, in writing, four minutes, then a compare in pairs, and take only the ones they disagreed on. Ex 1 on the same page (match the verb to the ending) is for the fast finishers.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 3a on p. 9: against each phrase they write D (every day), W (only at the weekend), S (sometimes) or N (never). Do three about yourself on the board first so they see it is about their own life. Three minutes, alone. Then ex 3b in pairs, as sentences, not letters: I have a lie-in at the weekend — what about you? Board that model and the two things the Teacher’s Book reminds them of: always and never before the verb, every day and at the weekend at the end. They find three things they both do and one they never both do. If there is time, change partners and ask them to find the person in the room whose weekend is most like theirs.
stages.avoid: If they simply show each other the lettered list, there is no speaking. Say before they start that the paper stays face down and they ask.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two or three pairs report the thing they both do. Then four sentences from your notes on the board, right and wrong mixed — a wrong verb with a noun (make exercise), an adverb in the wrong place, and one that was fine — and pairs decide which is which before you confirm.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised expressing graded likes and dislikes — I absolutely love, I really like, I’m quite keen on, I don’t mind, I’m not very keen on, I can’t stand — followed by a noun or an -ing form, to talk about how they spend their free time.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency asking and answering questions about their hobbies and free time.
slots.pages: New Total English Pre-int SB p. 10 (the three texts, read in the first lesson of the day) / SB p. 11 ex 6 (Active grammar, from the p. 10 texts), ex 7, ex 8a–8b – audio track 1.2, ex 10–11 / SB p. 129 (Student B’s questions for ex 10) / Workbook p. 5 ex 5

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Books closed. The class read about Marek, Lola and Henry in the first lesson today, so ask pairs to remember three things one of them likes or hates doing, and the exact words the text used — the Teacher’s Book suggests starting them off with I quite like … on the board. Collect the expressions they remember and board them in no particular order.
stages.avoid: Do not set the texts again. The first lesson read them twice; you refer back, you do not re-read.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 6 on p. 11, the Active grammar box, with the texts on p. 10 open: pairs fill the five gaps from the texts. A larger copy of the box as a handout is worth making. Check: 1 really like, 2 ’m quite keen on, 3 don’t mind, 4 ’m not very keen on, 5 really hate. Now the board has seven expressions in a scale from three smiles to three frowns.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning: the scale, drawn vertically on the board from I absolutely love at the top to I can’t stand at the bottom, with the faces. Concept-check by placing things, not by explaining — a hot Metrobus in August: where does it go; coffee on Monday morning. Form: the note under the box says a noun or an -ing form follows, so board I’m quite keen on art next to I’m quite keen on looking at art and elicit the difference; then the one they will break — don’t mind takes -ing or a noun, never to. Pronunciation is ex 8a: pairs predict the six stressed words in each of the two sentences, play track 1.2, check, then ex 8b — it is the content words, nouns and verbs, that carry the stress. Drill both sentences with the stress, then two of the scale expressions in a sentence of their own.
stages.avoid: Only two of these expressions are new to most of the room (keen on, don’t mind); the rest is grading and form. Spend the fourteen minutes on the scale, the -ing / noun choice and the stress, not on re-teaching like.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 7 on p. 11: eight prompts with faces, written as full sentences — two faces and my job is I really hate my job or I can’t stand my job; a frown and go ice skating needs the -ing. In silence, five minutes, then a quick compare in pairs, and take the two or three that split the room. Workbook p. 5 ex 5 (one word per gap: keen, mind, stand, absolutely) is the second pass for anyone done early.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 10: Student A asks the seven questions on p. 11, Student B the seven on p. 129, each noting the other’s answers. Model it first with a strong student asking you question 1 and answer with a full, well-stressed sentence from the scale — that is the model they copy. Pairs, four minutes each way. Then ex 11: which of the four descriptions from the first lesson fits your partner, and do they agree.
stages.avoid: Student B’s questions are on p. 129, not on p. 11. Say so when you set it, or half the room reads the same seven questions and the information gap is gone.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two or three partners’ verdicts from ex 11. Then say three sentences you heard with the stress flat, and the room says them back with the stress where it belongs. Finish with one sentence missing its -ing after keen on, for the speaker to put right.

1B.context: 24 hours – Monday to Friday: Valentino Rossi’s typical day, and how often we do things in our own

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised listening for gist and for detail to a conversation about what the motorbike racer Valentino Rossi does on a race day and on a normal day.
slots.sub: To review the daily-routine verb phrases in ex 2a — get up early/late, go to the gym, go out in the evening, go to bed early/late, talk to his family/friends — used to predict and then report what Rossi does.
slots.pages: New Total English Pre-int SB p. 12 ex 1a–1b – audio track 1.3 / ex 2a–2b, ex 3 – audio track 1.4 / ex 4 (response)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book warmer: famous sportspeople on the board — hand two pens out and let the room write ten names, local ones welcome. Then pairs pick two of them and talk about what a normal day is like for that person when they are not competing. Two minutes, a couple of ideas in open class, done.

stages.name: Prediction and first listening
stages.todo: Ex 1a: the photos of Rossi — what job does he do? Pairs guess, no feedback. Then ex 1b, track 1.3, the first part of the conversation: they check the job and fill the fact file. Pairs compare, then take it: Italian, motorbike racer, nine world championships. The date of birth is printed, so they are listening for three things.

stages.name: Pre-listening
stages.todo: Ex 2a: using the phrases in the box, pairs guess what Rossi does on a race day and on a normal day. The box is the sub aim: check the five phrases quickly (go out in the evening — is it 7 a.m.; talk to his family — on the phone or at breakfast), say them, and let pairs use them to predict. Ideas in open class but confirm nothing — the recording does that.
stages.avoid: Do not pre-teach the adjectives in the recording (stressful, lazy, unusual). They are the next lesson’s target language and the tasks do not need them.

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex 2b, track 1.4, the second part: they listen once to check their predictions for the race day and the normal day. Pairs compare for thirty seconds, then elicit: race day — up early, prepares for the race; normal day — up late, the gym, out in the evening, bed late. Tell them before you play it that they will not hear every phrase in the box.

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex 3: eight questions about the second part. Give them thirty seconds to read the questions first, then play track 1.4 again. Pairs compare, then nominate: 1 about six or seven, 2 eleven o’clock, 3 no, 4 between twelve and two, 5 music, computer games, sometimes a film, 6 parties and clubs with friends, 7 about three or four in the morning, 8 no. Have one extra question on the board for anyone who does not want a third play — what does the woman say about her own life — and only play a third time if the room asks.

stages.name: Speaking response
stages.todo: Ex 4 extended into an A/B handout of eight questions: the book’s two (is Rossi’s normal life really like being on holiday; would you like his lifestyle), then your own — which part of his day would you enjoy most and least, how is your day different from his, do you know anyone with an unusual routine. A and B get different questions. Model it with a student so they see it is a conversation with follow-up questions, not a questionnaire. A–B pairs for five minutes, then A–A and B–B so each student answers the questions they asked.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One finding per pair — who would and would not want Rossi’s life. Then four or five sentences you wrote down while they talked on the board, right and wrong mixed, for pairs to correct on paper before you confirm. Keep it general: the next two lessons take the adjectives and the present simple, so do not spend your feedback on them.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised using eight adjectives for describing a day and a lifestyle — boring, busy, exciting, fun, lazy, relaxing, stressful, unusual — to talk about their own routine and other people’s.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency describing a typical day in somebody’s life.
slots.pages: New Total English Pre-int Teacher’s Book p. 124 audioscript 1.4 (copied as the reading handout) / SB p. 12 ex 5, ex 6 / Workbook p. 6 ex 2a (definitions only, for the handout), ex 2b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: A photo of Rossi on the board: who is he, what does he do, what do they remember about his day. Two minutes — call on the students who said something interesting in the last lesson’s speaking. You are bringing the context back, not re-telling it.

stages.name: Reading task
stages.todo: The audioscript of recording 1.4 is printed in the Teacher’s Book on p. 124; copy it out, enlarged, as a handout, and under it put the eight definitions from Workbook p. 6 ex 2a without the words. They read the script and find the adjective that matches each definition — all eight are in it. On their own, four minutes, then check with a partner, then take the answers: boring, busy, fun, exciting, lazy, relaxing, stressful, unusual. The script is a text they have heard twice, so no gist task is needed.
stages.avoid: The script is the way in, not a reading lesson. Seven minutes and out; if you spend fifteen here the clarification has nothing left.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning from ex 5 on p. 12: seven sentences about Rossi with the definition in brackets, done in pairs, then checked — 1 boring, 2 busy, 3 stressful, 4 relaxing, 5 lazy, 6 fun, 7 unusual. Concept-check the two pairs that blur: busy and stressful (can a busy day be happy), fun and funny (is bungee jumping fun or funny). Form: have them find the eight in the script and say what comes before — is, are, very, really, quite — and what comes after: a full stop or a noun (a lazy lifestyle, an unusual routine). No metalanguage beyond adjective. Pronunciation: pairs mark the stress on the four with more than one syllable — BORing, exCITing, reLAXing, STRESSful, unUSual — then drill the ones they got wrong and the two short ones in a sentence.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 6 ex 2b: seven gapped sentences — my job is really stressful, an unusual person, relaxing hobbies, a lazy lifestyle, the film is exciting, he’s very busy, it’s great fun. Individually, a quick compare in pairs, take only the ones they disagreed on.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 6 on p. 12 first: the five questions in pairs, four minutes — a stressful lifestyle, an unusual routine, lazy or busy weekends. Then the guessing game: tell the room about a famous person’s typical day using three of the adjectives, job last, and let them guess who. Now each student thinks of a famous person and does the same in groups of three; the group may ask questions. Have slips with extra names ready for anyone stuck.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Which famous people were guessed. Then hot correction from your notes: say a sentence with the wrong adjective in it, stop, and let the speaker’s group fix it — two or three like that, then re-drill the two stresses that went wrong. The next lesson takes the present simple, so leave grammar slips alone.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised using the present simple with adverbs of frequency (always, usually, often, sometimes, hardly ever, never) in the right position to describe someone’s daily habits.
slots.sub: To give students practice writing a short description of a person’s habits for others to read.
slots.pages: New Total English Pre-int SB p. 13 ex 7a–7b (Active grammar), ex 8, ex 9 – audio track 1.5 / Workbook p. 7 ex 5

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Two questions to the room about Rossi — what time does he get up on a normal day, does he go to bed early. The class has spent two lessons on him, so this is a thirty-second reminder, and the answers put the present simple in the air without you naming it.

stages.name: Test
stages.todo: A handout of five questions answered in writing, from memory, books closed: What time does Rossi get up on race days? Does he talk to his family in the morning? How often does he go to the gym? What does he usually do in the evening? And one about themselves — How often do you go to bed late? Full sentences, individually, no help. Walk round and note what you see: the third-person -s, does / doesn’t, and where they put the adverb — those notes decide the next stage. Then they compare in pairs and you put the correct answers on the board, because the form stage works from them.
stages.avoid: Do not correct while they write and do not let the strong students help. You are finding out what they have; a test they pass together hides it.

stages.name: Teach
stages.todo: Teach what the test exposed and nothing else. Meaning is ex 7a part A: the present simple is for habits, not single events — check it with one pair of sentences (I teach every day; I’m teaching now). Then the table with do / does / don’t / doesn’t, but only the row they got wrong. Ex 7b, part B, is the part most of the room needs: the adverbs on a scale from always to never — write them up jumbled and let pairs order them — then the three rules, which they choose for themselves: before the main verb, after be, longer phrases at the end. Pronunciation is ex 9 with track 1.5: do and does are weak in the question and strong in the short answer; play it, let them hear it, drill the two exchanges.
stages.avoid: If nobody dropped the third-person -s, do not teach it. The temptation is to present the whole tense because you prepared it; the shape only works if you leave out what they already have.

stages.name: Test
stages.todo: Ex 8 on p. 13: four exchanges with a mistake in each question and each answer — Does you get up, I get up always early, Do your brother, he do, You go clubbing, I not, Your sister does go, phones sometimes. Pairs find and correct, aloud, saying the whole corrected line. Check in open class. Workbook p. 7 ex 5 (five jumbled sentences with an adverb to place) is the written second pass for the early finishers.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Describe a friend with an interesting job without naming it — he hardly ever sleeps at home, he often flies, he is always busy — and let them guess (a helicopter doctor). Then each student writes five or six sentences about an imaginary person’s habits, with an adverb in each, never naming the job; slips with jobs for the unimaginative — astronaut, zookeeper, night nurse. Six minutes, numbered sheets, then stick them round the room and everyone walks round guessing the jobs on a numbered list. Quick recap of the guesses.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Four or five sentences from the sheets on the board, one of them right — an adverb in the wrong place, a missing -s, a doesn’t with an -s after it. Pairs correct them on paper, then you confirm.

2A.context: 24 hours – At the same time: Joe buys a guitar on eBay while his friends comment; what we are doing now and around now

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised reading for gist and for detail in the context of a social-networking thread about buying a guitar at an online auction.
slots.sub: To clarify the online-auction and social-media words the thread needs — bid / bidding, top price, wall, comment, save your money, give me a chance.
slots.pages: New Total English Pre-int SB p. 14 ex 1 (lead-in), ex 2 (gist), ex 3 (detail), ex 4 (response)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book warmer: Facebook on the board, pairs have two minutes to write every word they connect with it, the pair with the longest list reads it out and wins if every word is accepted. Then ex 1 question 1 only, in open class for a minute: how often do they use these sites.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Ex 1 question 2 is the way in: how often do you bid for things on eBay? Bid is the one word the whole thread turns on, so teach it properly — you offer €50, someone offers €55, is your €50 still good; bid as a noun and bidding as the activity. Then top price and wall / comment in a sentence each. The rest the thread makes clear.
stages.avoid: Do not pre-teach the present continuous or the time phrases (at the moment, every time, all the time). Both belong to the next two lessons; the gist and detail tasks do not depend on them.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 2: read the thread quickly for one thing — what two things is Joe looking at on eBay. Two minutes, in silence, no dictionaries; it is a long page but the question only needs the first post and the last. Pair check, then the answer: a guitar, and a pair of ice skates. Ask one follow-up — did he buy the guitar — so they have read to the end.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 3: six questions, answered alone in five minutes with the line of the thread underlined for each — the time stamps are the clue for 3 and 5. Pairs compare by pointing at the line. Then nominate: 1 because he is having guitar lessons, 2 someone he works with, 3 €50, 4 at work, 5 €70, 6 €150. Have a harder question on a slip for the early finishers — why is Joe not writing a very good report.

stages.name: Speaking response
stages.todo: Ex 4 in groups of three, extended into two rounds. Round one is a reaction to the thread: Debbie says eBay is not exciting and Joe is crazy — do they agree, and was €150 a good price. Round two is personal: one good and one bad thing about social-networking sites, and what they themselves buy online and whether they have ever paid too much. Give them the questions on a slip. Then the Teacher’s Book’s finish — list the good and bad things on the board and vote: mainly good or mainly bad. You listen with a pen.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: The vote, in one minute. Then four or five sentences from the groups on the board, right and wrong mixed, for pairs to put right on paper before you confirm. Leave any present continuous slip alone — the next lesson is about it.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised using the present continuous for actions happening now and for temporary actions around now, in contrast with the present simple for habits and states, to talk about their own lives.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency describing their life now to an old friend they have not seen for years.
slots.pages: New Total English Pre-int SB p. 14 (Joe’s thread, read in the previous lesson) / SB p. 15 ex 5a–5b (Active grammar), ex 6, ex 10a–10b / Workbook p. 8 ex 3

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: One minute to bring Joe back — what did he buy, how much did he pay. Then the Teacher’s Book’s grammar lead-in, which is one question on the board: why did Joe write I’m having guitar lessons and not I have guitar lessons? Pairs talk for a minute. Take two ideas and confirm nothing — the next stage answers it.
stages.avoid: Do not set the thread as a reading again. The previous lesson read it twice; you point at it.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 5a on p. 15: the two headings go into the Active grammar box — A is temporary actions around now (2), B is actions at this moment (1). Then ex 5b: pairs go back to the thread on p. 14 and find more examples for each heading, using the time stamps — I’m working all the time and where are you having lessons go under A; I’m doing two things at once, I’m making my first bid now, someone else is bidding €70 go under B. Board them in two columns.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning on a timeline: now is a point, around now is a stretch of days or weeks that includes now — I’m having lessons at the moment: is he in a lesson this second? no; this week, this month? yes. Then the second half of the box, the present simple for states (I know it’s a lot of money, I love music) and for habits (I listen to music every day): can you say I’m knowing? Form: be + verb-ing, the negative (I’m not writing), the question (are you bidding?), and the contractions. Pronunciation is the contractions and the weak are: I’m looking, it’s all happening, are you bidding for it now — drill the three as whole lines, fast.
stages.avoid: The present continuous is not new at this level; what is new is the around-now use and the state verbs. Put the minutes there, not into a presentation of the -ing form from zero.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 6 on p. 15: six exchanges, present simple or continuous — go once a week, buy / don’t like, do you usually do / go, isn’t studying / ’s travelling, do you know / ’m learning, are you doing / ’m working. In silence, check with a partner, take the ones that split the room. Workbook p. 8 ex 3, Paola’s email (seven choices, with loves / is loving as the state-verb trap), for the fast finishers.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 10a: each student writes down a city, a job, a hobby, a foreign language and a musical instrument — and these are now their life. Then ex 10b: they meet an old friend they last saw six years ago and tell them about their life now. Board the book’s model — My life is very different now. I’m living in Bilbao and I’m not doing the same job — and ask for follow-up questions: do you like living there? Pairs, three minutes each way, then one swap.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two surprising new lives from the room. Then four sentences from your notes on the board, one correct, and pairs find the fault — expect I’m liking and a dropped am.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised using eight time phrases — at the moment, these days, all the time, 24 hours a day, every time, each time, at the same time, at once — to say when and how often they do things.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency asking and answering about their habits online and at work.
slots.pages: New Total English Pre-int SB p. 14 (Joe’s thread, re-read for the time phrases) / SB p. 15 ex 7, ex 8, ex 9

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Two lines on the board: I’m having guitar lessons at the moment and I’m having a guitar lesson. What is the difference? Pairs, one minute: the first is these weeks, the second is right now. Then one more minute: what other phrases do they know that say when or how often — board whatever comes.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Back to the thread on p. 14, which they have read twice today: pairs circle every phrase that says when or how often — at the moment, every day, these days, all the time, every Thursday evening, every time, right now, at once, at the moment again. Have spare copies; the earlier handouts will not all have survived. Collect them on the board.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex 7 on p. 15 does the first job: the three box phrases matched to the underlined ones — all the time is 24 hours a day, every time is each time, at the same time is at once. So the eight sort into three meanings on the board: how often (all the time / 24 hours a day; every time / each time), when (at the moment / these days), together (at the same time / at once). Concept-check the two that blur — every time versus all the time (every time I look, the price goes up: once or many times, and is there a gap between?). Form: every time and each time start a clause with the present simple; at the moment and these days go with the present continuous; at once and at the same time sit at the end. Stress and drill: ALL the time, at the SAME time, at the MOment, twenty-four HOURS a day — in the sentence, not the phrase on their own, and once as a stressed, busy person and once as a relaxed one, which is the intonation the Teacher’s Book is after.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 8: seven sentences, choose the right phrase — at the same time, Every time, at once, all the time, Each time, at the moment, 24 hours a day. On their own, a quick compare in pairs, and take only the two or three that split the room.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 9’s five questions, split into an A and a B set with two of your own added on social media and shopping — do you check Facebook every time you pick up your phone, do you shop online at the moment. Model one with a strong student, with a full answer and the phrase in it. Pairs, four minutes each way. Then the role-play: A has a very busy, stressful life, B an easy one; two minutes telling each other about their week, then swap roles. You listen with a pen.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One finding from the pairs. Then a correction slip per pair: four of their own sentences, two with the phrase in the wrong place or the wrong tense after it, to fix and read back to you. Collect the slips.

2B.context: Music – Music for 007: a radio programme about James Bond theme songs, the words for talking about music, and what happened when

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised listening for gist and for detail to a radio programme about the theme songs of the James Bond films.
slots.sub: To clarify the words the programme needs — spy, the Secret Service, came out, a classic, a mixed reaction — so the tasks are not blocked by them.
slots.pages: New Total English Pre-int SB p. 20 ex 1a–1b – audio track 1.9 / ex 2a–2b – audio track 1.10 / ex 3 (response)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book warmer: James Bond on the board, pairs say what they know about the films for a minute. Then seven names on the board — Carly Simon, Duran Duran, Jack White, Alicia Keys, Madonna, Paul McCartney, Shirley Bassey — and the question: what do these people have in common? Take guesses; they have all sung a Bond song. Thirty seconds of a theme tune from your phone does the rest.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Four items, and only because the tasks need them: spy and the Secret Service (what Bond is), came out (a film or song in a year), a mixed reaction (some people loved it, some did not). A sentence each, let them give you the word where they can, and move on. Everything else in the programme the picture and the song titles carry.
stages.avoid: Do not pre-teach duet, solo, lyrics, chorus, theme song, soundtrack, hit or flop. They are the next lesson’s target set, and ex 2a and 2b can be done without knowing them.

stages.name: Prediction and first listening
stages.todo: Ex 1a: four questions about Bond — who wrote the books, what his job is, who played him first, which film Jack White and Alicia Keys sang in. Pairs guess, no feedback. Then ex 1b, track 1.9, the introduction: listen and check. Ian Fleming; a spy for the British Secret Service; Sean Connery; Quantum of Solace.

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex 2a with track 1.10, the second part: match the artists a–f to the eight Bond songs. One play, individually, then pairs. Goldfinger, Diamonds Are Forever and Moonraker are all Shirley Bassey; A View to a Kill is Duran Duran; Live and Let Die Paul McCartney and Wings; Nobody Does It Better Carly Simon; Die Another Day Madonna; Another Way to Die they already have.

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex 2b: seven sentences to complete. Thirty seconds to read them first, then track 1.10 again. Pairs compare, then nominate: 1 2008, 2 Goldfinger, 3 three, 4 1971, 5 A View to a Kill, 6 the 1970s, 7 Die Another Day. A third play only if the room asks for it, and then only for the two or three they missed.
stages.avoid: Two full plays is the budget. If you play the whole programme a third time the response stage goes, and the response is where they speak.

stages.name: Speaking response
stages.todo: Ex 3 in groups of three, with two questions of your own added so it lasts: do they like Bond or other spy films and why; does a film need good music; which Bond song they know and like; and one film whose music they remember, and what it made them feel. Give the questions on a slip, four minutes, then re-group and report the most interesting answer.
stages.avoid: Stay off the music vocabulary and the past simple — the next two teachers have them. Your response is about films and feelings.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two groups report. Then reformulate: read out three things you heard, said correctly, and ask who said them and how they said it at the time.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised using ten words for talking about songs and singers — theme song, soundtrack, lyrics, chorus, duet, solo, lead singer, hit, flop, top of the charts — to talk about music they know.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency talking about their own musical tastes.
slots.pages: New Total English Pre-int Teacher’s Book pp. 124–125 audioscript 1.10 (copied as the reading handout) / SB p. 20 ex 4, ex 5 / Workbook p. 10 ex 1, ex 3

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Two minutes on the programme the class has just heard — which Bond song did they know, who sang three of them. You are bringing the recording back, not replaying it.

stages.name: Reading task
stages.todo: The audioscript of recording 1.10 is in the Teacher’s Book on pp. 124–125: copy it out as a clean, enlarged handout. They read it once and underline every word or phrase that is about music rather than films — the ten you want are all there: duet, lead singer, solos, lyrics, soundtracks, theme song, top of the charts, hits, flop, chorus. Individually, four minutes, then pairs compare their lists. Collect the ten on the board.
stages.avoid: This is the way in, not a reading lesson — they heard the script twice last lesson. Seven minutes, then the words.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning from the script: a matching handout with the ten words and ten short definitions (the Teacher’s Book gives you flop — no success at all — and catchy; write the rest), done in pairs with the script open, because the context decides it. Check with questions on the pairs that blur — a duet and a solo (how many singers), a hit and a flop, the lyrics and the chorus (all the words, or the part that repeats). Form: nouns, and the ones that take the — the lead singer, the top of the charts, the chorus — and hit and flop as both noun and adjective-like (a hit song). Pronunciation: CHOrus, LYrics, THEME song, SOUNDtrack, duET — mark the stress and drill the ones they mangle, chorus and theme especially.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 4 on p. 20: ten gapped sentences, singular or plural — duet, lead singer, solos, lyrics, soundtracks, theme song, top of the charts, hits, flop, chorus. In silence, check with a partner, take only the ones they disagree on. Workbook p. 10 ex 1 (five anagrams) and ex 3 (the dialogue about a vampire film) for anyone done early.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 5’s four questions in groups of three, with a fifth of your own: a song they know the lyrics to, a soundtrack they have downloaded, who is at the top of the charts now, a song and whether it is a solo, a duet or a group and who the lead singer is — and the last, a hit they think should have been a flop. Five minutes, then re-group and tell the new group the best answer you heard. Monitor for the words.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One song from each group. Then four sentences from your notes on the board, two of them using the target words, one of them right, for pairs to put right before you confirm.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised using the past simple of regular and irregular verbs, positive and negative, to describe completed events in a musician’s life and their own.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency asking and answering about their childhood and school days.
slots.pages: New Total English Pre-int Teacher’s Book pp. 124–125 audioscript 1.10 (the handout from the previous lesson, re-read for the past forms) / SB p. 21 ex 6a–6b (Active grammar), ex 7, ex 10a–10b / SB p. 149 (irregular verb table) / Workbook p. 11 ex 7a (the -ed sentences, said by you — no audio)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Goldfinger, 1964, on the board. When did it come out — then, or now? Pairs have one minute to remember any other things the programme said happened, and roughly when. Take three and write them up as they say them, wrong forms and all; you will come back to them.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: The script of recording 1.10 again (Teacher’s Book pp. 124–125; have spare copies, the earlier handouts will not all be there): pairs circle every verb that talks about the past — came out, was, had, didn’t have, got, sang, appealed, loved, didn’t like. Then two columns on the board: ones that end in -ed and ones that do not.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex 6a on p. 21: pairs complete the Active grammar box — started, became, expected, didn’t have, wasn’t, did she sing, was. Then ex 6b, regular or irregular: start and expect are regular; become, have, be and sing are not, and the table on p. 149 of their book has the rest. Meaning is one question — is it finished, and do we know when. Form: -ed for the regular ones, a form to learn for the rest, and didn’t + the infinitive for the negative, so didn’t had is the error to name. Pronunciation: the three -ed endings. Workbook p. 11 ex 7a has nine sentences built for it — say them yourself, they sort worked, kissed, wanted, finished, moved, ended, waited, loved, believed into /t/, /d/ and /ɪd/, and drill the /ɪd/ ones, which are the ones they will say as two syllables everywhere.
stages.avoid: The past simple is not new at pre-intermediate. The new content is the irregular forms in the script and the -ed sounds; keep the question form to the one line in the box and do not present the whole tense from zero — the source itself calls this a large subject for 45 minutes.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 7 on p. 21: the paragraph about Alicia Keys, ten verbs in the past simple — grew up, didn’t have, separated, appeared, began, went, started, didn’t finish, left, made. On their own, a quick compare in pairs, then take only the ones they disagreed on, and say the irregular ones aloud as you confirm them.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 10a: six questions from the prompts about a partner’s early life — when and where born, where grew up, what they liked and disliked about school, what job they wanted, what hobbies they had as a teenager, what they did when they left school. Check the questions in open class before anyone asks them. Then ex 10b in pairs, the asker taking notes, follow-up questions encouraged. Re-pair and tell the new partner what you found out.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Back to the three sentences from the lead-in: are they right now? Then four you heard, right and wrong mixed — a didn’t with a past form after it, an irregular verb regularised — and pairs find the fault before you confirm.

3A.context: Music – Barefoot music: Shakira, pop star and businesswoman — what she has done, and when she did it

slots.pages: New Total English Pre-int SB p. 22 ex 1 (gist), ex 2a–2b (jigsaw: Student A reads p. 129, Student B reads p. 133), ex 3 (response) / SB p. 129 / SB p. 133

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book warmer: pairs list ten pop stars, then describe one to another pair without the name, who guess. Finish with its last question — do any of these stars do anything for other people?

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Five items the texts do not explain: poverty, charity, a performer, determination, release an album. A sentence each, let them give you the word where they can, with one concept question each, and move on.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 1: the photo of Shakira with the child — what is the connection? One read of the p. 22 text, two minutes, to check: her charity builds schools for poor children in Colombia. Quick check with a partner, then the answer.
stages.avoid: The text is built on she’s sold, she has given, she started. Do not comment on the tenses; the next lesson is made of these sentences.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 2a as a jigsaw: Student A reads p. 129 (her childhood up to her first albums), Student B reads p. 133 (her career and her charity), each answering their own six questions alone. Then ex 2b: tell your partner about your half, and the listener writes down the three facts they find most interesting. Decide before the lesson how you will check twelve answers without reading both texts to the room.

stages.name: Post-reading discussion
stages.todo: Ex 3 in groups of three: the two most interesting things in her story, and whether rich, famous stars should do charity work. Add one question of your own about a local star who does, or does not.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One opinion per group on the charity question. Then one sentence per pair on a slip with a word underlined; they decide whether the underlined word is the problem and fix it. A quick round of the answers, with charity or poverty in at least one.

slots.pages: New Total English Pre-int SB p. 22 ex 4a–4b, ex 5a–5b (Active grammar, from the Shakira texts) / SB p. 133 (Student B’s text, for ex 5b) / SB p. 23 ex 6, ex 7, ex 8 – audio track 1.11, ex 9 / Workbook p. 12 ex 1

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book’s grammar lead-in: three questions on the board — have you ever met a famous person, which singers have you seen, have you ever played a musical instrument. Pairs, one minute, then two full answers in open class and the name of the tense.
stages.avoid: Do not set the Shakira texts again; the previous lesson read both halves. You point at sentences in them.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 4a on p. 22: the two underlined phrases — she’s sold and she started — which tense is each, and do we know when it happened? Then ex 4b, the two rules. Then ex 5b: pairs find more present perfect examples in the p. 22 text and in Student B’s text on p. 133 (she has earned, has done, has given, has paid for). Board them.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex 5a, the Active grammar box: have/has + past participle, the negative, the question with ever, and the past simple line beside it. Meaning on a timeline — some time up to now, time unknown or unimportant, against a finished time you can name — with ever and never. Pronunciation is ex 8 with track 1.11: have and has are weak in the question and strong in the short answer; drill the two exchanges.
stages.avoid: The error that matters is the present perfect with a finished time — I’ve seen her in 2008. Build one concept question for it; the rule alone will not stop it.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 6 on p. 23: the fan’s text, seven gaps in the present perfect — has had, haven’t met, haven’t paid, ’ve learned, ’ve downloaded, ’ve bought, haven’t had. Individually, a quick compare in pairs, take the disputed ones. Workbook p. 12 ex 1 (Nick’s interview, eight choices) for the early finishers.

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 7: three short dialogues, present perfect or past simple — Have you ever won… I won a singing competition when I was six. Pairs, aloud, because this is the stage that tests the contrast.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 9: the ex 7 questions asked and answered with true answers, and a past-simple follow-up after every yes — when, where, what. Swap partners once.
stages.avoid: The next lesson writes a biography with these tenses. Keep your freer practice to spoken question and answer.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two minutes: re-drill the question and short answer the room got wrong most, then one sentence on the board for them to fix.

slots.pages: New Total English Pre-int SB p. 136 Writing bank 2 ex 1a–1b, ex 2, ex 3a–3b, ex 4a–4b / SB p. 23 ex 10a (the achievement phrases, as useful language)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1a on p. 136: the five topics of a life — career, childhood and family, death, achievements, how it all started — numbered in the order a biography would tell them. Pairs, two minutes, no answer yet.

stages.name: Model text
stages.todo: Ex 1b: read the Bob Marley biography and check the order. Then ex 2, seven sentences completed with one or two words — Jamaica, England, father died, nineteen, solo singer, thirty-six, One Love. Then the shape, from ex 3a: three paragraphs — childhood and family, career, achievements.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: The achievement phrases from p. 23 ex 10a, matched in pairs — win an award, start your own charity, give a speech, pass an exam, earn a lot of money, get a good job, do a lot of work for charity, learn to speak another language — and checked against the Marley text and this morning’s Shakira texts. Add the time links the model uses: at the age of fourteen, five years later, in the 1970s. Board both sets and leave them up.

stages.name: Preparing to write
stages.todo: Ex 3b: Paul McCartney’s nine facts sorted into the three paragraphs (a, c, g / b, e, h / d, f, i). Then ex 4a: notes on their own person — a famous musician or someone in their family — one line for each paragraph.

stages.name: Writing task
stages.todo: Ex 4b: the biography, three paragraphs, about 120 words, with at least three of the achievement phrases and two of the time links. Silence, notes and board in front of them; answer questions by walking over.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Swap drafts with someone who wrote about a different person; the reader says which achievement impressed them most. Then two lines from the drafts on the board — one time link, one achievement phrase — for the room to correct.

3B.context: Music – The Mozart effect: what music does to us, and the questions we ask each other about music

slots.pages: New Total English Pre-int SB p. 24 ex 1 – audio track 1.12 (lead-in) / ex 2 (gist), ex 3 (detail), ex 4 (response)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1 with track 1.12: three pieces of Mozart. After each, pairs say how it makes them feel, with the adjectives in the box — relaxed, sleepy, awake, thoughtful. Check the seven adjectives before you play it.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Five items the text leans on: concentrate, alert, memory, reduce (pain), painkiller — and affect against effect, which the Teacher’s Book flags. A sentence each, with one concept question, and move on.
stages.avoid: Do not pre-teach anything from the grammar box on the next page. The grammar lesson later today is the question forms.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 2: match the three headings to the three paragraphs — 1 b, 2 a, 3 c. Two minutes, in silence, then a check with a partner and the answers.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 3: eight statements, true, false or not given. NG is new for most of the room, so show one example before they start. In silence, then pairs pointing at the line, then nominate: NG, F, T, NG, F, F, NG, T.

stages.name: Post-reading discussion
stages.todo: Ex 4’s two questions plus two of your own — does music help or stop you studying, and which music would you play in a hospital, and why. Pairs, then re-pair and report.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: The hospital playlist from two pairs. Then read three sentences from your notes aloud and stop at the error; the room supplies the next word. Make one of them concentrate or affect.

slots.pages: New Total English Pre-int SB p. 26 ex 1a–1b – audio track 1.15 / ex 2a–2b – audio track 1.16 / ex 3, ex 4a–4b – audio track 1.17, ex 5, ex 6a–6b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1a: the photo — what is the radio programme about? Then ex 1b, track 1.15, the introduction, to check: an actor alone on a desert island with three pieces of music.

stages.name: Model
stages.todo: Ex 2a with track 1.16: Mark’s three pieces and their artists in the table — Feelin’ So Good, Jennifer Lopez; Symphony No. 5, Mahler; Imagine, John Lennon. Ex 2b to compare, then ex 3 in groups: what do they think of his choices, and which they like best.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Ex 4a: six sentences from the programme completed from the box, then track 1.17 to check — it reminds me of, it makes me feel, it’s got great memories for me, it made me cry, I remember listening to it. These are the five ways of saying why a piece matters; the form is remind + me + of and make + me + feel / cry. Drill them as whole lines.
stages.avoid: Remind and remember are the pair they confuse. Check it in one question — who does the remembering — before the task.

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Ex 5: their own top three — the piece, the artist, and why, in notes, one line each with a phrase from the board. Silence.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Ex 6a in groups of three: two minutes each on their three pieces, listeners asking one question per piece. Then ex 6b: is the group’s taste similar or different? Re-group once if there is time.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One surprising choice from each group. Then two things said well, repeated by the room, and one with remember where remind was needed, for the speaker to put right.

slots.pages: New Total English Pre-int SB p. 25 ex 5, ex 6, ex 7 – audio track 1.13 / ex 8 (Active grammar), ex 9, ex 10 – audio track 1.14, ex 11a–11b / Workbook p. 15 ex 4

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book’s grammar lead-in: five answers about you on the board — I live in…, I can play…, I finished university last year — and pairs write the questions that get them. Collect them as they come; correct nothing yet.

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Ex 5 with track 1.13, two people talking about music: four statements, true or false (T, F, T, T). Then ex 6 on a second play: tick the questions they hear — 1, 3, 5, 6 and 9. Two plays and stop.
stages.avoid: This is not a listening lesson. If a third play is needed for the true-false, skip the true-false; the ticked questions are what the lesson is built on.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: The five ticked questions, sorted in pairs into three piles: starting with do/does/did, starting with can/have/are, starting with is. Ex 7 — what the woman answered — from memory in the same pairs, one minute.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex 8, the Active grammar box: before, before, before — the auxiliary, the modal or the verb be goes in front of the subject, and that is the whole rule in three patterns, A, B and C. Concept-check on the lead-in questions they wrote. Pronunciation is ex 10 with track 1.14: wh- questions fall, yes/no questions rise; drill the two and then one of each from ex 6.
stages.avoid: The lesson is word order, not tenses. If you re-teach the present perfect or the past simple here you have lost the aim.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 9: ten questions, eight with a mistake — Do you can, Has you ever, Who your favourite. On their own, a quick compare in pairs, take the disputed ones. Workbook p. 15 ex 4 (add one word to each question) for the fast finishers.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 11a: pairs write six survey questions about music; check them as you walk round. Then ex 11b: they ask four other students and note the answers.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One finding from the survey. Then three questions you heard on the board, one of them correct, for pairs to correct — word order, not content.

4A.context: Taste – Jamie’s kitchen: Jamie Oliver’s projects, and our own plans for the next two years

slots.pages: New Total English Pre-int SB p. 30 ex 1 (gist), ex 2 (gist), ex 3 (detail), ex 4 (vocabulary from context), ex 5 (response)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book warmer on cooking programmes and celebrity chefs: do they watch them, who watches them, what are the chefs like. Pairs, then two answers in open class.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 1: the photos and the first paragraph — who is Jamie Oliver and what has he achieved. Then ex 2: read the rest and choose which of the five areas he has worked in (a, d, e). Two short reads, two minutes each.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 3: five sentences completed with one word — pub, unemployed, chef, recipe, menus. Individually, pairs, nominate.
stages.avoid: The last paragraph is the next lesson’s target language — going to. If they ask, give the meaning in a word and move on.

stages.name: Vocabulary from the text
stages.todo: Ex 4: six phrases worked out from their context — his passion for, no previous experience, top-class chefs, success story, affordable food, cooking habits. Pairs, then check against the Teacher’s Book’s suggested meanings; drill the stress on affordable and previous.

stages.name: Post-reading discussion
stages.todo: Ex 5 in groups: which of the three projects is the most interesting and why, and would they train as a top-class chef. Add one of your own about school food here.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One verdict per group. Then a find-the-mistake race: three sentences on the board, pairs race to find the one mistake in each.

slots.pages: New Total English Pre-int SB p. 30 ex 6a–6b (Active grammar, from the last paragraph of the text) / SB p. 31 ex 7 / Workbook p. 17 ex 6, ex 7

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book’s grammar lead-in: one true plan of yours on the board — Next weekend I’m going to … — then the stem for them, and a chain round the room, each student saying theirs and asking the next.
stages.avoid: The text was read twice last lesson. Do not set it again; you go to its last paragraph.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 6a: the Active grammar box completed from the last paragraph on p. 30 — are going to eat, ’m not going to miss, What’s Jamie going to do. Then ex 6b: three more examples in the text.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning: a plan or intention decided before speaking — check it against a decision made on the spot. Form: be + going to + infinitive, with the contractions and the question. Pronunciation: the contracted I’m / he’s and the fast going to; drill three lines from the box.
stages.avoid: One structure, one meaning. Leave the present continuous for arrangements alone — it is tomorrow’s lesson.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 7 on p. 31: eight prompts written as full sentences, positive, negative and question. In silence, check with a partner, take the disputed ones. Workbook p. 17 ex 6 (pictures) and ex 7 (find the mistakes) for anyone done early.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book’s extension: you tell the room three plans for this week, one false, and they guess which with follow-up questions. Then each student writes three of their own and the group guesses.
stages.avoid: The next lesson is the speaking lesson on plans for the next two years (ex 10). Keep this to this week.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Who fooled their group. Then three sentences you wrote down while they talked on the board, one of them correct, and pairs find the fault.

slots.pages: New Total English Pre-int SB p. 31 ex 8 (How to… box), ex 9a–9b – audio tracks 1.19, 1.20, ex 10a–10b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: One plan of yours for the next two years, with a time and a reason, as the model they will copy. Then the question to the room: what are your plans for the next two years? Hands up, two answers.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Ex 8: the How to… box completed with its four headings — ask about plans, describe your plans, give a time reference, give a reason. Then the linking in ex 9a with track 1.19 and ex 9b with track 1.20: pairs mark where words link, listen, check and repeat.

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Ex 10a: notes on the six topics in the box — home, education, friends and family, hobbies and sports, travel, work — with a time and a reason for each plan, following the box. Silence.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Ex 10b in groups of three or four: take turns on your plans, and every listener asks one question per plan. Then the Teacher’s Book’s variation — one question per student on a topic, and a mingle to ask it.

stages.name: Feedback on content
stages.todo: Whose plans were most similar in each group, and one plan the room should hear.

stages.name: Delayed error correction
stages.todo: Four sentences you heard on the board, one of them fine as it is, and pairs decide which is which — a missing be, a to after going dropped, a reason without because.

4B.context: Taste – Let’s celebrate! A Thanksgiving dinner, the words for describing food, and arranging to meet for a meal

slots.pages: New Total English Pre-int SB p. 32 ex 1 (lead-in), ex 2a (pre-reading), ex 2b (gist), ex 3 (detail), ex 4 (response) / Teacher’s Book pp. 125–126 audioscript 1.21 (the book’s listening, copied out as the reading text)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1: the photo — which country, which festival. Groups, then the Teacher’s Book warmer: occasions people celebrate, and what they do to celebrate two of them.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Ex 2a: the six foods labelled on the pictures A–E — turkey and stuffing, sweet potatoes, maple syrup, cranberry sauce, apple pie. Pairs, then check, pointing at each picture as you go.
stages.avoid: The book wrote this page as a listening; your lesson reads the script instead. Do not play recording 1.21 — copy the script from the Teacher’s Book as a clean handout, and leave the adjectives in ex 5 to the next teacher.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 2b turned into a reading task: number the six foods in the order the text mentions them — turkey, sweet potatoes, maple syrup, cranberry sauce, stuffing, apple pie. Two minutes, on their own, then pairs.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 3: seven questions answered from the text with the line underlined. On their own, then pairs, then nominate — her house; walk or TV; no presents; maple syrup or fruit; bread and sausages; some have pumpkin or pecan pie; about two o’clock.

stages.name: Post-reading discussion
stages.todo: Ex 4: would they enjoy Tarin’s meal, and the Macy’s parade. Add the meal they would cook for a foreign guest to show their own country. Pairs, then re-pair.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One meal from the room. Then a correction slip per pair with three sentences you heard; they fix them, then swap slips with another pair and compare.

slots.pages: New Total English Pre-int SB p. 32 ex 5 / SB p. 33 ex 6, ex 7 / Workbook p. 18 ex 1, ex 2

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Back to the Thanksgiving meal the class has just read about: roast turkey, baked apple pie, sweet potatoes, spicy stuffing. Which words describe the food, not the food itself? Board the four.

stages.name: Presentation
stages.todo: Ex 5 on p. 32: the ten adjectives sorted by its questions — five ways of cooking (baked, boiled, fried, grilled, roast), three tastes (savoury, spicy, sweet), and the pairs roast / baked and fresh / raw. Pictures of dishes do the meaning; the two contrasts need a concept question each (raw: cooked at all?). Form: adjective before the noun, and roast with no -ed. Drill the stress — SAvoury, GRILLed — and the one-syllable ones in a phrase.
stages.avoid: Ten items is the cap. Do not add the kitchen words from the unit lead-in page.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 6 on p. 33: ten sentences, seven with the wrong adjective — boiled sausages, roast bread, raw curry. Individually, pairs, take the disputed ones. Workbook p. 18 ex 1 (gaps) and ex 2 (the email from Peru) for the early finishers.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 7 in groups: an important celebration at home — what people eat, how it is cooked, what else they do — and the foreign food they have tried and would like to try. Each speaker uses four of the ten; listeners tick them off.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One celebration from each group. Then four sentences you collected, one of them correct, at least two with the adjectives, for pairs to put right.

slots.pages: New Total English Pre-int SB p. 33 ex 10 – audio track 1.23 (How to… make arrangements), ex 11a–11b / Teacher’s Book p. 126 audioscript 1.23 (the dialogue, as a handout) / Workbook p. 19 ex 7

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Tarin and Marcos, from the first lesson: Marcos is invited to the Thanksgiving meal. How do you invite someone, and how do you say yes? Two ideas from the room on the board, uncorrected.

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Ex 10: track 1.23, the two extracts where Tarin invites Marcos. One question for the first play — does he accept, and when is he going? Then the script from the Teacher’s Book in their hands for the second play.
stages.avoid: Seven minutes: the dialogue is the way in, not the lesson. Ex 8 and 9 (the present continuous for arrangements) are not on your card.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: The How to… box: pairs add one phrase from the script to each of the four sections — I’m having a meal… and I’d really like you to come; Oh, thanks, I’d love to; Why don’t you come at about midday; Perfect! See you then.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Four moves, six exponents: suggest or invite (Let’s go to…, Why don’t you come…), accept (Great idea! I’d love to), reject with a reason (I’m busy, I’m afraid — I’m seeing Jo), arrange and confirm (Shall we meet at…? / Actually, 8:00 is better for me / See you then). Meaning by the move each one makes; form — why don’t you + infinitive, shall we + infinitive, and I’m seeing / I’m having as the fixed-arrangement present continuous; pronunciation — the intonation of the invitation and the polite refusal, drilled as whole lines.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 19 ex 7: the two phone dialogues with Jim, lines numbered into order, then read aloud in pairs with the intonation.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 11a: notes on a meal they want to cook or a restaurant to go to, a day in the next week and a time. Then ex 11b: a mingle to make as many arrangements as possible — one per time slot, and they may refuse with a reason.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Who made the most arrangements. Then two lines you wrote down while they talked on the board, one of them fine as it is, for the room to sort.

5A.context: Survival – Going to extremes: a free-diver and two climbers who pushed themselves to the limit, and how we compare people

slots.pages: New Total English Pre-int SB p. 39 ex 2c (the survival phrases, pre-taught) / SB p. 40 ex 1 (prediction and gist), ex 2 (detail), ex 3 (response)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Going to extremes on the board, the Teacher’s Book’s way in: what does it mean, who does it, why. Then a minute of sports in which people push themselves to the limit, boarded.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: The five phrases from p. 39 ex 2c matched to their definitions — control your fear, achieve your goal, a challenge, rely on, physical / mental strength — because all of them are in the texts. Add hold your breath and oxygen with a mime and a picture.
stages.avoid: Leave the comparatives alone — much deeper than, aren’t as famous as. They are the next lesson.

stages.name: Prediction and gist
stages.todo: Ex 1: from the photos and the two headings, what goal did each person achieve? Pairs guess, then one quick read of both texts to check — Everest without oxygen; the world free-diving record.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 2: eight statements, true or false, with the line underlined — F, F, T, F, F, T, T, T. In silence, then pairs, then nominate and make them correct the false ones.

stages.name: Post-reading discussion
stages.todo: Ex 3 in groups: how would they feel about diving that deep or climbing that high, who they admire more and why, and why people do this at all. Then one more from you — the most extreme thing anyone in the group has done.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: The most extreme thing from two groups. Then one sentence from each group, said back to them by you with its error in, and the group corrects you — one with a phrase from the pre-teaching.

slots.pages: New Total English Pre-int SB p. 40 (the two texts, read in the previous lesson) / SB p. 41 ex 6a–6b (Active grammar), ex 7a–7b – audio track 1.28, ex 8 – audio track 1.29 / Workbook p. 24 ex 2, ex 3

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book’s grammar lead-in, books closed: cat, horse, big on the board, and pairs make the sentence; then car, bike, expensive. Two sentences, the rule left unsaid.
stages.avoid: The texts were read twice last lesson. You go to them for sentences; you do not set them again.

stages.todo: Ex 6a: the table in the Active grammar box completed and checked against the p. 40 texts — deeper than, fitter than, happier than, more dangerous than, worse than, further than. Then ex 6b: the two questions on as … as and a bit / much.

stages.todo: Form by syllable count, with the three spelling traps the Teacher’s Book names — fit / fitter, brave / braver, happy / happier — and the irregulars. Meaning: as … as for the same, not as … as for different, a bit against much for the size of the gap; one concept question for each. Pronunciation is ex 8 with track 1.29: the extra stress on the word that carries the contrast — a BIT longer, MUCH more; drill the two lines.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 24 ex 2: eight sentences comparing two extreme-sports holidays. On their own, pairs, take the disputed ones. Ex 3 on the same page (rewrite with as … as) for the fast finishers.

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 7a on p. 41: Louisa and Carla compared from the stars in the box, with the modifiers and both forms. Gloss the four adjectives in one line — motivated, fit, determined, brave — then check with track 1.28.

stages.todo: Two people they both know — a teacher, two footballers, two singers — compared in pairs with four sentences, at least one with as … as and one with much. Then tell another pair.
stages.avoid: The next lesson is the personality quiz and the comparing of partners (ex 9–11). Compare famous people here, not each other.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two sentences from your notes on the board, one of them correct, for the room to sort.

slots.pages: New Total English Pre-int SB p. 41 ex 4a–4b (the adjectives for describing people, as useful language), ex 5, ex 9–11 (Student A’s questions) / SB p. 130 (ex 4a descriptions; Student B’s questions for ex 9)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Sara Campbell and the two climbers, from this morning: one word each for what kind of person they are. Take whatever adjectives come and board them.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Ex 4a: the nine descriptions on p. 130 matched to the adjectives in the box — generous, confident, funny, intelligent, reliable, motivated, determined, fit, talented, with brave in the example. Then ex 4b: each description rewritten with be + adjective. Check, drill the stress on deTERmined, MOtivated, inTELligent, reLIable, and ex 5 in one minute — which fit Sara and the climbers.
stages.avoid: Ten adjectives is the whole cap, and this is a speaking lesson. Twelve minutes, then the task.

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Ex 9: the class in two groups — As read the four questions on p. 41, Bs the four on p. 130 — and each group matches its questions to the adjectives (A: motivated, funny, reliable, confident; B: fit, intelligent or talented, generous, determined). They are preparing to ask, so make them say the questions aloud in their group.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Ex 10 in A–B pairs: ask and answer all eight questions, noting the answers. Then ex 11: with a new partner, sentences comparing themselves with their first partner — Alessandra is much more motivated than me, because… — with reasons.

stages.name: Feedback on content
stages.todo: Who is the most determined, the funniest, the most reliable in the room, by vote.

stages.name: Delayed error correction
stages.todo: Four sentences you collected on the board, one of them fine as it is, two with the adjectives, and pairs decide which is which.

5B.context: Survival – Survival school: a talk about the Hillside courses, the superlatives that sell them, and surviving in English abroad

stages.name: Lead-in

stages.todo: Ex 1: the six phrases matched to the underlined parts of the questions — survival skills, build a shelter, challenge, push yourself, cope with, the wilderness. Then ex 2: the five questions asked in pairs with the phrases, three minutes, because the talk uses every one of them.

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Ex 3 with track 1.30: the photos first, then three questions on one play — who David Johnson is, who he is talking to and why, where he is. Pairs, then the answers.

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Ex 4: the notes, ten gaps, read through first. Second play, pairs compare, then nominate — the army; working as a team; groups of friends; a weekend; all year; £175; November to February; £195; find it and cook it on a fire; build it and sleep in it.

stages.name: Post-listening discussion
stages.todo: Ex 5 in groups: would they do one of the courses, and how they would feel about the activities in the photos. Add which course they would send their colleagues on, and why.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One verdict per group. Then re-drill cope with and push yourself in two sentences you heard, and board the one sentence the whole room needs to fix.

slots.pages: New Total English Pre-int Teacher’s Book pp. 126–127 audioscript 1.30 (copied as the handout) / SB p. 43 ex 6a–6b (Active grammar), ex 7, ex 8, ex 9, ex 10 / Workbook p. 26 ex 2

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book’s grammar lead-in: two jumbled sentences on the board — the basic survival course is the most popular; January is the coldest month of the year — put in order in pairs, first and last words given.
stages.avoid: The class heard the talk twice last lesson. Do not play it again; they read the script.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: The script of recording 1.30 from the Teacher’s Book as a handout: pairs underline every the …-est and the most … — the most popular, the wettest, coldest weekend, the hardest thing, the most comfortable, the best weekend. Then ex 6a, the table, completed from what they found.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Form by syllable count, as in the comparatives lesson — the -iest, the doubled consonant, the most, the irregulars. Then ex 6b: the before the superlative, in after it for places and groups, of in other cases. Pronunciation: the sentence stress on the superlative — the WETtest, COLDest weekend EVer — which the script does not teach, so you supply it; drill three lines.
stages.avoid: The source notes the text gives you no pronunciation point. Sentence stress is yours to add; do not skip it.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 7: eight sentences, one mistake each — hardest without the, most big, of the world. Individually, pairs, take the disputed ones. Workbook p. 26 ex 2 (the dialogue about the Harry Potter film) for anyone done early.

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 8: the email and the note from two people who did the course, eight gaps from ten words — difficult, most, worst, exciting, of, best, noisiest, in. Pairs, then a check.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 9: the four questions written out in full (the most dangerous thing that has ever happened to you…), then ex 10 in groups, one follow-up question each. One report per group.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two sentences you heard on the board, one of them correct, for the room to sort.

slots.pages: New Total English Pre-int SB p. 44 ex 1a (lead-in), ex 1b (gist), ex 2 (detail), ex 3 (response), ex 4 (the Lifelong learning box: British and American words) / Workbook p. 28 ex 1a–1b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1a: the three photos — which three places, and what the title One language, three cultures might mean. Pairs, then the Teacher’s Book’s question: which countries have English as their main language?
stages.avoid: A new context, as the source says — this text sets up the next day’s grammar on the following page. Stay on p. 44.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Four items only: queue, tip, pedestrian, polite. A sentence each, with one concept question, and move on.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 1b: match the three headings to the three paragraphs — 1 a, 2 c, 3 b. Two minutes, individually, a quick compare in pairs, answers.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 2: eight questions answered from the text with the line underlined — stand in line; they say sorry; G’day; the US; the US; the check; the left; the sidewalk. In silence, pairs, nominate.

stages.name: Vocabulary from the text
stages.todo: Ex 4, the Lifelong learning box: the British word for each American one — flat, mobile phone, crisps, biscuit, lift, petrol, trousers, handbag, toilets, holiday — in pairs, with the pairs from the text added (queue / stand in line, bill / check, pavement / sidewalk). 6A.context: Stages – Turning eighteen: three eighteen-year-olds on what they have to do and should do, and the friends we keep in touch with

slots.pages: New Total English Pre-int SB p. 50 ex 1 (lead-in), ex 2 (gist), ex 3a–3b (jigsaw: Gregor on p. 50, Miguel on p. 130, Fei on p. 134), ex 4 (response) / SB p. 130 / SB p. 134

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1: the best year of their life so far and why, and the situations in the photos. Pairs, two answers in open class.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Four items the three texts share: military service, compulsory / optional, stand on your own two feet, a place of your own. A sentence each, with one concept question – can you say no to something compulsory? – and move on.
stages.avoid: Do not touch should, have to and can. They are the next lesson, and the texts are full of them.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 2: text 1, the website’s own introduction — who is it for and what does it ask readers to do? Two minutes; eighteen-year-olds, to send in what their life is like.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 3a as a jigsaw in threes: A reads Gregor on p. 50, B Miguel on p. 130, C Fei on p. 134, each ticking the subjects their person mentions. Then ex 3b: each tells the other two, who complete the rest of the table. Check the table in open class.

stages.todo: Ex 4 in the same threes: who they are most like and in what ways, and whether they enjoyed being eighteen. Add what is different about turning eighteen in their country.

stages.todo: One answer per group on being eighteen. Then a vote: three sentences on the board, right or wrong, hands up, then the fix from whoever voted right.

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book’s grammar lead-in: three sentences about this class on the board — you should speak English in class; you can eat in class; you have to be a good swimmer to study English — true or false in pairs, and the false ones fixed.
stages.avoid: Gregor’s text was read last lesson. You send them to it for sentences; you do not set it again.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 5: in Gregor’s text on p. 50, underline should, shouldn’t, have to, don’t have to, can and can’t — six sentences, boarded in that order. Then the Active grammar box on p. 51, rules A–F matched in pairs.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Obligation is the lesson: have to (no choice), don’t have to (a choice), should and shouldn’t (the right thing in your opinion). One concept question per pair — don’t have to against shouldn’t is the one they confuse. Form: have takes to and the do auxiliary, should does not, and nothing changes for he or she. Pronunciation is ex 8a–8b with track 1.36: the t of can’t and shouldn’t disappears before a consonant; drill the two lines.
stages.avoid: Six forms is more than one lesson. Treat can and can’t for permission as known — a one-line check — and spend the time on have to and should.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 6 (choose the word) and ex 7 (complete with should, can or have to) on p. 51. On their own, pairs, take the disputed ones. Workbook p. 31 ex 4 (the Spanish schoolboy’s day) and ex 5 (correct the mistakes) for the fast finishers.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: The five statements in ex 9a as discussion prompts — eighteen is too young to marry, children should help with housework, young people should do military service. Groups choose two and decide what young people have to, should and can do in their country. One report per group.
stages.avoid: Ex 9 and 10 are a listening with the opinion phrases; you are using only the five statements. Do not play track 1.37.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: The room votes on the most divisive statement. Then three sentences you wrote down while they talked on the board, one of them correct, and pairs decide which is which — expect must for have to and should to.

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The Teacher’s Book warmer: the name of a school friend they no longer see, and a minute of memories in pairs. Would they like to meet them again?

stages.name: Reading task
stages.todo: Ex 1 on p. 52: Tina’s profile read once for its purpose — to let old school friends find her. Then one more read: find the two phrases about friends that use touch (lost touch, get in touch). Six minutes and out.

stages.todo: Ex 7 on p. 53: the eight phrasal verbs matched to their definitions — get in touch, keep in touch, lose touch, catch up, get on, fall out, go out, split up. Pairs, then the answers.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning in pairs that contrast — get in touch against lose touch, go out against split up, get on against fall out — one concept question each. Form: all take with someone, and the verb changes (got on, went out, fell out). Pronunciation: the stress on the particle — get ON, fall OUT, split UP — drilled in a sentence.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 8: Tina’s story about Martin, eight gaps, verbs in the right form — got on, went out, lost touch, got in touch, catch up, split up, fall out, keep in touch. Individually, pairs. Workbook p. 33 ex 6 (Will’s email) for anyone done early.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 10: a diagram of three best friends with a word about each. Then ex 11a–11b: pairs write two questions about each person in their partner’s diagram, using the phrasal verbs, and ask them.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One friend story from the room. Then two phrasal-verb sentences you heard, one with the wrong particle, for the room to put right; finish by re-drilling the particle stress.
